Hezbollah recruiting convicts in Latin America for revenue, relaxing ideological requirements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:36:53 UTC
21:36:53 KST

Hezbollah is increasingly recruiting convicted felons in Latin America, targeting those facing financial difficulties and harboring resentment toward the courts, while relaxing its requirements for ideological alignment, according to a new assessment published by The Washington Institute and written by Lucas Gualtieri, a Brazilian federal prosecutor who specializes in organized crime and Hezbollah’s use of criminal networks.
Operation Trapiche, a counterterrorism operation launched by Brazil’s Federal Police in November 2023 with support from Israel’s Mossad, has shed light on Hezbollah’s efforts to outsource operatives, criminal revenue generation, and financial services in Latin America, building capabilities the group can plausibly deny if confronted.
Hezbollah has long outsourced operations in Latin America, as illustrated by the 2021 expulsion of two criminals hired by the Iran-backed group to target an Israeli in Bogotá. However, the investigation has uncovered what amounts to an assembly line for operatives. Rather than simply contracting hitmen, Hezbollah recruits men with no prior ties to the group, flies them to Lebanon for training, and sends them back to their home countries to scout for potential Israeli and Jewish targets.
Gualtieri said Hezbollah was specifically seeking to recruit financially vulnerable convicted felons with no prior ties to the group or Lebanon. In intercepted audio, recruiters discussed looking for aggrieved individuals who had been “locked up” and therefore felt they “owe the courts,” he said.
By recruiting men without prior ideological or personal ties to Hezbollah or Lebanon, Gualtieri said, the group could deny involvement in attacks, allowing any resulting unrest to be dismissed as hate crimes committed by fringe extremists.
Lucas Passos Lima, whose conviction was reinstated by Brazil’s Superior Court of Justice last month after a federal court ruled that his role in a network targeting Jews and Israelis was motivated by financial gain rather than terrorism, had returned from Lebanon with more than $5,000 in untraceable cash. Had the superior court failed to convict Lima of terrorism, Gualtieri said, Brazil could have been viewed as a permissive environment for the group, and individuals who support terrorism for personal gain could have escaped more severe sentencing despite their knowing involvement in plots.
Hezbollah relying on Latin American criminal network revenue
Hezbollah has also increasingly relied on revenue generated by criminal networks in Latin America, he said, offering the example of the discovery of Brazilian tobacco shops that helped fund plane tickets for recruits.
The shops were initially identified by tax inspectors investigating a tobacco shop in Belo Horizonte’s Mercado Central that was selling banned electronic cigarettes. The case was referred to counterterrorism police in October 2023 after an FBI warning about a criminal financial network funding Hezbollah raised alarm among Brazilian officials.
Although the shops were registered to Hussain Abdulmajid, investigators found that his brother, Mohamad Khir Abdulmajid, a Syrian-born naturalized Brazilian, was the real operator. The FBI memo also flagged Haissam Houssin Diab, a Lebanese-born naturalized Brazilian whose passport and travel bookings were later found in Abdulmajid’s cloud storage.
Abdulmajid is believed to have approached at least five Brazilians through social media and paid for their short trips to Beirut, including stays in upscale hotels. There, they allegedly received operational instruction and training in clandestine communications. This included learning a physical recognition signal and using shared email accounts as dead drops, leaving messages unsent in draft folders. They were also instructed to photograph Lebanese tourist sites to support a cover story that they had traveled for leisure.
Lima was recruited through Abdulmajid’s network and flew to Lebanon twice in 2023. After his first trip, researchers found that he had geolocated and filmed three synagogues, a Jewish cemetery, the Israeli embassy, and a rabbi in and around Brasília. He had also trained with firearms, purchased untraceable radios and surveillance equipment, and approached a pilot about exfiltration routes that would bypass migration controls.
Hezbollah, IRGC using cryptocurrency for money laundering
Although Hezbollah’s use of criminal enterprises to raise funds is not new, he argued the these cases matter because the group did not need to launder its own money to evade sanctions. Dante Felipini, a São Paulo cryptocurrency broker arrested in a separate money-laundering case as part of Operation Colossus, established three separate cryptocurrency wallets for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and Hezbollah. Prosecutors charged him with money laundering, currency evasion, membership in a terrorist organization, and terrorism financing.
Gualtieri argued that Felipini’s case showed Hezbollah views outsourcing as both a tactic and a recruitment opportunity. After the cryptobroker traveled to Baalbek in January 2023, where he fired rifles in the hills with Hezbollah terrorists, Felipini told a contact that the trip had been his “baptism” into the group.
Gualtieri argued that the cases highlighted the need for authorities to pursue terrorism-related charges alongside other criminal offenses where the evidence supports them. He noted that such charges can lead to longer sentences and that relying solely on formal terrorism charges can understate the extent of Hezbollah’s activities.
He also highlighted a precedent set by Brazil’s Superior Court of Justice, which affirmed that financial motivation does not preclude terrorism liability when suspects knowingly participate in a terrorist plot, even if they do not share the group’s ideological motives.
Finally, he said authorities should strengthen financial monitoring to identify suspicious cryptocurrency transfers and shell companies, continue tracking networks after assets are frozen, and expand national mechanisms for designating terrorist organizations. While international cooperation was crucial to Operation Trapiche, Gualtieri argued that domestic enforcement tools remained essential to disrupting Hezbollah’s networks and prosecuting those involved.

Iran deploys heavy weaponry to Kurdish regions amid fears of renewed conflict with Israel, US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:36:27 UTC
21:36:27 KST

Iran has deployed artillery and additional heavy weaponry to its northwestern Kurdish regions bordering Iraq as it intensifies its crackdown on the Iranian Kurdish opposition group Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK). Recent clashes have been reported in the Shaho Mountains and other areas near the border with the Kurdistan Region of northern Iraq.
Millions of Kurds live on both sides of the border, forming part of a larger Kurdish population that also extends into Syria and Turkey.
According to the Kurdish media outlet Rudaw, “Iran has deployed artillery and heavy weaponry to Kurdish areas in the west of the country amid growing fears of a wider conflict with Israel and the United States, as the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) intensifies operations against armed opposition groups along the country's western and southeastern frontiers.”
Meanwhile, the Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) reported that the IRGC has been moving military convoys into the areas of Sanandaj, Kamyaran, Sarvabad, Marivan, and Baneh.
The developments come as Iran has demanded that Iraq expel Iranian Kurdish opposition groups. Iran's ambassador to Iraq claimed this week that Baghdad had agreed to the demand.
Tehran has long pressured Baghdad to rein in Kurdish opposition groups operating from Iraqi territory and has carried out hundreds of attacks against them.
Over the past week, Iran has targeted the Kurdistan Freedom Party (PAK), the Democratic Party of Iranian Kurdistan (PDKI), Komala, and Khabat. In one attack this week, Iran reportedly used drones to strike a PAK camp near Mount Harir.
These four groups, together with PJAK, are part of an Iranian Kurdish opposition coalition formed in January and February 2026. PJAK is a left-wing organization linked to the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK).
Iran views Kurdish opposition groups as potential regional threat
Iran views Kurdish opposition groups as a potential threat and has sought to preempt any uprising among its Kurdish population by extending the conflict into neighboring Iraq, where Tehran maintains significant influence.
With reports circulating that Israel and the US could resume military operations against Iran, Tehran appears to be taking additional steps in preparation for another potential round of conflict.
Rudaw reported that “an informed source in Kamyaran told the rights network that “hundreds of IRGC special forces, believed to be members of the entity's Saberin Unit, have been dispatched over the past few weeks in military convoys to areas surrounding villages on the slopes of Mount Shaho in Kamyaran County.”
The situation in Iran's Kurdish regions is complex. Some Kurds cooperate with the Iranian government, and Tehran has frequently sought to recruit Kurdish fighters into its own units.
According to Rudaw, the IRGC has also mobilized Kurdish fighters. From Tehran's perspective, encouraging Kurds to fight one another offers several potential advantages. Kurdish fighters are familiar with the mountainous terrain, while any resulting backlash could be directed toward Kurdish communities rather than the Iranian government.
Iran has also used drones to attack PJAK positions inside the country.
PJAK said its positions in the mountainous and forested areas of Marivan had been attacked “with two suicide drones, followed by more than 30 mortar shells and heavy weapons on Sunday.”

I met Gadi Eisenkot. He did not perform leadership. He practiced it - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:36:22 UTC
21:36:22 KST

JERUSALEM — I have attended enough political events to recognize the usual performance: the polished entrance, loud promises and leaders who speak about “the people” while remaining distant from them, but when I observed Gadi Eisenkot in person, I encountered something different—a man who did not appear to be acting like a leader because he seemed too busy listening, standing among Israelis and carrying himself like a servant rather than an owner.
I did not feel that I was watching a political celebrity. I felt that I was meeting one of us.
That judgment is personal, not scientific. One encounter cannot answer every policy question. I am a religious Zionist with convictions about Jewish sovereignty, national security and Israel’s right to defend itself. I surrender those convictions to no politician. But leadership is revealed not only on platforms. It is also revealed in whom a leader notices, whom he brings into the room and whether he treats citizens as partners rather than scenery.
That is why Eisenkot’s inclusion of Yaffa Tabaja in his Yashar party matters to me.
The importance of Yaffa Tabaja
Tabaja is not a professional slogan-maker. She is a builder. She is an Ethiopian Israeli woman from a traditional family of eight children whose parents made aliyah during Operation Moses. Born in Karmiel, she grew up partly among Russian-speaking immigrants and later described herself as a human “gathering of the exiles”: Ethiopian, Russian-speaking, traditional and Israeli. Her parents did not raise her with wealth, political privilege or famous connections. They gave her discipline, dignity, and faith in education.
The first in her family to pursue higher education, she earned degrees in criminology and government, and communications. At Ashkelon Academic College, Tabaja became the first Ethiopian Israeli elected to lead a student union. She served two terms and represented public colleges nationally. Young people from the periphery asked her a question: Is higher education possible for someone like me? Tabaja did not answer with a speech. She answered by working. She later led Ashkelon’s MTech Innovation Center, building a community of thousands and connecting southern entrepreneurs with Google for Startups, Amazon Web Services, Cisco and Nvidia. She wanted technology to become an instrument of social mobility, bringing opportunity to communities too often told to wait.
“If we aren’t given a seat at the decision-making table, we build our own table,” she has said.
That sentence should disturb Israel’s establishment. Parties visit Ethiopian neighborhoods, photograph our elders, and praise our military service.
Yet Ethiopian Israelis are still invited to decorate politics more often than direct it. We provide loyalty, votes and immigration stories, but are seldom trusted with authority over diplomacy, technology, security or the economy. Tabaja represents a different demand. She is not asking to be included simply because she is Ethiopian. She is asking to serve because she has already demonstrated that she can build institutions, create partnerships and turn neglect into opportunity.
Eisenkot deserves credit for recognizing that leadership. Yashar placed Tabaja at No. 21 on its electoral list, a potentially consequential position for a party polling around that range. Representation becomes meaningful only when a candidate has a realistic path to power and is allowed to address the whole nation, not merely “community affairs.” Eisenkot’s story may explain why he recognizes quiet service. From a working-class Moroccan Israeli family, he rose through four military decades to become chief of staff. He also carries a sacrifice no parent should endure: his son and two nephews were killed in the war.
Grief does not qualify anyone automatically to govern, and military rank does not guarantee political wisdom. Israelis must examine Eisenkot’s policies and coalition choices. But his service and sacrifice give moral weight to his call for responsibility after October 7. Israel does not need another messiah. It does not need citizens to worship a leader or pretend one man can save the nation. We have paid too high a price for politics organized around personality. Israel needs servant leadership: leaders who understand that public office is borrowed authority, who can be strong without humiliating others and who place proven workers beside them including women from communities rarely entrusted with national power.
October 7 exposed failures of security, governance and political culture. Israel’s next government must restore border security, establish a credible state commission of inquiry, rebuild international diplomacy, lower living costs and ensure every community contributes to and benefits from the state.
Tabaja offers a practical model. When rockets made Ashkelon appear like a place to escape, she stayed and built. After October 7, her center assisted soldiers, women, businesses, and entrepreneurs. She understood that survival was insufficient; citizens also needed employment and hope. That is Zionism in work clothes.
I was moved by Eisenkot because he appeared simple in the best sense: approachable, disciplined and unpossessed by his importance. I am moved by Tabaja because she reflects the true colors of my community, not merely our struggle, but our competence, faith, endurance, and desire to contribute.
My admiration is not blind. I will challenge them when they are wrong. I will ask whether Eisenkot will give Tabaja and other underrepresented leaders genuine authority, not merely a place on a list. I will ask whether Yashar will bring the periphery into decisions about Israel’s economy, diplomacy, and security. But what I witnessed gave me hope.
In Eisenkot, I saw a leader who still looks like a citizen. In Tabaja, I see a citizen who has already become a leader. Israel will be renewed not by the loudest people in the room, but by those who enter ready to work. Gadi Eisenkot and Yaffa Tabaja may represent that renewal. Now they must prove that servant leadership can become national leadership—and that the table they are building has room for all Israel.

Israel Election 2026: Pollster Shmuel Rosner says Israelis have already made up their minds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:36:22 UTC
21:36:22 KST

With less than a week until Israelis vote, Benjamin Netanyahu has come back to mainstream television studios carrying a fresh, effusive endorsement from President Trump.
On this episode of The Deep Dive, host Jacob asks Shmuel Rosner, a JPPI senior fellow and Channel 13 election pollster, whether any of that can still move votes. His answer is blunt. After the judicial overhaul fight of 2023, October 7, and the long wars in Gaza, Lebanon, and with Iran, most Israelis already know what they want. Any last-minute shifts will happen inside the political blocs, not across them.
He argues that Netanyahu's late blitz is not a play for 61 seats. It is a defensive move meant to stop the opposition from forming a viable coalition, which would force yet another election in six months, one in which the prime minister might get luckier.
The conversation then turns to the scenarios likely to dominate the morning after. Rosner explains why a minority government backed by a 57–50 split is a very different thing from one resting on 52–51. He also covers how far President Herzog can actually push the rival camps toward the unity government many Israelis say they want. And he describes the one arrangement that could appeal to nearly everyone except one man: a plea deal that lets Netanyahu step aside. He takes on the theory that a post-election flare-up with Iran could be used to herd rivals into an emergency government.
Here, he points out that the opposition has already watched that approach play out twice, first with Benny Gantz and then after October 7. He also offers a clear explanation of Trump's endorsement: it carries no risk for Trump. If Netanyahu wins, Trump can collect on it, and if he loses, the winner will still need Washington.
The last striking moments
The most striking moments come near the end. Asked about warnings over election integrity and comparisons to America's January 6, Rosner defends Israel's voting system as one of the few institutions the public still trusts. He warns that leaders who spread false claims about the count would be creating a dangerous moment for the country's democracy.
He also offers a provocative thought about the stakes. Whether this vote really is the most important in Israel's history, he suggests, depends on its outcome, and the stakes are not equal for both sides. For many opposition voters, he believes, another term for the current coalition would be a crisis of identity and of attachment to the country itself.

Lockheed Martin enters deal with US Defense Department for 850 F-35 Lightning II fighter jets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:36:17 UTC
21:36:17 KST

Lockheed Martin has entered into an initial production and sustainment agreement with the US Defense Department to deliver at least 850 F-35 Lightning II fighter jets over the next 10 years, the department said Thursday.
The defense contractor will self-fund at least $7 billion in initiatives that support the F-35 program, the department said in a statement.
The F-35, built with stealth technology that helps it evade enemy detection, is considered the world's most advanced fighter jet and sits at the core of Lockheed's aeronautics division, which accounts for nearly 40% of its quarterly revenue.
Under the agreement with the Defense Department, which US President Donald Trump calls the Department of War, Lockheed aims to maintain annual production at 156 aircraft.
The agreement is not an order but is considered a prearranged long-term contract.
"If granted multi-year authority in the coming months, the F-35 Joint Program Office and Lockheed Martin will work to finalize contract terms, pricing, and schedules through a formal contract award," the company said.
The agreement also covers international orders for the F-35, along with initial spares and modification kits, Arlington-based Lockheed said in a statement.
"We have fundamentally changed how we stabilize the American defense industrial base to produce at speed and scale," said Under Secretary of Defense Michael Duffey.
"This agreement with Lockheed Martin proves it. By aligning financial incentives with actual performance, we are ensuring our warfighters are equipped with the lethal capabilities they need to fight and win."
Lockheed, defense industry, benefit from increased global defense spending
Lockheed and its peers across the US have benefited from increased global defense spending as geopolitical conflicts remain unabated.
Lockheed estimates the agreement will support 317,000 US jobs and generate nearly $79 billion in annual economic activity over the next decade.
It also expects the arrangement to lower production costs and ease supply-chain constraints from raw materials to finished parts.

Chinese-linked hackers used AI in ConnectWise breach: Microsoft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:30:46 UTC
21:30:46 KST

Dilara Hamit
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
A Chinese state-aligned hacking group used an artificial intelligence-powered security testing tool in a campaign that compromised IT services firm ConnectWise and targeted hundreds of organizations worldwide, Microsoft said Wednesday.
In a security blog, Microsoft attributed the activity to Storm-0940, a group it says has operated since 2021. Targets included government, defense, energy, financial services, and technology organizations.
The hackers used ARTEX, an open-source penetration testing framework that connects to AI models to automate tasks ranging from identifying weaknesses to stealing data.
Penetration testing is normally used to assess security, but Microsoft said the attackers used the framework to accelerate their operations.
In several cases, attackers gained high-level access to cloud systems less than three hours after selecting a target. Most attempts failed, but the group established persistent access at many organizations, Microsoft said.
Successful sign-ins did not necessarily mean customer data had been accessed or stolen, it added.
ConnectWise said its evidence, including Microsoft's threat intelligence, indicated that a Chinese state-aligned group was responsible for the attack on Cloud Backup, formerly known as SkyKick.
The company said it had contained the affected application connections and begun restoring services in phases following security checks.
However, it warned that those steps would not eliminate unauthorized access potentially established inside individual customer Microsoft 365 environments, which require separate investigation.
In an update Thursday, ConnectWise said restoration was expected to take several days. Existing backup archives remained encrypted, isolated, and preserved, with no indication they had been compromised, it said.
The company urged customers to keep affected connections disabled until it issued formal reconnection instructions.
ConnectWise said the original mechanism by which the credentials were exposed remained under investigation. It had not established whether a product vulnerability contributed to the incident.
China's Embassy in Washington rejected accusations implicating Beijing, saying China opposes hacking and what it described as attempts to smear the country.

HELSINKI, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Finnish telecommunications equipment maker Nokia reported on Thursday a 10-percent year-on-year increase in third-quarter net sales, driven by strong demand for artificial intelligence (AI) and cloud infrastructure.
According to its interim financial report, Nokia's net sales reached 5.15 billion euros (5.77 billion U.S. dollars) in the July-September period, up from 4.7 billion euros (5.26 billion U.S. dollars) a year earlier. On a constant currency basis, sales grew 9 percent.
Comparable operating profit rose 35 percent year-on-year to 605 million euros (677.42 million U.S. dollars), while reported operating profit declined 22 percent to 196 million euros (219.46 million U.S. dollars), reflecting higher restructuring and integration costs.
Growth was particularly strong in Nokia's Network Infrastructure division, where net sales increased 15 percent on a constant currency basis, led by a 43-percent increase in IP Networks and an 18-percent rise in Optical Networks.
The company said net sales to AI and cloud customers jumped 123 percent year-on-year, while order intake surged 118 percent, with new orders totaling 1.5 billion euros (1.68 billion U.S. dollars) during the quarter.
Nokia President and CEO Justin Hotard said the company expects its combined Optical and IP Networks businesses to grow between 25 percent and 30 percent in 2027, citing growing demand for AI infrastructure that is becoming "larger, more distributed and hyperconnected."
Hotard also noted that Nokia, together with T-Mobile and NVIDIA, had completed what the company described as the world's first AI radio access network (AI-RAN) call on a live operator network, marking progress toward commercial deployment of AI-powered mobile networks.
Nokia maintained its full-year 2026 outlook, forecasting comparable operating profit of between 2.1 billion and 2.6 billion euros (2.35 billion and 2.91 billion U.S. dollars).
Despite the stronger earnings, Nokia shares fell in Helsinki on Thursday, declining around 3 percent by midday, according to Finnish business daily Kauppalehti. The newspaper attributed the market reaction partly to weaker-than-expected cash flow. ■

Some estuarine fish may withstand warming oceans: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
20:30:08 CST
21:30:08 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Some estuarine fish may be able to withstand warmer ocean conditions expected under climate change because of their genetically determined resilience to temperature extremes, new research finds.
The study examined three economically important estuarine species, yellowfin bream, sand whiting and tarwhine, and found that they were "thermal generalists" capable of tolerating a broad range of temperatures, according to a statement released Thursday by Australia's Adelaide University.
Yellowfin bream and sand whiting were among the Australian east coast's most commonly caught inshore fish, making their ability to cope with warming estuaries important for coastal fisheries, according to the researchers.
While these estuarine fish can tolerate extreme conditions, climate change is already shifting marine species' distributions, with tropical fish moving further south as waters warm and reshaping local fisheries, researchers said. ■

EXPLAINER – What is Shamonda virus, detected in humans for 1st time?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:27:17 UTC
21:27:17 KST

- 1st documented human case involves ‘severely’ immunocompromised patient who died in early October
- French authorities say no risk to general population has been identified so far, but investigations continue
French health authorities reported Thursday the first documented human infection with the Shamonda virus, an emerging pathogen primarily affecting livestock.
France's Health Ministry said the infection was detected in a patient with "severe immunodeficiency" who was receiving treatment for a serious illness.
The patient died in early October, and clinical, biological and epidemiological investigations are ongoing.
 
What is Shamonda virus?
Shamonda virus is an orthobunyavirus transmitted primarily by Culicoides biting midges.
It belongs to the same broader group of viruses as Schmallenberg virus and Akabane virus, which are associated with infections in animals.
First detected in Nigeria in the mid-1960s, it was subsequently reported sporadically in parts of West, East and southern Africa, as well as Japan.
It was identified in Europe for the first time in summer 2026, including in France, Germany and Switzerland, according to the French Agriculture Ministry.
The UK's Animal and Plant Health Agency also detected the virus in cattle in Jersey, a British Crown dependency, in August.
 
What happened in France?
The patient was receiving treatment for a serious illness at the Hospices Civils de Lyon hospital group and had a severely weakened immune system.
French authorities said neurological complications observed before the patient's death were "very likely" linked to the infection, although the virus had previously been considered incapable of infecting humans.
They said the case shared characteristics with human infections caused by other orthobunyaviruses, including Oropouche virus.
Investigators believe the patient may have been infected through a Culicoides midge bite in eastern France, where the virus circulated among animals during spring and summer.
The case is considered exceptional because no human infection had previously been documented despite the virus circulating in parts of Africa and Asia for decades.
 
What symptoms does it cause in animals?
In cattle, the virus can cause fever, diarrhea, lethargy and reduced milk production. These symptoms are generally temporary, according to the French Agriculture Ministry.
Infections during pregnancy may also lead to reproductive complications, including abortions and fetal malformations, similar to those associated with Schmallenberg virus.
Although cattle are considered the main animal hosts, the virus has also been detected in small ruminants, including sheep and goats, as well as horses and alpacas in some European countries.
The UK agency reported detections in horses with neurological disease in Germany and Switzerland. Investigations are continuing into the relationship between the infection and those symptoms.
 
How does the virus spread?
Shamonda virus spreads primarily through bites from Culicoides midges, small biting insects that transmit several animal viruses.
According to the French Agriculture Ministry, there is no evidence of significant direct transmission between animals, apart from transmission from a pregnant animal to its offspring.
The ministry said no scientific evidence currently documents transmission through meat, milk or dairy products.
Even so, products from sick animals are excluded from consumption, it added.
 
Is there a vaccine or treatment?
No vaccine is currently available, and there is no treatment that eliminates the virus in infected animals, according to the French Agriculture Ministry.
Veterinarians can provide treatment to relieve symptoms. Farmers are advised to seek veterinary assistance if cattle develop fever, diarrhea or reduced milk production.
Veterinary monitoring is also recommended for potential reproductive complications following infection.
Authorities recommend reducing exposure to midges by eliminating breeding sites, including liquid manure and stagnant water and treating transport vehicles against insects.
The virus is not currently classified as a regulated animal disease under European Union animal health legislation, according to the French Agriculture Ministry.
No mandatory culling is required under the regulations in the event of an infection.
 
What happens next?
French authorities are continuing investigations involving specialists in human, animal and environmental health to better understand the infection and the virus's circulation.
No risk to the general population has been identified based on current knowledge of the virus, the Agriculture Ministry added.
France has notified the World Health Organization and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control.

Italy, Spain agree to end border controls after nearly 3 months of tensions over Ceuta
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22

21:22:15 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
Italy and Spain agreed Thursday not to extend temporary border controls introduced nearly three months ago amid tensions over mass migrant arrivals in Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta.
Italian Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi and his Spanish counterpart Fernando Grande-Marlaska reached the agreement during a telephone conversation, the Italian Interior Ministry said in a statement.
The call followed a meeting between Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on the sidelines of a European Council meeting.
The ministers agreed that "the Schengen suspensions in force in the two countries will not be extended further," according to the statement.
The ministry said the decision followed a "careful" assessment of the situation and would be accompanied by increased information-sharing to ensure security across the Schengen area.
The Schengen area normally allows travel between participating European countries without routine border checks, although governments can temporarily reintroduce controls in response to serious security threats.
Italy introduced the checks on Aug. 1 after around 72,000 people crossed irregularly from Morocco into Ceuta on July 30-31, according to the Spanish central government’s estimate.
The Spanish government described Italy's move as “unjust,” stressing that Ceuta has a special status under the Schengen system and that migrants who entered the territory cannot travel freely into Europe's passport-free area.
On Aug. 8, Madrid responded with random checks on travelers arriving from Italy, citing migration pressure along the Central Mediterranean route and unauthorized onward movements to other Schengen countries.

Africa’s richest man expands fuel empire into Kenya

Africa’s richest man expands fuel empire into Kenya
Africa’s richest man Aliko Dangote has bought a roughly 25% stake in Kenya’s fuel pipeline operator as part of a wider push to expand petroleum distribution across the continent.
The Nigerian industrialist announced the acquisition at the Financial Times Africa Summit in London on Wednesday. Kenya Pipeline Company (KPC) operates pipelines and storage facilities supplying Kenya and other regional markets.
“We bought 25% of their pipeline network for the distribution of petroleum products,” Dangote said.
The purchase involved 4.5 billion KPC shares worth $335 million, bought at a slight premium to the last-traded price, the FT reported. Dangote said the acquisition and planned network expansion formed part of a continent-wide fuel distribution strategy. “We are going very aggressively with that,” he said.
Dangote also plans to invest $1.5 billion in expanding the pipeline network as part of a wider African refining, storage, and distribution business, the FT reported.
KPC operates about 1,342 km of pipelines transporting refined petroleum products inland from the port of Mombasa. Its infrastructure supports supplies to Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan, and eastern DR Congo.
Kenyan President William Ruto said on Tuesday that private investors had acquired a quarter of KPC from public entities, without identifying the buyers. The government sold a 65% stake through an IPO earlier this year to raise revenue, with the company listing on the Nairobi Securities Exchange in March.
The purchase follows the September 30 groundbreaking for Dangote’s planned 700,000-barrel-per-day refinery in Kenya’s coastal Lamu County. The project is intended to supply the wider East African market and is scheduled for completion in 2030.
Dangote already operates Africa’s largest refinery near Lagos, Nigeria’s commercial capital. The roughly $20 billion facility began commercial operations in 2024, helping the country reduce its reliance on imported fuel. In September, the company launched a $1.6 billion public offering to help finance an expansion intended to double its capacity to 1.4 million barrels per day.

Who is Lana Nusseibeh, the UAE nominee for UN General Secretary?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:16:54 UTC
21:16:54 KST

Breadcrumb
Who is Lana Nusseibeh, the UAE nominee for UN General Secretary?
The UAE has formally nominated veteran diplomat Lana Nusseibeh to become the next UN secretary-general, placing one of its most experienced international representatives in the race to succeed Antonio Guterres.
The nomination was submitted on Wednesday by UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in a letter to the presidents of the UN General Assembly and Security Council.
Nusseibeh, 48, is a former UAE ambassador to the UN who spent more than a decade in international diplomacy, including during the country's 2022-23 membership of the Security Council.
If successful, she would become the first woman to lead the UN and the second person from the Middle East and North Africa to hold the position, following Egypt's Boutros Boutros-Ghali.
Who is Lana Nusseibeh?
Nusseibeh is the daughter of Zaki Nusseibeh, a senior Emirati presidential adviser who has served successive UAE leaders for decades. However, the Nusseibeh family are originally from Palestine and have longstanding connections to Jerusalem.
Her grandfather, Anwar Nusseibeh, was a prominent Palestinian politician and lawyer who served in senior government positions in Jordan.
She studied history at the University of Cambridge before obtaining a master's degree in Israeli and Jewish Diaspora Studies from the School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS) in London.
Nusseibeh founded the UAE foreign ministry's Policy Planning Department in 2009, becoming its first director, and subsequently served as a joint special envoy to Afghanistan and Pakistan.
In September 2013, she became the first Emirati woman appointed as the country's permanent representative to the UN, a position she held until April 2024.
During her tenure, she served as president of the executive board of UN Women in 2017 and as a vice-president of the General Assembly. She also co-chaired negotiations concerning UN institutional reform.
Her most prominent diplomatic role came during the UAE's membership of the Security Council between 2022 and 2023, when she twice presided over the body.
During Israel's war on Gaza, Nusseibeh helped secure Security Council Resolution 2720 in December 2023, establishing a UN mechanism intended to facilitate humanitarian assistance to Palestinians.
She was also involved in securing resolutions condemning the Taliban's restrictions on Afghan women working for the UN and addressing the relationship between hate speech, discrimination and international security.
Following her departure from New York, she continued serving in senior positions within the UAE foreign ministry, becoming a minister of state in September 2025.
Can she become UN secretary-general?
Nusseibeh enters the contest as the organisation confronts financial pressures, questions over its effectiveness in responding to conflicts and growing divisions between major powers.
Her campaign programme, titled 'A United Nations for the Next Eighty Years', advocates strengthening conflict prevention, reducing institutional duplication and improving accountability.
Her extensive diplomatic experience could prove advantageous in a contest where leading candidates have struggled to secure the consensus required for appointment.
Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan, head of UN Trade and Development, and Argentina's Rafael Grossi, director-general of the International Atomic Energy Agency, are among her principal rivals.
However, Nusseibeh's candidacy could encounter geopolitical obstacles.
The UAE has faced serious allegations of supplying weapons and financial support to Sudan's Rapid Support Forces (RSF), whose members and allied militias were determined by the US in January 2025 to have committed genocide.
Amnesty International has documented weapons it believes reached the RSF through the UAE, while Abu Dhabi has consistently denied providing military support to either side in Sudan's war.
The controversy could complicate Nusseibeh's candidacy, although no evidence has been presented implicating her personally in the alleged arms transfers.
Regional rivalries, particularly the UAE's complicated relationship with Saudi Arabia, could also influence the contest, alongside expectations that the next secretary-general should come from Latin America.
Ultimately, her prospects will depend on securing at least nine Security Council votes without facing a veto from any of its five permanent members.
The successful candidate will take office on 1 January 2027, succeeding Guterres after two five-year terms.

The Turkic world: From shared history to a shared future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:16:44 UTC
21:16:44 KST

The Turkic world: From shared history to a shared future
Ahead of the 13th OTS Summit in Ankara and as his tenure as Secretary General draws to a close, H.E. Ambassador Kubanychbek Omuraliev shares his reflections on the progress achieved within the Organization of Turkic States and the road ahead. In his article, he looks back on the key developments of recent years and considers how the Turkic States can build on their shared heritage to deepen cooperation, strengthen connectivity, and create new opportunities for their peoples. Qazinform News Agency offers its readers the full text of the article titled The Turkic world: From shared history to a shared future.
By H.E. Ambassador Kubanychbek OMURALIEV
Secretary General of the Organization of Turkic States
Istanbul, October 2026
The Turkic World: From Shared History to a Shared Future
There are critical moments in the life of nations and states when shared history ceases to be merely a memory and becomes a force shaping the future. I believe the Turkic World is living through such a moment today.
Across a vast geography connecting East and West, the Turkic World brings together a population of around 180 million people, bound by deep historical and cultural ties and increasingly connected through trade, transport, investment, education, technology and people-to-people cooperation. What for centuries was sustained through common language, culture, traditions and collective memory is increasingly taking institutional and practical form under the umbrella of the family Organization of Turkic States (OTS).
The transformation has been remarkable. Since its establishment in 2009, the OTS has evolved from a platform focused primarily on political dialogue and cultural affinity into a comprehensive and action-oriented framework of cooperation.
As I approach the completion of my tenure as Secretary General, I see this moment not simply as an occasion to look back at what has been accomplished. More importantly, it is an opportunity to reflect on what makes our cooperation distinctive, what it can offer to our peoples, and what kind of Turkic World we wish to build together in the decades ahead.
A Unity Rooted in Something Deeper
The OTS possesses a quality that is rare among international organizations.
International institutions are often created in response to a particular political challenge, economic necessity or security concern. The foundation of the OTS is different. Our cooperation rests upon something that existed long before the establishment of the Organization itself: centuries of shared history, linguistic affinity, common cultural traditions, values and a profound sense of belonging to the same civilizational space.
Common history, language, identity and culture are not simply references to our past. They provide a foundation of trust upon which strong and sustainable cooperation can be built.
Few, if any, international organizations enjoy such a natural foundation. Yet heritage alone does not guarantee a shared future. The responsibility of our generation is to transform this historical closeness and affinity into opportunities, connectivity and cooperation that respond to the realities and challenges of the 21st century.
There is a simple expression that captures this idea particularly well: “Together, We Are Stronger”.
Remarkably, these words are understood across the Turkic World and require almost no translation, reflecting the deep linguistic and cultural bonds among our peoples. Today, “Together, We Are Stronger” is not merely an expression of solidarity, but a guiding principle for practical cooperation.
From Shared Identity to Institutional Strength
One of the most important transformations of recent years has been the gradual conversion of this natural affinity into institutional capacity.
Today, the OTS continues to make significant strides in strengthening cooperation among its Member States. Currently, 65 cooperation mechanisms exist under OTS umbrella, which range cover– from economy, trade, transport and customs to energy, digitalization, industry, science and technology, health, education, youth, agriculture, labour and social protection, intellectual property, space and many others. Since 2023 alone, 32 new mechanisms have been established – matching the total number created by the end of 2022. This reflects not only the expansion of our agenda but also the growing determination of our Member States and Observers to translate shared priorities into concrete institutional cooperation.
What matters even more than the numbers is a change in how we work together. Political consultations have become more frequent and substantive; ministries and specialized institutions are in closer contact; and our ability to think together, plan together and act together has grown. I would describe this stage of our development in three words: implementation, transformation and institutional deepening.
As Chair of the Coordination Committee of the Turkic Cooperation Organizations, the OTS maintains close and structured cooperation with affiliated and related organizations, including the Parliamentary Assembly of Turkic States (TURKPA), the International Organization of Turkic Culture (TURKSOY), the Turkic Academy, the Turkic Culture and Heritage Foundation, the Turkic Investment Fund (TIF) and the Union of Turkic Chambers of Commerce and Industry (TCCI). Together, these institutions contribute to a multidimensional framework of cooperation, strengthening institutional ties and advancing shared priorities across the Turkic World.
The establishment and operationalization of the Turkic Investment Fund represent an important milestone in this evolution. For the first time, the Turkic States have created a joint financial institution designed to mobilize their economic potential, support investment and entrepreneurship, strengthen small and medium-sized enterprises and facilitate joint projects. The Council of Central Banks, the Turkic Green Finance Council and the Turkic Investment Promotion Network (TurkIPAnet) further reinforce this emerging financial and investment architecture.
Yet among the most encouraging developments I have witnessed during my tenure is the emergence of cooperation networks beyond governmental and formal institutions, including within the private sector and professional communities.
Notaries, auditors, engineers, trade unions and representatives of other professions are establishing contacts, creating networks and exploring institutional forms of cooperation within a broader Turkic framework. This growing cooperation is also reflected in initiatives such as the Union of International Road Transport Associations of the OTS, the Union of Turkic Ski Resorts and the Turkic Red Network, bringing together stakeholders across transport, tourism and humanitarian cooperation. Business communities, universities, young people, experts and professional associations are finding their own reasons – and increasingly their own ways – to connect.
When people and professional communities begin building connections on their own initiative, cooperation acquires a life beyond institutions. It becomes rooted in society itself.
For me, this is one of the clearest signs of the growing maturity of Turkic cooperation.
An Emerging Economic and Strategic Space
The growing importance of the Turkic World is shaped not only by our shared heritage, but also by the scale of our collective economic and strategic potential. According to figures reported for the end of 2025, the combined GDP of OTS Member States and Observers exceeded $2.4 trillion, and their aggregate trade turnover reached approximately $1.27 trillion.
Together, the Turkic States would represent the world’s 11th largest economy and third-largest energy provider. With substantial reserves of oil, natural gas, coal, and critical minerals, including over 40 percent of global uranium production, our countries possess significant energy potential while increasingly investing in renewable energy development.
In a time of rising demand and fast changes in global energy systems, working together is not optional – it is a necessary thing to do. Recent OTS Summits stress the importance of energy security, which depends on connecting pipelines, power grids, storage, and transport routes to ensure stable supply, increase trade, and strengthen economic and geopolitical stability.
The Turkic States are strengthening regional and international energy connectivity through major infrastructure projects, including the Southern Gas Corridor, the Central Asia -Azerbaijan Green Energy Corridor, the Kambarata-1 Hydropower Plant and the Black Sea Submarine Cable. These initiatives reflect the growing role of the Turkic World in enhancing energy security, diversifying supply routes and advancing renewable energy cooperation.
In this regard, the Turkic World Vision-2040 provides an important strategic framework. It calls on us to deepen economic integration, improve connectivity, strengthen institutions, invest in knowledge-based industries, and promote sustainable and inclusive growth.
Perhaps nowhere is this logic more visible than in connectivity.
The Trans-Caspian International East - West Middle Corridor is becoming an increasingly important link between Asia and Europe, with freight volumes potentially reaching 11 million tons by 2030. The China - Kyrgyzstan - Uzbekistan railway, with a projected capacity of up to 15 million tons annually, will further strengthen regional connectivity and expand trade opportunities across Eurasia.
But a modern corridor is more than railway tracks, roads and ports. Goods must cross borders efficiently; information and documentation must move with them.
The OTS is complementing physical infrastructure with customs and digital solutions, including the Simplified Customs Corridor, e-Permit, e-CMR and digital TIR, to facilitate cross-border trade and reduce administrative barriers. The Digital Economy Partnership Agreement and ongoing efforts to conclude a free trade agreement in services and investment will further strengthen economic integration among our countries.
We also welcome the recently established cooperation among competition authorities, financial intelligence units, investment promotion agencies, supreme audit institutions and tax administrations. These partnerships strengthen institutional connectivity and improve economic governance across the Turkic World.
The digital economy remains at the center of this agenda. Digital trade platforms, interoperable e-customs systems, fintech cooperation, secure data exchange, and common approaches to digital regulation can make economic relations more efficient and accessible. Digital transformation is not simply a technical matter. It is one of the foundations of modern economic integration.
The objective is straightforward: to make connectivity work better for those who actually use it.
Taken together, these developments point towards the gradual emergence of a more connected Turkic economic space – one in which infrastructure is reinforced by efficient borders, trade is supported by investment, and the strengths of individual countries increasingly become sources of shared opportunity.
Towards a More Connected Turkic World
For the younger generation, the Turkic World should be a living space of opportunity. The Turkic Universities Union (TURKUNIB) and Orhun Exchange Programme help bring students, academic staff and universities closer together. Youth initiatives, including the Youth Volunteering Educational Programme, the Multilateral Youth Exchange Programme and the International Youth Camp, further promote people-to-people contacts, mutual understanding and a sense of shared identity among young people across the Turkic World. Meanwhile, initiatives under discussion, such as the Turkic ID and Common Museum Card, aim to facilitate travel and access to our shared cultural heritage.
A transport corridor becomes more valuable when businesses use it. Business cooperation becomes stronger when supported by investment. Investment becomes more productive when connected with technology and human capital. And all of these become more sustainable when our societies participate in and benefit from the process.
The future of the OTS therefore lies not simply in expanding the number of areas in which we cooperate, but in bringing existing mechanisms together into a more coherent space of opportunity.
Our strength lies precisely in building upon our unique foundations while remaining open to the wider world.
Our long-term direction is set out in the Turkic World Vision-2040. Deeper connectivity and integration, pursued with full respect for the sovereignty and national priorities of our States, should strengthen our common capacity to address climate change, food and health security, emergencies and other cross-border challenges.
A Turkic World Open to the World
A stronger Turkic World should also mean a more connected and outward-looking Turkic World.
Our geography gives us a natural role in this regard. For centuries, the lands of the Turkic World have connected peoples, cultures, markets and ideas across Eurasia. Today, we have an opportunity to give this historical role a modern meaning.
By improving transport links, facilitating trade, connecting energy networks, encouraging innovation and strengthening contacts among societies, the Turkic States can contribute not only to their own prosperity, but also to greater connectivity and cooperation across the wider Eurasian region.
This approach is reflected in the OTS’s growing engagement with the United Nations system and other international and regional organizations, as well as in the development of the OTS+ format, which provides a flexible platform for cooperation with countries and partners beyond the Organization. Our aim is to develop mutually beneficial, practical partnerships that contribute to peace, stability, connectivity, sustainable development and dialogue.
Our objective is not to build walls around the Turkic World, but to build bridges that connect it with the wider world.
A Turkic World that is more connected within can also be more open, more relevant and more capable of contributing to dialogue, development and shared prosperity beyond its own borders.
The Road Ahead
Over the past years, I have had the privilege of witnessing and making my humble contribution to the Turkic World move closer together in ways that are increasingly diverse and increasingly tangible.
Yet perhaps the most important conclusion I draw from these years is that we are still at the beginning of what is possible.
The foundations have been laid. The commitment of our Member States is strong. The institutional architecture has expanded. Our collective economic and strategic potential is increasingly recognized. And our societies themselves are discovering new ways of connecting with one another.
The forthcoming 13th OTS Summit in Ankara, to be held under the theme “Turkic Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Deed”, which will mark the beginning of Türkiye’s Chairmanship, offers an important opportunity to carry this momentum into the next phase of our common work.
Looking ahead, the success of our cooperation must be measured not only by the agreements we sign or the mechanisms we establish, but by the tangible benefits we deliver to our peoples. Our priority must remain to translate our collective ambitions into meaningful opportunities and lasting progress for future generations.
I remain deeply grateful to the Heads of State of our Member States and Observers for their vision and unwavering support, as well as to our governments, institutions, Permanent Representatives, experts and colleagues at the OTS Secretariat. Their dedication, professionalism and shared commitment have been indispensable to every step of our collective progress.
It has been a great honour to contribute to this journey as Secretary General.
Although my tenure as Secretary General is drawing to a close, my commitment to the unity, cooperation and prosperity of the Turkic World will remain unchanged. I will always regard it as a privilege to have contributed to this common endeavour and will continue to believe in the extraordinary potential of our shared future.
The Turkic World must continue its journey from affinity to connectivity, from potential to capacity, and from cooperation to tangible benefit for its people.
Our ancestors gave us a shared heritage. What we leave to future generations must be more than the memory of that heritage.
It must be a shared future built upon it.
Across our languages and across our geography, the following message should continuously resonate:
Together, We Are Stronger.

Kazakh schoolers build AI platform to translate sign language in real time
Students at the Nazarbayev Intellectual School in Kyzylorda have developed an AI platform that translates sign language into text and speech in real time, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Aishabibi Yerlankyzy and Gainizhamal Berikkyzy piloted their web platform, QOLDAU AI, at Kyzylorda Specialized Boarding School No. 6 for Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Children.
Requiring only a standard web camera and an internet connection, the system recognizes Kazakh sign language gestures and converts them into text and audio formats, helping hearing-impaired individuals communicate with others without the need to install additional applications.
While testing, children evaluated the platform and shared their impressions. Teachers highlighted the platform's practical benefits, urging developers to add more gestures and noting its potential to support literacy development.
"I thank the girls for creating a useful platform that can become a good assistant for specialists and parents. Some of the sign language elements still need refinement, but they can be improved. In the future, I would like to see more educational materials and video tutorials," said sign language specialist Zukhra Kalzhanova.
NIS Kyzylorda physics teacher Ainur Kurakbayeva and deputy principal Madina Rashitova are supervising the project. Feedback gathered during testing will help the project authors refine the system to suit users' needs.
Alongside the technology demonstration, the NIS students also organized an art contest titled "Kazakhstan is My Pride" for the boarding school pupils ahead of Republic Day.

OpenAI expands ChatGPT ads to 26 more countries
The expansion includes 14 new markets in Latin America, as well as countries across Europe, the Middle East, Africa and Asia. New markets include Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Peru, Nigeria, South Africa, Serbia, Ukraine, Cambodia, Bangladesh and Pakistan.
Advertisers can launch campaigns through OpenAI's Ads Manager or its technology partners, depending on the market.
OpenAI says more than 1.2 billion people use ChatGPT each week to explore ideas, compare options and make decisions. The company aims to place advertisements alongside relevant conversations, allowing businesses to reach users while they consider products and services.
For example, someone planning their first marathon might discuss meal planning with ChatGPT and then see an advertisement for a grocery delivery service.
OpenAI says advertisements will appear only on its Free and Go plans. Users subscribed to Plus, Pro and Enterprise will not see ads, according to the announcement.
The company also says advertisements will be clearly labeled and displayed separately from ChatGPT's answers. OpenAI states that it does not share users' conversations with advertisers or sell their personal data, and that advertisements do not influence the answers ChatGPT provides.
According to OpenAI's advertising guidelines, the system selects ads based on factors such as the current conversation, the user's apparent intent and the advertisement's content. When ad personalization is enabled, the system may also use certain signals from a user's broader interactions with ChatGPT.
Advertisers can pay for impressions or valid clicks and can use supported conversion tracking to measure campaign performance. OpenAI recommends starting with a maximum bid of $3 to $5 per click for campaigns using cost per click pricing.
OpenAI plans to introduce additional advertising formats, campaign objectives, purchasing options and measurement tools as the service expands.

Libya’s National Oil Corporation says individuals shut valve on Hamada-Zawiya crude oil pipeline

Muetaz Wannes and Ikram Kouachi
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
Libya’s National Oil Corporation (NOC) said Thursday that individuals had shut a valve on the Hamada-Zawiya crude oil pipeline in the country’s west, which transports crude from the Hamada and al-Tahara oil fields.
In a statement, the corporation said “individuals,” whose identities were not disclosed, had entered the crude oil reception station operated by Arabian Gulf Oil Company, adjacent to the Zawiya refinery, and closed the isolation valve on the Hamada-Zawiya pipeline.
The corporation warned that the continued closure would lead to “the loss of quantities of crude oil production, negatively affecting oil revenues.”
It called for oil facilities to be kept free from any interference that could disrupt operational activities.
The NOC also urged the relevant authorities to “intervene immediately” to reopen the valve and secure the site.
The statement did not identify those responsible for closing the valve, while oil facility guards have been demanding higher monthly wages for some time as part of protests across several sectors.
In September, the corporation said a group of guards had “illegally shut a valve” on the main Hamada-Zawiya oil loading pipeline.
That same month, the NOC said armed members of the Petroleum Facilities Guard had closed a crude oil transport valve at the Sharara oil field in the country’s southwest, leading to a decline in production.
The corporation put the losses at the time at $95 million in a country that relies on oil exports for about 90% of its public budget.

Elena Teslova
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
A deal between Russia and the US on Russian diesel supplies will be effective from Friday, Russia's special envoy said Thursday.
Speaking in Istanbul on the sidelines of the Verona Eurasian Economic Forum, Kirill Dmitriev, the special envoy for investment and economic cooperation with foreign countries, said Russia was also open to diesel supply deals with European nations if requests were made.
“We all know about the diesel deal, it will begin to be implemented literally tomorrow,” he said.
The official added that Moscow and Washington were discussing potential Russian fertilizer supplies to the US market, other energy projects and technological cooperation, including the possible creation of joint artificial intelligence data centers.
Dmitriev said economic cooperation between Russia and the US would continue to expand despite opposition from some European officials, adding that European countries themselves purchased significantly more Russian energy resources than the US.
 
Europe's fuel crisis to 'intensify'
He also predicted that Europe’s fuel crisis would worsen, attributing it to attempts to abandon Russian energy supplies.
“We see a fuel crisis in Europe, and it will only intensify,” he said.
“I have no doubt that the more deals we have with the US, the more European companies will want to join. They will not want to be left out,” he said.
Dmitriev also said European businesses were suffering from high energy prices as a result of the EU’s policies and the shift away from Russian energy supplies.
According to him, European business representatives had approached the Russian delegation at the forum to express support for maintaining dialogue with Moscow.
The Russian envoy also predicted that the Nord Stream 1 and 2 gas pipelines would eventually resume operations.
“There is absolutely no doubt that Nord Stream 1 and 2 will operate again at some point. It is inevitable,” he said.
Nord Stream 1 and 2 were designed to deliver Russian gas directly to Germany via the Baltic Sea.
Nord Stream 1 operated from 2011, while Nord Stream 2 was completed in 2021 but never entered service.
Explosions damaged three of the four pipeline lines in September 2022. Germany’s investigation into the sabotage remains ongoing, with a Ukrainian national suspected of coordinating the attack arrested in 2025.

Iran reveals ‘offensive’ doctrine, US issues alert: Is war imminent?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:12:32 UTC
21:12:32 KST

Iran reveals ‘offensive’ doctrine, US issues alert: Is war imminent?
US orders diplomatic staff out of Saudi Arabia amid escalating conflict and reports of potential US and Israeli strikes on Iran.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says renewed attacks by the United States could prompt Tehran to invade neighbouring countries and hit bases used in US military operations as part of its new “offensive” strategy.
The warning on Wednesday came amid escalating attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a global energy chokepoint, and uncertainty over diplomatic efforts to end the nearly eight-month war.
“Our defence doctrine was previously defensive; we used to say that if a country attacks us, we will respond. Now we say that if a country attacks us, we will both respond and launch an offensive,” IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebi said.
Washington ordered some diplomatic personnel to leave Saudi Arabia amid attacks from Yemen’s Houthis while US President Donald Trump has signalled that a decision on the conflict could come soon.
According to media reports, the US and Israel are planning potential attacks on Iran in the coming weeks.
As negotiations seem stalled and both sides exchange threats, could the region be heading towards another military escalation?
What is Iran’s new doctrine?
The IRGC on Wednesday announced a shift towards an “offensive and asymmetrical” defence doctrine, threatening to invade countries that launch attacks against it.
Mohebi said Tehran would no longer limit its military operations to retaliatory strikes.
Mohebi stressed that Iran’s missile stockpile has increased 1.5 times since the 12-day war between Iran and Israel in June 2025. He did not provide specific figures.
“The quality of the missiles has improved significantly, and their range, destructive power and accuracy in hitting targets have increased,” the spokesman said.
Moreover, Mohebi said Iranian forces were in the “stage of preparing to unveil the ‘father of all bombs’. This is something new for the enemy.”
Meanwhile, attacks in the Strait of Hormuz continued unabated.
The IRGC’s navy said on Thursday that four vessels it accused of being involved in illegal oil transfers were struck and caught fire in the northern Gulf. Three other vessels hit mines west of the strait, it added.
Before the war, one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas supplies passed through the Strait of Hormuz. While shipments through the strait are still below those levels, oil shipments from the region returned to pre-war levels last month as exporters found alternative ways to ship out their oil and gas, including using pipelines.
However, a flurry of recent attacks in the key waterway and the fighting between Yemen’s Houthis and its Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government, which has resulted in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, have once again sent oil prices surging. Brent crude climbed above $110 a barrel on Thursday amid fears of further disruptions to regional energy supplies.
Why the shift?
Iran’s shift towards an offensive military doctrine reflects Tehran’s determination to make future US-Israeli attacks significantly more costly, according to analysts.
Negar Mortazavi, senior fellow at the Centre for International Policy, told Al Jazeera that Tehran was drawing lessons from the wars of 2025 and 2026 after its previous strategy of retaliation failed to prevent repeated attacks.
“Tehran now wants to establish a new equation: Any future attack on Iran will come at a much higher cost for the aggressors,” she told Al Jazeera.
Unable to match conventional US military capabilities, Iran is increasingly relying on asymmetric warfare, including missiles, drones and its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, Mortazavi explained.
She said Tehran was pursuing a broader strategy aimed at imposing military, economic and political costs on Washington, including potentially influencing the November 3 US midterm elections.
“Iran wants to teach Washington a lesson: Attacking Iran comes with a high price, one that can even cost elections,” Mortazavi said, referring to US surveys that are predicting electoral losses for Trump’s Republican Party.
She added that Iranian officials were closely monitoring the elections, believing the economic fallout from the war could damage the Republican Party’s prospects of retaining control of Congress.
“The long-term objective is to establish deterrence so that future American administrations think twice before daring to attack Iran again,” she said.
Political analyst Rami Khouri said the doctrine was also intended to ensure that the consequences of attacks extend to the US, Israel and regional countries supporting their military operations.
“That’s one part of the strategy, that the suffering and the damage have to be equal and reciprocal,” Khouri, nonresident senior fellow at the Arab Center, told Al Jazeera.
Khouri argued that Tehran was also seeking to challenge what it views as longstanding Western domination of the region.
“The Iranians are actually working to try to end the colonial period,” he said.
He added that Iran’s strategy could extend the economic consequences of conflict far beyond the Middle East, affecting energy supplies, transportation, insurance costs and shipments of essential goods.
“The pain is going to go way beyond just the Middle East and Israel and the US and will hurt people in other parts of the world,” Khouri said.
What has the US said about resuming the war?
Trump has offered conflicting signals about Washington’s next steps.
On Wednesday, he said the US was no longer negotiating with Tehran and suggested developments were imminent. “We are going to have something one way or the other that’ll happen fairly soon,” he told reporters.
He also said Washington could end the war immediately but wanted a lasting outcome. “It’ll end very soon. We could leave now, but we want to make sure it lasts for a long time,” Trump said at a campaign rally in South Carolina.
Trump previously pledged not to attack Iran before the November 3 elections.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said this week that reaching a peace agreement is extremely difficult and insisted that Iran must stop targeting commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
In recent weeks, Iran’s enrichment of uranium has re-emerged as a point of contention.
Rubio has maintained that Washington will reject any agreement allowing Iran to develop nuclear weapons, which require highly enriched uranium. “The United States will not support any deal that creates a pathway for Iran to ever have a nuclear weapon,” he said on Wednesday.
Tehran insisted its right to enrichment is guaranteed under the Non-Proliferation Treaty.
Iran has offered a seven-day plan to restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for Washington ending its blockade of Iranian ports, easing sanctions and unfreezing Iranian assets.
Meanwhile, the US Department of State on Wednesday ordered nonemergency personnel and their families to leave Saudi Arabia after recent Houthi attacks.
The US embassy in Riyadh has warned of further attacks while American officials told the Reuters news agency that family members could be withdrawn from other Gulf missions.
State Department spokesman Tommy Piggott said departure orders for mission personnel across the Gulf have not been ordered, saying the current orders were for “employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only”.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reiterated on Sunday his pledge to topple Iran’s government, saying it was key to preventing it from rebuilding its nuclear programme and the “axis of resistance”, further raising prospects of an escalation.
Netanyahu made the comments as Israel’s longest-serving prime minister is locked in a tough battle to remain in power in Tuesday’s elections.
Is war imminent?
Analysts warned that renewed US-Israeli attacks on Iran are increasingly possible with both sides preparing for another confrontation despite the continued possibility of diplomacy.
“Another round of war seems to be approaching,” Mortazavi said.
“Both sides appear to be preparing for renewed confrontation while escalating tensions in the Strait of Hormuz increase the risk of a wider conflict,” she said.
Mortazavi added that the elections in the next two weeks in the US and Israel could influence the timing of military action but warned that the current trajectory appeared to favour escalation over negotiations.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, on Wednesday said, “Everyone must know that any action against Iran comes at a cost.”
“If diplomacy can create this understanding, we prefer diplomacy, but if the war continues, Iran has the necessary means to sustain its response,” Rezaei said, according to the IRNA news agency.
Echoing Mortazavi, Khouri warned that another confrontation could be approaching although he said US threats might still be part of a negotiating strategy.
“I think imminent conflict is on the cards, but I don’t know if war is the right word to use,” Khouri told Al Jazeera.
He said renewed strikes could target Iran’s critical infrastructure, including electricity networks, transportation systems, bridges and essential services.
“We’re probably going to get some severe attacks on a few targets that will try to make life in Iran very difficult,” he said.
However, Khouri cautioned that Iran’s ability to withstand another major military offensive while inflicting comparable damage on its adversaries remained uncertain.
“It’s not clear if Iran has the ability to withstand major new assaults against it,” he said, while stressing that Tehran was unlikely to surrender to military pressure.

Congressmen urge Trump, Musk to give Ukraine ability to destroy missile launchers in Russia – media

2026-10-22
15:06:11 EEST

American congressmen, including 16 members of the Democratic Party and seven members of the Republican Party, have signed a letter urging U.S President Donald Trump and SpaceX founder Elon Musk to grant Ukraine access to Starlink satellite systems to detect missile launchers on the territory of Russia.
"We are writing to urge you to ask Elon Musk to let Ukraine use the Starlink satellite internet system to hunt for missile launchers inside Russia. With one phone call, you could both save lives and give Vladimir Putin greater incentives to negotiate," reads the text of the letter sent on Wednesday, as cited by The Hill.
Among the Republicans who signed the letter are Joe Wilson (South Carolina), Brian Fitzpatrick (Pennsylvania), Don Bacon (Nebraska), Carlos Gimenez (Florida), Jeff Hurd (Colorado), Andy Harris (Maryland), and Max Miller (Ohio).
"Mr. President, we all share the goal of ending the war in Ukraine and the devastating loss of life it has caused... If Ukraine cannot reliably intercept Russian arrows, it must be able to strike the archer. The Starlink system, operated by Mr. Musk's SpaceX, could help with this," the letter states, with the congressmen noting that Vladimir Putin "currently has no intention of stopping the bloodshed."
As reported, Ukraine began using StarShield in 2024. Standard StarLink (Starlink Mini), installed on drones, has a limited speed of up to 160 km/h, which is insufficient to perform certain missions. To make an aircraft fly faster, it is necessary to gain access specifically to the military version of StarLink – StarShield.
SpaceX, without warning the Ukrainian Defense Forces on the night of October 14, unilaterally restricted the operation of StarShield terminals; this complicated the work of UAV missions, in particular interceptors and middle strikes. By the end of that same day, the operation of terminals at speeds of 160 km/h resumed, but Ukraine received confirmation that the 160 km/h restriction applies only within its territory.
On the same day, Musk stated that decisions regarding restrictions on the operation of military StarShield systems are made by the U.S military and the president, and commercial StarLink cannot be used for offensive military actions. However, Trump later stated that Washington was not involved in slowing down StarShield for Ukraine, and U.S Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that StarShield was allegedly unavailable to Ukraine and the White House had nothing to do with disruptions in StarLink's operation. U.S Secretary of War Pete Hegseth reported that his department refrained from issuing any directives regarding restricting StarShield's operation. Later, the British newspaper The Telegraph, citing its own sources, reported that Musk personally appealed to Trump with a proposal to limit StarLink's operating speed for the Ukrainian military.
Following this, a number of senators and congressmen stated the unacceptability of such actions, Musk's influence on the course of the war in Ukraine and U.S security, and that they would demand an investigation into the restrictions on the operation of StarShield systems in Ukraine and hold those responsible accountable.
On October 20, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that the American side had restored the operation of Ukraine's early warning system for Russian ballistic missile launches and announced a conversation with Rubio, while Rubio himself stated that he had nothing to do with decisions made by Musk and SpaceX regarding the operation of StarLink and StarShield.
The European Commission stated that SpaceX's restrictions on StarLink services for Ukraine contradict agreements, and the company must ensure full access for Ukraine.
