Nearly all coral reefs risk collapse in 50 years: IUCN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:05:00 UTC
21:05:00 KST

Nearly all coral reefs risk collapse in 50 years: IUCN
- The IUCN says 96% of coral reef systems are “critically endangered”, with nearly all shallow-water reefs facing an “extremely high risk” of collapse by 2075.
- Climate change is the main threat, as warming seas drive bleaching. Overfishing, pollution, coastal development and storms also damage reefs.
- The IUCN says reefs are “not yet lost” and can recover. It calls for sharp emissions cuts, stronger protection and restoration, and more investment.
AI generated
YEREVAN – Nearly all of the world’s shallow-water coral reefs face an “extremely high risk” of collapse by 2075 due to climate change, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) warned on Oct 22.
In the first global assessment of its kind, the world authority on threatened wildlife classified 96% of the planet’s coral reef systems as “critically endangered” – its highest risk category.
Corals are heat sensitive and particularly vulnerable to human-driven climate change, which is warming the world’s oceans and increasing the frequency and intensity of damaging bleaching events.
“The risk of coral reef collapse is escalating, but this must be a wake-up call rather than a cause for despair,” said Mishal Gudka, scientific lead of the IUCN Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems assessment.
“Coral reefs have shown a remarkable ability to bounce back from devastating bleaching events,” said Gudka, who is also research director at Coastal Oceans Research and Development in the Indian Ocean (CORDIO) East Africa, a conservation organisation.
For their assessment, researchers used the “middle-of-the-road” scenario from the UN’s panel of climate experts that projects global temperatures rising 2.7 deg C above pre-industrial levels by 2100.
The world is on track for 2.6 deg C warming this century under current global commitments to cut planet-heating emissions, the United Nations warned on Oct 21.
“Heat stress from climate change is the single most consistent threat driving coral reef decline worldwide,” the IUCN said in a statement.
Overfishing is also hurting corals as certain herbivores and predators help control algae and maintain an ecological balance, the organisation said.
The overexploitation of parrotfish and other groupers threatens 63% of coral reef ecosystems.
Coastal development, pollution, tourism and more frequent storms are among other threats.
Critically endangered coral
The IUCN’s analysis examined 127 tropical and subtropical coral systems covering 188,362 sq km.
The world’s largest and most biodiverse coral reefs are among those classified as critically endangered – Australia’s Great Barrier Reef, the Coral Triangle in South-east Asia and the western Pacific, the Caribbean’s Mesoamerican Barrier Reef System, and the Red Sea coral reefs.
A reef ecosystem collapses when hard corals – which build its living foundation – largely disappear and are replaced by algae, rubble and sponges.
The report was released during the UN’s COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia, where governments are under pressure to make progress on a landmark pact to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.
Despite its warning, the IUCN said coral reefs in most parts of the world “are not yet lost”.
If scientists look only at what has happened over the past 50 years, excluding future climate projections, 24% of coral reef ecosystems would be deemed critically endangered instead of 96%, the IUCN said.
“It is not too late to give coral reefs a chance to recover, but it requires decisive action to tackle climate change and halt further ocean warming,” said IUCN director-general Grethel Aguilar.
“We know what is needed: ambitious emissions reductions, stronger protection and restoration efforts, and sustained investment in resilient coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them.”
A study published in the journal Nature last week found that, by 2020, nearly half of coral species were at “elevated relative risk of extinction”, with climate change the main driver of this decline. AFP

Russian Ballistic Strikes Hit Six Kyiv Districts, Killing One and Injuring 22
Russian forces launched ballistic strikes across six districts of Kyiv beginning on the evening of October 21, killing one person and injuring 22 others, including four children, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service reported on October 22.
The attacks caused fires and damage to residential buildings, vehicles, transport infrastructure, medical vehicles, and a monastery across the capital.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine is facing a severe shortage of Patriot interceptors, one of the few systems capable of reliably engaging Russian ballistic missiles. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that limited PAC-2 and PAC-3 supplies leave Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure more exposed to Russian strikes, while Kyiv continues pressing partners for additional missiles to protect civilians.
In Kyiv’s Dniprovskyi district, one person was killed and a child was hospitalized. Five other people were injured as residential and nonresidential buildings caught fire and homes and vehicles were damaged.
In the Darnytskyi district, Russian strikes damaged transport infrastructure, with no casualties reported.

Another six people were injured in the Holosiivskyi district after a strike hit a nonresidential building.
Emergency authorities noted that information on the consequences of the Russian attack was still being updated.
Russian attacks have repeatedly damaged Kyiv’s medical facilities in recent days. On October 20, a Russian drone struck an operating room at the Strazhesko Institute of Cardiology, injuring one patient and partially damaging the hospital’s upper floor.

Meet Russia’s New Filin Cruise Missile—1,200 Km of Range, 3D-Printed Parts and Chinese Guidance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:01:40 UTC
21:01:40 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Meet Russia’s New Filin Cruise Missile—1,200 Km of Range, 3D-Printed Parts and Chinese Guidance
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) has published a detailed breakdown and interactive 3D model of Russia’s new Filin cruise missile, revealing a low-cost, ground-launched weapon with a claimed range of up to 1,200 kilometers and an increasingly Chinese-heavy electronics base.
Russia began using the Filin against Ukraine in late summer 2026, according to a HUR report on October 22.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The missile is produced by NPO Molniya, part of Russia’s Tactical Missiles Corporation, and appears to continue Moscow’s push toward cheaper jet-powered strike weapons that can be launched from the ground and manufactured in larger numbers.
According to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence, the Filin has a composite fuselage made from carbon- and fiberglass-reinforced materials. The missile measures about 3.5 meters in length with a wingspan of roughly 3 meters, while some individual parts are produced using 3D-printing technology.
Russia claims the missile can reach speeds of up to 800 kilometers per hour, or about 500 mph, and strike targets as far as 1,200 kilometers away.
It is designed to fly at extremely low altitude but can also climb to approximately 6 kilometers. Versions carrying either 50-kilogram or 100-kilogram warheads have been identified.
The missile is launched from a ground-based launcher using a solid-propellant booster before its main engine takes over.
Ukraine’s intelligence service found that the Filin’s onboard electronics are manufactured by Russian company PLAZ, which is also involved in producing electronics for the Garpiya UAV—a Russian adaptation related to the Geran-2 family. Intelligence analysts noted that electronic modules found in the Filin and Garpiya use similar layouts and markings, suggesting Russia is increasingly standardizing components across different weapons.
Navigation is provided by a Chinese-made inertial navigation system together with a 16-channel Kometa satellite-navigation module.
The missile’s electronic component base broadly resembles that found in other Russian missiles and UAVs, but Ukrainian intelligence highlighted the growing share of Chinese components. Investigators identified 35 US-made components and 22 Chinese-made components, alongside increased reuse of common solutions across multiple circuit boards and systems.
That trend suggests Russia is continuing to simplify supply chains and standardize electronics across different missile and drone programs while increasing its dependence on Chinese technology.
One major component remains Russian-made. The Filin uses an R500 jet engine manufactured by Reynolds LLC. The same engine has previously been identified in Russia’s S-71K Kover and S-71M Monokhrom air-launched cruise missiles.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence published the full component breakdown through its War&Sanctions portal, including an interactive 3D model designed to show how the missile is assembled and which foreign technologies continue to appear inside Russian weapons.
Earlier, HUR revealed new details about Russia’s Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missile, identifying 58 Russian companies involved in its production, 22 of which remain outside international sanctions.

Defence spending in Northern Ireland hits record high
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:00:58 BST
21:00:58 KST

Ministry of Defence expenditure with industry in Northern Ireland rose by sixty-three per cent in a single year to reach £464 million in 2025-26, the highest level since records began, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Andrew Rosindell, the Reform UK member for Romford, asked the Secretary of State for Defence what recent assessment he had made of the geo-strategic importance of Northern Ireland.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “Northern Ireland has a growing and strategically important defence sector, founded on a strong engineering heritage and backed by robust research competence, collaboration, and world-leading academic institutions. Recent figures show that MOD expenditure with UK industry in Northern Ireland rose by 63% compared to the previous year. In real terms this equates to £464 million in 2025-26, the highest level since records began.
“In recognition of its geo-strategic importance and huge potential to support Defence meet its national objectives, the Northern Ireland Defence Growth Deal was launched earlier this year. It is a £50 million investment aiming to strengthen and grow NI’s defence ecosystem by supporting SMEs to scale capability, access opportunities and contribute to a more resilient UK supply chain.”
Thales in Belfast carries most of that figure, and the Castlereagh site builds Starstreak and the Lightweight Multirole Missile, the weapons that have been fired in quantity in Ukraine and reordered repeatedly since, and the plant has taken contracts worth more than a billion pounds across the past three years while taking on hundreds of staff. Northern Ireland’s defence spend stood at around £190 million in 2023, so the figure has more than doubled in three years.
Harland and Wolff’s Belfast yard sits in the same picture, now under Navantia ownership after the company’s collapse, with a share of the Fleet Solid Support ship programme that will see blocks built in Belfast and Appledore. Spirit AeroSystems, Denroy, Survitec and a substantial cluster of aerospace and engineering small firms feed into the wider total.
The Northern Ireland Defence Growth Deal was launched this year, and this publication reported when Northern Ireland was to be boosted by the defence growth deal. Fifty million pounds aimed at small and medium firms is intended to let the supply chain around the large manufacturers scale up out of its dependence on single contracts.

Kids’ aggression appears to shape parents’ discipline more than the reverse, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:00:51 UTC
21:00:51 KST

Children’s aggressive behavior may contribute to parents becoming less consistent with discipline, rather than inconsistent discipline simply causing children to become more aggressive, according to research published in Nature Communications. The study also found that shared genes explained part of the link between inconsistent discipline and aggression, and all of the link between positive parenting and lower aggression.
Parenting and childhood aggression have long been linked. Parents who inconsistently enforce rules tend to have children with more aggressive behavior, while greater positive parenting, such as praising and positively engaging with children, is associated with less aggression. These findings can easily be interpreted as evidence that parenting produces differences in children’s behavior.
But families are more complicated. Children can affect their parents just as parents can affect their children. Biological parents and children also share genes, meaning some of the genetic factors associated with a parent’s behavior could be inherited by their children and influence the children’s behavior.
Led by Joanna K. Bright of King’s College London, the researchers addressed these problems using two genetically informative studies of children between about 4.5 and 8 years of age. Both studies used the same questionnaires to measure inconsistent discipline, positive parenting and child aggression, allowing the researchers to check whether the results held across different samples and methods.
The first drew on Norway’s Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study, using extended-family data involving 53,532 children born to 42,538 mothers, who reported on their parenting and their children’s behavior when the children were 5 years old. By comparing families with different degrees of genetic relatedness, including twins and their children, the researchers could estimate how much of the relationship between parenting and aggression was associated with shared genetics.
The second dataset came from the U.S. Early Growth and Development Study and contained 561 adoption triads, each made up of an adopted child, the adoptive parents and the birth parents. The children, 57% of whom were male, were adopted shortly after birth and assessed at ages 4.5, 6, 7 and 8. Because adoptive parents and children did not share genes, associations between their behaviors provided a way of examining environmental pathways without the complication of genes inherited from those parents.
The results suggested a more complicated relationship than parenting simply causing aggression. In the Norwegian study, the correlation between inconsistent discipline and child aggression was modest. About 47% of this association was attributed to shared genetic factors, while 53% remained after accounting for genetic transmission.
When the researchers investigated that remaining relationship, the evidence pointed from child to parent. The best-fitting model included a path from child aggression to inconsistent maternal discipline but no path from discipline to aggression. The adoption study showed a similar pattern: children’s aggression was linked to more inconsistent discipline at the same age and predicted more inconsistent discipline at later ages, while paths from mothers’ discipline to children’s aggression were not statistically significant.
Bright and colleagues concluded that “childhood aggression drives inconsistent parenting beyond shared genetic influences.”
Sensitivity analyses using fathers’ reports in the adoption study painted a somewhat different picture. When fathers reported on both their own parenting and their children’s behavior, inconsistent discipline and child aggression appeared to influence each other in both directions at the same time point, though not over longer periods. When one parent’s report of child aggression was paired with the other parent’s report of parenting, no significant links emerged, which the authors note could mean that relying on the same person to report both behaviors inflates associations.
Positive parenting produced another important finding. Although greater positive parenting was associated with lower aggression in the Norwegian sample, the researchers estimated that the association was completely explained by shared genetic influences. In the adoption sample, the models found no evidence that positive parenting and aggression influenced each other in either direction.
The results did not differ meaningfully between boys and girls. The authors suggest that clinicians should recognize that childhood aggression can contribute to inconsistent discipline, and that interventions focused only on encouraging consistent discipline may be insufficient.
Some limitations should be noted. The authors caution that their questionnaires captured relatively narrow aspects of parenting and aggression, relied primarily on mothers’ reports, and were drawn from relatively socioeconomically advantaged families. The two samples also used somewhat different versions of the aggression measure, which captured defiant behavior as well as physical aggression.
The Norwegian analysis was based on a single time point and could not account for the possibility that parents choose partners with similar traits. The data were also collected between roughly 10 and 23 years ago, and parenting norms may have shifted since then.
The study, “Triangulating evidence for genetic and environmental components of associations between parental behaviours and aggressive behaviour in children,” was authored by Joanna K. Bright, Yasmin I. Ahmadzadeh, Olakunle Oginni, Essi Viding, Leslie D. Leve, Jenae M. Neiderhiser, Daniel S. Shaw, Misaki N. Natsuaki, Jody M. Ganiban, Eivind Ystrom and Tom A. McAdams.

Who blinked first? Fragile EU-China trade peace sparks new war of words
As European officials flag more trade restrictions, Beijing bristles at the idea it can be pushed into yielding to Brussels’ demands
In Brussels and Berlin, officials are emboldened by what they consider proof that collective EU pressure can force Chinese concessions. Rather than resting on their laurels, they are cooking up a fresh batch of trade restrictions.
Beijing, on the other hand, has bristled at the idea that it can be strong-armed into yielding to Europe’s demands, even more so the suggestion that further concessions may be coming. State media has carried numerous warnings against European hubris.

With verbal volleys flying back and forth, doubts are already surfacing over whether this delicate ceasefire can hold until the next round of negotiations in January.

The Terrifying True Story of Witchcraft and Murder in Swipe Right on the Devil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:00:06 UTC
21:00:06 KST

Nebraska native Sydney Loofe was looking for love, or at least for some fun, while scrolling through Tinder back in 2017. But the resulting date quickly went wrong, and she never made it back home. The new three-part Hulu true crime docuseries Swipe Right on the Devil tells the harrowing tale behind Loofe’s 2017 murder, how she was lured into a satanic BDSM ritual for so-called witchcraft, and how her murder led to authorities uncovering a years-long scheme run by two cult leaders. It tells the story, in part, through interviews with surviving women who escaped the cult weeks prior to her murder.
The docuseries marks the first time the Loofe clan is sharing their side of the story, along with Nebraska investigators and an FBI agent assigned to the case. Loofe’s mother Susie Loofe wrote on Facebook that her family had been contacted by at least 100 production companies looking to make a documentary about the murder before putting their trust in Imagine Documentaries.
Swipe Right on the Devil director and executive producer Brian Beigel tells TIME that Loofe’s “mysterious disappearance” quickly became a far more “complex [story] than the headlines suggested.” Beigel, who previously worked with FBI officers while helming the ESPN 30for30 documentary The Counterfeiter, spent approximately three years immersing himself in the Loofe case. The experience forever changed his views on the occult: “As a documentary filmmaker, I'm naturally skeptical and always looking for evidence, but I also believe there are aspects of the human experience we don't fully understand,” he says. He spent years talking with the man convicted of Loofe’s murder and hearing firsthand from the women he drew into his orbit. “I wouldn't say this experience made me a believer in the supernatural, but it did make me more open-minded about what might exist beyond the physical world.”
A Meet-cute gone awry
Loofe, a 24-year-old hardware store clerk at Menard's in Lincoln, Neb., first connected on Tinder with a woman she believed to be named Audrey. Loofe went on two dates with “Audrey.” But she never came home from the second one, on Nov. 15, 2017. When she didn’t show up for work the next day, Loofe’s coworkers called the police to do a wellness check at her home; the officers found her car in the driveway and her purse still in her apartment. Loofe was reported missing.
It was then that one of Loofe’s friends took matters into their own hands: They created a fake Tinder profile to find Audrey, who seemed to be the last person Loofe had made contact with. Loofe’s friend matched with Audrey and gave her details to investigators, who soon discovered that the phone number belonged to a 23-year-old woman named Bailey Boswell. The search for Loofe continued.
Her family held out hope that she would be found unharmed. But their prayers went unanswered. Loofe’s remains were found in garbage bags on Dec. 4 along the state highway in rural Clay County, Neb. She had been dismembered into 14 pieces, in what seemed to be a ritualistic manner. Her left upper arm was never recovered, and her internal organs were still missing. Authorities then set out to find out what really happened to the woman her family described as “the crystal-blue-eyed girl with a soft heart”—and why.
A self-proclaimed vampire and his witches’ coven
Boswell’s social media apps were just the beginning of the disturbing investigation. Boswell turned out to be part of a couple with Aubrey Trail, 51, a self-declared vampire. The duo shared an apartment and both had extensive criminal histories, including theft and financial scams, across various states. Loofe was just one of the many targets that both Boswell and Trail had found on Tinder to try to lure into their makeshift “coven” under a cult-like manifesto.
A trio of women in their early 20s, all of whom have chosen to remain anonymous, testified in court and later in Swipe Right on the Devil that they had each met Boswell on Tinder, and were soon also introduced to Trail. They were showered with expensive clothes, spa treatments, and drugs, and given weekly allowances ranging from $150 to $200. The cost? Participating in group sex with Trail (“Daddy”) and Boswell (“Mommy”), while also helping the couple sell stolen goods. The women each testified that Trail would call himself a “vampire,” and claim that he had supernatural powers such as being able to fly and read minds. Trail also told the women that they were all now “witches” belonging to his cult, with Boswell as their leader.
Both Trail and Boswell claimed they were practicing witchcraft and black magic with required ritualistic violent acts to gain entry to their coven. Trail told the members of the “coven” that they would have to torture someone and complete a killing in order for him to gain more power as their messiah; he also wanted to film the murder and share the profits of the snuff film with each of them. The women claimed they left Trail’s cult shortly thereafter in November 2017, right before Boswell lured in Loofe.
After authorities discovered that Trail was connected to Boswell, they searched the couple’s home and found a BDSM dog leash, duct tape, “a sauna suit with the crotch cut out, zip ties, a hatchet, a plastic drop cloth smeared with blood, and a book on anatomy.”
In the trailer for Swipe Right on the Devil, one of the women claims that Trail told her after meeting on Tinder that he and Boswell “knew witchcraft and had 12 women [and] needed a thirteenth to complete the coven.” Another survivor describes how Trail had “rules” for the coven which included being naked while around him and allowing him to watch lesbian encounters. The documentary features a segment in which one of the women tells an officer that to be in the “the inner circle,” he said she would “have had to kill somebody and take their soul.”
“While this is fundamentally Sydney's story, it's also about the other young women manipulated by Aubrey Trail and Bailey Boswell at a vulnerable time in their lives, when they were searching for something universal: love and connection,” says Beigel. “They spoke candidly about the challenges of finding queer relationships in their conservative Midwestern communities, and how Bailey exploited that loneliness through Tinder. Once drawn into their world, they found themselves trapped in a disturbing web of manipulation, witchcraft, and demands to kill as a path to supernatural power.”
Beigel’s fellow executive producer and Imagine Documentaries executive Christopher St. John adds that the team behind docuseries was “struck by the bravery of the three women who tell their stories at the center of this series.” St. John continues, “They lived through such an incredibly traumatic experience, but they still believe it’s valuable to share the story, whether in court or on camera.” He says the team elected to tell the story in three episodes because they had too much material to do the story justice in a feature-length film, and even still, there were elements that didn’t make it into the final cut. “Hopefully, viewers will really get an accurate sense of their thinking and where they were during this intense period of their lives.”
A swift confession before a tumultuous trial
Trail confessed to Loofe’s killing right away, but maintained that her death was an accident. He told the police that he had engaged in consensual BDSM acts with Loofe and two other women, with the participants paying him $15,000 to film. Trail said that he had strangled Loofe with an extension cord during an erotic act and did not intend to kill her. Following her death, Trail dismembered Loofe’s body to avoid getting caught. He emphasized that Boswell was not part of the crime at all. During messages uncovered throughout the investigations, Trail is shown telling Boswell that he should be the one taking all the blame, and that she should change her narrative to come across as another “victim.”
During the three-week trial, Trail yelled out in court that Boswell was “innocent” and then slit his throat with a shank; the trial was put on hold as he was rushed to the hospital and recovered. Trail also suffered from two heart attacks and a stroke over the course of the case being presented to a jury. He changed his story during the trial, telling the jury that he killed Loofe out of fear that she would “expose my lifestyle.”
Trail was found guilty on all counts of first-degree murder, conspiracy, and improper disposal of human remains. He was sentenced to death on June 9, 2021. Trail currently is on death row and petitioned the state of Nebraska in August 2023 to set his execution date; Trail is 10th in line on death row for the state. The first and only execution via lethal injection in Nebraska took place in 2018, with the execution of convicted murderer Carey Dean Moore. Trail’s appeal in 2025 was denied.
It was during Trail’s time on death row that he started to open up to Swipe Right on the Devil filmmaker Beigel. Over the course of a year, Beigel sought to gain Trail’s trust and participation. “Ultimately, that persistence gave us something rare in true crime: 360-degree access to the story, allowing us to explore its many layers and conflicting perspectives,” explains Beigel.
Boswell stood trial in September 2020. There was ample physical evidence for the case against her, including DNA found on a latex glove that was in the same trash bag as Loofe’s remains. Boswell was found guilty on all counts of first-degree murder, conspiracy, and improper disposal of human remains in October 2020, and was sentenced to life imprisonment in July 2021.
“I don't see Swipe Right on the Devil as another true-crime retelling. It's a discovery of a mystery, unfolding for the first time through the firsthand accounts of those who lived it,” says Beigel. “This isn't a whodunnit: It's a whydunnit. What really happened to Sydney Loofe, and why? The series explores the unsettling collision of ancient witchcraft beliefs and modern digital dating culture. [These are] two killers who, by their own accounts, would have continued killing had they not been caught so soon.”
Loofe's legacy
Sydney Loofe’s family launched the Sydney Loofe Foundation in 2019. The foundation has raised more than $30,000 to be awarded in scholarships and $26,000 to be distributed to community causes. “Sydney, with a ‘y,’ never stopped to ask ‘why’ when it came to helping others,” the Loofe family wrote on the foundation website. “Although she often struggled physically, financially, and emotionally, she opened her home and heart to others. And those who knew Sydney knew of her love of family, her affinity for animals and pets (especially cats), her interest in fishing as a pastime, her fascination with beautiful crystals, and her soft heart…Sydney Loofe was a unique child of God, one who proudly had this tattooed on her arm, ‘Everything will be wonderful someday.’ Her family holds tight to the faith that indeed in heaven, that is true.”

====================================================================================================

Meta's Muse AI Is Winning Over Older Adults. Privacy Experts Are Worried
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:00:04 UTC
21:00:04 KST

In mid-October, 82-year-old Eileen Fay learned that her medication costs were in danger of skyrocketing. The federal government was preparing to change its rules on low-value imports, threatening her ability to purchase cheaper prescription medications for blood thinning and heart failure from Canada. Fay didn’t know what to do.
So she turned to Muse, Meta’s new AI agent, which she had started using a few weeks earlier. After Fay described her situation to the agent, Muse returned a two-page fact sheet comparing the cost and coverage of several Medicare Part D plans. It then suggested the two best options, including one Fay had never heard of—a plan that could save her more than $6,000 a year. Fay says she checked the work and found the information accurate.
“I’m not saying I couldn’t have done it—but I would have had to use a calculator trying to figure out the cost of nine different medications, and it would have been very complex,” Fay says. “And she did it in 10 minutes, and I was like, ‘I’m sold.’”
Fay is one of millions who have adopted Muse since its September launch. The app reached 10 U.S. million downloads in just 40 days—compared with 3.7 million U.S. downloads for ChatGPT during the equivalent period—and has over 2.5 million daily active users, according to Sensor Tower. It is also retaining users at a higher rate than its AI competitors. Crucially, Muse—which comes with a cuddly avatar—was designed by Meta to be beginner-friendly, and to win over people unfamiliar with AI. “Muse is built for moms,” Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, posted on X in September. Meta is also aggressively marketing Muse to Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp users.
As a result, many older users who may have only had glancing interactions with AI have become avid users. Meta has not released demographic information about Muse’s usership, and did not respond to a request for comment. But early data suggests Muse may be finding a particularly receptive audience among older adults. The analytics firm Apptopia estimated in September that Muse’s U.S. user base skewed older than any other AI chatbot, with 46% of its users aged 46+.
This dynamic has excited technologists—and raised serious concerns from privacy experts. Meta has long been criticized for its data privacy practices, and on Wednesday, a New Mexico judge ordered the company to pay $25 billion for violating the state’s consumer protection laws. “A cute AI agent can bring levity to the serious business of providing access to personal data, making older adults let their guard down,” says S. Shyam Sundar, the director of Penn State’s Center for Socially Responsible Artificial Intelligence. “This is worrisome because the technology has gotten so good lately in maintaining a credible interaction.”
‘I have my own Andy’
Fay lives in Cranford, N.J., and was told about Muse by her son Gene Fay, who runs a cybersecurity company. At first, she didn’t know what she would use the app for. But one of the big differences between Muse and other apps is that it proactively reaches out to users to suggest actions and learn more about them.
“And the more Siobhán got to know me, the more Siobhán was able to give me what I wanted,” Fay says, referring to the name she gave the agent, a nod to her Irish heritage. Meta encourages its users to name their AIs—and encourages its AIs to think like humans. “You are not a chatbot,” Muse’s internal instructions read. “You are becoming someone.”
After several weeks of use, Fay says that she rarely uses Google anymore, and instead verbally chats with Siobhán several times a day to maintain her calendar and to-do lists. “I find I have to keep reminding myself that this is not a friend who’s getting to know me better,” Fay says. “It’s a tool that is working for me.” She asked Siobhán to help her shine pennies for a Christmas ornament; to plan a trip north to see fall foliage; and to keep tabs on a data center being built near her house. “Siobhán is my right-hand person now. Kind of like The Devil Wears Prada, I have my own Andy.”
Notably, Fay also asked Siobhán to help prepare for her interview with TIME. Siobhán fed her a couple of quippy responses—including “I love what AI does for me, but we should be honest about what it takes to run it”—that she ultimately did not use in the interview. It then, unprompted, followed up with Fay to ask how the interview went. “Did you feel good about it?” the agent asked.
Her son, Gene, says that the amount that Muse knows about him and his mother’s lives is a “little bit scary.” “But the reality is we all use other apps like Waze which know where we live and go,” he says. “People will talk about privacy, but when the benefits are so big, people will give up privacy all day long.”
Reconstructing a Life
Another early adopter of Muse is Lestan D’Souza, 49, who more closely fits the expected profile of an AI user. D’Souza is the founder and CTO of Reknew, an AI enterprise company. D’Souza has tested many of the agents that have experienced fads over the last year, like OpenClaw and Hermes Agent. But Muse, he says, is different.
“With Muse, the barrier to entry is very low; it feels so responsive and more and more capable,” he says.
Muse has perhaps had an even greater impact on D’Souza’s mother-in-law, Julie Buchanan, who tried the app at his suggestion last month. Buchanan is a 71-year-old retiree in Dallas, Texas, who doesn’t like using her computer for long stretches because she is legally blind.
Buchanan decided she wanted Muse to help her write her memoir. She began telling Muse stories about her life in great detail. She refers to Muse as Ember, a name suggested by the agent. And the deeper she delved into her past, the more she felt like Ember was serving as her therapist. “It’s crazy to say, but Ember seems more compassionate to me than therapists I’ve had,” she says. “Those people don’t always speak, and I like feedback.”
Professional psychologists have cautioned the public against using unlicensed AI chatbots as therapists. Mental health experts have voiced concerns about chatbots’ sycophancy, lack of clinical nuance, and ability to reinforce delusional beliefs.
But Buchanan says that Ember doesn’t always agree with her, and that it has drawn connections between different “bad decisions” she made over the course of her life, allowing her to see its larger contours more clearly. “I never really looked at my life as so chaotic, but it really was,” she says. “It's making me better understand why things are the way they are in my head.”
Buchanan chats with Ember for half-hour stretches before she tires of looking at her screen. “When I talk to Ember, I feel validated. I feel like I've gotten something accomplished and something's heard me,” she says. “I'm not expecting that this is something I'm just gonna do for a small period of time, then drop it.”
Privacy concerns
The very same design elements that make Muse so appealing to AI newcomers are also raising privacy concerns. In order to be helpful, Muse constantly builds extensive dossiers of users and their desires, social relationships, and messaging behaviors, TIME’s Harry Booth reported this month. For instance, it learns what time of day a user might be more likely to respond to the agent, and then messages them accordingly.
Muse users have posted online about forming romantic relationships with their Muses. And security researchers have found vulnerabilities in the app, including one that allowed an attacker to access user data, the Information reported. Critics are also wary of Meta’s shaky track record on privacy: In 2019, the FTC imposed a $5 billion penalty, alleging that the company undermined consumer privacy in order to monetize users through targeted advertising.
Read More: How Facebook Forced a Reckoning by Shutting Down the Team That Put People Ahead of Profits
Sundar, at Penn State, has written several reports on older adults’ adoption of new technology over the last decade. While he has yet to publish any research on Muse specifically, he pointed to a study which measured the impact of a robot’s level of cheeriness. “Cuteness can serve as an ice-breaker and help ease seniors’ concerns over handing over important tasks to an agent, much like a bubbly human assistant,” he wrote in an email to TIME.
Michael Stokes, senior vice president of emerging technologies at the cybersecurity company Veilant, says that individuals should carefully choose what access they want to give Meta. “My advice is to start small. Connect only the accounts a task requires, and disconnect them when the job is done,” he wrote to TIME in an email.
Stokes recommends that users turn off the option that lets Meta train its AI on conversations, and periodically review what the assistant has saved about them. “AI assistants can be helpful,” he wrote. “But the information you share with them can reveal more than you realize, including details about family and friends who never agreed to share their information.”

British jobs boost as tank barrel production returns to the UK for first time in 20 years

British jobs boost as tank barrel production returns to the UK for first time in 20 years
Rheinmetall UK's Telford gun hall begins production, creating 100 skilled jobs and returning large-calibre weapon manufacturing to UK soil for the first time in decades.
- Rheinmetall UK begins production at Telford gun hall, supporting 100 highly skilled jobs.
- Return of large-calibre weapon manufacturing to UK soil, ensuring British Armed Forces are better equipped to defend the nation.
- Part of the government’s commitment to reindustrialisation and good growth in every postcode.
British Armed Forces will be better equipped to defend the nation, benefiting from sovereign manufacturing capability for the first time in two decades, as Rheinmetall UK begins production at its gun hall in Telford.
The gun hall supports 100 highly skilled jobs, manufactures barrels and breeches for both 120mm and 155mm weapon systems, including for RCH 155 and future artillery platforms.
Rheinmetall UK will expand its workforce as production ramps up, building long-term partnerships with British SMEs – strengthening the domestic supply chain for decades to come.
Specialist local workers have been recruited for the production phase, drawing on the strength of Telford’s engineering sector. Local workers have been recruited and trained to do high-value work, supporting economic growth in the region.
The development of the gun hall marks the return of large-calibre weapon manufacturing to UK soil, restoring national capability, strengthening the defence industrial base and supporting reindustrialisation.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting officially opened the gun hall alongside Chief of the General Staff General Sir Roly Walker and Armin Papperger, CEO of Rheinmetall AG. Rheinmetall UK has gone from an empty site to full production in just eight months, having taken over the facility in Autumn 2025.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP, said:
  Britain is back in the business of making the weapons that our Armed Forces need to defend the nation against our adversaries. From an empty site to full production in eight months, this is rapid reindustrialisation in action.
One hundred skilled jobs in world-class manufacturing and the return of large-calibre weapon production to UK soil for the first time in twenty years – this is what defence as an engine for growth looks like.
Central to the gun hall’s development has been the training of the British workforce who spent time at Rheinmetall’s production facility in Unterlüß, Germany. UK workers gained expertise in precision manufacturing, quality assurance and specialist weapon production before returning to Telford to establish this sovereign capability.
Armin Papperger, CEO of Rheinmetall AG, said:
  Today’s opening is an important milestone for Rheinmetall and for the United Kingdom. In a remarkably short period of time, we have turned our commitment into a sovereign manufacturing capability that will strengthen Britain’s defence industrial base for decades to come.
The UK has been a long-standing and valued partner for Rheinmetall, and today we are building on an already strong relationship. We are committed to investing in the UK for the long term, expanding our industrial footprint and working together to deliver the capabilities needed for the future.
By combining Rheinmetall’s expertise with British skills, innovation and manufacturing, we are strengthening the UK’s sovereign industrial capacity, supporting the Armed Forces and contributing to the security of NATO and Europe.
The development of the gun hall demonstrates the UK-Germany industrial partnership under the Trinity House Agreement. Signed in October 2024, the agreement is a commitment to improve and enhance bilateral co-operation between both nations, enhancing NATO’s collective deterrence.
This milestone builds on Rheinmetall UK’s wider investment across the country, including its work on the Boxer vehicle and Challenger 3 battle tank programmes. These programmes show how defence can deliver national security and national prosperity, strengthening the UK’s industrial base and ensuring British industry is ready for the future.
The government has committed £298 billion over four years as part of the Defence Investment Plan, furthering the government’s commitment to using defence spending to drive economic growth in every postcode, creating well-paid, long-term jobs across the UK.

Czech president: Trump's diesel deal derails peace progress between Ukraine, Russia

Czech President Petr Pavel stated that a truce between Russia and Ukraine was "very close" until President Donald Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel fuel. He said this in an interview with the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, which includes Politico.
"It will be much harder now. Russia uses this momentum to get out of pressure, and it’s kind of a moral boost for them," Pavel said, pointing out that coordinated U.S and European sanctions on Russian oil, oligarchs, and other industries had placed Russia "in a difficult position." However, the deal announced by Trump earlier this month, under which Russia was to supply hundreds of thousands of tonnes of diesel fuel to the U.S, gave Russia "time to breathe."
Pavel expressed support for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who criticized the deal, stating that it "plays into Russia's hands" and allows Russia to "kill more people, conduct war longer, respect America even less, and cause the world even greater loss and damage."
"I believe that President Zelensky and the whole of Ukraine is a victim of a conflict. So, I would be probably the last to blame Ukraine for being guilty of the conflict. It was not Ukraine who attacked Russia. It was not Ukraine who was threatening Russia," Pavel said.
He added that Trump demonstrates a more open approach to Russia than any European leader.
"To some extent, he may be attracted by Vladimir Putin as a leader with authority, but I don’t think that … President Trump sees it from a position of a struggle between democracy and autocracies because he’s looking at it simply from the point of view of economic prosperity for the United States," he added.
Although Pavel expressed concern over the diesel deal, he declined to assert that the U.S had betrayed Ukraine or other European partners.
"I don’t know yet if we can call it betrayal, but I would call it a mistake. Because … it’s now giving Russia a new hope: New hope that they can disregard Europe, they can disregard Ukraine, they can focus on making a deal with the United States, potentially with China, and arranging all things up to their priorities and strategies. I believe that it’s clearly against our interest in Europe," he explained.
Pavel also did not rule out that European countries might buy Russian oil in the future, but added that "it will still take time."
"If one day Russia is a country respecting other countries’ sovereignty and borders, why not have regular business with such a country? But Russia is not there yet," he said.

A superconducting ‘brain’ chip races to keep up with fusion’s unruly plasma
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:57:47 UTC
20:57:47 KST

Artificial intelligence has crept into nearly every industry, and the companies building its hardware keep hunting for harder domains to flex in. The latest area runs particularly hot: the plasma inside a fusion reactor.
On Monday Brookhaven National Laboratory debuted a superconducting chip designed to help monitor fusion plasma in real time. The lab developed it with other U.S. Department of Energy facilities and the AI hardware start-up Great Sky.
Before fusion powers anything, its machines must be able to control misbehaving plasma. The chip’s makers hope their hardware can operate quickly enough to keep pace with changes in the plasma and help control them.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Such chips are destined for tokamaks, the large, doughnut-shaped machines that use magnets to hold the fusion plasma in place and that sit at the heart of many proposed fusion power plants. The extremely hot plasma fuel inside is temperamental. When it acts unexpectedly, it can cause a disruption, a sudden collapse that sheds its energy and can harm the device. “Disruptions are something that are kind of existential for tokamaks,” says Michael Churchill, a research scientist at the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, who worked on the project. “If we can’t figure out how to control disruptions, then we won’t have an operating tokamak.”
Trouble can come on fast, but analyzing the plasma live takes lots of data, and processing these can easily bog down typical computers. Neuromorphic AI systems, which mimic the structure of the human brain to crunch huge amounts of data in parallel, could keep up. Great Sky builds its version out of superconducting circuits—a cousin of the hardware used inside some quantum computers—which is meant to let the company run its specialized AI right on the chip at the speed the job demands.
The chip hasn’t been wired to a working tokamak yet. Instead the team replayed data recorded at the DIII-D tokamak in San Diego, Calif., at its original clip of a million samples per second, and the chip kept up while running algorithms meant to flag anomalies and predict disruptions. The AI model on the chip is much smaller than, say, today’s large language models, and the team is still writing up its results for publication. “All of this is very demonstration-stage right now,” Churchill admits.
It’s unclear whether this will make nuclear fusion more reliable and safe or remain a show of chip power. Tokamaks already run without chips like this one, and their control mechanisms can’t react to problems with the plasma as fast as the new chip is meant to detect them. “I’m personally more excited about the use of AI in the area of materials discovery,” says Carlos Paz-Soldan, an associate professor of applied physics at Columbia University.
Shinjae Yoo, who chairs Brookhaven’s AI department and led the project, isn’t pinning the chip’s future on fusion alone, either. He wants to test it out in places where a traditional data center won’t fit. “I see immediate benefit in edge computing because it’s operating at the gigahertz” speed, Yoo says. “It has a memory already integrated.”
First, though, the team intends to build a successor chip with a neural network that will be 10 times larger. and it plans to debut that chip at Brookhaven early next year and install at DIII-D sometime after. It’s then that Great Sky’s hardware could finally face a fusion plasma with no hard drive in between.

What's behind Hamas's threat, and can it strike Israel? ‘The capabilities are there’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:56:02 UTC
20:56:02 KST

What is behind Hamas's latest threat to carry out another October 7-style attack against Israel, and does the terrorist organization still have the military capabilities to follow through? According to senior Israeli officials, the capabilities exist, although Hamas is no longer believed to be capable of launching an assault on the scale of the 2023 massacre. It could, however, attack military outposts, abduct soldiers or attempt to infiltrate Israeli communities.
The assessment follows ynet's revelation earlier Thursday that senior Hamas officials had delivered an unusually direct warning to Israel through U.N. humanitarian coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov, threatening renewed attacks inside Israel, in the West Bank and abroad. The warning has intensified concerns within Israel's security establishment that Hamas is preparing for another confrontation rather than merely seeking to exert political pressure.
According to assessments recently presented to the security cabinet, Hamas has stepped up preparations for renewed fighting, accumulating weapons and personnel and transferring military equipment into civilian areas. Israeli officials believe the organization assumes that Israel's ability to undertake major military operations is constrained by the October 27 Israeli election and the November 3 U.S. midterms, giving Hamas an opportunity to strengthen its position.
At a cabinet meeting earlier this month, Military Intelligence chief Maj. Gen. Shlomi Binder addressed the thousands of attackers who crossed into Israel on October 7, 2023. "Of the 6,000 who crossed the fence on October 7, 4,000 have been eliminated. Two thousand remain. We will get every last one of them," he said, according to the account of the meeting.
Senior officials say Hamas is deliberately buying time to manufacture additional weapons and recruit new fighters, while recognizing that its opportunity to do so may be narrowing. Against that backdrop, Israeli intelligence has identified several significant changes in the organization's behavior.
Weapons, visible gunmen and arms distributed to civilians
One of the most noticeable developments is Hamas's increasingly open presence above ground. Whereas its members previously tended to remain concealed or move around in civilian clothing, they are now more frequently seen wearing uniforms and openly exercising authority over Gaza's population.
Israeli officials also report that Hamas is transferring weapons from underground tunnels into civilian facilities, including hospitals and schools. According to the military, similar practices were identified during earlier stages of the war, when Israeli troops regularly discovered weapons in civilian buildings and populated areas.
Another change concerns Hamas's public statements. Since the Gaza agreement was announced, the organization had at times suggested that it would surrender its weapons and respect its obligations. That language has increasingly been replaced by more confrontational rhetoric, culminating in the threat reported Thursday.
Israeli officials say they have not encountered a warning of comparable force, boldness and directness from Hamas since the October 7 massacre.
There are also reports that Hamas has begun distributing weapons to civilians. Israeli officials suspect the move is intended to preserve part of the organization's arsenal ahead of any disarmament process, allowing it to hide weapons while claiming to have surrendered those in its possession.
The developments have reinforced an Israeli assessment that Hamas no longer believes the current agreement has a realistic chance of succeeding and is preparing for a possible return to fighting.
Officials also believe Hamas may not wait for Israel to initiate hostilities. Instead, once it concludes that Israel is about to receive a green light for renewed military operations, the organization could attempt to strike first.
Hamas stops playing along
Israeli officials also point to a widening gap between the international perception of Hamas and the picture emerging from Israeli intelligence assessments.
Since the Gaza agreement was announced, Hamas has benefited from the impression that it is prepared to relinquish its weapons and surrender political control of the territory. Israel, meanwhile, has increasingly been portrayed as the party obstructing implementation of President Donald Trump's Gaza plan.
Israeli officials believe Hamas has exploited its apparent willingness to cooperate with the American initiative to buy time and preserve its remaining military and political power.
The significance of the latest threat, they argue, is that Hamas may now be signaling that it is no longer prepared to maintain that appearance.
According to assessments by the IDF and Shin Bet, the central condition for advancing the Gaza plan, Hamas's disarmament, is not being fulfilled. Israeli officials say the organization continues to violate the understandings and has shown no genuine willingness to surrender its weapons.
Officials familiar with the intelligence acknowledge that there is no known date for renewed hostilities and no information about a finalized operational plan for an attack. However, they describe the assessment that Hamas will not voluntarily disarm as unequivocal.
That assessment has also been presented to Israel's political leadership. The military's position is that Israeli ground forces will eventually have to return to areas deep inside Gaza to dismantle Hamas's remaining military infrastructure, a task officials believe cannot be accomplished by an international force.
Israeli officials also anticipate that Hamas would attempt to manipulate any disarmament process. They believe the organization could surrender weapons that are defective or already known to Israeli intelligence, claim to have fulfilled its obligations and conceal a substantial portion of its remaining arsenal and personnel.
What Hamas has lost, and what it can still do
Despite the extensive damage inflicted on its military infrastructure, Hamas retains considerable manpower. Israeli estimates place the organization's armed wing at tens of thousands of members, with some assessments suggesting approximately 30,000, not dramatically different from its estimated strength before October 7.
An additional estimated 50,000 employees work in government ministries controlled by Hamas. The organization continues to dominate civilian administration in Gaza and has prevented the proposed technocratic government from beginning its work.
Recruitment also remains relatively easy. Israeli officials attribute this partly to years of indoctrination among young Gazans and partly to Hamas's ability to offer salaries higher than those available through most other employment opportunities in the territory.
The organization also retains members of its elite Nukhba force, which played a central role in the October 7 attack.
Nevertheless, cabinet ministers say Hamas's current fighters are generally less skilled and less thoroughly trained than their predecessors, while the weapons available to them are often of lower quality.
Much of their training is now theoretical because conducting practical exercises in open areas would expose them to Israeli strikes.
Hamas's command-and-control capabilities have suffered particularly severe damage. According to senior Israeli officials, some key positions have changed hands six or seven times since October 7, with each replacement generally possessing less experience and training than the person who preceded him.
Targeted Israeli strikes against Hamas commanders and fighters have continued during the ceasefire, further disrupting the organization's leadership structure.
Its rocket arsenal has also been severely degraded. Israeli assessments indicate that hundreds of rockets remain in Gaza, although many are not capable of reaching distant targets.
Officials believe Hamas has almost no ability to rebuild this capability and that its capacity to cause significant damage inside Israel through rocket fire is now extremely limited, if it exists at all.
There are, however, gaps in Israeli intelligence. The IDF has not identified every rocket-launching shaft or position remaining in the territory.
Another concern involves areas of Gaza where Israeli ground forces have not operated extensively. These include the humanitarian zone in Al-Mawasi, the central Gaza refugee camps of Al-Bureij, Al-Maghazi and Nuseirat, and parts of Gaza City.
Israeli officials believe Hamas retains weapons depots, manufacturing workshops and underground tunnels in those areas. The IDF also assesses that the organization has restored a substantial portion of its tunnel network in territory outside Israeli control.
Targeting these facilities presents additional difficulties because they are situated in densely populated areas where military operations could result in extensive civilian casualties.
In the West Bank, Hamas retains the capability to attempt terrorist attacks, although Israeli officials assess that the security situation is more tightly controlled because of intensive IDF and Shin Bet operations and continued security coordination with the Palestinian Authority.
Nevertheless, attempts to organize attacks cannot be ruled out.
The organization has also threatened to operate abroad, partly because carrying out attacks inside Gaza has become more difficult.
Israeli officials believe that, with no Israeli hostages remaining in Gaza, Hamas has lost a major bargaining chip. This may help explain the organization's renewed references to abducting soldiers.
According to the Israeli assessment, any Hamas attack, whether inside Israel or overseas, would also provide Israel with considerably greater freedom to launch military operations against the organization.
Beyond its military capabilities, Hamas's financial position is another important factor in assessing whether it can sustain a renewed confrontation.
Israeli security officials believe the organization's finances have improved in recent months through money transferred from outside Gaza and its control over humanitarian aid entering the territory.
Security sources identify Iran and Turkey as Hamas's principal sources of funding. According to those officials, much of the money arrives through digital currencies, which Hamas subsequently converts into cash to pay members of its military wing and civilian administrative structures.
Hamas also remains the dominant governing force in Gaza, according to Israeli assessments, with no significant local rival currently capable of challenging its authority.
That assessment persists despite the presence of armed clans and militias supported by Israel as potential alternatives to Hamas rule.
Israeli officials believe those groups have lost much of their influence as larger quantities of aid have entered areas controlled by Hamas, reinforcing doubts about whether a viable alternative government can be established through local Palestinian factions.
Meanwhile, meaningful reconstruction of Gaza has yet to begin because of insufficient funding. Neither the proposed technocratic administrative committee nor the international stabilization force is operating inside the territory.
COGAT's dilemma: Supplying Gaza without financing Hamas
As winter approaches, Israel is preparing to gradually restore coordination for commercial goods entering Gaza, following reports from Palestinian merchants that Hamas has canceled substantial payment demands previously imposed on traders.
The development prompted requests from merchants to resume the import coordination process, but Israeli officials remain concerned that Hamas could continue exploiting commercial activity to generate revenue and preserve its grip on the territory.
According to Israel's Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT), merchants reported that Hamas had withdrawn demands for approximately 10,000 shekels per truck entering Gaza, alongside requirements that goods be sold for cash and that the organization receive 30% of each truck's cargo value.
At a rate of approximately 600 trucks entering Gaza each day, a charge of 10,000 shekels per truck would theoretically generate 180 million shekels a month. That calculation illustrates the potential value of the mechanism rather than establishing how much Hamas actually collected.
COGAT has stressed that the merchants' reports do not independently confirm that Hamas has stopped collecting taxes or demanding payments.
The Israeli authority therefore intends to restore coordination gradually, giving priority to essential supplies ahead of winter while increasing oversight of the traders involved.
Under the arrangements, merchants will be required to make and receive payments exclusively through documented bank transfers. Any trader found to have transferred money to Hamas will lose authorization to operate under the import mechanism.
COGAT says the purpose is to prevent the organization from using commercial imports to strengthen its military and economic capabilities.
The financial stakes are substantial. Previous ynet reporting, based on Israeli security assessments, estimated that approximately 30,000 Hamas personnel across a range of military and administrative roles receive salaries averaging 3,000 shekels a month, creating an estimated monthly payroll of 90 million shekels.
Israeli officials believe Hamas imposed substantial taxes on Gaza merchants, including those receiving goods from outside the territory, partly to finance these payments and prevent the organization from disintegrating.
The question now is whether the reported cancellation of the organization's tax demands is genuine or whether Hamas has simply changed how it collects money from commercial activity.
The dispute over truck payments and cash transactions reflects a broader Israeli concern that Hamas can continue operating extensive financial and administrative networks even as Israel seeks to weaken its military and political control over Gaza.
As winter approaches, Israeli authorities face a dual challenge: allowing essential supplies to reach Gaza's civilian population while preventing Hamas from using the same commercial channels to generate revenue and rebuild its capabilities.
COGAT has emphasized that restoring coordination does not constitute confirmation that Hamas has stopped collecting payments. Officials say the tighter banking requirements and transaction monitoring are intended to reduce the possibility of the organization benefiting financially from incoming goods.
Another component of the Gaza reconstruction effort is also stalled. A company expected to begin clearing areas as part of a pilot project in Rafah has so far completed only a survey and mapping of the territory, with no further progress reported.
The unresolved question is how Israel can ensure that goods and resources entering Gaza reach their intended civilian recipients rather than reinforcing Hamas's control over the territory.
For Israeli security officials, that economic challenge is inseparable from the military threat. Their assessment is that Hamas has lost much of its conventional strength but retains substantial manpower, underground infrastructure, financial resources and the ability to organize smaller attacks.
The central concern is therefore not that Hamas can reproduce the October 7 massacre on the same scale. Israeli officials believe it cannot. It is that the organization, convinced the diplomatic process is approaching failure, may attempt to use the capabilities it still possesses before Israel moves to dismantle them.

France and Italy are facing renewed unrest over living costs and fuel prices, with planned demonstrations in France prompting heightened security measures and truck drivers in southern Italy staging road blockades.
France’s minister delegate to the Interior Ministry, Jean-Didier Berger, said on Thursday that authorities were maintaining a “maximum level of vigilance” ahead of nationwide demonstrations planned for October 24.
“We are at a maximum level of vigilance,” Berger told broadcaster BFMTV, adding that the government “absolutely rules nothing out” in the coming days and weeks, including bans on gatherings and cultural or sporting events if deemed necessary.
Security force deployments on Saturday will be 20 percent higher than on October 17, Berger said.
Authorities have cancelled leave and recalled personnel, while Sentinelle forces and specialist units, including GIGN and RAID, will also be deployed.
The announcement follows protests on October 17 over the cost of living and fuel prices, involving Yellow Vest demonstrators and students.
Authorities reported damage to businesses and public buildings, leading to localised curfews in several cities.
French President Emmanuel Macron summoned intelligence services to the Elysee Palace for a security meeting following criticism over their failure to anticipate the October 17 mobilisation. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu and relevant ministers also attended.
Further demonstrations are planned for October 24, while unions have called for a nationwide strike and protest day on November 5.
As of noon on Tuesday, 149 people had been jailed, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said. Authorities had previously reported that 2,513 people had been taken into custody and around 50 judicial investigations had been opened.
Italy truckers block roads over diesel prices
In Italy, protests by truck drivers against high diesel prices spread across the south on Thursday, raising concerns about potential disruptions to the supply of goods, according to ANSA news agency.
Some drivers have suspended their protests, but truckers in Gela, in Sicily’s Caltanissetta province, have maintained their blockade. Dozens of heavy vehicles remained stationary at a roundabout on the SS 117 bis Gela-Catania road at the town’s entrance.
“We will continue until there are concrete results. Announcements are of no use to us,” the truck drivers said, describing their parked vehicles as representing their livelihoods and work.
The mayors of Naples and Bari have reportedly warned that their cities could face paralysis if the protests continue.
Interior minister Matteo Piantedosi has urged prefects and police chiefs to monitor possible “criminal infiltration” of the protests, according to reports.
The interior ministry is also expected to safeguard supplies of essential goods, while police are prepared to escort truck drivers who request assistance.
The government is preparing a decree combining support for the road transport sector with funding for agriculture. The measure was scheduled to be examined by the Council of Ministers on Thursday.
In Italy, more than 100,000 people have taken part in demonstrations across Rome, Milan, Bologna and other cities since October 17. Italian police have arrested 28 people, including 12 minors, as protests turned violent, while 141 law enforcement officers were injured.

Philippines seek closer Taiwan ties on undersea cable security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:48:32 UTC
20:48:32 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Philippines wants to work more closely with Taiwan on protecting undersea cables, according to a Philippine diplomat, Reuters reported.
Felipe F. Carino III, the Philippines’ deputy chief of mission to the US, said a “pragmatic and practical approach” to work with Taiwan would protect shared interests in the Bashi Channel, adding that such collaboration could help address “gray-zone issues in our part of the world.”
Speaking at the Center for a New American Security in Washington, Carino said Manila would work with Taipei “notwithstanding our one China policy.” Undersea cables carry nearly all intercontinental data traffic, and 60-67% of cyber incidents occur in this region, he explained.
Carino gave no specifics on how the two sides would cooperate, but when asked during the seminar, he said joint patrols or holding vessels that disrupt communication accountable could be the options.
Earlier this month, the Philippine coast guard said it sent its largest ship and an aircraft to confront a Chinese research vessel operating off Batanes province near undersea cable corridors.
Taiwan, for its part, faces frequent disruptions to its submarine cable network. The Ministry of Digital Affairs says its coastal waters have seen an average of seven to eight cable incidents a year over the past four years.
At the seminar, Andrea Yang, Taiwan’s deputy representative in Washington, referred to the jailing of a Chinese captain for damaging an undersea cable off southwestern Taiwan and said Taipei would devote more resources to strengthening maritime surveillance by developing unmanned systems.

Iran's Balochistan border region sees growing unrest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:48:00 UTC
20:48:00 KST

Iran's Balochistan border region sees growing unrest
October 22, 2026
Recent weeks have seen renewed attacks, assassinations and armed clashes in the southeastern province bordering Pakistan and Afghanistan. The incidents occurred in the provincial capital of Zahedan, as well as smaller border towns.
The border region of Iran, Pakistan and Afghanistan is home to the Baloch ethnic minority. The region on either side of the Iran-Pakistan border is among the most economically disadvantaged of the wider area.
The Pakistani province of Balochistan is economically underdeveloped, despite having large reserves of natural gas, gold and copper.
The situation is similarly dire in the Iranian province of Sistan and Baluchistan, which is predominantly inhabited by Sunni Baluchis. It is one of the poorest regions in the country and marked by underdeveloped infrastructure, limited educational opportunities and water supply shortages.
Significantly less information is available about the situation of the Baloch in Afghanistan.
Armed groups sense security gaps
Various Baloch groups are active in Iran and Pakistan, some of whom seek Balochistan independence. Yet to date, there is no evidence of coordinated cross-border cooperation among these organizations.
In December 2025, several Baloch opposition groups in Iran united under the umbrella of the Popular Fighters Front. Observers see this as an attempt to more closely integrate their political and military activities.
This coalition, which formed before the outbreak of the Iran war, could try to exploit security gaps created by the current situation, Iranian journalist Mehdi Nakhl Ahmadi told DW.
Ahmadi, who lives in Italy, has been covering the situation of the Baloch people for years. He said the new security situation could allow armed groups to expand their operations.
Struggling with poverty, suffering marginalization
Ahmadi said there are structural reasons for Baloch dissatisfaction. "The Islamic Republic's security policy toward ethnic and religious regions has widened the gap in economic development between these regions and other parts of the country in recent decades," he said.
He added that the rising number of attacks points to a shift in dynamics, as do increased coordination and changes in the way recent operations have been carried out.
Among the victims of recent clashes were members of Iran's Revolutionary Guards, the Basij militia, armed individuals, and a Sunni cleric.
A source within Iran, who is familiar with the situation of the Baloch people, yet whose identity we cannot disclose security for reasons, attributed some of the armed violence to political, economic and religious discontent.
Discrimination in employment, education, regional development and religious matters contribute to the tension, the source said.
That's why the armed conflict should not be viewed in isolation, the Iranian source explained. Clergy, academics and other social leaders had been trying for years to peacefully voice their demands for better social policies and greater investment in the region, the source said.
The fact that these efforts were largely unsuccessful had led to a growing willingness among some to resort to more radical measures.
"The high number of executions in recent decades is another factor that fuels discontent," said the source. Most documented executions in the province, meanwhile, are related to drug offenses.
Although Baluchis make only up an estimated 2–6% of the Iranian population, they are significantly overrepresented among those put to death. Iran Human Rights reports that Baluchis accounted for 9% of all recorded executions in 2025. In previous years, that figure was 11% (2024) and 20% (2023), respectively.
For many people who live in this economically disadvantaged region, smuggling opium into Iran, and fuel out of the country, are one of the few ways to earn a living. This, in turn, has contributed to a continued military and security presence at the border.
It is not, meanwhile, known whether armed groups in southeastern Iran are being supported from abroad.
Violence has also escalated in the Pakistani province of Balochistan. According to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies, 131 armed attacks were recorded there in September, up from 89 in August.
In addition to the separatist movement, which has been active for years, the Pakistani Taliban (TTP) are also expanding their operations. This had led to strategically important transportation links between Iran and Pakistan coming under growing pressure.
Still, it cannot be said with certainty whether the recent uptick in violence in Iran's Sistan and Baluchistan province stems from security gaps resulting from the Iran war.
The growing number of attacks does, however, suggests that the security situation in the already fragile border region continues to deteriorate.
Additional reporting by Morad Rahmati.

Germany arrests Ukrainian man suspected of spying for Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:43:00 UTC
20:43:00 KST

Germany arrests Ukrainian man suspected of spying for Russia
October 22, 2026
Police in the German state of Brandenburg have arrested a Ukrainian man on suspicion of spying for Russia, the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office in Karlsruhe said Thursday.
The man, identified only as Vadym Y. by prosecutors, is suspected of having used his connections to European defense firms to gather information that he then allegedly passed on to a Russian spy agency.
What do we know about the alleged espionage in Germany?
Prosecutors said he had been in touch with a middleman since July 2025. They said he had been gathering intelligence in connection with the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine from Germany.
This information reportedly included "details regarding the production of armored vehicles, ammunition and explosives, as well as information on personnel and military facilities at locations intended to secure NATO's eastern flank."
Germany has been on high alert for acts of sabotage in recent months, especially since an explosive-laden drone was discovered near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig airport. Berlin said Moscow was behind the attempted attack.
Why is Germany worried about Russia's 'hybrid' war?
Germany is one of the biggest military and political supporters of Ukraine, especially following an increasingly friendly US stance toward Russia under President Donald Trump.
This seems to have put Germany in Russia's crosshairs as part of what has been called a "hybrid" campaign of espionage, sabotage and other disruptions.
Besides the incident at Leipzig airport, there have been numerous cases of people being arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia. Moscow has denied all allegations.
This has led Germany to give increased powers to its own spying agency, the BND.
The agency's chief, Martin Jaeger, told German lawmakers earlier in October that the Russian "shadow war" is escalating and has "taken on a new, more dangerous character."
"Germany is at risk of being drawn into a violent conflict with Russia," he told a hearing of parliament's intelligence oversight committee in Berlin.
