Brain scans suggest first graders don’t engage their control networks like adults when talking to ChatGPT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:00:26 UTC
19:00:26 KST

A small brain imaging study suggests that young children show less communication within and between the brain networks responsible for self-regulation and focused attention when brainstorming with an artificial intelligence chatbot than adults do. Although first graders and adults scored similarly, relative to their age groups, on a standard test of creative thinking outside the brain scanner, only adults showed a link between higher creativity and stronger coordination among these mental control systems during the conversation. The findings, published in Cerebral Cortex, suggest that young children may not yet have the mature brain wiring needed to actively direct and evaluate a collaborative conversation with generative artificial intelligence.
Generative artificial intelligence programs, such as ChatGPT, are powered by large language models, which are computer systems trained on massive amounts of text to predict how words fit together, allowing them to produce human-like responses and brainstorm ideas in real time. As these tools enter homes and elementary classrooms, children are increasingly using them for storytelling and collaborative problem-solving, a process known as co-creativity. Keeping up with a fast-talking, unpredictable digital partner requires cognitive control, which is the mind’s ability to plan ahead, stay focused on a goal, remember what was already said, and filter out unhelpful distractions.
Generating original and useful ideas relies heavily on how different systems in the brain communicate with one another. For instance, a 2018 neuroimaging study of adults (covered by PsyPost at the time) indicated that people who come up with more original ideas tend to have stronger synchronization among three major brain networks: one involved in spontaneous daydreaming and memory, another that flags important new thoughts, and a third that handles cognitive control and goal-directed planning. Instead of operating separately, these systems team up so a person can both brainstorm freely and judge whether an idea actually makes sense.
In young children, however, the brain networks that manage cognitive control and focused attention are still under construction, only reaching full maturity in a person’s mid-twenties. A 2019 neuroimaging study of young children, conducted by the same research group behind the new study, found that across children ranging from 17 months to nine years old, older children tended to show stronger connections within and between their cognitive control networks while listening to stories. In addition, a neuroimaging study covered by PsyPost in 2023 indicated that the way cognitive control networks relate to creative thinking shifts across development, with stronger connectivity in these control regions linked to higher creativity in adolescents but lower creativity in adults.
First grade, around ages six and seven, is a sensitive developmental window when children are first learning to evaluate text and speech on their own, while still tending to trust perceived experts and technology without much skepticism. The research was led by Tzipi Horowitz-Kraus, an associate professor with the Educational Neuroimaging Group in the Faculty of Education in Science and Technology and the Faculty of Biomedical Engineering at the Technion – Israel Institute of Technology, who is also affiliated with the Kennedy Krieger Institute and Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine.
She and her Technion colleagues Yoed Kenett, Dafna Link-Sourani, Emeel Ashqar, and Rola Farah examined whether first graders engage their cognitive control and attention networks to the same degree as adults when brainstorming with ChatGPT, and how that brain activity relates to their underlying creative ability. Part of the motivation came from a 2025 preprint, which has not been peer reviewed, in which adults who wrote essays with ChatGPT showed less coordinated brain activity than those who used a search engine or no tools at all.
“Generative AI is entering children’s lives, and classrooms, much faster than the evidence about how young brains engage with it,” Horowitz-Kraus told PsyPost. “Studies in adults have suggested that people recruit fewer cognitive resources when they work with ChatGPT, but adults have mature cognitive control systems, and these systems keep developing into the mid-twenties. We focused on first graders (ages 6–7) because this is when formal schooling begins, when executive functions are developing rapidly, and when children tend to place a great deal of trust in sources they perceive as experts. We wanted to know what the brain of a young child is actually doing during a real conversation with ChatGPT, compared with an adult given exactly the same task.”
To investigate this, the researchers recruited 15 first-grade children with an average age of about 6.4 years and 16 adults with an average age of about 38 years. All participants came from average to above-average socioeconomic backgrounds, had no history of neurological or psychiatric conditions, and completed standard tests to confirm typical verbal and nonverbal intelligence. Before entering the brain scanner, each participant took a behavioral creativity test called the Divergent Association Task, which asks a person to name 10 words that are as unrelated in meaning as possible.
Inside a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scanner, which measures brain activity by tracking changes in blood flow, participants engaged in a five-minute spoken conversation with ChatGPT. Using a specialized microphone and noise-canceling audio system built for the scanner, both children and adults were given the same open-ended goal: they had to plan the opening of any kind of store they wanted, anywhere and for anyone, by consulting out loud with ChatGPT. Immediately before the scan began, children were told they would be speaking to “the smartest computer in the world,” also known as ChatGPT, whereas adults were simply told they would be speaking to ChatGPT.
“I would also like to note that holding a live spoken conversation with ChatGPT inside an MRI scanner, with six-year-olds, required dedicated infrastructure developed at the Technion Human MRI Research Center,” Horowitz-Kraus noted. “I am very grateful to the children, parents and students who took part.”
The researchers recorded and transcribed every conversation to measure how original and varied the spoken exchanges were. They used a computer model to calculate a “divergent semantic integration” score, which measures how far apart the meanings of all the words in a conversation are from one another; for example, the words “cat” and “democracy” sit much farther apart in meaning than “cat” and “dog.” On the brain scans, the team measured functional connectivity, which reflects how closely different brain regions synchronize their activity over time, across seven major brain networks after statistically controlling for head movement inside the scanner.
These seven systems included the frontoparietal and cingulo-opercular networks, which manage cognitive control and task goals; the dorsal and ventral attention networks, which handle voluntary focus and automatic reactions to new information; the salience network, which acts as a switchboard by detecting important ideas; the default mode network, which supports spontaneous imagination; and the memory retrieval network.
On the word-association creativity test taken outside the scanner, children and adults scored at comparable levels relative to others their age, with average percentile scores of 28.61 and 26.16, respectively, a difference that was not statistically significant. During the actual five-minute conversation with ChatGPT, however, adults produced slightly more diverse and wide-ranging spoken narratives than the children did, scoring an average of 0.82 on the semantic integration measure compared to 0.81 for the first graders, a small difference that was nonetheless statistically reliable.
When the researchers examined the brain scans, they found pronounced differences in how the two age groups engaged their mental control and attention systems while talking to the chatbot. Within individual brain networks, adults showed substantially stronger internal synchronization in the frontoparietal control network, where adults averaged a connectivity score of 0.201 compared to 0.113 in children. Adults also had higher internal connectivity in the salience network (0.289 versus 0.198 in children) and the dorsal attention network (0.211 versus 0.162 in children). Only the frontoparietal difference held up after the researchers adjusted for the number of comparisons they ran.
In contrast, internal connectivity within the default mode network, which handles spontaneous imagination, did not differ between the two groups, averaging 0.187 in adults and 0.181 in children. Communication across different brain networks was also more integrated in adults than in first graders during the AI conversation. After adjusting for multiple statistical comparisons, the most robust difference appeared in how the frontoparietal control network linked up with the dorsal attention network (averaging 0.126 in adults versus 0.039 in children).
Before correcting for multiple comparisons, adults additionally showed stronger cross-network ties linking memory retrieval regions to cognitive control and attention systems, as well as stronger coupling between the default mode network and memory retrieval (0.150 in adults versus 0.111 in children). The researchers then tested whether a person’s baseline creativity score outside the scanner predicted how strongly their brain networks communicated while using ChatGPT.
They found that in adults, higher creativity scores were positively linked to stronger communication between the frontoparietal control network and the salience network during the AI dialog. Among the first graders, however, baseline creativity showed no statistically significant relationship with the strength of these brain network connections. That adult pattern differs from the 2023 study described earlier, which tied stronger connectivity within the executive control network to lower creativity in adults, though that study looked at connections within a single network rather than links between networks.
“Two things” surprised the team, Horowitz-Kraus explained. “First, children and adults looked similar in creative ability on the standard test, yet the neural route they took during the conversation was quite different; the difference lay in how creativity is implemented in the brain, not in baseline capacity. Second, the default mode network, which is central to most models of creativity, did not differ between the groups. One possible explanation is that conversing with ChatGPT in a scanner was novel for everyone, but that needs to be tested directly.”
Taken together, the results suggest that even when young children have age-appropriate creative potential, they engage their control, attention, and memory systems in a less integrated way than adults do during a conversation with generative AI. The authors propose that adults use their salience and frontoparietal networks to filter ChatGPT’s rapid responses and steer the brainstorming toward their goal, a role these networks may not yet play in six- and seven-year-olds.
“Talking to a chatbot looks effortless, but it draws on planning, monitoring, attention and memory systems that are still under construction in a six-year-old, which is why adult guidance matters when young children use these tools,” Horowitz-Kraus said.
“The practical message is that young children should not be left to use generative AI on their own,” she added. “For parents and teachers, this means sitting with the child, asking questions about the answers, and treating the AI as a shared activity instead of an independent tutor. For educators, pediatricians and policy makers, it means that the age at which children start using these tools deserves the same careful attention we already give to screen exposure. This study cannot set a specific ‘safe age’ since it focused on two very distinct age groups, but it is a clear signal that tools designed around adult abilities should not simply be handed to young children.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. Because the study did not include a comparison task where participants brainstormed on their own or talked with a human partner inside the scanner, the design cannot separate general age differences in brain maturity from effects caused specifically by ChatGPT. In other words, the lower network connectivity seen in children may reflect how six-year-old brains handle this kind of complex task in general, rather than showing that ChatGPT actively suppresses or harms their brain activity.
“This study does not show that ChatGPT reduces cognitive control in children or harms their brains,” Horowitz-Kraus emphasized. “We compared children with adults doing the same ChatGPT task; we did not compare children with and without ChatGPT, or ChatGPT with a human conversation partner. So we cannot yet separate what is specific to AI from general developmental differences in how the brain handles this kind of conversation.”
The way the chatbot was introduced may have also influenced how the children behaved. Telling first graders that they were about to talk to “the smartest computer in the world” may have encouraged them to passively accept the machine’s suggestions rather than questioning or evaluating its ideas, which could naturally lower their use of cognitive control networks. Future research will need to give children and adults the exact same instructions, or intentionally test how calling an AI an “expert” changes how critically kids think.
In addition, the sample size of 15 children and 16 adults was relatively small, and the groups were unevenly split by sex, with 11 boys among the 15 children and four men among the 16 adults. The study had enough participants to detect large differences between age groups, but the analyses linking creativity to brain connectivity were exploratory and likely underpowered.
The researchers also did not control for differences in everyday vocabulary size, how fast participants spoke, how many turns they took in the conversation, or how much prior experience they had with ChatGPT before the experiment (and adults likely had far more experience with the tool). Tracking children over several years in larger studies will help educators and pediatricians determine the developmental stage at which kids build the mental control needed to actively collaborate with artificial intelligence tools.
“The next steps are larger samples, a direct comparison of talking with ChatGPT versus talking with a human partner or working without AI, and longitudinal follow-up to identify when in development the control networks begin to engage in an adult-like way and to relate to creativity,” Horowitz-Kraus said. “We also plan to measure children’s familiarity with AI and to test how the perceived authority of the AI shapes their engagement. The long-term goal is to give educators, pediatricians and policy makers evidence for developmentally appropriate use of generative AI, in the same way that guidance exists for screen exposure.”
“Technology can support learning, but it cannot lead it; children learn best alongside an adult who guides and challenges them,” she added.
The study, “Lower engagement of cognitive control in children on ChatGPT,” was authored by Tzipi Horowitz-Kraus, Yoed N. Kenett, Dafna Link-Sourani, Emeel Ashqar, and Rola Farah.

Press review: Russia-US-Ukraine peace hopes rise as Moscow offers Iran-US mediation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. The prospects for peace and trilateral talks between Russia, the US and Ukraine following the October 21 St. Petersburg meeting; Moscow’s willingness to mediate between Tehran and Washington; and Russia’s potential agreement with the US to start shipping fertilizers alongside diesel. These stories topped Thursday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Media: Chances of peace and Russia-US-Ukraine talks following St. Petersburg meeting
US efforts to end the conflict between Russia and Ukraine have resumed, perhaps the main visible and indisputable outcome of the October 21 talks between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US special presidential envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg. The envoy left Russia with news of the release of an American citizen from a Russian prison and Moscow’s assurances that the proposals he brought would be reviewed. In addition, Putin expressed readiness to launch trilateral talks in the Russia-US-Ukraine format. The talks are scheduled for mid-November, after the US congressional elections, which are likely to bring significant changes.
Witkoff’s visit to St. Petersburg wrapped up a busy diplomatic round, international affairs expert Nikolay Novik told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. The St. Petersburg talks were preceded by consultations in Oslo. Witkoff and Kushner, who participated remotely, met with Zelensky, European leaders, and EU and NATO representatives there, the expert recalled. "It is likely that Witkoff presented an updated plan to end the conflict and a proposal for direct talks involving Trump and Zelensky. There may also have been discussions about a meeting between Putin, Trump, and Xi Jinping in China during the APEC summit on November 18-19: Washington doesn’t need a technical pause, but rather an outcome from the summit that can be presented as a tangible result," Novik said.
At the same time, the package of conditions that the US envoy might have brought - if these were the ones recently mentioned in the Western media - does not suit Russia, Russian International Affairs Council President Dmitry Trenin told Vedomosti. According to the expert, Moscow agreed to discuss not so much the settlement itself as possible ways to establish a security framework for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends. "By 2027, we will most likely still be in the midst of ongoing hostilities, though the US administration had certainly hoped to achieve tangible results by the end of this year," Trenin noted. The expert stressed that the future prospects of the negotiation process, including the development of specific terms, will be determined by the actual situation on the battlefield.
The current round of talks differs from previous ones because the agenda will include the issue of security guarantees for both Russia and Ukraine, an issue that was not included in negotiations with Kiev following the Istanbul consultations, Nikolay Silayev, a leading researcher at the MGIMO Institute of International Relations, said. However, the expert does not expect the upcoming negotiations with Ukraine to conclude any differently from the previous ones. "The main reason for the lack of confidence in a breakthrough is the public statements made by Ukrainian and European officials. Their position remains the same: an unconditional ceasefire," he stressed.
Izvestia: Russia ready to mediate between Tehran and Washington
Moscow is prepared to act as a mediator in settling the conflict between the US and Iran, provided both parties are interested. Talks between Washington and Tehran have reached an impasse, partly due to the unresolved question of Iran’s nuclear program. Russia previously proposed transporting Iran’s enriched uranium to its territory, but this initiative has yet to receive support.
The eight-month conflict between the US and Iran has stalled. Washington’s initial plan to quickly topple the country’s government has failed. Passage through the Strait of Hormuz remains difficult, and diplomats have yet to make progress toward resolving the conflict. Under these circumstances, Russia could assume the role of mediator. Moscow is ready to take such a step, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko told Izvestia. "If all parties express interest, then we are ready [to act as mediators]," he noted. "We previously offered our services regarding how the Iranian nuclear program could be resolved, but our proposals have not yet been supported," the senior diplomat said.
Thanks to its good relations with both Iran and Israel, Russia occupies a unique position as a universal intermediary in the Middle East, political analyst Alexander Kargin said. Moreover, Moscow is currently pursuing a negotiating track with the US as well. The expert noted that Pakistan, another potential mediator, has no diplomatic relations with Israel at all, whereas Russia does not face this problem.
Russian mediation would at least help establish a ceasefire, paving the way for a comprehensive resolution of the crisis, Kargin said. The analyst expects that, ultimately, the practical necessity of Moscow’s involvement will prevail, and the parties will bring Russia into the negotiations. At the same time, according to him, the parties to the conflict have diametrically opposed views on the nuclear program. While Russia’s proposal to remove the uranium would be ideal, heightened tensions in the Middle East are preventing the parties from making even the smallest compromises, Kargin stressed.
Izvestia: Russia may begin exporting fertilizers to US alongside diesel
Russia is ready to supply mineral fertilizers and fuel to the US, but expanding fertilizer exports would require a reallocation of shipments: currently, about 69% of fertilizer production is exported, experts said. Russian President Vladimir Putin has discussed the prospect of supplying fertilizers to the US market on a significant scale. In addition, the first shipment of 40,000 metric tons of Russian diesel fuel is scheduled to leave for the US on October 22, with other countries set to receive shipments by the end of the year.
During a meeting with US special presidential envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on October 21, Russian President Vladimir Putin said that Moscow could supply fertilizers to the American market in large quantities. However, it is difficult to gauge potential export volumes, since a significant portion of Russian production is already under contract with foreign buyers, Denis Prikhodko, an equity market analyst at Alfa-Capital Asset Management, told Izvestia. According to him, shipments will increase gradually, primarily through the redistribution of export flows among foreign markets rather than through higher production.
Increasing fertilizer and diesel fuel shipments to the US market could help bring down prices for these products both in the US and globally, which is especially important for agricultural producers. Such agreements with Russia would benefit both the Donald Trump administration and the Russian authorities, Igor Yushkov, a leading analyst at the National Energy Security Fund, stressed.
The European factor is also relevant. According to political scientist and German studies expert Yegor Belyachkov, the current leadership of most European countries will likely react negatively to an agreement between Russia and the US on fertilizer supplies, just as they did with the diesel deal. This approach directly reflects European countries' policy in recent years, under which the slightest compromise between Moscow and Washington prompts EU nations to attempt to block such agreements. Brussels could do so by tightening sanctions against Russia and coordinating with American Democrats, the expert said.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Possibility of routing Persian Gulf oil around Strait of Hormuz
New pipelines that bypass the Strait of Hormuz and lead to seaports outside the Persian Gulf will address the problem of supplying Middle Eastern oil to the global market. In five years, the strait may become obsolete for oil trade as shipments are redirected along new routes. This is not the first attempt to find alternative ways to deliver oil from Persian Gulf countries. Previously, this idea was also proposed by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. According to him, the construction of oil pipelines will render the Strait of Hormuz "a worthless piece of water" in as little as two to three years.
Bypass routes are currently more profitable, not because transporting oil via pipeline is inexpensive, but because of the increased costs linked to transit through the Strait of Hormuz, Maxim Malkov, a Kept partner and head of the firm’s oil and gas practice, told Rossiyskaya Gazeta. Before the crisis, tanker transit cost the same as or less than pipeline transport, while now, that balance has reversed, the expert noted. However, maritime transport is cheaper in peacetime. The cost of pumping oil through a pipeline is up to five times higher than the cost of moving it by oil tanker per kilometer, Oleg Abelev, head of the analytical department at the Rikom-Trust investment company, pointed out.
Existing alternative routes do not resolve the problem because their combined capacity is less than half of the volumes that previously passed through the Strait of Hormuz, Malkov emphasized. Moreover, the Red Sea poses its own risks, such as Houthi attacks, and there are virtually no alternatives to tankers for transporting refined petroleum products, the expert noted. But even if the existing infrastructure that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz is expanded and new oil pipelines are built in parallel, the economic viability of these projects will be questionable, economist Boris Kopeikin stressed. If the situation in the region stabilizes in the long term, oil will once again follow the traditional route, through the Strait of Hormuz, he said.
At the same time, the main advantage of alternative routes is the diversification of risks. They reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz and allow exports to continue in the event of shipping restrictions, but they do not guarantee complete supply security, Ivan Timonin, a senior manager at the Implementa consulting firm, said. According to Abelev, pipelines are no safer than maritime transport. They are vulnerable to drone and missile attacks, and protecting them along their entire length is quite difficult. Unlike seagoing vessels, a pipeline is stationary and its location is precisely known. It cannot be replaced or rerouted. Maritime transport offers greater flexibility. Oil pipelines for the Persian Gulf states are an expensive insurance policy, not a cheap alternative, the expert stressed.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: French authorities trying to ease protests with talks and concessions
Ahead of another round of large-scale protests scheduled for the weekend, the authorities are trying to reach a deal with the protesters. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu met with union representatives on October 21. The meeting produced no results; the government did not receive any promises to call off the protests. In fact, a general strike has been announced.
Nevertheless, Lecornu remains undeterred. The government has proposed an aid program for businesses affected by the unrest. Following his trip to the Persian Gulf states, President Emmanuel Macron issued a statement saying that he had secured additional fuel shipments to bring down prices in the country. The authorities are hoping these measures will have a rapid effect.
Rather than resorting to force, the French authorities have decided to address the wave of protests sweeping the country through persuasion. They have chosen to respond to the demonstrators’ main demands. Perhaps there is no other option: last weekend, more than half a million French citizens took to the streets across the country. The protests are no longer limited to schoolchildren and their parents who are dissatisfied with the education system. Labor unions are actively participating in the protests, which are directed against the rising cost of living and ultimately against the economic policies of the current president and government.
At the same time, the situation in the country is gradually returning to normal, although this will take some time, Tatyana Zvereva, a professor at the World Economy and World Politics Faculty of the Russian National Research University Higher School of Economics, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. "The composition of the protesters is complex. It includes high school students, members of the ‘Yellow Vests’ movement, and others, including members of fringe political organizations," she noted. According to the expert, the French authorities are pursuing two main lines of action. On the one hand, they are restoring order, which society as a whole expects. The far-right National Rally party has been particularly vocal in demanding this. On the other hand, the authorities are negotiating with moderate protesters.
"The logic is this: the most aggressive protesters must be held accountable, and positive-minded citizens must be reached out to by addressing their socio-economic demands. However, the second point is much more difficult to achieve. Therefore, it seems unlikely that we can expect quick results from the negotiations. But dialogue can help defuse the situation and let off some steam," Zvereva emphasized.

U.S. Reportedly Considering Major Strikes on Iran After Midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

The U.S. and Israel are reportedly developing plans for major strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections in November.
Citing people familiar with the deliberations, the New York Times reported on Wednesday that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth discussed the possibility of renewed strikes on Iran with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel this week. Possible targets of the strikes reportedly include Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
U.S. officials have repeatedly asserted that the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps are teetering on the edge of collapse but are deliberately prolonging the war in an effort to meddle with Republican prospects in the midterm elections. Once the elections are over, President Donald Trump promised last month, the Iranian regime would quickly capitulate.
“I think the war is going to end immediately after the election,” Trump said. “They can’t hold out any longer.”
Renewed strikes could complicate that outlook.
Some officials have reportedly argued that resuming attacks for an intense but limited campaign would hasten Iran’s economic collapse, especially as the country has been squeezed by an ongoing U.S. blockade on Iranian ports and economic sanctions campaign. The officials hope the blow will make Iran more amenable to negotiations.
Trump has at times shared that view.
Last week, Trump told Newsmax he was considering additional military action in Iran, including a possible strike on Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, a nuclear facility deep underground. His comments came amid reports that he was weighing deploying a 22,000 GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, also known as the “mother of all bombs.”
The President added the war would end soon, be it through negotiation or escalation.
“Do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he said in a speech to the United Nations General Assembly last month.
“But I believe we’ll make a deal,” he added, “right after the election.”
Will the U.S. renew strikes on Iran?
Intensified fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthi rebels and the Saudi and Yemeni governments has threatened to create a broader regional crisis that could be harder to disengage from. The State Department on Wednesday ordered nonemergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia amid escalating attacks by the Houthis on Saudi infrastructure.
Houthi attacks on Saudi airports and Aramco facilities, as well as their attempts to disrupt shipping through Bab El-Mandeb, which has become an important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz for energy trade, could prompt direct U.S. strikes in support of Saudi Arabia, analysts have said. Trump said earlier this month that the U.S. “may” join Saudi strikes on the Houthis, although that has yet to transpire.
Israel’s Oct. 27 election could also raise the stakes of additional military action. Netanyahu, whom Trump has endorsed, would remain in office until a new government is formed, even if his bloc loses the election, and his government would retain the authority to order strikes during that transition. But renewed strikes before the election, or after an electoral defeat, could invite scrutiny. “One ordered in the last weeks of a deadlocked campaign would be judged in Israel as politics as well as strategy,” Gregg Roman, executive director of the Middle East Forum, wrote in a September analysis.
Nevertheless, the forum assessed that a large-scale Israeli strike on Iranian territory, with or without U.S. participation, was probable before the end of the year. Analysts told the Times Netanyahu could use the prospect of joint strikes to form a unity government that could allow him to stay in power.
“The larger constraint,” Roman argued, “is Washington.”
Trump has not yet approved the proposed strikes, the Times reported.
Trump has also called off plans to renew attacks on Iran before. He reportedly blocked an Israeli plan for a multi-day offensive against Iran earlier this month, and rejected five proposals for major operations against Iran or the Houthis in recent months.
The U.S. and Iran have not exchanged major fighting in recent weeks. The last reported U.S. strikes on Iran were on Sept. 8, even as Iranian attacks on commercial shipping have continued. Earlier this month, Trump ruled out attacking Iran before the midterms.
How might Iran respond to new strikes?
Tehran’s reluctance to make concessions to the U.S. appears to have strengthened, rather than weakened, over the course of the war. Iranian leaders reiterated this week that they will not directly negotiate with the U.S. unless Washington accedes to certain demands, which include ending its naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian funds.
The initial U.S. and Israeli bombing campaign on Iran that began the war on Feb. 28, as well as June 2025 attacks during an earlier round of U.S.-Iran nuclear diplomacy, also hardened the Iranian view that the U.S. is not serious about negotiating. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in March that the previous disruptions of negotiating rounds had increased distrust in Washington.
Last month, the IRGC published an open letter appealing to American voters to “wrest control” from their government. In the letter, the IRGC said: “Despite all the hardships that our enemies impose on us, we will continue fighting, as we have done for the past 47 years.”
Both the U.S. and Iran appear to believe they hold enough leverage to achieve their goals, and those “dueling perceptions” have impeded progress towards a deal, according to an Oct. 1 analysis by the New York-based nonpartisan research organization The Soufan Center.
Iran’s key point of leverage is its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway vital to global energy trade. Iran’s militarization of the strait has disrupted global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, leading to soaring energy prices and inflation.
Analysts previously told TIME that the higher prices are politically costly for Trump. In recent weeks, a growing number of Republicans have broken with Trump on Iran. The President has also seen his lowest approval ratings of his second term.
Iran’s ability to choke off regional oil exports, however, appears to be waning. Middle East oil exports topped prewar levels last week as shipping companies use alternative routes to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. HSBC Group Chief Executive Georges Elhedery also projected that Hormuz could be “redundant” in five years thanks to investment in alternative logistics routes.
Iranian officials told the Times that they are aware of the U.S. and Israel’s war planning and are developing their own tactics.
Earlier this week, IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi told the Tehran Times that “even a limited” attack from Washington would provoke a “serious energy crisis” for the world. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said that an attack on Pickaxe Mountain would be met with a response “just as hard,” if not “stronger.”
And earlier this month, Iranian officials said Iran had prepared potential retaliatory operations that would depart from the U.S. and Israel’s assumptions. Security Chief Mohsen Rezaei told Press TV that Iran could respond to renewed attacks by targeting new targets, including U.S.-linked data centers and AI facilities in the Gulf, as well as subsea communications cables. Last month, Iran threatened to retaliate against any further U.S. attacks by targeting U.S. oil and gas assets in the Gulf.
In a post on Telegram on Sunday, Mahdi Mohammadi, a senior adviser to Iran’s negotiator Gen. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said, if the U.S. and Israel attack, “they may want to keep it short, but we will not allow it.”
He added on Wednesday: “The war will continue longer and across a wider geography than the enemy calculates.”

Hugging Face’s New AI Biology Model Lets You Chat With DNA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

The AI platform Hugging Face on Thursday released a new open-source model for understanding DNA that can run locally on a laptop.
Developed in collaboration with researchers at Zhongguancun Academy in China and the University of Naples Federico II in Italy, the model is trained on genomic sequences and natural language so that people can ask questions about the effects of DNA changes on gene activity and health and get conversational answers in return.
Lewis Tunstall, a senior research scientist at Hugging Face, says the tool is meant to help researchers design new drugs and genetic therapies, and it could potentially aid patients in interpreting their own genomes.
“We've unlocked a new capability in language models, which is fundamentally about being able to chat with DNA,” he says of the new model, dubbed Carbon-X. Using natural language means even nontechnical users “can actually ask questions about DNA that wouldn't be accessible through any other tool.”
Known as essentially GitHub for AI models, Hugging Face provides a library of readymade AI tools and a platform for running primarily open-weight and open-source AI applications for developers, researchers, businesses, and people who want to experiment with AI without building everything from scratch. In September, Nvidia agreed to acquire the company for nearly $13 billion. (Hugging Face was also at the center of a major hack by OpenAI’s models earlier this year.)
DNA is more like computer code than natural language. Instead of 0s and 1s, though, it uses As, Cs, Gs, and Ts to encode information. A human genome contains 6 billion of these letters. While the human genome has been sequenced end to end, scientists still don’t understand how most of it works.
Now, AI models are helping researchers decipher some of those mysteries. Last year, Google DeepMind released AlphaGenome, which predicts the effects of DNA sequences and genetic mutations but does so in a numeric format. It also requires more compute power. Evo 2, a model developed by the Arc Institute and Nvidia, along with academic partners, speaks the language of DNA and can generate entire genomes from scratch.
Carbon-X integrates both DNA and natural language in a conversational interface. Think of it like a ChatGPT for DNA.
The team started with an existing language model and expanded its vocabulary to read DNA in groups of six letters. They then continued training on 300 billion chunks of data, or tokens, that combined DNA sequences, English text, and examples linking DNA to biological descriptions. The DNA sequences came from mammals (including humans), other vertebrates, invertebrates, plants, fungi, and protozoa. Tunstall says the team didn’t train the model on viruses because they didn’t want it to be used for potentially dangerous applications.
Users won’t be able to upload full human genomes. The model was trained to be able to ingest DNA sequences of roughly 50,000 base pairs, so users will only be able to query small parts of the genome at a time.
One of the ways scientists could use Carbon-X is to help understand whether a genetic mutation is benign or disease-causing, a key step in developing a targeted drug or genetic therapy. If an intervention targets the wrong mutation, it could be totally ineffective or, worse, cause unintended harm.
Researchers face restrictions when it comes to uploading identifiable or sensitive patient data to frontier AI models, so Tunstall says his team intentionally designed a small model with 14 billion parameters. That will allow it to run locally on the user’s hardware, rather than rely on cloud-based models. No data is sent to Hugging Face or any other company, he says.
The developers of Carbon-X caution that they haven’t validated the model yet with actual wet lab experiments, so they can’t say how accurate its predictions are.

Other people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
31 minute listen
Earlier this year, I surfaced from sleep to a strange noise, a loud, human singing reverberating through our bedroom ceiling, then a low, almost animal groaning. My husband and I looked at each other. ‘I think Hatty’s in labour,’ he said.
The rest of the day proceeded in the usual way, getting breakfast for our children, dropping them off at school, meetings, emails, booking in the car for an MOT, but these activities were interspersed with opening the door to midwives, making cups of tea for Hatty, and finding towels to drape around the birth pool that had appeared in our living room. Towards evening, our eighth housemate appeared in a rush of fluids. Two ambulance-loads of paramedics stood around like a flock of green and yellow London parakeets, blessedly unrequired. At one point, there were nine medical professionals, seven housemates, two grandparents of the new arrival and a cat in our terraced London house. It didn’t even feel that full, I thought later, as I poured bleach on bloodstained towels and binned a discarded catheter that had been overlooked in a corner.
I am 42, and I did not expect to end up here. Like most of my peers, I was handed a vision of a home worth striving for with far, far fewer people in it and, to begin with, I followed that script. A middle-class 1980s child, I did well at school, moved away from my home county dormitory town for university, and never went back. London, jobs at the BBC, running a think tank all followed. I lived with good friends, and juggled seeing others between our clashing personal schedules. Then people began to pair up and procreate. I met someone, followed suit, and we clawed our way onto the very bottom of the housing ladder. It was a lovely life. A bit relentless, perhaps, a bit lonely around the edges, too, as the schedules got ever harder to tessellate, the work and care burdens heavier. But we had done it. Our little dyad, with dependants, was standing on its own feet, even if something felt decidedly unstable underneath.
More space, more privacy, more control – all are sold as natural, unquestioned goods to be sought in the unconscious script that most of us carry. For the nuclear family, they are tokens of success and maturity, whereas forgoing these ‘goods’ and living with people you are neither shagging nor parenting has an association with low-status, studenty seasons. Not for proper grownups. My husband and I began to feel the strengthening drag of this story. I sometimes saw it in my mind’s eye as a tide, washing young adults from their family homes into temporarily intertwined clusters (largely in cities), then out again, to the suburbs and beyond, in pairs or alone, in search of a garden, a bigger kitchen, storage space for the mountains of stuff we inevitably accumulate. Swept away from each other, everyone further and further apart.
Every policy issue we researched at the think tank led back inexorably to disconnection. It was labelled different things (overconsumption, fraying trust, the corrosion of democracy, crises of loneliness, mental health, care, climate, housing). But a thread linked them all: our inability to bear each other, to share (our stuff, space, skills, and deepest selves) was actively making the world worse. I came across thinkers who shared my intuition that something largely invisible but all-encompassing was getting in the way of our being together as healthier cultures remembered how to do. Some called it individualism or modernity. Others blamed ‘the machine’ of late-stage capitalism. I never settled on a name I liked, but I felt the disquiet of it. Still, all the intelligent analysis and critique never quite seemed to lead to progressive action, but instead to a conservative turn that half-appealed in its communitarianism and rooted localism, but not in its approach to women and ‘outsiders’.
The message seems to be that the price we pay for the freedoms of liberal individualism is loneliness. You can have personal autonomy, privacy and endless choice; you can outsource most of your needs to the market rather than navigate complex non-transactional relationships with other people that tie you into reciprocity; you can optimise your surroundings, appearance and experiences to your exact preferences, but what gets bundled in for good measure is a sense of existential weightlessness.
I rebelled. Surely there was something between atomisation – what the philosopher Charles Taylor calls the ‘buffered self’ – and hierarchical, authoritarian community; between girl-boss and trad-wife. The final push to try and find it, ultimately, was fear. When my first child was born, the reality of the climate crisis moved from a theoretical policy problem to one that bubbled acidly in my belly, settled itself in my bones. I had brought this powerless being into a world on fire, and the idea that hard work and individual accumulation could keep her safe stopped making sense. The need to be part of a thick web of humans who would not play a passing role in each other’s lives but commit to costly mutual care felt urgent as the ground bucked and roiled beneath our feet. I wanted ‘a village’, as we say now, not for the golden Instagram images of laughing friends around a photogenic table, but because, in my bleakest moments, I thought it might be essential for survival.
It is a truism that early parenthood is isolating and relentless, but does it have to be? We started questioning accepted norms, not idly fantasising about building a commune but taking serious steps. I wanted to live this season of our lives up close with others, witnessing each other, supporting each other. Not uploading the tidied-up details into group chats, after the fact, or smoothing the misery into memes, holding back the joys for fear of sounding smug. This realisation cracked outwards, connecting with a deeper intuition: I wanted all of life to be like that. I wanted to see and be seen. It felt wrong that everyone didn’t live this way, like something important had been lost in the rush to accumulate stuff and protect our security, status and autonomy by disappearing behind our own front doors.
Whether you call the present a polycrisis or just a gigantic roiling clusterfuck, I became more convinced that the medicine for most of our ills is to actively and counterculturally move towards other people. To resist the powerful forces driving us apart. There are lots of ways of doing this, of course. But letting go of the idea that our homes must be private retreats from other people seemed a decent place to start. I believe that our homes can be places to relearn the habits of reciprocity, sharing and mutual care that for most of history (and, in many parts of the non-Western world, still) are the defining characteristics of a culture worthy of the name. A culture we are urgently going to need.
This sounds much, much simpler and easier than it is.
For us, it took years of intentional conversations, initial enthusiasm from others that then petered out, bureaucratic wrangling, and research. We eventually found people who were equally committed (who were not, interestingly, friends already), and rented together to test it. We learned to navigate sex noises and bathroom smells (sound-proofing and background music helps a lot with the first). We had tense conversations about kitchen storage, our different expectations around spending and cleanliness. It surfaced stuff from our childhoods, which we then had to be honest about and confront. The process (much of which happened during COVID-19 lockdowns, which I’m sure accelerated it) was challenging and exposing, almost unbearably uncomfortable at times.
As I held him at 4 am, my son asked: ‘Why couldn’t we stay in our flat, just us?’
We also practised rupture and repair, realising that, even as we saw the most ridiculous, fragile, defensive parts of each other, we were not running away. In his play The Real Thing (1982), Tom Stoppard aptly defined love as ‘Knowledge of each other … knowledge of self, the real him, the real her, in extremis, the mask slipped from the face.’ In the course of our building trust, it did feel a lot like love. Not love based on surface similarities or romance, but on a mutual commitment to each other. It felt like growing up. The existential emptiness, the unsteady sense of vertigo eased.
Having tested the concept, we embarked on a labyrinthically complex joint house-purchase. It fell through on the day of a long-delayed exchange, after we’d reached the end of the notice period on our rental. For months, we had no fixed address and scattered to the sofas and spare beds of friends and family. My youngest child began having nightmares. As I held him at 4 am, he asked: ‘Why couldn’t we stay in our flat, just us?’ The script glowed temptingly. If living with others was the answer, surely it shouldn’t be this difficult. We held our nerve.
To date, we have lived up close – bodily fluids close – with people we are not related to for nearly six years. We share all the space in our jointly mortgaged home except the bedrooms. We pool most of our money, cook, shop, pray and host hundreds of guests a year, together. And we manage countless petty conflicts, over the milk or the dishwasher or the crumbs on the side, conflicts that often mask deeper questions: who do I belong to? Where can I be really at home, be really myself? Who am I becoming, alongside these people? And are we able, when it comes down to it, to be each other’s safety?
There are very few models for what we are doing. Perhaps the most robust is the monastic tradition. Most orders of religious Sisters or Brothers see the proximity of living up close with each other as essential to spiritual growth. It is precisely in the discomfort of being witnessed, up close, at our worst, in being asked to compromise preferences, to share and serve others, they argue, that we really grow up.
Living with others has shown me things in myself that I would prefer to ignore
My policy-wonk brain knew there were systems keeping us apart. Not just social scripts but monetary policies, mortgage terms, HMO (house in multiple occupation) legislation. Yet living communally has taught me that it is also what is inside us that makes it hard to be together. My romantic ideas about cultures worthy of the name, marked by interdependence and mutual care, clearly also require certain kinds of people – with emotional skills, developed character, an ability to make lasting commitments. None of which my individualistic formation had gifted me an abundance of.
Living with others has shown me things in myself that I would prefer to ignore. How much of me is still a child, wanting my way, quick to cry ‘it’s not fair’. I have been learning all this as the world around us unravels. The contrast is disconcerting. If it really is the end of the world, at least as we have known it, then what kind of people will be needed? What would it take to be braver, more resilient and flexible, more joyful, creative and free? A person who could, at bloody least, wait patiently to go in the bathroom, or let someone else use a favourite mug. Someone able to sacrifice sleep to care for another’s child, and have the hard conversation about a failure to mop the kitchen floor, rather than avoiding it. I want to learn these habits. I have a hunch that much more than this might be asked of me. Of all of us.
This project finds faint echoes in the self-improvement, self-development, self-optimisation we are all constantly hectored into – therapy (or psychedelics, or stoicism) for the mind and Hyrox (or reformer Pilates, or yoga) for the body (with those who are not working on themselves in some way being the exception). Interestingly, the unconventional way our household lives is rarely recommended to those seeking self-knowledge or self-development. The standard advice is an inward turn in order to facilitate a private excavation of an authentic self, along with strong personal boundaries that draw distinct lines between that self and others. Porousness tends to be framed as deleterious to Project Self. Most monastic orders encourage periods of solitude and silence, to be sure, but much of daily life is spent in an exposing proximity to others, the very idea of which would bring most of us out in hives.
This difficult proximity, where we witness and are witnessed without our protective, polished personas is an immensely powerful change agent. You can see it in action in group therapy, the recovery movement and some short-term intensive self-development programmes, but this powerful ‘technology of the self’, to use Michel Foucault’s phrase, is vanishingly rare. This kind of witnessing (during my housemate’s labour, for example, I witnessed parts of her that only her partner otherwise sees) is effective because change requires us to be honest about who we currently are. Living in community is where illusions about the self go to die!
One of the phrases we use a lot in our household is ‘We are made for each other and we are made by each other.’ Marxists such as Silvia Federici call this ‘social reproduction’. Neurologically, this makes sense: human interaction shapes our brains from our very earliest moments. Every human comes into the world in search of a gaze.
The day the baby was born, while their mother was being stitched up and I was moving bins for the paramedics, my primary-school aged son was one of the first people to hold the tiny form. They’d wrapped the baby in a yellow foil survival bag, and he gazed down for long minutes with as much attention as if he was indeed holding a giant Quality Street toffee. This baby had moved from deep bodily entanglement, hidden in just one of us, to a less visible but no less profound interdependence. They have now been held by more arms than your average Western infant, and whether it’s mum, dad, us housemates, family, neighbours or church friends, we all adopt the same posture as my son. Face turned towards face. Eyes meeting eyes. The baby makes noises, and we make noises back. And as we gaze and gurgle, the mycelia of their brain are forming.
Dan Siegel, the clinical psychiatrist and founder of interpersonal neurobiology, says that our earliest relationships ‘shape the very neural structures that create representations of experience and allow a coherent view of the world: Interpersonal experiences directly influence how we mentally construct reality.’ The connections formed by the face-dancing we all instinctively do with babies help create the conditions that enable them to experience what is real. More than this, these gazes are where their sense of self comes from. Siegel says that, beyond these earliest experiences of connection, relationships shape, throughout our lives, ‘how we feel, how we think, how we remember things, how we tell the story of who we are, the sense of self … what gives you a sense of purpose.’ We become who we become because of who we gaze on, and who gazes back at us.
We talk a lot about exits, about the fact that we will probably not live together forever
The porousness of babies to their caregivers, and especially their need for face-to-face connection is widely understood. The neuropsychologist Allan Schore calls a baby an ‘open dynamic system’. What our house is helping me see is how much humans remain ‘open systems’, and how much mind/self/soul (all translations of the word ‘psyche’) arises within and between us. We are not closed selves, semaphoring information to each other and making free rational choices. We are always makers of each other – the act of mutual witnessing, or its lack, moulding us like wet clay.
One way of thinking about our unconventional living situation, then, is that it offers a way of choosing who we want to be formed by, as if consciously curating the powerful gaze of others. Our bet is that the real costs, in control, convenience and comfort, the exposure of being seen and known ‘with masks slipped from faces’, are worth it. I believe that it is a demanding but effective method of becoming the kind of people the world needs now.
I could be wrong. I am not rosy-tinted about the realities of experiments like these, how badly they can hurt people if done poorly. The way we live may not last. We commit, unlike monks and nuns, only in five-year increments. This season has been the most meaningful, the most beautiful and the most fun of my life, despite the challenges. It has made me braver, and freed up swathes of time and energy that I would have otherwise spent on home admin in a household of only two adults. It is working, really working, for now, but we are realists. We talk a lot about exits, about the fact that we will probably not live together forever. Perhaps we’re trying to have our cake and eat it, keeping one foot in the autonomy of liberal individualism even as we experience the benefits of rooted, committed mutual care. Our experiment is imperfect. My hunch, though, is that we are going to need more of them.
As a society, we are still largely in denial about the scale of the existential threats facing us, and against which individualism cannot keep us safe. In times of deep ecological, technological and political crisis, we may be forced to remember how to be each other’s safety. To unpick, laboriously, the conditioning of the weird, prosperous West and call bullshit on the lie that control, accumulation and a frictionless, precision-optimised life was ever going to make us happy. Though I know it’s a lie, a lot of me still wants it. However, as I learn every day how deeply the script of individualism has formed me, I also see how poorly it serves us.
Each day that I wake up in this house, I am choosing to enact a different script, one in which other people’s concerns are more real to me. My housemate’s labour pains, this baby’s cries, are my business. Conversely, my occasional existential terror or my children’s school struggles are tangible to a wider group of people than they would otherwise be. We have a stake in each other. There is a fierce tenderness in it that often brings me to tears. Iris Murdoch describes something like it in ‘The Sublime and The Good’ (1959) when she writes:
Love is the extremely difficult realisation that something other than oneself is real. Love … is the discovery of reality … The exercise of overcoming one’s self, of the expulsion of fantasy and convention … is indeed exhilarating. It is also, if we perform it properly which we hardly ever do, painful.
Isolation allows us to maintain all kinds of illusions about ourselves and about others. In contrast, remaining tethered to a shared reality requires us to really see others, not in the refracted fun-house mirror of social media, but in regular, embodied ways. We triangulate the world via other people, taking readings from a range of perspectives to build a more accurate picture of things. My image of this process is of humans echolocating like bats, where the objects sounding back are the voices and faces of other people. René Descartes might have thought he needed to withdraw from society completely to find truth but, respectfully, he was wrong. Turning in, pulling away disorientates us. The social theorist Sarah Stein Lubrano argues that the more time we spend alone, the more prone we are to delusion. Communities like ours are often laughed at, written off as naive, but if our minds do indeed require a thick web of strong relational connections in order to grasp reality, then we weirdos are possibly learning to see the world more clearly.
Our community (and other lasting ones) hold together by turning attention beyond ourselves
Why, then, are experiments like ours so rare? Why do I, a public advocate, a recipient of the very real benefits of communal living, still feel conflicted about arguing more strongly for it to become the norm? It is partly that such a life is, as Murdoch says, painful. Decentering my preferences, letting go of my self-aggrandising illusions hurts. These are growing pains, every one worth it – but still. Inviting others into something this rigorous, and costly, is not in fashion.
There is another reason. The community we live in offers mutual witnessing, mutual recognition, increased capacity and care, and economies of scale, but this alone is not enough to hold us when it all feels too much. When people come to our home wanting advice about setting up something similar, we always tell them: community for the sake of community doesn’t work. Communes might be highly effective sites of self-formation, but the ones designed primarily to do that will likely collapse. My experience is that our community (and other lasting ones) hold together by turning attention beyond ourselves. The ability to locate the project in a vision of the good – political, ecological, philosophical or other – is an essential foundation.
There is something about our house I have not mentioned much. You may have caught that throwaway line about praying together. One of the arguments made by Charles Taylor and others about the isolating tendencies of modernity is that it is linked to secularity. He argues that pre-moderns had a much stronger sense of how porous they were, how bound up with each other, with nature, and with divine or magical presences. He links our increasingly boundaried or buffered sense of self to the loss of religion: we moderns are not made by and for god(s), by and for each other, but by and for ourselves. I have some sympathy with the argument, because without a robust, collective wisdom tradition, it is challenging to keep choosing to move towards each other. Despite believing in this way of life for policy reasons, emotional reasons, neurobiological reasons, even goddamn survival reasons, I am not sure I would be able to do it without a powerful, and in our case, religious, reason why.
When asked to sum up his teaching, Jesus offered two, interlinked commands. Firstly, love of the divine (Love the Lord your God ‘with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength’) then, love of the other (‘Love your neighbour as yourself’). No moral prescriptions or religious ritualism, but relationality as The Way. I have spent a lot of time sitting with the work that the word ‘as’ is doing in ‘love your neighbour as your self’. In the same measure you love yourself? At the same time as? Because they are yourself? Even when they have left beard clippings all over the sink?
The petty squabbles between early believers trying to share are there in the New Testament for all to see
Helpfully, Jesus had a lot of other less cryptic things to say about learning to bear each other and be together. The New Testament takes it as a given that humans are messy, dishonest, selfish, misguided, that we will hurt and anger each other. We may be made for and by each other, but it assumes there will be days when we wish we were not. This tendency to disconnect, this almost gravitational pulling away from each other led Martin Luther, building on Augustine, to call us ‘Homo incurvatus in se’: humanity turned in on itself. I find it one of the more useful definitions of sin.
The New Testament is largely a set of letters between what we might see as communitarian experiments, and reckoning with our inward-turning tendencies. The petty squabbles between early believers trying to share their lives and possessions are there on the page for all to see. The difficulty was part of the point, not a reason to avoid it.
This realism might be why, despite its very real benefits, this is not a full-throated advertisement for communal life. The costs are real, so you need a powerful story to hold you. A completely different script of what a good life looks like. I don’t think it necessarily has to be a religious one, but it does need to be powerful, and go beyond individual interest. Setting up my life for mutual care and reciprocity is the best thing I have ever done, but its chafing against the script I was born into still leaves blisters sometimes. On days when it asks more of me than I am receiving, it is the ‘why’ that makes me stay.
I hope that, collectively, we can (re)discover some big whys, that more people are inspired to experiment with moving towards each other. I think the upending of the world by climate change, AI and all their currently unforeseen effects will likely force us into it. It is, ultimately, soul work. Our household has had a few years’ head start, no more than a foundation course, yet it is getting easier as the vestiges of the old script become threadbare. I think – I hope? – that I am more patient and less petty; more steady and less resistant to sharing. More oriented towards a rigorous love, and so a tiny bit more of use in this hurting world. Whether that is in fact reality or self-delusion is a question you would have to ask my housemates.

South Korea's stranded celebrity shark swims back into canal after rescue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
09:59:38 UTC
18:59:38 KST

An endangered dusky shark that had been trapped in a canal in South Korea’s southeastern port city of Busan for more than a month returned hours after authorities guided it out to sea, local media reported on Thursday.
The female shark, nicknamed Bukang-i, was spotted on Thursday morning near the entrance to the canal at Busan’s North Port Waterfront Park after crossing a floating barrier late on Wednesday, according to The Korea Herald.
It was the second time the shark had slipped past barriers following rescue attempts.
Authorities had declared Wednesday’s operation successful at around 6.10 pm local time (0910GMT), but the shark was seen crossing the barrier again at around 11.05 pm (1405GMT).
Officials are considering reinforcing the barriers or capturing the shark and transporting it to open waters.
Lee Gwang-seok, an official with the oceans and fisheries ministry, said Bukang-i was unlikely to slip past more barriers and move farther up the canal, considering the density of the nets and the narrow waterway in that section that leaves little room for the shark to squeeze through.
The shark’s repeated returns have puzzled authorities, who remain concerned about its deteriorating health and falling water temperatures.
The National Institute of Fisheries Science has not observed Bukang-i feeding, while apparent injuries and footage showing it striking a canal wall have raised further concerns.
Sharing the Korean name of Busan’s North Port, where it was first spotted in mid-September, Bukang-i has become a major local tourist attraction as it slowly circled the canal, its fins slicing through the water’s surface. It has drawn more than 1.6 million visitors as of Sunday, according to Yonhap News Agency.
Previous rescue attempts on September 29 and October 2 failed. Authorities fear the shark could die if temperatures continue to fall.

Researchers warn of global decline in childhood measles vaccination
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:56:27 CST
18:56:27 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Researchers have warned of a global decline in childhood measles vaccination rates since the COVID-19 pandemic, contributing to a resurgence of the highly contagious disease.
Routine vaccine program disruptions and under-resourced health systems are driving the global decline, with estimated measles cases among children under five rising to 15.6 million worldwide in 2023, a 40 percent increase from 2019, according to a statement released Thursday by Australia's University of Queensland (UQ).
The study, published in Nature Medicine, examined measles cases, deaths and vaccination gaps among children under five across 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023.
Associate Professor Benn Sartorius from UQ's Frazer Institute said the resurgence coincided with pandemic-related disruptions to immunization programs, health systems and funding, reversing decades of progress, with measles cases falling nearly 80 percent worldwide between 1990 and 2019.
An estimated 23.7 million infants, or one in five worldwide, missed their first measles vaccine dose in 2023. Sub-Saharan Africa accounted for 50 percent of the missed doses, followed by South Asia at 20 percent, Sartorius said, adding the study's data could help authorities identify under-vaccinated populations to prevent future outbreaks. ■

Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, delivers an important speech during a gathering commemorating the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Red Army's Long March held at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 22, 2026. BEIJING, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday called for new achievements on the new Long March as China commemorates the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Red Army's Long March.
"Only by remembering history can we create a brighter future," said Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, when addressing a gathering held in Beijing to mark the anniversary.
Under Xi's proposal, all participants stood up and observed a moment of silence for the revolutionary heroes who gave their lives during the Long March and in revolutionary struggles across China.
From October 1934 to October 1936, the Red Army marched through more than 10 provinces during the Long March, opening up a new chapter in the Chinese revolution, Xi said.
"This earth-shattering revolutionary feat holds great significance in the history of our Party, country and military, and has a profound impact on our path toward the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation," he noted.
Xi stressed that the Party's right leadership and the establishment of Mao Zedong's core position were decisive for the victory of the Red Army's Long March.
The Party and the Red Army relied on firm conviction, Xi said, adding that troops with noble ideals and firm beliefs are invincible.
Xi emphasized the importance of integrating the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities in addressing the country's issues and problems.
He further underscored that the people will always be the source of strength and a strong support for the Party and the people's armed forces.
Xi said the great spirit of the Long March demonstrates the power of loyalty, truth, justice and unity. "It will always be a precious treasure and a powerful driving force inspiring us to overcome difficulties and forge ahead courageously."
He said the road of the Long March continues to extend. "On our new journey, we are now committed to realizing the Second Centenary Goal of building China into a great modern socialist country in all respects and advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation on all fronts through a Chinese path to modernization," he said.
To forge ahead on the new Long March, Xi said, it is imperative to stay committed to the Party's ideals, convictions and purpose and rely closely on the people to create new achievements.
He underscored the need to unswervingly advance high-quality development and promote common prosperity for all.
Efforts must be made to better ensure both development and security and seize the historical initiative to overcome difficulties, combat risks and meet challenges, he stressed.
Xi also emphasized the importance of moving more quickly to reinforce the people's armed forces to world-class standards and adhering to the Party's absolute leadership over the military.
It is also vital to uphold the leadership of the Party, strengthen Party building and persevere with full and rigorous Party self-governance, he added.
Li Qiang, Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang and Li Xi, who are members of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, as well as Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, attended the gathering.
Zhao, who presided over the event, said Xi's speech was of immense political, ideological and guiding significance, urging earnest efforts to study and grasp its essence and ensure its effective implementation.
He called on the whole Party, the entire military and the Chinese people of all ethnic groups to rally more closely around the Party Central Committee with Xi at its core and strive to build a great country and advance national rejuvenation on all fronts through Chinese modernization.
Around 3,000 people participated in the gathering at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing. ■

Explainer: What's the cost of biodiversity loss?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:55:59 CST
18:55:59 KST

YEREVAN, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Your first glass of water today comes with an invisible bill.
Behind it is a vast network of life, from forests and wetlands to microscopic organisms, helping keep water supplies clean and reliable.
The United Nations calls this interconnected system the "web of life," on which we depend for food, water, medicine and a stable climate.
Biodiversity is the variety of life that makes up this web.
At the ongoing 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in the Armenian capital, Yerevan, countries are grappling with how to halt biodiversity loss and translate pledges into action.
VALUE OF BIODIVERSITY
From bacteria and fungi to forests and coral reefs, the biodiversity we see today is the product of 4.5 billion years of evolution, increasingly shaped by human activity.
Pollinating plants, dispersing seeds, sustaining food webs ... every species has a role to play in nature. Losing a single species can mean losing ecological relationships and genetic resources accumulated over millions of years of evolution.
The scale of the loss is alarming.
The 2026 Living Planet Report of the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) shows that the average size of monitored wildlife populations shrank by 73 percent between 1970 and 2022.
Conservation, meanwhile, is making progress.
In Colombia, conservationists are breeding, reintroducing and monitoring the critically endangered Orinoco crocodile, aiming to restore self-sustaining wild populations rather than simply releasing more animals.
Armenia has applied for funding from the Kunming Biodiversity Fund to cover projects bolstering the biodiversity of Lake Sevan, including the protection of the Sevan trout, an endemic species, said Armenian Environment Minister and COP17 President Hambardzum Matevosyan.
And the projects go beyond saving a particular fish species. They aim to preserve genetic diversity, which helps species adapt to changing conditions.
Such diversity is practically valuable for humans: crop varieties may carry genes for drought or disease resistance, while natural organisms provide compounds used in medicine. According to the WHO, more than half of modern medicines came from nature.
INVISIBLE SERVICES
Scientists call the benefits nature provides -- including water purification, pollination and carbon storage -- "ecosystem services."
They rarely appear on household bills or business balance sheets, but their loss can bring very real costs, from poorer water quality to damaged crops and increased exposure to environmental disasters.
According to the United Nations, more than half the world's gross domestic product is moderately or highly dependent on nature. More than 1 billion people rely on forests for their livelihoods. And land and the ocean absorb more than half of all carbon emissions.
As COP17 opened, forest fires in Indonesia's Kalimantan region had affected more than 57,000 hectares, with haze reaching communities in Malaysia and Singapore, said Theiva Lingam, co-chair of Friends of the Earth International.
She described the fires as "a stark reminder of the deeper biodiversity crisis which is unfolding across the Global South."
The vulnerability of peatlands helps explain why such environmental damage can have consequences far beyond the areas affected.
Peatlands cover only about 3 percent of the world's land but store roughly twice as much carbon as all the forests on Earth. When drained or burned, these ecosystems can release large amounts of stored carbon while losing their ability to regulate water and support wildlife.
FOOTING THE BILL
The economic gains from activities that harm biodiversity are often shared globally, while the environmental and social costs fall disproportionately on developing countries and local communities, Lingam said.
To help redress this imbalance, Article 20 of the Convention on Biological Diversity requires developed countries to provide "new and additional financial resources" to help developing ones cover the agreed costs of implementing the convention.
Likewise, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted in 2022, calls for international biodiversity funding to developing countries to reach at least 20 billion U.S. dollars annually by 2025 and 30 billion dollars by 2030.
Preventing damage is particularly important as extinction is irreversible, while restoring degraded ecosystems can be costly and the outcome uncertain, experts said.
Celine Beaulieu, who works on biodiversity finance at the WWF, said funding must also translate into results, urging countries to "judge biodiversity finance not only by what is being pledged, but by what reaches implementation."
As Armenian Deputy Environment Minister Aram Meymaryan put it, conservation must be judged by results on the ground: Have threats been reduced? Have species' chances of survival improved? Are their populations recovering?
Nature may never send a bill, but the cost of losing the ecosystems behind it is real. Protecting biodiversity is not simply an act of generosity toward nature. It is an investment in the systems that sustain everyone's life. ■
