Far-left leader Melenchon in firing line as France blame-game heats up
PARIS, Oct 22 - Rivals from the centre-left to the far right have turned on Jean-Luc Melenchon and his France Unbowed (LFI) party, accusing them of fuelling France's worst civil unrest in years.
Melenchon, who launched his fourth presidential bid in May and remains the hard left's strongest hope of reaching next year's election run-off, has faced mounting criticism since unrest engulfed several French cities, with opponents saying years of confrontational rhetoric helped fuel tensions now spilling onto the streets.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu sharpened those attacks on Tuesday, telling an LFI lawmaker that the party's "political agenda of instilling violence and chaos in the country was now on full display".
The 75-year-old leader has rejected suggestions that LFI bears responsibility for the unrest, accusing the government instead of failing to address deep-rooted social and economic grievances in France's poorer suburbs.
But criticism has come from across the political spectrum.

Laurent Jacobelli, a spokesperson for Marine Le Pen's National Rally (RN), blamed "the ultra-left, including France Unbowed", as well as what he called uncontrolled immigration, for creating a revolutionary climate.
Marc Fesneau, of centrist party MoDem, said Melenchon had long promoted the idea that "everything must be a battleground".
"When you turn everything into a confrontation, you run serious risks," Fesneau told Reuters.
The attacks underscore both Melenchon's central place in French politics and the unease he provokes as the country heads toward a presidential election expected to pit increasingly strong anti-establishment forces against a weakened political centre.
The unrest has reinforced that contrast, shifting scrutiny onto the hard left while allowing Le Pen to strike a more presidential tone on law and order, an issue that traditionally favours the far right.
Yet with France's political landscape fragmented into three rival blocs and traditional centre-left and centre-right parties struggling, analysts say Melenchon remains a formidable political force.
YOUTH APPEAL AND THE 'NEW FRANCE'
LFI has built its support by mobilising younger voters, many of whom have grown disillusioned with mainstream politics. An IFOP poll for LCI published this month put Melenchon on 16.5%, behind Le Pen's 36% but ahead of all other mainstream candidates.
A Cluster17 poll found nearly half of 18-to-24-year-olds and more than a third of 25-to-34-year-olds would back Melenchon.
That has made him a prominent voice for many students involved in the protest movement and wider unrest that has shaken France in recent weeks.
However, Frederic Dabi, head of pollster IFOP, said the unrest risked reinforcing one of Melenchon's biggest electoral weaknesses: his inability to win over older voters.
"The perception that Jean-Luc Melenchon has been too indulgent towards perpetrators of violence is an absolute red line for a large part of the electorate," Dabi said.
Nevertheless, the party has also built strong support in poorer urban areas and among many voters from immigrant backgrounds who see themselves reflected in Melenchon's vision of a "New France" — a multicultural republic that embraces ethnic and religious diversity and gives greater political representation to communities that often feel overlooked.
Supporters say that reflects social realities rather than identity politics.
"It's the unique synthesis between a programme of revolutionary rupture and the desire to govern the country," LFI lawmaker Hadrien Clouet told Reuters.
Clouet said that meant tackling inequality and reversing a decades-long transfer of wealth towards finance and a narrow oligarchic elite.
Yet critics say LFI often blurs the line between democratic protest and more radical political agitation.
UPRISING LANGUAGE DRAWS SCRUTINY
Melenchon has frequently invoked the language of popular uprising. During the pensions crisis of 2023, he urged supporters to "tear down the citadel" of President Emmanuel Macron's government and has at times spoken favourably of "citizen insurrection" as a democratic force.
Supporters say such language refers to mass political mobilisation, not violence. The party officially advocates non-violent action.
LFI and its allies argue some of the accusations are politically motivated. This week, investigative news outlet Mediapart reported, citing an anonymous intelligence officer, that officials had been instructed to portray LFI as being behind the protest movement despite what the source described as a lack of evidence. The government denied the allegation.
Still, opponents say Melenchon's messaging is often deliberately ambiguous.
"They say they are against vandals, but at the same time they justify masks at demonstrations," said Sylvain Maillard of Macron's Renaissance party. "They never calm things down. They always say it's the police's fault. They want chaos."
Former Socialist President Francois Hollande, however, warned against making Melenchon the sole focus of the debate.
"It is not one political party or one individual that poured fuel on the fire," Hollande told France Inter. While criticising LFI for sometimes drawing an equivalence between rioter violence and police violence, he said: "To fixate on LFI is to fail to see what is happening in the country." REUTERS

Riot-ravaged luxury stores in Paris fear more mayhem, looting
Brands like Louis Vuitton and Hermes boost security measures ahead of Saturday’s protests as residents and firms brace for fresh violence
Across Paris’ toniest shopping districts, luxury boutiques bear the scars of a weekend of rioting that filled social media feeds around the world. Now they are bracing for the possibility of another round.
On the avenue Champs-Elysees, Louis Vuitton’s flagship store has metallic grates protecting its windows that are not there at quieter times, as does the Christian Dior Couture emporium on avenue Montaigne, a nexus of high-end shopping in Paris’ eighth arrondissement. Boarded up windows and doors line the rue Saint-Honore, not far from France’s presidential palace, where mobs on Saturday broke into and looted shops including those of Burberry, Christian Dior perfumes and Guerlain. All three boutiques remained closed on Wednesday, as did a Salomon sportswear store on the nearby boulevard de la Madeleine that was similarly ravaged.
An Hermes boutique on avenue George V, close to the Champs-Elysees, suffered broken windows. The brand’s store in Marseille fared far worse and “won’t reopen any time soon” after being ransacked by rioters, chief financial officer Eric du Halgouet told reporters on a call on Thursday. Hermes has since boosted security measures, he said.

Burglaries soar in Switzerland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
09:38:40 UTC
18:38:40 KST

Burglaries soar in Switzerland
Burglaries are soaring in Switzerland. Thieves are particularly active during the winter months and in French-speaking Switzerland, with the cost per incident reaching record levels, according to an analysis by the Swiss insurance company AXA.
Since 2020, AXA has recorded a steady rise in the number of burglaries per insured household, the insurance company announced on Thursday. In 2025, the company recorded 4% more burglaries than in the previous year and 15% more than in 2022.
The switch to winter time and the resulting earlier onset of darkness contributed to the rise in burglaries. From October to March last year, for example, AXA recorded 45% more offences than during the summer months. December proved to be the month with the highest number of burglaries, followed by November.
More
Geneva super-rich rocked by luxury home burglary spree
On Christmas Eve and New Year’s Eve, the insurance company recorded more than twice as many burglaries as on ordinary days. Burglaries were least frequent between April and June.
The risk of burglary also varied greatly depending on where people lived: between 2019 and 2025, the likelihood of falling victim to a burglary in the canton of Geneva was more than twice as high as the Swiss average. During this period, there were 8.4 burglaries per year per 1,000 households in Geneva. The cantons of Vaud, Basel-City, Basel-Country as well as Jura, Solothurn and Neuchâtel were also affected more frequently than average.
In central and south-eastern Switzerland, however, the risk was significantly lower. In Uri and Graubünden, AXA recorded just one burglary per year per 1,000 households since 2019, while in Glarus the figure was 1.2 burglaries. The Swiss average stood at 3.3 burglaries.
Claims costs at record levels
Average claim costs also rose. Last year, AXA paid out over CHF22 million for burglaries, representing a 9% increase on the previous year and a 60% rise compared with three years earlier. The average claim per incident reached a record high of over CHF7,000 ($8,534) in 2025, making it 30% more expensive than three years earlier.
AXA attributes this trend to several factors. For instance, many people now own increasingly expensive valuables such as smartphones, laptops or e-bikes. Furthermore, these same goods are more expensive than before due to higher prices. Another reason is the significant increase in major claims, i.e. cases costing over CHF30,000. Since 2023, AXA has recorded around twice as many such cases per year as in previous years. Experts at AXA suspect that such complex offences point to organised structures and that professionally executed burglaries and organised crime have increased significantly.

AI uncovers critical flaws in software powering much of the web
The vulnerabilities, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell by Wiz, could allow attackers to take control of affected servers or steal sensitive information without logging in.
According to Wiz’s findings, researchers demonstrated attacks against WordPress, Drupal and Joomla installations. The weaknesses lie in PHP’s core engine, meaning websites can be exposed even when their own application code is secure.
Wiz said AI helped researchers turn complex, longstanding flaws into working exploits and adapt them to different applications.
“With frontier AI models and the right tools, a single researcher completed in a week what previously would have taken a world-class team months of work,” the company said.
The PHP project released security updates on October 21, covering versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. Its official advisory urged users to update immediately and warned that temporary mitigations do not provide complete protection.
The PHP Foundation said the release was brought forward by one day after vulnerability identifiers circulated online before the planned disclosure. Both vulnerabilities carry a severity score of 9.2 out of 10.
The official reports do not confirm widespread website shutdowns. The 70% figure describes PHP’s estimated reach across websites, rather than the proportion confirmed compromised or taken offline.

Kazakhstan and Chinese company advance $1 billion Kuryk port project
Kazakhstan’s Baiterek Holding has signed a memorandum of cooperation with China’s Guoyou Materials Group for a 1 billion US dollars investment project to develop port infrastructure at Kuryk Port. The agreement was signed during the Kazakhstan Global Investment Roundtable 2026 (KGIR-2026) in Shymkent, Qazinform News Agency reports.
A delegation from Baiterek Holding attended the forum, led by Chairman of the Management Board Rustam Karagoishin. The delegation also included Managing Director Anna Lukina and Deputy Chairman of the Board of the Development Bank of Kazakhstan Vladimir Lee.
The forum brought together representatives of government agencies, international financial institutions and foreign companies. The plenary session focused on Kazakhstan’s new investment cycle, including attracting long-term capital and implementing projects in the country’s priority economic sectors.
The memorandum, signed by Karagoishin and Guoyou Materials Group Chairman of the Board Yu Boyang, outlines cooperation on the construction of a multifunctional terminal as part of the first phase of Kuryk Port’s development. Baiterek Holding is considering providing comprehensive support for the project through the financing and other instruments available through its subsidiaries.
Guoyou Materials Group specializes in international trade, logistics and supply chain management. Headquartered in Tianjin, China, the group comprises 33 subsidiaries. In Kazakhstan, it operates through Kazakhstan Guoyou Investment, which is implementing a port and logistics project in Mangistau region.
The first phase of the Kuryk project envisages the construction of a multifunctional terminal with an annual cargo handling capacity of 15 million tons, with scope for further expansion.
The development of port infrastructure is expected to increase cargo transportation capacity along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, strengthen Kazakhstan’s transit potential and expand domestic exporters’ access to international markets.
The business program will continue with bilateral meetings with foreign partners. In particular, Baiterek Holding’s delegation is scheduled to hold talks with Guoyou Materials Group’s management to discuss the project’s financial model, potential support mechanisms and the next steps toward implementation.
Earlier, Qazinform reported modernization of loading bridges at Kuryk Port had cut ferry processing times and increased handling capacity.

It is worth noting that Kazakhstan will also host UEFA’s 51st Congress in Astana on 22 April 2027. The gathering, the organization’s highest governing body, will include elections for the UEFA president and members of its Executive Committee.

Libya seeks to increase grain and meat exports from Kazakhstan
Libya is looking to expand imports of grain and meat from Kazakhstan as the two countries work to strengthen agricultural trade cooperation, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Kazakh Agriculture Minister Aidarbek Saparov and Libiya's Minister of Agriculture and Livestock Abdel Latif Al-Tahir met to discuss prospects for bilateral cooperation, the ministry’s press service reports.
During the meeting, Aidarbek Saparov emphasized the importance of strengthening trade and economic ties with Libya and increasing the presence of Kazakh agricultural products in North African markets.
Kazakhstan is prepared to increase exports of grain, beef and lamb to Libya, he said, adding that the focus is now on turning existing potential into concrete trade projects, expanding business contacts and establishing reliable supply chains.
The minister highlighted Kazakhstan's strong agricultural production capacity. Grain harvests have exceeded 27 million tons for two consecutive years, while oilseed production reached 4.8 million tons and legume output surpassed 1 million tons. Agricultural exports have doubled over the past five years, exceeding 7 billion US dollars.
As stated there, during the last marketing year, Kazakhstan exported 15.3 million tons of grain, up 70% compared to the previous period.
The Libyan minister expressed interest in expanding cooperation, exchanging expertise and creating additional opportunities for mutual trade. Both parties agreed that direct engagement between relevant agencies would help identify the most promising areas for partnership.
The ministers also discussed prospects for exports of Kazakh meat products. Kazakhstan currently has 9.3 million head of cattle and 24.3 million head of small livestock, providing a solid resource base for expanding meat exports.
To support future trade growth, the two sides reviewed veterinary and phytosanitary requirements, food safety measures and procedures for market access. Aligning standards and import conditions will be a key step toward increasing agricultural exports between the two countries.

This Preamp Costs More Than a Fancy Sports Car
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

In the world of hi-fi, there’s “high end,” and then there’s Goldmund. Since 1978, the Swiss manufacturer has produced exquisitely designed, astonishingly high-performance and staggeringly expensive audio equipment. As it nears half a century of proudly uncompromised engineering, its determination to position its products as credible alternatives to jewellery, art, or other pricey indulgences for the superrich shows no sign of abating—quite the opposite.
I was recently invited to Goldmund's headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, to experience the new Mimesis Statement, the company’s flagship analog preamplifier. Goldmund's HQ, incidentally, features the sort of high ceilings, generous use of concrete and glass, and fanatical tidiness that puts me in mind of a Bond villain who's decided to devote their time to audio gratification rather than global tyranny.
In a traditional stereo chain, a preamplifier takes the low-level signals from your source gear, handles volume and input selection, and feeds that clean signal to a power amp to drive your speakers. Most people use an integrated amplifier, one that combines pre-amplification and power amplification in the same box.
Those who want to take things to the next level often separate pre-amplification and power amplification into two boxes—to keep the precious audio signal away from any electrical activity that might compromise its integrity. Goldmund, naturally, is convinced that a preamplifier alone needs to occupy three separate boxes.
The first box, the one with the buttons, dials, and display, houses the pre-amplification electronics. It’s where your source equipment—turntable, network streamer, whatever you fancy—connects using the generous selection of balanced and unbalanced inputs. The other two boxes are external power supplies serving the left and right channels of your stereo signal.
Goldmund reckons this radical separation, along with painstaking internal architecture featuring complete symmetry, voltage regulation stages, and optimized heat dissipation, guarantees signal integrity and utterly consistent operating conditions in all circumstances.
It’s apparently not enough to make a preamplifier with such a low total harmonic distortion figure (0.0002 percent) that it’s extremely difficult to measure in the first place. No, it has to be housed in three chassis with mirrored-glass displays, metal-coated controls, and Goldmund’s signature slender gold-line design flourish to confirm its identity.
In the US, the Goldmund Mimesis Statement analog preamplifier costs $240,000. No, I didn't accidentally add a few zeros. We’re already into “fairly fancy European sports car” territory here, but a preamplifier by itself doesn’t constitute an audio system. For the Mimesis Statement to do its thing, it needs a music input signal, which it will output to a power amplifier. From there, it goes to a pair of speakers.
Thankfully, Goldmund offers plenty of options. During my listen to the Mimesis Statement, it is connected to the company’s Eidos network streamer (yours for $27,000) at one end and a pair of Thelos 9800 power amplifiers (nearly 800 pounds per amplifier, 1,560 watts per channel, an imposing aesthetic, and $500,000 each) at the other. The amplified signal then moves to a pair of Theia Passive four-way floor-standing loudspeakers ($215,000 for two). That’s a total system price of $1,482,000—not so much “sports car” as “very nice apartment, probably with a balcony.” And I haven’t even added in the price of cables.
What does all that money buy you? Well, it most certainly buys a distinctive industrial design language, attention to detail and precision where fit and finish is concerned that’s beyond OCD, hand-soldered circuit boards, military-grade alloys crafted using established Swiss watchmaking techniques, and the sort of overall physical presence that’s more commonly associated with the stuff they build at NASA.
But can a stereo system possibly be worth $1.5 million? The answer has to be “no.” I’ve been a part of the audio equipment appraisal process for over two decades, and I know full well that the law of diminishing returns kicks in long before you’ve spent six figures, let alone seven. But Goldmund isn’t selling you a hi-fi any more than Rolex is selling you a wristwatch—it’s selling you an unmistakable symbol of status, wealth, and success. It’s selling you exclusivity. It’s selling you what it sincerely believes is the pinnacle of artisanal engineering.
And it’s also selling you a serving of detailed, tremendously insightful, and eloquently communicative sound. I am not a prospective Goldmund customer, but if I had the disposable income, I really think I might be.

Russia and Türkiye back South Africa in G20 row with US
Russia and Türkiye have called for South Africa’s swift return to G20 activities after the US barred the country from participating during America’s presidency amid tensions over Pretoria’s domestic policies and foreign ties.
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Aleksandr Pankin and his Turkish counterpart, Berris Ekinci, discussed the issue during consultations in Moscow, according to a Russian Foreign Ministry statement released on Tuesday. They said any changes to G20 membership must be agreed on by consensus, with greater representation for countries of the Global South and East.
The diplomats also discussed preparations for the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta on October 30-31 and the leaders’ summit in Miami December 14-15. They stressed that the forum should remain a platform for equal dialogue on global economic challenges.
Russia and Türkiye are both members of the G20, which comprises 19 countries, the EU, and the African Union.
US President Donald Trump announced in November 2025 that South Africa would not be invited to the Miami summit, saying it demonstrated that it is “unworthy of membership.”
The Trump administration boycotted the G20 leaders’ summit in Johannesburg that month over allegations that the African country allows “horrific” abuses against its white minority, including killings and land confiscation, which Pretoria denies.
Trump also accused Pretoria of refusing to hand over the G20 presidency to a US Embassy representative. South Africa said it would breach protocol for President Cyril Ramaphosa to hand over to a junior diplomat. The transfer later took place at the Department of International Relations and Cooperation between officials of similar rank.
The South African presidency said US punitive measures are based on “misinformation and distortions.” Prior to the Johannesburg summit, Ramaphosa also rejected US pressure against issuing a joint declaration without Washington’s support. He told reporters on November 20 that South Africa “will not agree to be bullied.”
In December, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio extended the exclusion to all G20 meetings during America’s presidency. South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola rejected the move, saying no single member can unilaterally exclude South Africa, a founding member.
Relations have since deteriorated, with the US announcing visa restrictions in September against officials and people it accuses of enabling racial discrimination, uncompensated land seizures, and inciting violence against minorities in South Africa. US Ambassador Brent Bozell also criticized Pretoria’s ties with Russia, China, and Iran, pledging to challenge its “geostrategic drift” toward America’s competitors.
Ramaphosa warned on Monday that South Africa, which already faces steep US tariffs, must prepare for possible exclusion from America’s preferential trade program for African countries.

Expert sees creation of ‘nuclear belt’ as next step in militarization of the Arctic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
09:24:32 UTC
18:24:32 KST

MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. The next stage of Arctic militarization will likely involve the expansion of nuclear military infrastructure across the region and the emergence of a nuclear belt along Russia’s northern borders, encompassing Northern Europe and Greenland, Alexander Stepanov, a military expert at the RANEPA Institute of Law and National Security, told TASS.
He was commenting on the European Commission’s new Arctic strategy, which, for the first time in more than 30 years, places primary emphasis on military development.
According to Stepanov, the EU’s formal adoption of a militarization agenda, driven in part by efforts to exploit the Arctic’s natural resources, will entail a strengthening of NATO’s northern flank. This trend aligns with the strategic priorities of Northern Europe’s military-industrial complexes, Finland and Sweden’s accession to NATO, and the designation of the Baltic and North seas as priority areas for Europe’s geo-economic and military presence.
"The next step will most likely be the ‘nuclearization’ of the Arctic, specifically through the expansion of nuclear military infrastructure into the region. I envisage a ‘nuclear arc’ stretching from the Baltic Sea to the northern seas. A nuclear belt is taking shape in the areas adjacent to the Arctic along Russia’s borders, encompassing Northern Europe and Greenland, which has recently de facto legalized an expanded US military presence. This will likely involve the deployment of nuclear-capable assets, including US strategic bombers and nuclear-powered submarines," Stepanov said.
He noted that the necessary legal frameworks are already being prepared in several countries. In Finland, steps are being taken to remove restrictions on the potential deployment of nuclear weapons, effectively reversing a policy that had been in place since 1987. A similar trend is evident in Sweden, where the country’s leadership has signaled a possible willingness to host nuclear weapons. Lithuania, meanwhile, has removed restrictions at the constitutional level, effectively opening the way for the deployment of nuclear arsenals.
"The Arctic is becoming a key area of interest not only for the United States but also for the European Union, which urgently needs access to hydrocarbons and rare-earth metals. This creates additional threats to the peaceful development of the Arctic and to the maritime trade routes that are vital to Russia," Stepanov concluded.

FACTBOX: What we know about one of largest Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
09:23:14 UTC
18:23:14 KST

MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. Air defense systems on duty intercepted and destroyed a total of 808 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones overnight over Russian regions, the Defense Ministry said.
A nighttime Ukrainian drone attack injured two people in Moscow and one person in Lipetsk.
Kiev’s attempted drone attack on Moscow on Wednesday evening and overnight became one of the largest since the beginning of this year.
TASS has compiled the main details of the aftermath.
Scale
- Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed a total of 808 fixed-wing Ukrainian drones over Russian regions between 8 p.m. Moscow time (5 p.m. GMT) on October 21 and 8 a.m. Moscow time (5 a.m. GMT) on October 22, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
- The Defense Ministry said the drones were shot down over the Belgorod, Bryansk, Vladimir, Voronezh, Kaluga, Kursk, Lipetsk, Leningrad, Oryol, Rostov, Ryazan, Smolensk, Tambov, Tver, Tula and Yaroslavl regions, as well as the Moscow Region, the Republic of Crimea and the Black Sea.
- The attempted Ukrainian drone attack on Moscow from Wednesday evening into Thursday morning was one of the largest of the year, according to TASS’s analysis of data published by Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin on the Max messenger.
- Sobyanin said that 630 drones headed toward the Moscow Region between 8:30 p.m. Moscow time (5:30 p.m. GMT) on October 21 and 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) on October 22.
- On-duty air defense systems destroyed most of the drones at long range and intercepted 163 on their approach to Moscow.
- Seventy Ukrainian drones were shot down over the Tula Region in western Russia overnight, regional Governor Dmitry Milyaev reported on Max.
- A total of 44 Ukrainian drones were destroyed over the Voronezh Region in southwestern Russia overnight, regional Governor Alexander Gusev wrote on Max.
- About 20 Ukrainian drones were shot down over the Lipetsk Region in western Russia, regional Governor Igor Artamonov reported on Max.
- Air defense crews downed 17 Ukrainian drones over the Kaluga Region in western Russia overnight, regional Governor Vladislav Shapsha said on Max.
- Shapsha specified that air defense forces shot down the drones over the Babyninsky, Dzerzhinsky, Zhukovsky, Maloyaroslavetsky, Peremyshlsky, Sukhinichsky, Ulyanovsky, and Ferzikovsky municipal districts, the Kuibyshevsky District, and the outskirts of the city of Kaluga.
- Twelve drones were intercepted over the Oryol Region in western Russia overnight, regional Governor Andrey Klychkov said on Max.
- Ten drones were downed over the Ryazan Region in central Russia overnight, regional Governor Pavel Malkov reported on Max.
Aftermath
- A nighttime drone attack on Moscow injured two people in the capital’s Troitsky Administrative District, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said on Max.
- Medical and emergency personnel are providing the injured with all necessary assistance.
- A drone attack injured a civilian in Lipetsk, a city in western Russia, regional Governor Igor Artamonov reported on Max.
- The injured person is receiving necessary medical care at a hospital.
- Drone strikes also damaged the windows and facades of several private houses and apartment buildings in various parts of Lipetsk.
- Drone debris struck an outpatient clinic on Merkulova Street in Lipetsk. The building was empty at the time, so no one was injured.
- The outpatient clinic on Merkulova Street will remain closed on Thursday, Lipetsk Mayor Mikhail Shcherbakov said on Max.
- The regional government’s press service later clarified that a drone’s unexploded warhead remained on the building’s roof following the nighttime attack.
- Falling drone debris damaged the roofs and facades of several private houses and apartment buildings, as well as one social infrastructure facility, in a municipal district of the Voronezh Region, Governor Alexander Gusev reported on Max.
- A man injured in the large-scale drone attack on Lipetsk underwent surgery and remains under medical supervision, Shcherbakov later added.
- Drone debris also damaged several passenger cars with shrapnel.
- The attack also damaged power supply networks in another district, which now require repairs.
- Emergency response teams are working at the affected sites.
- A drone attack damaged private homes in the Zaoksky District of the Tula Region and in the city of Tula, regional Governor Dmitry Milyaev reported on Max.
- A drone attack damaged four private houses in the Zhukovsky District of the Kaluga Region, regional Governor Vladislav Shapsha said on Max.
- Drone debris damaged the windows and fence of a private house in the Maloyaroslavetsky District.
- The attack also caused minor damage to a power line serving a settlement in the Dzerzhinsky District.
- Repair crews are carrying out restoration work.

Dmitry Yadrov, the ex-head of the Russian Federal Air Transport Agency, Rosaviatsiya, took the post of the Minister of Transport.
The first meeting of the new Cabinet will take place this Thursday, the government’s press service told TASS.

Northern Fleet ships hold drills to protect Russian military facilities in Arctic

MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. A detachment of the Russian Navy’s Northern Fleet warships has held an exercise to defend Russian military facilities in the Arctic, the fleet’s press service reported.
"A detachment of Northern Fleet warships conducted an exercise with a Northern Fleet tactical group to defend Russian military infrastructure facilities in the Arctic," the press service said.
According to the exercise scenario, a group of simulated enemy ships was preparing to seize military facilities on Alexandra Land Island. After receiving the mission, a battalion of the Bastion coastal missile launcher, stationed on the Franz Josef Land archipelago, moved to its designated area. The Bastion crews carried out simulated missile launches against the naval group. The targets were located 350 kilometers away. The surviving enemy landing forces reached Alexandra Land from assault boats.
Exercise events
A detachment of Northern Fleet warships practiced reinforcing the protection and defense of military infrastructure facilities. The crew of a Ka-29 ship-based helicopter, which took off from the Ivan Papanin patrol ship, delivered a counterterrorism team to the island. During the combat exercise, the simulated enemy forces were destroyed. Mobile air defense teams practiced intercepting unmanned aerial vehicles.
The press service emphasized that the tasks of simulating a missile strike by the Bastion coastal missile launcher crews against a detachment of enemy warships, as well as reinforcing and defending the Northern Fleet’s tactical group, were fully accomplished.
The fleet noted that the exercise was conducted using lessons from the special military operation. The exercise took place in challenging weather conditions, including snowfall and winds reaching speeds of up to 30 meters per second. However, the personnel completed all assigned tasks.

Taiwan study links childhood family difficulties to aggression in teenage boys
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
09:10:21 UTC
18:10:21 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — National Taiwan University researchers found that boys who experienced family difficulties during childhood showed greater aggression in their late teens, CNA reported Thursday.
Associate Professor Chang Ling-yin (張齡尹) led the research using data from the Taiwan Birth Cohort Study, which followed children born in 2005. Her team conducted two analyses examining childhood adversity in relation to aggression and sleep.
The aggression study followed 7,800 participants until ages 17 or 18. Researchers found that boys who experienced family problems around age five and a half, or repeatedly during childhood, showed greater aggression in their late teens.
Depressive symptoms at age 12 could partly explain the association. The researchers estimated that these symptoms accounted for 20% to 33% of the link, depending on the timing and duration of family difficulties.
Chang urged parents and professionals to look beyond aggressive behavior when assessing a child’s needs. They should also consider emotional distress and difficulties at home, she said.
The separate sleep analysis tracked 16,666 children from six months to 12 years old. Researchers examined childhood adversity, including parental mental illness, imprisonment, unstable living arrangements, and bullying.
Children who faced such difficulties tended to sleep fewer hours, particularly boys and those aged three to eight. Children with greater emotional resilience generally slept longer, but this benefit weakened when they experienced adversity.
Chang said building children’s emotional resilience was important, but a supportive environment was equally necessary. She called for greater support for caregivers’ mental health and stronger efforts to prevent bullying.
The research team recommended monitoring children’s sleep and family conditions from preschool through early elementary school. It also called for emotional and behavioral assessments to become part of routine child healthcare.
Schools, healthcare providers, and social workers should consider children’s past experiences when offering support, the researchers said. They recommended continued assistance through adolescence while avoiding labels based on family backgrounds or behavior.

Taipower on standby as Typhoon Champi nears Taiwan
Unknown

2026-10-22
09:10:19 UTC
18:10:19 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipower said Thursday it had mobilized 7,400 personnel, along with thousands of vehicles and pieces of equipment, ahead of Typhoon Champi.
Taipower has positioned repair crews and equipment in mountainous areas and outlying islands particularly vulnerable to storm damage, per CNA. It expects stronger impacts in northern and northeastern Taiwan and some mountainous regions, and has stepped up power line inspections and arranged cross-regional support.
The company urged local governments to help clear fallen trees, damaged signs, and other obstructions, as well as reopen roads blocked by landslides, to ensure repair crews can reach affected areas. It said it would monitor wind and rainfall conditions and deploy additional support as needed.
Taipower has also completed flood-protection measures in low-lying areas, including placing sandbags and testing pumping equipment, to reduce the risk of flood damage.
Taipower said that if the typhoon causes power outages, crews will restore electricity in stages, beginning with key substations, followed by main power lines and branch lines. Priority will also be given to restoring power to essential public services and infrastructure.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Air Force plans to spend NT$997.2 million (US$30.63 million) on 18 fire trucks from the US due to a shortage of spare parts for its existing trucks, reports said Thursday.
Taiwan’s Champion Auto Co., Ltd. won the bid to supply the 3,000-gallon trucks by the end of May 2028, per Liberty Times. The new vehicles will help ensure safety at military airfields supporting fighter jet operations, the Air Force said.
The current fire trucks are aging, and in several cases spare parts are no longer available because the vehicles are no longer manufactured, according to the military. Repairing the trucks has become more difficult and expensive each year.

The previous trucks were Oshkosh Striker aircraft rescue and firefighting vehicles made in Wisconsin.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Nvidia said Wednesday it will work with Siliconware Precision Industries Co. (SPIL) to expand optical engine manufacturing capacity 15-fold by mid-2027, citing demand for equipment that connects AI computing infrastructure.
The plan was announced at GTC Berlin as part of a broader effort with suppliers to strengthen supply chain resilience. Nvidia said it aims for “another doubling” of SPIL’s expanded capacity by the end of 2028.
“We are in the midst of the largest infrastructure buildout in human history,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said. “Demand is extraordinary. Capacity is the constraint.”
SPIL will provide packaging, assembly, and testing services to support Nvidia’s growing production of co-packaged optics, which combine optical engines and electronics in a single package to improve data transmission performance and efficiency.
“We’re very excited about bringing co-packaged optics to the AI data center and working with SPIL and others to expand our capacity,” said Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president and general manager of hyperscale and high-performance computing.
In the past two years, SPIL has poured roughly NT$200 billion (US$6.1 billion) in new facilities to expand its advanced packaging capacity in Taiwan.
Speaking at a groundbreaking ceremony for its Yunlin plant, Vice Chair Chang Yen-chun (張衍鈞) said the spending reflects the company’s confidence in demand for advanced packaging over the next five years.
In the same press release, Nvidia also announced an expansion with King Yuan Electronics (KYEC). Nvidia pledged an advance payment of NT$35.8 billion to reserve testing capacity at KYEC’s new US facilities, with high-volume production targeted for April 2027.

Taipei Zoo’s premature orangutan moves from intensive care to nursery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
09:09:44 UTC
18:09:44 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei Zoo’s premature orangutan Yi Bao, also known as Da Bao, was discharged from the animal medical center Monday and moved to a nursery after months of intensive care, with zookeepers continuing to act as surrogate parents.
The baby orangutan was born prematurely by cesarean section on June 29 to Bornean orangutan Ke Yi, along with a twin, Xiao Bao, who died shortly after birth from complications including respiratory distress syndrome. Yi Bao was born with underdeveloped lungs and other organs and initially required intubation and a ventilator, per a press release.
By late July, it had begun breathing independently, allowing the medical team to remove the breathing tube and switch to a high-flow nasal cannula to provide supplemental oxygen. In late September, the team gradually reduced the oxygen flow and concentration as its breathing improved.
After assessments showed stable breathing, heart rate, and blood oxygen levels, the orangutan was discharged from the medical center and transferred to a nursery prepared by keepers. Under round-the-clock care, Yi Bao has gradually gained weight, while activity levels, limb movements, and responses to external stimuli have improved.
For months, the infant lived in an incubator under the care of veterinarians and zookeepers, who took turns feeding, burping, changing diapers, and weighing the orangutan. Caregivers have been bottle-feeding Yi Bao to help develop sucking and swallowing skills.
After feeding, they rock the infant to help it burp and massage its abdomen to encourage bowel movements. Recently, keepers have also begun taking it outdoors on sunny days to get fresh air and sunlight and practice grasping, helping prepare the orangutan for eventual life with its mother.
During the transfer to the nursery, keepers pushed a specially made crib and symbolically folded and discarded a paper fan, expressing their hope that it would continue to grow stronger and would not need to return to the hospital.
Although Yi Bao has made progress, keepers will continue monitoring the infant day and night in the nursery. The next stage will involve gradual physical development and training to strengthen muscles and develop grasping, movement, and other skills.
A reunion with Ke Yi will depend on Yi Bao becoming sufficiently mature and medically stable. Taipei Zoo has previously emphasized that the infant’s health and welfare will determine when that can happen, per the press release.
Bornean orangutans are critically endangered, facing threats including deforestation, habitat loss, poaching, and illegal wildlife trade. Their slow reproductive rate and the long period young orangutans depend on their mothers also make population recovery difficult.

Websites go dark worldwide as AI uncovers flaws in code powering much of the internet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
09:06:38 UTC
18:06:38 KST

Websites go dark worldwide as AI uncovers flaws in code powering much of the internet
- AI found two critical PHP flaws that can let hackers enter servers without a username or password. PHP runs about 70% of the world’s websites.
- Governments, companies and groups like Wikipedia took sites offline or rushed patches after the fix on Oct 21. The US National Security Agency and others urged immediate updates or shutdowns.
- Experts called it a major security crisis, with OpenAI saying it marks “a new phase” for using AI to find software flaws. Some sites may stay vulnerable for days or months, raising phishing and malware risks.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Governments and companies around the world shut down websites as they raced on Oct 22 to protect themselves from hacks after artificial intelligence uncovered critical flaws in a widely used programming language called PHP.
PHP helps run about 70% of the world’s websites, from online stores and news outlets to government services, according to Wiz Research, one of the cybersecurity firms that found the two flaws.
Created in the early 1990s, PHP originally stood for “personal home page” but now means “hypertext preprocessor” and sits underneath popular web design platforms.
“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” a Wiz blog post said.
Increasingly powerful AI models can spot weak points in back-end computer code that have gone unnoticed by humans for years.
That has heightened cybersecurity fears, with the number of software vulnerabilities discovered worldwide in 2026 on track to roughly double the record total in 2025.
PHP programmers released a fix on Oct 21, and the US National Security Agency told organisations to patch their sites immediately or pull vulnerable systems offline, a call echoed by the authorities from Japan to the European Union.
A platform affiliated with China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology urged the same, warning of “two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities with severe impact” in PHP.
On the same day, the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (CSA) issued an alert urging firms to apply the fix for PHP, as the exposed vulnerabilities affect all versions of the scripting language.
Even though there are no known cases of websites in Singapore taken down by hackers, CSA said: “There have been reports of widespread exploitation attempts targeting these vulnerabilities, as well as the development of multiple proof-of-concept exploits.”
When contacted, GovTech Singapore said on Oct 22 that there was “currently no indication” that any Government systems were compromised as a result of the vulnerabilities, and that it is working closely with agencies to implement precautionary measures.
“Where necessary, affected services may be temporarily taken offline to facilitate remediation,” GovTech added. “Such measures are precautionary and do not indicate that the systems have been compromised.”
Only sites that run PHP on their own servers are exposed. Many large platforms are built on other programming languages or use operators that could install the fix quickly and were able to stay online.
Rahat Masood, senior lecturer in cybersecurity at the University of New South Wales, Sydney, described the discovery as “quite devastating”.
It could allow “attackers to get into your servers without any authorisation, without any username or password”, she said.
“Once they are in the servers, they can do anything they want”, from stealing sensitive information to modifying website content, she added, urging institutions to “take it seriously”.
‘New phase’
Government agency sites in countries from Australia to Finland and the Netherlands were among those that went dark, while services from insurance firms, transport operators and media outlets were under emergency maintenance.
Popular apps, including a Pokemon sleep tracker, were also temporarily taken offline while the fix was implemented, while the foundation that runs Wikipedia warned users they could see outages while it addressed the flaws.
“If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now,” the PHP Foundation, which funds developers working on the language, said in a blog post.
Volker Dusch, a security engineer at the foundation, told the Wall Street Journal it was the most serious problem PHP has faced in more than a decade, comparing it to Heartbleed, a 2014 flaw that set off a worldwide rush to patch.
Security firm Calif found the flaws in August using OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model, as part of an OpenAI-funded audit of PHP’s code.
OpenAI said the discovery “marks a new phase, where AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact”.
Wiz, which is owned by Google, said it found them independently weeks later with help from AI models, including Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol.
The flaws were reported privately to PHP’s developers and kept confidential while a fix was prepared.
AI fuels urgency
Details leaked online on Oct 20, a day before the planned release of the fix, prompting the rush to take sites offline before hackers could exploit them.
Steve Kerrison, senior lecturer in cybersecurity at the Singapore campus of James Cook University, said the fear of hackers using AI to quickly and easily exploit the PHP vulnerabilities fuelled the urgency to react.
So far, there has been little evidence of damaging attacks, although data breaches could lead to a wave of so-called phishing attacks, where hackers use personal details to steal passwords, down the line.
Larger institutions, from government agencies to news outlets, should be able to fix their websites relatively fast, Kerrison said, but others may be left vulnerable.
“There are sites, systems and people out there who will have no idea about this and still won’t for days, weeks and months,” Kerrison warned.
That may include user-run blogs that could be weaponised to spread computer viruses, spam people or distribute malicious content, he said. AFP
- Additional reporting by Sarah Koh.

Lula hopes older voters can help power him to victory against Flavio Bolsonaro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22

Lula hopes older voters can help power him to victory against Flavio Bolsonaro
BRASILIA, Oct 22 - Rony Amaral, 71, is terrified right-wing Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro will slash healthcare and pension spending if he wins Sunday's runoff vote, so he is supporting leftist Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva instead.
Amaral and his 91-year-old mother Aisa form part of a growing cohort of voters in fast-ageing Brazil who could play a decisive role in the razor-tight election.
Since 2010, the number of voters over 60 has grown by 74%, according to IBGE, the government statistics agency, and they today make up nearly 25% of Brazil's electorate, increasing their political weight.
Polls show a growing share of them support Lula, who has overseen one of the largest and most generous welfare programs in Brazil's history during his three presidential terms. He is neck and neck with Bolsonaro going into Sunday's vote.
"What I see is a fear among people over 60 that they will be left without care," Amaral said. "Even some on the right share this fear."
According to pollster Quaest, Lula leads among seniors with 48% of voting intention. It found 42% plan on voting for Bolsonaro, who scores less highly than his father, ex-President Jair Bolsonaro, did among the same demographic at this stage in the 2022 presidential election.
OVERLOOKED DEMOGRAPHIC
Despite their growing importance, seniors have traditionally been overlooked in Brazilian campaigns, said Cila Schulman, chief executive of polling firm Ideia.
Lula's campaign is now actively targeting the so-called "Lula generation" — seniors aged over 70, close in age to the 80-year-old president — hoping their support can help overcome the two-point gap between Bolsonaro and Lula in the first round.
The party has launched a website aimed at seniors with the aim of persuading more older voters to go to the polls.
"In the first round, I wasn't enthusiastic, but now that the race is so close, I'm going," said Ana dos Reis, 76, who lives in a low-income neighborhood in northern Sao Paulo. "Who knows, maybe my vote is what Lula needs to win?"
FEAR OF LOSING WELFARE GAINS
Unlike younger voters, who polls show tend to back Bolsonaro, older voters' support for Lula is linked to memories of improvements in living standards, including minimum wage hikes, investment in public health, and other benefits linked to Lula's earlier governments, Schulman said.
"It's a memory that younger people don't have," Schulman said.
Some seniors fear their benefits could diminish under a Bolsonaro government, since he is under pressure to trim Brazil's heavy public debt, and could target welfare spending.
Others are concerned about what a Bolsonaro win would mean for Brazilian democracy, remembering how supporters of former President Bolsonaro attacked government buildings in January 2023 after he lost to Lula in Brazil's last election, according to research from the leftist incumbent's Workers' Party, known as PT.
Near Manaus, in northern Brazil, Olga Darc Pimentel, 78, told Reuters she was deeply concerned by the runoff.
"We remember the terror of the pandemic here," Pimentel said, referring to the elder Bolsonaro's widely criticized handling of the coronavirus outbreak, adding that she plans to vote for Lula and is encouraging others to do the same.
Bolsonaro's campaign did not respond to requests for comment, but he can still count on plenty of elderly voters.
Isaltina Rosa Peixoto, 73, a retired civil servant, said she believes Bolsonaro will continue and refresh his father's legacy.
"I'm not afraid because I know he'll do what's best," she said at a pro-Bolsonaro rally in Rio de Janeiro. REUTERS

The shift will apply to all cars, motorcycles and mopeds operated by state agencies or owned by their staff, except for special-purpose vehicles, the report said.
The information was shared by Bui Hoa An, deputy director of the municipal Department of Construction, at a ceremony Thursday to launch a campaign promoting sustainable transport in the city.
Under the green energy transition roadmap, the city's officials, civil servants and public employees are expected to take the lead, he said, adding that the shift should be accompanied by practical support measures, including charging infrastructure, parking facilities, financial incentives and support programs from vehicle manufacturers.
According to the department, the city currently has about 12.82 million vehicles, with motorcycles accounting for 90 percent.
The city's authorities have drafted a roadmap for the transition to green transport and the establishment of low-emission zones, which is currently open for public feedback, local daily Thanh Nien reported.
Under the draft roadmap, low-emission zones will be introduced from 2028 in the city's central area and the new Thu Thiem urban area, covering a total of about 15.6 square kilometers. ■

World Insights: Japan PM Takaichi's 1st year in power marked by adventurism, predicaments
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:04:41 CST
18:04:41 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi marked one year in office Wednesday, having pressed ahead with a right-wing agenda centered on military buildup and constitutional revision while making little progress on economic and livelihood issues. A series of scandals and growing public discontent have also cast a shadow over her administration.
Analysts said Takaichi's approval ratings have begun to lose momentum amid mounting challenges, warning that her political future would become increasingly uncertain unless she reverses misguided policies and responds to people's concerns.
ACCELERATED MILITARY BUILDUP
A prominent figure in Japan's right-wing political camp, Takaichi has long advocated a hard-line foreign and security policy. Since taking office, her administration has significantly accelerated Japan's military expansion.
On the budgetary and policy fronts, the Takaichi administration has brought forward by two years its target of raising defense spending to 2 percent of gross domestic product, revised the "three principles on transfer of defense equipment and technology" and their implementation guidelines to lift the ban on exports of lethal weapons, and pushed for a centralized intelligence system through the establishment of a national intelligence bureau.
The government also plans to revise by the end of this year, ahead of schedule, the country's three key security documents. Takaichi and senior officials in her administration have repeatedly floated proposals to revise Japan's Three Non-Nuclear Principles, introduce nuclear-powered submarines and even acquire nuclear weapons, testing public reaction to the controversial ideas.
In military deployment and industrial development, Japan under Takaichi has deployed long-range missiles capable of striking enemy bases for the first time. Her administration has also promoted the expansion of the defense industry as a driver of economic growth and technological innovation, while pursuing the development and introduction of additional long-range missiles, hypersonic weapons and "new ways of warfare" designed to ensure sustained combat capabilities, including through the large-scale deployment of unmanned equipment.
To rally public support for its right-wing agenda, the administration has repeatedly played up so-called threats from neighboring countries, with Takaichi going so far as to claim that a contingency involving China's Taiwan could constitute a "survival-threatening situation" for Japan. Seeking external backing, the government has courted other countries, promoted bloc confrontation and frequently held military exercises, heightening regional tensions and drawing criticism and countermeasures from neighboring countries.
On historical issues, Takaichi has also taken steps that critics view as a revival of Japan's militarist legacy. She has sought to restore Japanese military ranks used in World War II for members of the Self-Defense Forces and repeatedly made ritual offerings to Yasukuni Shrine, which honors convicted Class-A war criminals, including performing a remote act of worship on the anniversary of Japan's surrender in WWII.
These moves have raised alarm among Japanese intellectuals and members of the public. Protests against the administration's military buildup have continued across Japan over the past year, while scholars and civic groups have repeatedly warned of the dangers posed by its defense policies and underlying historical views.
Former Japanese Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba criticized the Takaichi administration and right-wing forces for a lack of honesty in addressing the country's wartime history in a television program aired on Monday, saying such an attitude made it impossible to build solid diplomatic relations.
LIVELIHOOD CONCERNS LEFT UNRESOLVED
Takaichi has touted her economic policy as "responsible proactive fiscal policy," but it has yet to provide a meaningful boost to Japan's long-stagnant economy.
Although Japan's economy has expanded over the past year, growth has remained limited. Meanwhile, the fiscal 2026 budget prepared by the administration has reached a record high, rising substantially from the previous fiscal year, with planned government bond issuance also increasing markedly.
Market confidence in Japan's fiscal position has weakened further, pushing government bond yields sharply higher. The yen has continued to depreciate, while domestic prices have kept rising, leaving the Bank of Japan caught between maintaining low interest rates to support economic activity and raising rates to curb inflation and shore up the currency.
High prices have weighed heavily on Japanese households in recent years. Takaichi pledged upon taking office to make tackling inflation a priority, but the problem has shown little sign of easing after a year. A recent Bank of Japan survey found that more than 95 percent of respondents believed prices had risen from a year earlier, while nearly 90 percent expected prices to continue increasing over the coming year.
Japan has also been hit by frequent natural disasters over the past year. Although Takaichi stressed the importance of disaster prevention and relief early in her tenure, her administration has faced criticism for its handling of actual emergencies. Some commentators have argued that Japan's response to the Kumamoto earthquake this year showed no improvement over its response to the 2016 disaster. Takaichi and senior officials also drew widespread criticism for staged publicity during post-earthquake visits and for offering prayers aboard helicopters.
Izuru Makihara, a professor at the University of Tokyo, said the Takaichi administration had prioritized military expansion over people's livelihoods. The substantial increase in defense spending has squeezed funding for social security, education and welfare, with the resulting burden inevitably affecting people's lives, he said.
POLITICAL DECLINE BEGINS TO EMERGE
Takaichi has cultivated an image as a hard-line conservative and has effectively used online platforms and social media to mobilize support among conservative voters. Buoyed by high approval ratings, she dissolved the lower house early this year and called a snap election, in which the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) won more than two-thirds of the seats on its own, dramatically reversing the ruling coalition's previous minority position in both houses of parliament.
The electoral victory, however, appears to have reinforced an increasingly unilateral and overconfident governing style. Public discontent over the LDP's political funding scandals, commonly referred to as the "slush fund" scandals, has persisted, yet Takaichi has continued to appoint lawmakers implicated in the controversies to key positions in her cabinet and the LDP leadership despite public criticism.
Jiji Press recently quoted a senior LDP official as saying that power was concentrated in Takaichi's hands and that people around her "dare not say anything."
Her leadership style has already exacted a political toll. Among those appointed during a cabinet reshuffle in September was Agriculture Minister Kazuo Yana, a lawmaker implicated in the slush fund scandal. Less than a month after taking office, Yana came under intense criticism over a separate controversy regarding alleged remarks about local road budget cuts and ultimately resigned.
Takaichi initially sought to defend Yana after the budget scandal emerged, only distancing herself from him after the affair continued to escalate. The personnel scandal dealt a significant blow to both the prime minister and her administration.
With a limited record of achievements and controversies mounting, public support for Takaichi's cabinet has continued to decline. Recent polls released by several Japanese media outlets showed the ratings falling to new lows. Surveys by Kyodo News and other media organizations also indicated that the proportions of Takaichi's supporters who trusted her personally and viewed her economic policies favorably had fallen substantially from the early days of her tenure.
Meanwhile, a considerable number of her supporters fell into the category of "passive support" -- they only offer their backing because there is currently no better alternative, according to the polls.
Japanese newspaper Shimbun Akahata criticized the developments of Takaichi's first year in office as highly dangerous, arguing that peace, people's livelihoods and fiscal stability had suffered serious damage. Unless the administration corrects its policy course, which places military expansion and constitutional revision at the center of its agenda, contradictions between the government and the public will only intensify. ■

U.S. Army tests Patriot battalion’s readiness in Texas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
09:01:39 UTC
18:01:39 KST

- The U.S. Army’s 1st Battalion, 62nd Air Defense Artillery Regiment held a battalion-wide Patriot readiness exercise at Fort Hood, Texas, on Oct. 21, 2026.
- Soldiers positioned M903 launchers, an OE-349 antenna mast group and an M985 missile transporter to test setup, operation and sustainment.
A U.S. Army Patriot air defense battalion at Fort Hood, Texas, has put its launchers, radars and support vehicles into the field for a battalion-wide readiness exercise, according to photos released by the service on Oct. 21, 2026.
The exercise involves the 1st Battalion, 62nd Air Defense Artillery Regiment, part of the 69th Air Defense Artillery Brigade, and tests the unit’s ability to set up, operate and sustain its Patriot systems while coordinating across all of its firing batteries.
Patriot is the U.S. Army’s main system for defending troops, bases and cities against ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and aircraft. A Patriot battery brings together a radar, a control station, several launchers and support vehicles, and the exercise photos show three key pieces of that chain.
The centerpiece is the M903 launching station, the current version of the Patriot launcher, which can carry up to 16 PAC-3 interceptors, 12 of the newer and longer-range PAC-3 MSE, or four of the larger PAC-2 GEM-T missiles, depending on the configuration. Delta Battery positioned one of these launchers during the exercise, while soldiers from Alpha Battery performed maintenance on another.
Alpha Battery also set up an OE-349 antenna mast group, a raised communications mast that links Patriot units so they can share data and coordinate engagements across a wider area. Charlie Battery positioned an M985 guided missile transporter, a heavy truck fitted with a crane that carries reload missiles to the launchers, a job that becomes critical once a battery has fired its first load of interceptors.
The battalion has recent operational experience in Europe. In late 2023, 1-62 ADA deployed to southeastern Poland, where it operated under the 52nd Air Defense Artillery Brigade as part of the U.S. Army’s air defense presence on NATO’s eastern flank, and in February 2024 the U.S. Army extended that deployment by three months.
The unit has continued regular field training since returning to Texas, including an April 2026 exercise in which Alpha Battery soldiers drilled on equipment maintenance and crew proficiency at Fort Hood.
The October exercise is focused on the full battalion, with the batteries working together to establish their positions, keep the systems running and maintain coordination across the formation through the course of the training.

10:00:55 BST
18:00:55 KST

Canada’s involvement as an observer in the Global Combat Air Programme will further strengthen British bilateral defence cooperation with Canada, building on decades of close collaboration as Five Eyes members and NATO allies, according to answers given in Parliament.
James MacCleary, the Liberal Democrat member for Lewes, asked what assessment the department has made of the potential merits of Canada joining the Global Combat Air Programme as a full participant, and in a second question asked what discussions the Secretary of State has had with his Canadian counterpart on the same point.
Luke Pollard gave the same answer to both: “Canada’s involvement as an Observer in the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP) will further strengthen the UK’s bilateral defence cooperation with Canada, building on decades of close collaboration as Five Eyes members and NATO Allies.”
Canada joined the programme as an observer nation this year, alongside a British commitment of £708 million into the technologies feeding the aircraft. Observer status gives Ottawa access to programme information and a seat from which to judge whether to go further, without the funding share, workshare and governance obligations that come with full membership.
GCAP runs between the United Kingdom, Italy and Japan, with the industrial work carried by Edgewing, the joint venture formed by BAE Systems, Leonardo and Japan Aircraft Industrial Enhancement Company, and the aircraft is intended to enter service in 2035. Adding a fourth full partner would mean reopening the workshare and governance arrangements that took the three founding nations years to settle.
Canada’s interest arrives while Ottawa is reviewing its own fast jet plans, having committed to the F-35 and then reopened the question amid the wider deterioration in its relationship with Washington. A European-led sixth generation programme offers an alternative industrial partnership for a country that builds aerostructures and avionics at scale.

Health Care Costs Are Becoming Unsustainable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
09:00:04 UTC
18:00:04 KST

Amber Kostka, who owns The Stockpot restaurant in Hampton Roads, Va., says she has tried to do right by her employees by offering them health insurance, alongside good wages and a 401k.
But as costs have risen—premiums have roughly tripled since the company first started offering health insurance in 2018—her employees are increasingly telling her they can’t afford health insurance. That’s even though she splits the cost of premiums with employees, which are roughly $400 a month.
Instead, employees are dropping out of the plan and going uninsured, she says. About 35% of her eligible employees now buy the employer-sponsored health insurance, she says, down from 50% prior to COVID. She wants to warn them about the risks of going without insurance, she says, but also knows their finances are extremely tight. “It’s just a cost thing, at the end of the day,” she says. “You can’t stop paying for groceries.”
Her employees aren’t alone. The share of working-age U.S. adults without health insurance rose to 11.2% in 2026, up from 8.9% in 2024, according to new research from the Commonwealth Fund. People don’t have health insurance because the costs of everything—including gasoline, housing, and food—are rising, and they’re deciding they can’t afford to pay for even employer-sponsored plans like Kostka’s. “The whole system just seems like a complete gamble with people’s lives,” she says.
Some people are looking at the price of plans on the Affordable Care Act marketplace and deciding they can’t afford health insurance. Premiums on the ACA marketplaces increased by an average of 58% in 2026 after Congress decided last year not to renew expiring subsidies.
Ironically, these uninsured Americans may be helping drive the cost of health care even higher, fueling a cycle in which health insurance gets more expensive, forcing more people to drop coverage. As hospitals field more uninsured patients, they have to pass the costs of uncompensated care onto someone. “When providers have to provide a lot of uncompensated care, how do they make themselves whole? They raise prices,” says Beth Umland, director of employer research for Marsh, the health benefits consultant company formerly known as Mercer.
Of course, having more uninsured Americans isn’t the only reason costs are rising. A Marsh survey of employers recently found that they expected total health benefit costs per employee to rise 8.2% in 2027, the highest increase since 2003. One reason was that the consolidation of health systems was leading to higher prices, as some systems had monopolies in certain markets. Another was that lower government spending for public health programs was leading to higher costs for private sector plans.
“This is starting to feel—’unsustainable’ is the word you hear,” she says.
Many of the reasons why health care costs are rising may seem minimal until you start adding them up, Umland says. For example, more doctors are using AI scribes in care, which are helping them bill for more services, making care more expensive, she says. A clause of the No Surprises Act, which was passed by Congress in 2020 to protect patients from surprise medical bills but which allows disputes to be settled by arbitration, has also added billions to costs, she says.
There are also increasingly more treatments available for patients, and those treatments are more expensive than the ones they’re replacing, she says. One example: GLP-1s, which may save insurers money in the long run on health costs but which are expensive upfront. “That’s just a whole new category of expense that didn’t exist before,” she says.
In its survey, Marsh found that many employers were planning to pass costs onto employees after years of trying not to do so.
Overall, workers are paying on average about $7,471 annually towards premiums for employer-sponsored family health benefits this year, up 9% from 2025, according to a new employer health benefits survey from KFF. Workers at small firms with less than 200 employees—like Kostka’s—are especially hard hit, paying about $9,687 towards family coverage: $2,847 more than workers in larger firms.
And even as they pay more for health care, the plans available to them are getting costlier to use. The average deductible for employer sponsored plans has increased 34% over the last 10 years, according to KFF.
What employers are doing
Kostka says there have recently been fewer health insurers in her area to choose from. Two years ago, she switched from just buying insurance outright for her employees, which many small businesses do, to self-funding the plan. She was able to do this because her employees are relatively young and healthy, she says, making her risk of incurring big medical costs for cancer or a catastrophic illness relatively low.
But she knows she’s just a major diagnosis away from being dropped from the self-funded plan, she says. “It’s a little bit of a gamble right now,” she says.
There are some things employers can do to push back against high health care costs, says Jim Winkler, chief strategy of the Business Group on Health, which published its own recent survey of employers which projected health care costs to rise 9% in 2027, the highest forecast the group has ever recorded.
Some employers are dropping coverage for GLP-1s for weight loss to save money, he says. Others are trying to drive employees toward what are called Centers of Excellence—essentially hospitals or medical practices with high ratings that may save money in the long-term since employees won’t need to return again and again for care. Some employers are also telling employees to try to find cheap, legitimate medications where they can—from sites like GoodRx, for example—and reimbursing them, rather than getting medications from a pharmacy benefit manager.
“We’re just painting a really challenging picture for health care costs,” he says, “which leads employers down the path of needing to find things to do to take action to mitigate them.”
A small number of employees are deciding not to offer health care at all and are instead offering employees cash to buy their own plans through the ACA marketplace. This option, called an ICHRA (Individual Coverage Health Reimbursement Arrangement) is pushed by Republicans, Winkler says, and was introduced during the first Trump Administration.
Small employers, though, often can only choose from available plans, and if there aren’t many, they don’t have much room to negotiate.
It’s a problem facing Mas Torito, owner of Kokoro restaurant in Denver. He spent close to $150,000 in premium payments for his employees in 2025 and is on track to spend $200,000 in 2026. That’s about 2.7% of revenues; most restaurants only have margins of 2-3%.
“Really since COVID, every single year feels like there are these extra pressures on us,” he says.
Kokoro has been in business for 40 years, and some of Torito’s employees have been working at the restaurant the whole time. He suspects that having an older pool of employees is part of what’s driving his health care costs up every year.
“I think they see the number of claims and costs every year going up,” he says, “and that translates into higher premiums.”
Like Kostka, Torito is committed to offering health insurance for his employees, even as his own costs rise. And like Kostka, he’s hearing from more employees that they can’t afford it. Now, only about 40% of his employees buy the insurance, he says.
“I get it,” he says. “The deductible keeps going up every year, the insurance keeps going up. It’s enough where people are really thinking, ‘Hey, do I want insurance or not?’”

U.S. Air Force F-22 squadron arrives in southern Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
08:54:06 UTC
17:54:06 KST

- U.S. Air Force F-22 Raptors from the 525th Expeditionary Fighter Squadron deployed to Tsuiki Air Base, Japan, for Keen Sword 27 on Oct. 19, 2026.
- Keen Sword 27 runs through Oct. 29 with about 45,000 Japanese and 12,000 American personnel taking part.
U.S. Air Force F-22 Raptor stealth fighters from Alaska are operating from Tsuiki Air Base on Japan’s southern island of Kyushu as part of Keen Sword 27, the largest iteration so far of the biennial U.S.-Japan military exercise.
A photo released by the U.S. military shows an F-22 from the 525th Expeditionary Fighter Squadron parked at Tsuiki on Oct. 19, 2026, the opening day of the exercise. The squadron deployed from Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Alaska, home to the U.S. Air Force’s F-22 units in the Pacific.
The F-22 is a fifth-generation air superiority fighter built to hide from enemy radar and win control of the skies, and its presence at a Japan Air Self-Defense Force base brings one of the U.S. Air Force’s most capable jets into close training with Japanese forces on their home territory.
Keen Sword 27 runs from Oct. 19 to Oct. 29 and involves roughly 45,000 Japanese personnel and about 12,000 American service members, along with close to 300 aircraft and ships. Japan’s Joint Staff said the drills take place at Japanese and U.S. military facilities, civilian airports and ports, and in the sea and airspace around Japan, with the stated goal of training both countries’ forces to respond together to a range of contingencies.
The U.S.-Japan bilateral exercise series began in fiscal year 1985, and Keen Sword 27 is its 18th iteration. The 2026 edition is significantly larger than the 2024 exercise, which involved about 33,000 Japanese personnel, 30 ships and 250 aircraft.
Much of this year’s activity is focused on the defense of Japan’s southwestern islands, which stretch toward Taiwan. On Yonaguni, Japan’s westernmost island about 110 km (68 miles) from Taiwan, the U.S. Marine Corps has deployed its NMESIS ground-based anti-ship missile system and the MADIS short-range air defense system for the first time, while Japan has brought its new Type 25 surface-to-ship missile to the island, with a range of about 1,000 km (620 miles). Japanese officials said no live firing of the Type 25 is planned during the exercise.
The U.S. Navy is also taking part with major surface forces, including the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN 71), the cruiser USS Chosin (CG 65) and the destroyer USS Decatur (DDG 73), which docked at Yokosuka ahead of the drills.
The exercise program covers air and ballistic missile defense, parachute and amphibious landings, casualty evacuation, logistics, facility protection and operations in space and cyberspace. Australia, Canada, France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand and the Philippines are listed as participants this year, several of them stepping up from observer status in 2024, while South Korea and the United Kingdom have sent observers.
The F-22s at Tsuiki are scheduled to train alongside Japanese forces through the end of the exercise on Oct. 29.
