World Insights: Protests reflect France's economic, fiscal dilemmas
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:42:58 CST
14:42:58 KST

PARIS, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- France has been shaken by a wave of protests that began in classrooms and spilled onto the streets. What started as student anger over crumbling schools, overcrowded classes and chronic staff shortages has escalated into violent unrest in several regions.
Soon other groups, angered by soaring energy bills, a cost-of-living squeeze and deteriorating public services, joined the protests. Beneath the disorder lie deeper, intertwined pressures: feeble growth, shrinking fiscal room for manoeuvre and a welfare model under strain, all of which highlight the acute economic and fiscal challenges confronting France.
COST-OF-LIVING SQUEEZE
Soaring fuel prices are one of the drivers behind this concentrated outburst of public anger.
Buffeted by turbulence in global energy markets, French energy prices have kept climbing. The rise has not merely lifted household bills for transport and everyday living; it has also rippled through supply chains and production costs, pushing up prices across the wider economy and further tightening family budgets.
Data released by the French National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (INSEE) on Oct. 15 showed that France's consumer prices rose by 3.1 percent year-on-year in September, up from 2.4 percent in August. The acceleration was mainly driven by faster increases in energy prices, which surged 21.3 percent year-on-year in September, up from 16.7 percent in August.
For French residents who rely on cars for daily commutes, fuel is an unavoidable routine expense. In 2018, a fuel tax hike triggered the nationwide "yellow vest" movement. Years later, fuel prices becoming the focal point of public discontent once again demonstrates that certain long-standing issues affecting people's livelihoods have not been fundamentally resolved.
Sluggish economic growth has further eroded citizens' ability to cope with the rising cost of living. According to INSEE data, the French economy contracted by 0.2 percent in the first quarter of this year, posted zero growth in the second quarter, and household purchasing power per consumption unit declined by 0.6 percent in the second quarter.
LIVELIHOODS VS FISCAL CONSOLIDATION
High public debt and rising borrowing costs leave the French government with limited fiscal leeway to address social grievances.
INSEE data indicates that by the end of the second quarter of this year, France's public debt stood at 119 percent of its Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
Meanwhile, yields on government bonds have continued to climb. French radio station Europe 1 reported that the yield on France's 10-year government bonds exceeded the symbolic 5 percent threshold on Wednesday for the first time since 2002. Rising financing costs will increase the government's debt servicing burden, squeezing space for other public expenditures.
The French government estimates that interest payments on public debt will rise from 79.2 billion euros (88.96 billion U.S. dollars) this year to 91.2 billion euros next year.
Substantial social protection spending also complicates fiscal consolidation efforts. Data show that in 2024, French social protection benefits expenditure accounted for 31.9 percent of GDP, higher than the European Union average of 27.3 percent. As population aging accelerates, spending on pensions, healthcare and related areas faces sustained pressure.
The French government finds itself in a dilemma: on the one hand, in response to rising energy prices and calls to improve public services, it needs to provide subsidies, adjust taxes, and increase public spending; on the other, heavy debt burdens, rising interest expenses, and pressures for fiscal consolidation constrain its ability to expand expenditure.
UNREST-FUELING ECONOMIC RISKS
The protests and violent riots have damaged shops, public buildings, and infrastructure across France. The government estimates that around 3,000 businesses nationwide have been directly affected, with economic losses likely to reach hundreds of millions of euros.
In the longer run, persistent social unrest could also undermine consumer and investment confidence, dragging down an already fragile French economy. The OFCE, an independent economic research institute affiliated with Sciences Po in Paris, released a report on Oct. 14 forecasting that the French economy would grow by 0.4 percent in 2026 and 0.5 percent in 2027, noticeably below the eurozone average. If social unrest intensifies further, it could place additional strain on economic performance.
At the same time, social turmoil creates greater political headwinds for fiscal consolidation. As the 2027 presidential election approaches, debates over public services, social welfare, fiscal austerity and governance are growing increasingly fierce.
Divergent views among political forces on the root causes of social conflicts and their solutions make it harder for the government to build consensus to cut spending and rein in deficits.
On Oct. 19, Gilles Moec, chief economist at French insurance group Axa, told French daily Le Monde that while France's debt problem was serious but manageable, political instability could significantly aggravate the situation.
The deep-seated economic and social contradictions behind these protests cannot be resolved solely through short-term measures. Striking a balance between easing livelihood pressures, restoring economic growth, and managing public debt remains a long-term challenge for the French government. ■

LONDON, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Government websites throughout Europe became unavailable on Wednesday as operators raced to patch two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a scripting language widely used in website development.
The security issue involves two flaws that could allow attackers to trigger an out-of-memory condition, resulting in memory corruption and potentially enabling code execution under certain conditions.
PHP is a widely used, open-source general-purpose scripting language. It runs on servers to generate web content, interact with databases and perform other functions. It is also integrated into a wide range of software products.
Researchers at cybersecurity firms discovered the flaws with the help of artificial intelligence (AI) tools, according to the BBC. The vulnerabilities had reportedly gone undetected for more than a decade.
The incident affected a range of public services. Finland suspended public online government services, while the Dutch cybersecurity agency temporarily shut down its website because of the vulnerabilities.
Britain's Oxford City Council said on Wednesday that its website was temporarily unavailable as a precautionary "because of a worldwide issue affecting the underlying technology."
Britain's National Cyber Security Centre issued an alert on Wednesday, urging organizations to take immediate action to install the available security updates.
The BBC reported that patches were released on Wednesday afternoon.
Dane Knecht, chief technology officer at cloud cybersecurity services company Cloudflare, said on the social platform X that this would not be the last time such vulnerabilities were discovered. AI models, he said, would continue to identify similar flaws in widely used software.
"Maintainers, researchers, providers and governments need a new shared playbook so the response scales with the findings and critical Internet infrastructure gets patched," he said. ■

Colombian frontline police unaware of new AFP anti-drug taskforce
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:38:51 UTC
14:38:51 KST

Colombia's frontline anti-drug police unaware of new AFP international taskforce
In short:
Two Colombian National Police departments say they have no evidence of an agreement with the Australian Federal Police for its newly announced anti-drugs taskforce, based in Bogotá.
Five months after the taskforce's announcement, the departments say drug-related intelligence has not been shared and no substance seizures or arrests have been made in cooperation with the AFP.
The AFP says the taskforce is not yet operational, but agreements have been made that would allow it to "focus on transnational organised crime networks".
Two police departments on the frontline of Colombia's fight against cartels say they have no evidence of an agreement with the Australian Federal Police (AFP) for its newly announced anti-drugs taskforce based in the South American nation.
In May, Commissioner Krissy Barrett announced the AFP and New Zealand Police would fund an international joint investigations team (IJIT) "to gather evidence about illicit drug shipments".
The team would include AFP officers in the capital Bogotá, working with Colombian, US, INTERPOL and Mexican authorities to curb the flow of drugs through the Pacific to Australia, the commissioner said.
A joint investigation by the ABC and the Colombian newspaper El Tiempo can reveal the anti-narcotics department of Colombia's National Police (PNC) has no recorded data that shows subscribed "protocols, agreements, or procedures" relating to the IJIT.
In a response to a freedom of information request filed by El Tiempo and shared with the ABC, the department said drug-related intelligence had not been shared with the AFP and no "operational activities" such as illicit substance seizures or arrests had been made in cooperation with Australian police as part of the IJIT.
The department also said there was currently only a "letter of intent" outlining a "framework for cooperation and exchange of information", which the ABC understands was signed jointly by PNC Major General Jesús Alejandro Barrera Peña and the AFP in August.
"The instrument does not identify the so-called 'IJIT', nor does it establish specific functions, responsibilities or procedures for this department in relation to said mechanism," the department said.
The letter made no connection between the IJIT and joint drug seizures, destruction of narcotics production infrastructure, disruption of criminal groups or the identification of international trafficking routes, the department said.
The ABC understands the IJIT agreement was made with — and expected to be overseen by — the PNC's Office of International Relations and Cooperation (ORECI) and not the anti-narcotics department.
ORECI coordinates Colombia's international policing efforts by connecting other PNC departments to global counterparts, such as the AFP.
The department focuses on strategic decision-making and intelligence and sits above the anti-narcotics and criminal investigations agencies, which oversee frontline drug and domestic crime policing operations.
An AFP spokesperson told the ABC the IJIT was not yet operational, but an "annex" agreement was made with the PNC in August in addition to the letter of intent that would allow the taskforce to "focus on transnational organised crime networks".
The AFP did not specify when the IJIT would become operational.
In a separate response shared with the ABC, the PNC's criminal investigations department said it had no data that was able to determine whether the AFP was involved, supported, funded or shared intelligence in 174 drug trafficking investigations conducted between January 1, 2025 and October 6 this year.
The department said those figures were collated based on aggregate numbers of cases and investigations outcomes that did not list specific agencies involved.
But the department also said it had no knowledge of Colombian anti-narcotics intelligence being used to "identify, locate, track, monitor or intercept" suspected drug trafficking vessels in the Pacific Ocean or Caribbean Sea as part of the IJIT.
The revelations follow ABC questions posed to the AFP in June about the IJIT's allocated budget, operational commitments and measure of how it would be deemed successful, as part of a separate Freedom of Information request.
In response, the AFP said it had 60 documents that would answer the questions.
The AFP declined to release them, citing national security and international relations concerns, and said at the time that the IJIT was "still in the negotiation phase".
It also said publishing the information would be harmful to relations between Australia and Colombia, or could divulge confidential details regarding how AFP officers operate.
In this year's federal budget, more than $1.16 million was allocated to the AFP for "ordinary annual services" in policing assistance efforts abroad and on Australian external territories in 2026-27.
That figure is expected to rise to $1.4 million next year, before dropping to $1.01 million and $1.03 million in the following two years.
But the budget does not detail how much is set aside specifically for the IJIT.
Commissioner Barrett said 17 tonnes of illicit drugs, mostly cocaine, have been seized by "local and international" police since January this year and stopped from reaching Australia through the Pacific.
The ABC understands, to July this year, most of the offshore seizures were made in French Polynesia, AFP officers were not physically involved in any interceptions and none were in Australian territorial waters.
The PNC this month announced an Australian-Iranian national, Arash Ebrahimi Far, was detained in Colombia as a subject of an INTERPOL Red Notice for alleged drug trafficking and money laundering, which was not believed to be related to the IJIT.

Pentagon extends Raytheon deal for missile defense radars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:33:32 UTC
14:33:32 KST

- The Missile Defense Agency extended Raytheon’s AN/TPY-2 radar sustainment contract by two years, raising its ceiling from $2.6 billion to nearly $3 billion.
- The ordering period now runs to Oct. 31, 2028, with $112.3 million obligated at award.
The Missile Defense Agency has extended Raytheon’s contract to operate and maintain the U.S. military’s AN/TPY-2 missile defense radars for two more years, adding $394 million to the deal and lifting its ceiling to nearly $3 billion, the Department of War announced.
The sole-source modification raises the maximum value of the contract from about $2.6 billion to $2.999 billion and keeps the ordering period open until Oct. 31, 2028, with $112.3 million in fiscal 2027 operations and maintenance, research and development, and procurement funds obligated at the time of award.
The AN/TPY-2 is a transportable X-band radar that sits at the heart of the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense system, better known as THAAD, and also serves as a standalone early warning sensor for U.S. ballistic missile defense. The radar can work in two ways: deployed far forward to spot ballistic missiles shortly after launch and pass tracking data to other defenses, or as part of a THAAD battery to track an incoming warhead and guide interceptors to hit it as it descends.
Under the extension, Raytheon will continue to run and support the radars from its facility in Woburn, Massachusetts, and at radar sites in the United States and overseas, where the company’s field teams help keep the sensors operating around the clock. The work combines cost-plus-incentive-fee, cost-plus-fixed-fee and firm-fixed-price contract items, and the Missile Defense Agency at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, is also extending the task orders that fund individual radar sites.
The U.S. Army fields eight THAAD batteries, each with one AN/TPY-2 radar, including units at Fort Bliss, Texas, in South Korea and on Guam, while forward-based radars have been stationed at sites including the Shariki area in Japan, Türkiye, Israel and Qatar. The radar is also sold abroad, and in 2020 the Missile Defense Agency awarded Raytheon a production contract worth up to $2.3 billion for seven AN/TPY-2 radars for Saudi Arabia, built with gallium nitride components that extend the radar’s range and sensitivity.
The radars have come under direct fire during the war with Iran this year, and satellite images analyzed by CNN showed that a THAAD radar at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan was apparently destroyed by an Iranian strike in early March, along with damage at radar sites near Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia and in the United Arab Emirates. Each AN/TPY-2 costs hundreds of millions of dollars and takes years to build, which makes keeping the existing fleet working a priority for the Missile Defense Agency while new radars are produced.
The original contract was awarded to Raytheon on a sole-source basis in 2018 as the radar’s designer and builder, and the extension was likewise issued without competition. The new ordering period gives the Missile Defense Agency two more years to keep the current support arrangement in place before it decides how to handle long-term sustainment of the AN/TPY-2 fleet beyond October 2028.

British submarine hunters delayed by Norway frigate sale
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:30:04 BST
14:30:04 KST

The Royal Navy will not meet its requirement for eight frigates fitted with the Sonar 2087 towed array until 2037 if two Type 26 frigates being built for Britain are sold to Norway, and the government appears to have taken a conscious decision to prioritise defence exports over sovereign capability, according to a report by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, published its findings following an inquiry that took evidence between March and July this year and included visits to Norway, Denmark and Greenland.
Dhesi said: “The UK needs to be willing to address a hard truth: it does not currently have all the capabilities to operate successfully in the High North. Russian submarine and sabotage forces in the High North pose direct risks to the North Atlantic and the UK, including the nuclear deterrent. Despite this, the Ministry of Defence has accepted a serious anti-submarine warfare gap. Publicly available evidence of low availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines calls into question whether the UK can meet its commitments in the High North.”
The report states: “Analysis suggests (Figure 4) Sonar 2087-towed array equipped frigate numbers could remain as low as five vessels for the next three years. This assumes two Type 26 frigates being built for the Royal Navy are sold to Norway, as the latter has ordered at least five Type 26s for £10 billion—which the government says will sustain 4,000 UK jobs. This reinforces the government’s goal to use defence exports to contribute to its Plan for Change, based around its three foundations of good government: economic stability, secure borders and national security.
However, Norway wants its first ship in service by 2029–30. Based on this scenario the Royal Navy will take until 2037 to meet its requirement for eight frigates to be equipped with the Sonar 2087 towed array sensor. In this case the government seems to have taken a conscious decision to prioritise defence exports over sovereign capability.”
A chart published with the report shows the combined Type 23 and Type 26 anti-submarine frigate line falling to two vessels in 2031 before recovering to eight by 2037.
Norway selected the Type 26 in 2025 to replace its Fridtjof Nansen class, in an agreement the Ministry of Defence valued at £10 billion and said would sustain four thousand British jobs. The ships are being built by BAE Systems at Govan and Scotstoun on the Clyde, and Britain’s own order is for eight.
The committee elsewhere records that the Royal Navy has a requirement for eight of its thirteen frigates to carry the Sonar 2087 towed array, that all five remaining Type 23 frigates are fitted with it, and that HMS Richmond and HMS Iron Duke were both decommissioned in mid-2026.
On the wider relationship with Norway, the report describes the 2025 Lunna House agreement and the Type 26 purchase as “therefore strategically more significant than a conventional defence export”, and says a joint class of British and Norwegian anti-submarine frigates “should improve NATO’s ability to detect and track Russian submarines moving from the High North into the North Atlantic”.
The committee’s recommendation asks the government to set out how major naval export programmes, including the Norway agreement and any future uncrewed maritime systems, will support High North deterrence while protecting Royal Navy capabilities, including an assessment of their effect on British delivery timelines, industrial capacity, shared training, sustainment, interoperability and the availability of critical anti-submarine warfare capabilities.
In written evidence to the inquiry the Ministry of Defence described anti-submarine warfare as a core strength of Britain’s armed forces. The government is expected to respond to the report within two months.

U.S. Navy pays Johns Hopkins to find its subs’ weak spots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:28:03 UTC
14:28:03 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Johns Hopkins APL a contract worth up to $47.7 million to study vulnerabilities of submarines and seabed warfare assets.
- The work supports the Navy’s Undersea Security Program and runs through October 2031, managed by Strategic Systems Programs.
The U.S. Navy has hired the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory to look for weaknesses that adversaries could exploit against American submarines and other assets used in subsea and seabed warfare, under a contract worth up to $47.7 million announced by the Department of War on Oct. 21.
The laboratory in Laurel, Maryland, will provide research and development support for the Navy’s Undersea Security Program, studying both present and future technological and operational vulnerabilities, with work running until October 2031.
The contract went to the lab through full and open competition under a Broad Agency Announcement, and it is managed by the Navy’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive Strategic Systems Programs in Washington, D.C., the office that runs the Trident II D5 missile carried by the Navy’s ballistic missile submarines. About 80 percent of the work will take place at the laboratory in Laurel and the rest in Washington, and the Navy obligated only $50,000 in fiscal 2026 research and development funds at the time of award, with the remaining money to come through future task funding.
Keeping submarines hidden has been one of the core missions of the Applied Physics Laboratory for decades, since the Navy’s work on ballistic missile submarine security began with a 1968 Pentagon directive to investigate how vulnerable the boats were to detection. That effort grew into a long-running program that studies how a submarine could be found through sound, wakes, magnetic signatures, radar and infrared sensors, as well as through predictable patrol routines and lapses in operational security, and the laboratory has supported the Navy’s development of patrol tactics for its nuclear deterrent fleet.
The new contract widens that focus to the seabed, where cables, pipelines, sensors and other infrastructure have become a growing concern for NATO navies. Russia’s Main Directorate of Deep-Sea Research, known as GUGI, operates specialized submarines and deep-diving vehicles able to work on the ocean floor, and Western officials have accused Russian vessels of mapping undersea cables in European waters, while several Baltic Sea cables were damaged in incidents blamed on ships dragging their anchors.
The work also comes as the Navy prepares to replace its Ohio-class ballistic missile submarines with the new Columbia class, the most expensive shipbuilding program in its history, and in November 2025 General Dynamics Electric Boat received a $2.28 billion contract modification for advance work on five more Columbia-class boats. The first Columbia-class submarine is now tracking for delivery in 2028, and the new boats are expected to carry the sea-based leg of the U.S. nuclear deterrent into the 2080s.
The Applied Physics Laboratory is one of the Pentagon’s largest university-affiliated research centers, and its defense work has been expanding quickly, with DARPA awarding the lab a sole-source contract worth up to $499.8 million for engineering and research work just a week earlier. The Undersea Security Program contract combines cost-plus-fixed-fee and cost-no-fee work, and the specific tasks the laboratory will carry out over the next five years will be set through individual funding actions by the Navy.

Ramirez introduced the bill, H.R. 3565, last year with Democrats Sara Jacobs, Pramila Jayapal and Mark Pocan.
The legislation would block transfers to Israel of BLU-109 bunker-busting bombs, MK80 series bombs, GBU-39 small diameter bomb variants, Joint Direct Attack Munitions, SPICE gliding bomb assemblies and 120mm tank ammunition and 155mm artillery ammunition, including white phosphorus munitions.
Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others since October 2023, as well as caused widespread destruction affecting approximately 90 percent of civilian infrastructure.
According to the latest figures from Gaza’s Health Ministry, Israeli violations of a ceasefire agreement in place since October 2025 have killed 1,534 Palestinians and injured 5,486 others.

Flights will soon take off from Australia's newest airport. Here's where they're going
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:01:58 UTC
14:01:58 KST

In Brief
- Sydney's second airport opens on Sunday, offering 24-hour flights and new domestic and international routes.
- Seven airlines have signed on, taking jetsetters to both domestic and international locations.
Sydney's second airport is about to open, marking the first new international airport built in Australia in more than 50 years.
Western Sydney International Airport, officially named Nancy-Bird Walton Airport, will welcome its first passengers on 25 October.
Located at Luddenham near Badgerys Creek, about 45km from Sydney's CBD, the airport is expected to reshape travel across Greater Sydney, offering an alternative to Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport and providing airlines access to a 24-hour aviation hub.
From flight routes and transport links to where it's located and how it differs from Sydney Airport, here's everything you need to know.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Where can you fly from Western Sydney International Airport?
Western Sydney International Airport will have one significant advantage over Sydney's existing airport: it can operate around the clock.
Unlike Kingsford Smith Airport, which is subject to an overnight curfew between 11pm and 6am, flights at the new airport can arrive and depart 24 hours a day.
That flexibility has helped attract domestic and international carriers, with seven airlines already committing to operate services from the airport.
Here's where they'll fly:
- Qantas: Four weekly flights to Melbourne and Brisbane from March 2027.
- Jetstar: Four weekly flights to the Gold Coast, three weekly flights to Brisbane, and daily services to Melbourne.
- Qatar Airways: Three weekly flights to Doha's Hamad International Airport from 15 December, with additional services planned in coming years.
- Air New Zealand: Three weekly flights to Auckland from 26 October.
- Singapore Airlines: Daily flights to Singapore from 23 November.
- Fiji Airways: Three weekly flights to Nadi.
- Vietjet Air: Two weekly flights to Ho Chi Minh City from 10 January 2027, increasing to three in March 2027, plus four weekly flights to Bangkok via Vietjet Thailand.
Emirates has also been cleared to add seven weekly flights from the airport but is yet to announce a schedule.
Airport operators expect additional airlines and destinations to be announced as passenger numbers grow.
How do you get to Western Sydney International Airport?
One of the biggest questions facing travellers is how they will reach Sydney's newest airport.
Unlike Kingsford Smith Airport, which is connected to Sydney's rail network, Western Sydney International Airport will initially rely on road connections and bus services while major transport infrastructure is completed.
A Sydney Metro line linking the airport with St Marys is under construction and expected to open next year.
Until then, passengers can connect to St Marys via a free airport shuttle bus, or travel by express coach, public bus, taxi, rideshare or private vehicle.
If you're driving, the airport is accessible via the new toll-free M12 Motorway and is about an hour from Sydney's CBD, depending on traffic conditions.
An express shuttle service will also connect the airport with Parramatta, Sydney CBD and Sydney Airport.
Current fares are:
- Parramatta: $25 one way, $45 return.
- Sydney CBD: $55 one way, $80 return.
- Sydney Airport: $65 one way, $90 return.
From St Marys, passengers can connect to Sydney's wider rail network, though journeys to some parts of Sydney may take considerably longer than travelling via Kingsford Smith Airport.
State-run bus services will also link the airport with centres including Penrith, Liverpool, Campbelltown, Mount Druitt and Leppington.
For those driving, the airport has about 6,000 parking spaces available on site.
Where is Western Sydney International Airport?
Western Sydney International Airport is located at Luddenham, near Badgerys Creek, in Sydney's west.
The airport is approximately 45km from Sydney's CBD, 20km from Penrith and 15km from Liverpool.
It sits within the broader Western Sydney Aerotropolis precinct and will become Sydney's second major airport when passenger operations begin on Sunday.
Why is Western Sydney International Airport a big deal?
Plans for a second major Sydney airport have been debated for decades as governments looked for ways to meet the city's growing aviation demand.
The airport is expected to become the centrepiece of the Western Sydney Aerotropolis, a major business and infrastructure precinct that planners hope will drive jobs, investment and development across the region.
When it opens, Western Sydney International Airport will be able to handle up to 10 million passengers a year.
That capacity is expected to expand significantly over coming decades, with airport operators forecasting it could eventually handle 82 million passengers annually.
While flight options will initially be limited, airport operators expect additional airlines and destinations to be added as the airport grows.
Will Western Sydney International Airport make airfares cheaper?
Aviation experts have previously told SBS News that the change will fundamentally alter the country's airfare market and could drive prices down for consumers by opening up air travel capacity.
However with rail links that may not be ready until 2028, getting to the airport could theoretically incur a cost that would be similar or more than the savings on a ticket.

There is no current requirement for the procurement of new 105mm artillery barrels for the Light Gun, and consequently no plans to restore domestic production capacity or to deliver British-designed barrels from Sheffield, according to an answer given in Parliament.

The design was exported widely and the American M119 is a licensed version of it.
Barrel forging in Britain has been the subject of a deliberate rebuild over the past two years, and this publication has covered the work to rebuild the ability to manufacture large calibre guns and the point at which the first British made artillery barrels headed to Ukraine. That programme runs on 155mm, the calibre used by the AS90 and by the Archer system bought to replace it.

Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield, and what they mean to Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
04:52:53 UTC
13:52:53 KST

Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield, and what they mean to Ukraine in the war against Russia
Over the past week, Ukraine has received a stark reminder of its growing dependence on uninterrupted access to Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield networks in its drone-heavy war against Russia, now in its fifth year.
Ukraine has a fraction of Russia's resources, but its aggressive development of drone warfare on defensive and offensive fronts has helped it endure an onslaught from its much bigger adversary, which invaded Ukraine in early 2022. That was true until last week, when Ukraine reported a throttling of the Starshield network that was causing its drones to stop midflight and fall out of the sky.
The two SpaceX networks operate on a constellation of thousands of low-Earth satellites — Starlink is the commercial version, while Starshield is a military product licensed to the U.S. government and its partners, among them Ukraine.
Kyiv's reliance on drones has made Starlink and Starshield nearly indispensable to its arsenal. When Ukraine experienced a disruption to those networks, it lost the shield of interceptors and drones that offered some protection against Russian drone and missile strikes.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy believes Musk throttled Starshield at the request of U.S. officials, though the world's richest man has denied any role and said it's the U.S. government that controls the military-grade network. President Trump has also denied he's responsible for slowing the network. However, CBS News reported Tuesday that Musk was behind the disruption, though a number of questions remain unanswered.
There has also been conflicting information about whether full access to the networks has been restored. As of Wednesday afternoon, Starlink remained throttled, Zelenskyy's office confirmed.
Here's what's known about Starshield and Starlink — and their role in the Ukraine war.
What happened in Ukraine?
On Oct. 13, Ukraine's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment, making it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones, officials and soldiers told CBS News.
Ukrainian soldiers said they noticed "speed limits" had been imposed on their use of SpaceX's Starshield internet dishes, the military-grade Starlink dishes that Ukrainians strap onto their drones so remote pilots can maintain their connection with the unmanned aircraft as they fly toward Russian targets.
Access was restricted by turning off dishes on Ukrainian drones flying above a certain speed, causing them to fall out of the sky. Ukraine's Ministry of Defense sources said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions without informing them beforehand.
Zelenskyy said Saturday the speed limits had prevented Ukraine from using Starshield to shoot down Russian Shahed attack drones.
What are Starshield and Starlink?
Starshield, the military-grade satellite network, runs on the same constellation of satellites as its civilian sister, Starlink, but has fewer technical limitations and more advanced security features. Both are operated by Musk's company SpaceX.
The U.S. government pays SpaceX to license the use of Starshield and controls who can access the technology. Its use has been limited to Ukraine and occupied territories. It is not available in Russia.
There is no working alternative to Starlink, as no direct competitor approaches Starlink's coverage of 11,150 satellites. Amazon Leo aims to compete, but at this point, it has under 400 satellites in low Earth orbit and has been hampered by the launchpad explosion of a Blue Origin rocket in May.
Regular Starlink terminals have a 70 km/hr (43.5 mph) speed cap, which is the speed at which internet can be used in a vehicle in motion. At rates exceeding the cap, the internet degrades and is no longer usable.
Starshield has no artificial speed cap and is known to work at speeds of at least 160 km/hr (99.4 mph). Starshield-equipped strike drones cruise at 160 km/h or more, and they're the backbone of Ukrainian mid-range strikes.
During the throttling over the last week, Ukrainian units reported link drops at speeds as low as 90 km/hr (55.9 mph), making those drones inoperable. The degradation of Starshield is estimated to have cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses, according to an analysis by Dimko Zhluktenko, a drone pilot and analyst in the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
On Oct. 15, some Ukrainian officials said that the Starshield restrictions had been lifted. But Zelenskyy told NBC News on Sunday the maximum speed was still 161 km/hr.
Zelenskyy told Fox News on Wednesday that the service was "still limited," but he added that Secretary of State Marco Rubio told him he would "work with his team on this to unblock" it.
Is Ukraine using Starshield or Starlink?
It uses both. Starlink has been providing internet service to Ukrainian civilians and military forces since 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, according to Reuters.
Initially funded by private donors and a U.S. foreign aid contract, SpaceX won a Pentagon contract to pay for Starlink for Ukraine in 2023, along with a contract for 500 Starshield terminals.
In August 2024, SpaceX signed another Defense Department contract to expand Starshield usage to 3,000 terminals for the front lines, Bloomberg reported.
Beyond communicating with and guiding drones over long distances, Starshield also serves another function: It connects every sensor and weapon system on the battlefield. Disruptions to the service have an impact that can be compared to an office having to function without being able to connect to Wi-Fi.
Ukraine's military uses Starlink for general battlefield communications, and Ukrainian civilians rely on it for communications needs, too.
On the Russian side, the Kremlin had also been using Starlink until February, when SpaceX cut off its access. As a result, Ukraine gained more than 150 square miles of territory.
Musk and throttling Ukraine's access to Starshield
CBS News reported Tuesday that a decision by Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, though it remains unclear how Musk's order to curtail service was executed.
Musk had spoken with administration officials multiple times, seeking clarity on the president's thinking on the matter. He has in the past expressed distaste for the perception that his company could be seen as profiting from the Ukraine war.
The temporary restrictions came as a surprise to some Trump administration officials, who said neither Mr. Trump nor the Pentagon had specifically ordered any limits meant to deliberately disrupt drone operations and battlefield communications.
The president said Monday he was seeking information about who had ordered the slowdown. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday denied the Pentagon had manipulated the service, saying, "We haven't made any directives or anything like that."
Can Elon Musk stop the use of Starlink and Starshield?
Musk has not admitted to imposing restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starshield.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," the world's richest person wrote on X.
He added that Starlink is a "commercial service," writing that it is "limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action."
Rubio, however, seemed to attribute the network constraints to Musk.
"The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr. Musk," Rubio told reporters in Mumbai on Wednesday.
Within a few minutes, though, he seemed to concede that Starshield was different: "We don't control what a private company — how they decide their product can be used. Now, if they're in a contract with the United States military, like Starshield, that's a different matter, because that's something we are purchasing and using for our use."
Intelligence-sharing
At around the same time as the Starlink and Starshield disruptions, Ukraine also did not receive warnings from U.S. intelligence about major Russian strikes.
Ukraine relies on a mixture of American sensors, aircraft, surveillance and human intelligence to map Russian positions and launch sites.
The early warning system, which is distinct from the SpaceX products, notifies Ukraine when Russia has launched a ballistic missile in its direction. It failed in at least two instances, on Oct. 13 and Oct. 18.
On Oct. 13, Zelenskyy said Ukraine "received no advance warning" when Russia launched a ballistic missile barrage. That overnight attack targeted energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv and Kharkiv, killing six people and leaving some 600,000 without power.
Ukrainian sources said U.S. officials said the warning system had failed due to "bad weather." Ukrainian officials expressed doubt about that explanation and accused the U.S. of "playing" with the system. By 3 a.m., that system seemed to have been restored.
Then on Monday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had been hit by another wave of Russian missile and drone strikes, "and again, there was no warning from partners."
A senior Pentagon official told CBS News Monday there had been "no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."
By Wednesday, however, the warning system appeared to have been restored: "Now intelligence works. Thank you so much. That was crucial for us," Zelenskyy said on Fox News.
Rising pressure to end the war
Deliveries of key Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine have also slowed, Ukraine has said.
Rubio on Tuesday called interceptors the "most in-demand product right now in the defense field," and said that "when a country doesn't get interceptors from the United States, it's not because we're denying. We have our own needs, too."
"There's nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine," he said. "It's simply a balance between our obligations."
Mr. Trump has grown impatient with the more than four-year-long war. He has sought to portray the ongoing Ukraine war as the reason for high energy prices and has vented his frustration with Zelenskyy more frequently in recent weeks, accusing him of not doing enough to end it.
He waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel earlier this month in an effort to ease pressure on the price of the commodity, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. And Mr. Trump also waived sanctions on Russia last week.
Mr. Trump said earlier this month that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire." Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The Russian government never confirmed that it had agreed to a ceasefire.
Mr. Trump told reporters Tuesday that Russia keeps "grinding away" and is more capable of sustaining casualties than Ukraine, arguing "it's time" for Zelenskyy to make a deal.

India hit out at the UN rapporteur for bias in a counter-terror report after UN rapporteur Ben Saul described Dawood Ibrahim as leader of "India-based" D-Company criminal gang with terrorist ties
NEW DELHI: India has pushed back against a United Nations special rapporteur’s description of fugitive gangster Dawood Ibrahim’s D-Company as an “India-based” criminal group, flagging “glaring inaccuracies” in a counter-terrorism report. India warned that such factual errors, coupled with a lack of accountability for UN experts, risk undermining the credibility of the world body.Raghoo Puri, first secretary at India's Permanent Mission to the UN, raised the objections on Wednesday during a meeting of the Third Committee of the UN General Assembly, responding to a report by Ben Saul, the special rapporteur on the promotion and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms while countering terrorism.
“My delegation has been pointing out in other forums as well our serious concern at the unacceptable situation of the SR (Special Rapporteur) releasing reports with factual inaccuracies, while not being held accountable for them,” Puri said.
He argued that the publication of reports containing factual errors without adequate accountability left member states with little scope to respond before the findings entered public discourse.
According to news agency ANI, he added, “It is in this context that we would like to point out some particularly glaring inaccuracies as far as my country is concerned.”Puri took issue with Saul's report, which stated that the UN Security Council had listed the leader of “the India-based D-Company” in 2003 for association with Al-Qaeda.“Read in isolation, this line paints a very different picture from the actual reality,” Puri said, rejecting the description of the criminal organisation as India-based.He said Ibrahim and his organisation had been wanted in India in connection with terror attacks since 1993, adding that the circumstances were documented in the UN Security Council's Al-Qaeda sanctions listing.“This is clearly written in the narrative summary of reasons of listing under the 1267 sanctions regime,” Puri said.
“Not mentioning this fact is regrettable, and such incompetence on part of special mandate holders does this organisation tremendous harm,” he added.Seeking to clarify the timeline, Puri said, “Let me correct it for the record. This individual fled India much before the 2003 listing, and it was during this period from outside our country that he was listed for being associated with Al Qaeda and with Osama bin Laden.”Puri also said the UN listing placed Ibrahim in the same country where Al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden was found and killed, referring to Pakistan. Bin Laden was killed by US Navy SEALs in a raid in Abbottabad in 2011.

Cuban FM slams U.S. strong-arm diplomacy ahead of key UN vote
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:50:33 CST
13:50:33 KST

HAVANA, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez on Wednesday denounced the United States' unprecedented campaign of coercive diplomacy to pressure third countries to vote against a Cuban-backed draft resolution that condemns Washington's decades-long trade embargo against the Caribbean island.
The draft resolution, titled "Necessity of ending the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States of America against Cuba," is to be put to a vote at the United Nations General Assembly on Oct. 28, the 34th time for such a vote.
This year's draft resolution is the first to address the fuel and energy blockade imposed by Washington in January 2026, and the "collective punishment" it inflicts on all Cubans, Rodriguez told a press conference.
The resolution is a response to the extreme ramping up of the embargo, which has cost the small island more than 178.7 billion U.S. dollars in economic losses over the course of more than six decades, he said.
U.S. political pressure and economic threats "aim to compel those sovereign states to change their position regarding this draft resolution, to alter a state policy that many of them have, in the exercise of their sovereignty, maintained for decades," Rodriguez said.
Washington's methods, including threatening to impose sanctions and punitive tariffs, suspend cooperation programs, deny visas, and interfere in electoral processes, amount to "genuine political violence, coercion, and blackmail," the minister said.
The United States seeks to obscure the fact that a superpower "is committing an atrocious and ongoing act of abuse against a small, peace-loving nation, an attempt to destroy the nation's very fabric, constituting an act of genocide as defined under the Geneva Convention," Rodriguez added, saying that the debate at the UN General Assembly is not a bilateral matter, as it will address the sovereign rights of all peoples on the planet.
In January, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order imposing sanctions and tariffs on countries and entities that export or supply fuel to Cuba, a move Havana denounced as an "energy siege."
"This is an attempt to suffocate an entire population, to destroy a small nation," Rodriguez said. "What is happening to Cuba today could happen to any other state tomorrow."
A similar draft resolution, presented by Cuba at the UN General Assembly last year, received 165 votes in favor, seven against, and 12 abstentions. ■

Cloudflare sees millions of exploit attempts after PHP disclosure
- Cloudflare saw “millions” of exploit attempts after PHP’s critical flaws were disclosed, rising from “thousands” before the announcement to “tens of thousands” and then “hundreds of thousands” within hours.
- PHP developers released urgent fixes on Oct 21 and told users to “update immediately” after AI helped uncover long-hidden vulnerabilities in the language.
- Website operators and governments rushed to respond, with some European sites going offline and Japanese services, including Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group and the Finance Ministry, temporarily suspending functions.

Cloud services firm Cloudflare saw millions of exploitation attempts after the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in the widely used programming language PHP, CEO Matthew Prince said in a post on X late on Oct 21.

Taiwan’s National Symphony Orchestra pairs Britten’s bold sounds with Haydn’s surprises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
04:35:44 UTC
13:35:44 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s National Symphony Orchestra will explore Britain’s musical heritage through works by Benjamin Britten and Joseph Haydn at Taipei’s National Concert Hall on Thursday.
Conducted by Chien Wen-pin (簡文彬), the concert will feature German violinist Viviane Hagner, who is reuniting with the orchestra for the first time in 13 years. The program marks the 50th anniversary of Britten’s death in 1976.
It will open with Britten’s “The Young Person’s Guide to the Orchestra, Op. 34,” followed by Haydn’s “Surprise” Symphony. Hagner will join the orchestra for Britten’s “Violin Concerto, Op. 15,” which will close the evening.
“The Young Person’s Guide to the Orchestra” introduces the distinctive sounds of orchestral instruments. Chien said Britten captured the defining characteristics of each instrument, from the clarinet’s rapid runs to the French horn’s layered, full-bodied harmonies and the trumpet’s distinctive technical flair.
The violin concerto, meanwhile, reflects the youthful energy of Britten’s early compositional period and his willingness to challenge conventional forms. Its opening creates a striking contrast between percussion and strings, Chien said, while its tonal structure pays tribute to Ludwig van Beethoven, connecting the work to the broader classical tradition.
Haydn’s “Surprise” Symphony is one of 12 symphonies he composed during his later years in connection with his musical activities in London. It is best known for a sudden loud chord in its second movement, which helped make the work one of his most popular symphonies.
Chien noted that the symphony’s playful character extends beyond that famous passage. Haydn alternates between sudden bursts of sound and unexpected moments of softness, using shifts in dynamics, melody, and rhythm to give the music its wit and sense of mischief.
The concert will also feature Yang Zhe-yu’s (楊喆宇) “A Dialogue between Wind and Poetry,” part of the One-minute Symphony Project. The initiative is a collaboration between TSMC, the NSO, and the Taipei National University of Arts, designed to nurture young composers in Taiwan.

Taiwan issues land warning for Typhoon Champi

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Central Weather Administration issued a land warning for Typhoon Champi at 11:30 a.m. Thursday as the storm approached, with work and classes on Lanyu and Green Island suspended from noon.
The storm is expected to bring its strongest winds and heaviest rain to Taiwan on Friday and Saturday. Taipei, New Taipei, Keelung, and Taoyuan are expected to announce whether work and classes will be suspended Friday at 8 p.m. Thursday, per UDN.
Under existing regulations, authorities may suspend work and classes based on forecast winds, rainfall, and local conditions. The final decision rests with local governments.
Suspensions may also be announced when rising rivers, damaged bridges, flooding, or dangerous changes in terrain affect transportation and the safety of traveling to work or school.
Rain is forecast across the country Friday, with heavy or extremely heavy rain possible in northern and eastern areas through Saturday. The CWA has warned that the storm could slow or linger near Taiwan, potentially prolonging its effects.
Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) said Thursday that he would receive the latest forecasts from meteorologists in the evening before announcing whether work and classes would be suspended Friday, per CNA.
Chiang visited a pumping station Thursday after visiting the city’s disaster response center Wednesday night, where he received departmental reports and called for preparations. He said public safety was the top priority and announced the immediate suspension of all campaign activities.
Chiang said Taipei, New Taipei, Keelung, and Taoyuan form an interconnected metropolitan area and that authorities would continue to follow existing procedures. He said differing views on the rules had been raised previously and further coordination with the central government was possible, but the immediate priority was typhoon preparedness.

Could China’s 100-channel single-photon detector enable broadband quantum internet?
New design shatters quantum network bottleneck, creating ‘robust and scalable infrastructure’ for large-scale applications, scientists say
Chinese scientists have developed a 100-channel single-photon detector, a breakthrough promising to pave the way for broadband quantum networks.
State-of-the-art single-photon detectors – essential components underpinning photonic quantum technologies – could previously support a maximum of 32 detection channels for photon signals.
Now, a newly developed interconnect scheme by a Shanghai-based team has broken this bottleneck, supporting more than 100 detection channels while maintaining accurate and stable operation.
“This work establishes a robust and scalable infrastructure, paving the way for large-scale quantum photonic applications,” the authors said in their paper.

British warship should ‘stand up’ to Russia in north
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:30:39 BST
13:30:39 KST

The government should prepare options for a British state-owned vessel to transit the Northern Sea Route in support of international freedom of navigation rights, according to a report by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, sets out concern that Russia may seek to turn its control of the route into a de facto monopoly as it becomes more accessible.
Dhesi said: “The High North poses a major strategic challenge for the UK’s security. This is a demanding, hostile environment, and one that our greatest adversary, Russia, is seeking to dominate for military advantage.”
Its recommendation states: “The government should prepare options for a UK state-owned vessel to transit the Northern Sea Route in support of international freedom of navigation rights, including an assessment of the legal basis, operational risks and potential Russian response.”
The conclusion preceding it states: “As the Northern Sea Route becomes more accessible, Russia may seek to turn its control of the route into a de facto monopoly. A transit by a UK state-owned vessel through international waters could help uphold freedom of navigation rights under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, but this action would need to be carefully assessed against the operational and escalatory risks.”
The Northern Sea Route is a roughly 5,600 kilometre shipping lane running along Russia’s Arctic coast from the Kara Sea to the Bering Strait. Dr Marc De Vore, senior lecturer in international relations at the University of St Andrews, told the committee: “If we do not act to contest Russia’s illegal efforts to territorialise the northern sea route—these are their laws of 2012, 2018 and 2022—we will find after 2030, when the northern sea route becomes navigable all year long, that the Russians have set up a de facto monopoly on transit. They will make money off that, but they could also use it as a form of leverage—for example, if they do not like the level of support that Denmark is providing to Ukraine, they can cut off Maersk ships from sailing the northern sea route. Failing to contest that through freedom of navigation operations will give Russia a tremendous amount of both wealth and geopolitical leverage.”
The report records that in September 2018 the French Navy’s offshore support and assistance vessel Rhône transited the route from Tromsø in Norway to Dutch Harbor in Alaska without informing the Russian authorities. Russia subsequently stated that all foreign naval vessels would have to provide details of any proposed voyage at least forty-five days in advance and carry a Russian maritime pilot, and warned that if a voyage did not comply with Russian regulations it reserved the “right to take extraordinary measures including its forced halt, arrest and in extreme cases elimination.”
Freedom of navigation operations are actions taken by a country to sail or fly through contested international waters and airspaces to challenge maritime claims that break international law. The United States has conducted them in the Gulf of Sirte and the South China Sea, and Britain has done so near the Sea of Azov.
The committee notes such operations carry inherent risks, and in 2021 the Type 45 destroyer HMS Defender exercised its right of innocent passage through Ukrainian territorial waters off Crimea, which Russia had annexed in 2014, and Russia claims to have fired warning shots and dropped bombs near the vessel.
China is focused on using the route, with the sailing distance between Shanghai and Rotterdam approximately 25,500 kilometres via the Cape of Good Hope, 19,500 kilometres via the Suez Canal and 14,900 kilometres via the Northern Sea Route.

ADB report calls for action as Asia-Pacific coasts face mounting flood risks
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:01:34 CST
13:01:34 KST

MANILA, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Asia-Pacific coastlines face growing threats as sea levels rise and floods intensify, but investing in resilience could generate benefits up to 20 times greater than the cost, according to an Asian Development Bank (ADB) report.
Annual coastal flood damages in the Asia-Pacific region could increase more than sixfold by 2050 and nearly twentyfold by 2100 without adaptation, according to the Asia-Pacific Climate Report 2026: Coastal Risks on the Rise-Actions for a Resilient Future released on Wednesday.
Based on estimates across 30 coastal economies, the report estimates that annual flood damages could reach 172 billion U.S. dollars to 199 billion U.S. dollars by 2050 and 520 billion U.S. dollars to 739 billion U.S. dollars by 2100, compared with approximately 27 billion U.S. dollars today.
The report said keeping flood damages near today's levels would require an estimated 9 billion U.S. dollars to 19 billion U.S. dollars a year in coastal protection, an investment that could avoid 178 billion U.S. dollars to 360 billion U.S. dollars in flood damages each year.
According to ADB, over 400 million people in the region live within 10 kilometers of the sea. Coasts are hubs for ports and trade, as well as tourist and heritage spots. Without adequate adaptation measures, larger economies could face some of the highest economic losses in absolute terms, while relative impacts are particularly severe in atoll nations, where annual flood damage could reach 30 percent to 60 percent of GDP by 2100.
In major coastal cities such as Bangkok, Jakarta, Kolkata, and Mumbai, coastal floods that historically occurred once every 100 years could become annual events by the end of the century, said the report. ■

China-Russia ties entering new stage of greater achievements with resilient cooperation at milestone of strategic partnership
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:01:16 CST
13:01:16 KST

ST. PETERSBURG, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- China and Russia have leveraged more dynamic and resilient cooperation to cushion the impact of external uncertainties and instability, and bilateral ties are entering a new stage marked by greater achievements and faster development, said Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Wednesday.
Li made the remarks while co-chairing the 31st regular meeting between Chinese and Russian heads of government with Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin.
This year marks the 30th anniversary of the establishment of the China-Russia strategic partnership of coordination. For three decades, the regular meeting, held every year since its inception in 1996, has served as an important mechanism for implementing the consensus reached by the two heads of state and promoting bilateral cooperation and people-to-people exchanges, no matter how the international situation evolves.
China and Russia have in recent years stood side by side and moved forward together in the face of a complex and turbulent international landscape, Li said.
"This environment calls for continuous coordination and timely adjustment of plans. By advancing all-round cooperation, our two countries (Russia and China) are effectively countering the destructive forces and trends," said Andrei Vinogradov, head of the Center for Contemporary China Studies at the Institute of Oriental Studies under the Russian Academy of Sciences.
During the regular meeting on Wednesday, both sides agreed that China and Russia should advance cooperation in key areas such as economy and trade, investment, energy and resources, foster new drivers of development in frontier areas such as artificial intelligence, biotechnology and the digital economy, jointly ensure the success of the China-Russia Years of Education, and strengthen people-to-people and cultural exchanges.
These commitments build on the strong foundation of practical cooperation between the two countries, with economic and trade ties remaining a major pillar of the bilateral relationship.
Data from China's Ministry of Commerce showed that in 2025, China-Russia trade reached 227.9 billion U.S. dollars, staying above 200 billion dollars for the third consecutive year. China remained Russia's largest trading partner for the 16th consecutive year.
The structure of bilateral trade has also continued to improve, with electromechanical and high-tech products accounting for a growing share. Chinese automobiles, home appliances and machinery have maintained strong exports to Russia, while Russia has remained a stable supplier of energy, minerals and agricultural products to China.
"It is noteworthy that the two countries are working not merely to identify new converging interests, but also to explore new development avenues by leveraging the combined potential of their two economies," Vinogradov said.
Bilateral trade maintained relatively rapid growth in 2026. Statistics from China Customs showed that in the first seven months of the year, China-Russia trade reached 159.2 billion dollars, up 26.3 percent year on year.
"Russian and Chinese economies are complementary. This allows each side to pursue its own development path and advance its national interests," said Vladimir Lvovich Nezhdanov, an expert at the Institute of Contemporary International Problems, Diplomatic Academy of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Russian Federation.
"Russia needs a stable and dynamically growing China, just as China needs a stable and dynamically growing Russia. This is a mutual interest," he added.
On the global dimension, a joint communique issued after the 31st regular meeting said that China and Russia firmly uphold the United Nations-centered international system and the international order based on international law. The two countries also support consolidating fair international relations on the basis of mutually beneficial cooperation among sovereign states and oppose dividing the world into rival regions or blocs, it said.
"China proceeds in a steady manner, recognizing that no initiative or policy measure can be implemented without mutual trust," said Nezhdanov, noting a white paper titled "More Just and Equitable Global Governance: China's Principles, Proposals and Actions" released by China in June.
Cultivating mutual trust under the Global Governance Initiative is a practice that major countries, which are willing to assume responsibility for international affairs, have long followed to normalize and strengthen international dialogue, he added.
This year also marks the 25th anniversary of the signing of the Treaty of Good-Neighborliness and Friendly Cooperation Between China and Russia. Over the years, the two countries have always adhered to the treaty's established principle of non-alliance, non-confrontation and not targeting any third party, and stayed committed to equality, mutual respect, good faith and win-win cooperation, making important contributions to safeguarding international fairness and justice and promoting a new type of international relations, and serving as a vital constant amid century-defining changes sweeping across the world, said Xi in May during Putin's state visit to China.
The two sides should deepen multilateral coordination, further increase coordination and collaboration on multilateral platforms such as the United Nations, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, BRICS and APEC, unswervingly uphold the postwar international order and the authority of international law, unite the Global South, and steer the reform of the global governance system in the right direction, Xi said then.
"Russia-China relations are a truly high-quality model of relations between major countries, delivering benefits and shared interests at every level, from grassroots communities to national governments and the global stage alike," Nezhdanov said. ■

WELLINGTON, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand's annual inflation eased to 3.7 percent in the September 2026 quarter from 4.1 percent in the previous quarter, still remaining above the central bank's target band of 1 to 3 percent, official data showed on Thursday.
Petrol was the largest contributor to annual inflation, with prices rising 19.1 percent from a year earlier. If petrol prices had remained unchanged, annual inflation would have been 3.2 percent in the period, according to a statement from Stats NZ, the country's statistics agency.
The cost of constructing new housing rose 3.2 percent over the year, with higher material, subcontractor, labor and fuel costs contributing to the increase, Stats NZ prices and deflators spokesperson Nicola Growden said in the statement.
Other major contributors to annual inflation included electricity, up 9.3 percent, international airfares, up 12.5 percent, and local authority rates and payments, up 6.2 percent, statistics showed.
More than 85 percent of items in the consumer price index (CPI) basket increased in price over the year, while about 13 percent fell in price, the lowest proportion since the December 2023 quarter, according to Stats NZ.
Quarterly, the CPI rose 0.7 percent in the September quarter from the previous quarter, with international airfares the largest upward contributor, up 14.3 percent, mainly due to higher fares to Europe and Asia, the agency said.
Petrol prices fell 6.5 percent over the quarter, after rising 20.1 percent in the June 2026 quarter, it said.
Finance Minister Nicola Willis told reporters that Thursday's inflation figures were encouraging, but overseas events and the international oil shock continued to pose pressures. ■

The Ministry of Defence plays a key role connecting with industry, local resilience fora, the voluntary sector, and working with our active reserves and local cadet groups to facilitate a whole of society approach to defence and security.
“Government messaging on defence and security will continue to build ahead of ALBISTON SHADOW, a major UK Home Defence exercise, and NATO’s Crisis Management Exercise in spring 2027.”
Briefing company bosses directly on the threat picture marks a change in how the state handles this material, since the intelligence assessments behind it have traditionally stayed inside government and inside cleared parts of industry. Splitting the work between the Security Minister for critical national infrastructure and the Minister for the Armed Forces for industry gives each a defined audience.
University leaders and political parties were given equivalent briefings earlier this year on foreign interference, covering Chinese and Russian activity aimed at research, funding and candidate selection. Extending the same treatment to energy, water, telecommunications and transport operators brings it to the sectors that would be targeted first in a campaign of sabotage.
Exercise ALBISTON SHADOW is the largest home defence exercise Britain has run in decades, and has been described as a test of whether the public would know what to do and where to go if the country came under attack. Pairing it with NATO’s Crisis Management Exercise puts the national and alliance rehearsals in the same window in spring 2027.

Australian hospitalizations following e-scooter falls on rise: report

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:00:44 CST
13:00:44 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- The number of Australians hospitalized with injuries sustained in incidents involving e-scooters has more than tripled since 2019, according to a government report.
The report released on Thursday by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) showed that there were 4,089 hospitalizations for falls involving powered scooters in 2024-25, up 216.7 percent from 1,291 in 2019-20.
It said that the population-wide hospitalization rate for falls involving powered scooters increased from 5.1 per 100,000 people to 14.9 per 100,000 people in the same period, while the hospitalization rate for falls involving non-powered scooters fell from 6.8 to 4.9 per 100,000 people.
According to the report, males accounted for 69 percent of hospitalizations for falls involving powered scooters. The increase in hospitalizations was largest among people aged 12-15, with the rate growing from 3.1 hospitalizations per 100,000 people in 2019-20 to 33.4 per 100,000 in 2024-25.
Among boys aged 12-15, the hospitalization rate was 54 per 100,000 compared to 12 per 100,000 for girls.
"While the data cannot tell us exactly how much of this change is due to increased use, it is consistent with the growing popularity of e-scooters in Australia over recent years," AIHW spokesperson Jacqueline Rek said in a media release.
The proportion of hospitalizations following e-scooter falls that involved fractured bones increased from 46 percent in 2015-16 to 58 percent in 2024-25.
The report noted that new hospital codes that were introduced in July will allow future data to distinguish between e-scooters, e-bikes and other mobility devices more clearly. ■

US and Israel create plans for 'short but intensive' strikes on Iran after midterms - report
The New York Times reported that American and Israeli military planners have reportedly developed options for an operation against Iran lasting roughly three days
The United States and Israel are preparing for a possible new attack on Iran after the American midterm elections, even as questions persist over whether another military campaign would secure concessions from Tehran, The New York Times reported.
The proposed campaign would concentrate strikes into roughly three days, concentrating operation on nuclear facilities, missile and drone capabilities, and parts of Iran’s energy infrastructure.
US officials and others familiar with the discussions said the United States is also assembling additional forces. Its planned deployment, including three aircraft carriers, Marines, combat aircraft and Special Operations personnel, is expected to be fully positioned by early November.
President Donald Trump has not approved an attack. The Times reported that he has repeatedly held back proposed operations, including one earlier this month that both militaries had prepared to launch.
At the center of the deliberations is a disputed calculation: whether a short burst of military force could achieve diplomatic results that months of fighting and economic pressure have failed to deliver.
Iranian officials have warned that retaliation could extend to data centers, undersea internet cables and regional oil facilities. Mahdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran’s negotiating team, called expectations of a 72-hour campaign a “fantasy.”
“Our attacks will be more fierce, creative and different,” Mohammadi wrote on social media.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of Education conducted drug-prevention sessions in more than 50,000 classes last year to help students recognize the dangers of etomidate, CNA reported.
Education Minister Cheng Ying-yao (鄭英耀) said Thursday that etomidate had become the second most common drug encountered by students since 2024, surpassing marijuana and amphetamines.
The sedative, used for general anesthesia, can cause dependence and has been mixed with chemical additives to produce liquid for e-cigarettes, according to the Keelung City Government.
Lessons on the dangers of drugs and e-cigarettes were incorporated into health and physical education courses, and the ministry reached all targeted classes last year. Through September this year, it had conducted similar sessions in more than 48,000 classes.
Cheng said emerging drugs and e-cigarettes were constantly changing in appearance, with some featuring cartoon characters or resembling USB drives and bubble tea. The ministry has stepped up efforts during school visits to teach students how to recognize these products and understand their risks.
The ministry is also considering saliva tests to help schools identify potential drug use early and has coordinated with the National Police Agency on joint procurement. The tests could be introduced after amendments to the Narcotics Hazard Prevention Act are passed.
According to the Keelung City Government, inhaling etomidate can cause hand tremors and full-body shaking. Severe cases may result in permanent neurological damage or respiratory arrest.

Russia, Ukraine exchange strikes as US envoy leaves after talks

Russia pounds Kyiv, Ukraine launches drones, despite talk of renewing negotiations
KYIV/MOSCOW, Oct 22 - Russia pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles and Ukraine sent hundreds of drones towards Moscow overnight as the warring sides kept up a barrage of attacks despite the latest US push to end the conflict.
Russia said on Wednesday it was ready to resume US-mediated talks with Ukraine next month, after President Vladimir Putin hosted US envoy Steve Witkoff for talks in St Petersburg.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said he hoped negotiations, which would be the first since February, would take place early in November.
Ukraine said Russia fired at least 21 ballistic missiles in three waves. Russia said Ukraine launched 630 drones towards the capital Moscow during the night.
The two sides held an exchange of war dead, with Moscow handing over 252 bodies and Ukraine handing over 25, according to the Belta state news agency in neighbouring Belarus. Such exchanges have accompanied moves towards talks in the past.
But while Witkoff spoke of "some degree of momentum" after meeting Zelenskiy and European and NATO officials in Oslo earlier in the week, the Kremlin expressed doubts.
"The Americans sensed some new nuances (in Oslo) and told us about this. But these nuances, so to speak, do not entirely satisfy us," Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said.
A senior Russian official, briefed on the results of the Putin-Witkoff talks, said they were relatively short and not substantive. The American brought a set of proposals drafted in Oslo and handed them to Putin for review, the person said.
Another source close to the Kremlin said the US proposals included a scenario where Ukraine would cede all of its Donbas region to Russia in return for receiving a guarantee of its future security from NATO.
Russia says it launched the war, the deadliest in Europe since World War Two, in part to prevent Ukraine from joining NATO. It has repeatedly said it would not end fighting unless Ukraine cedes more land, limits the size of its forces and is permanently barred from forming alliances.
Ukraine, which says the invasion was an unprovoked war of conquest, has long dismissed Russia's conditions as a demand for capitulation that would leave it defenceless against future Russian attacks.
US PRAISE FOR 'HUMANITARIAN' PUTIN GOES DOWN BADLY WITH KYIV
Zelenskiy's meeting with Witkoff was aimed in part at smoothing over a deterioration in relations with Washington this month, after President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and lifted sanctions on Moscow.
Kyiv says Washington failed to provide early-warning data on Russian missile launches, throttled the SpaceX satellite system used to guide Ukrainian drones, and withheld missile defence systems bought on its behalf by Europeans. Washington denies any shift in policy to intentionally hamper Ukraine's forces.
Trump has repeatedly rebuked Ukraine for attacking Russian oil refineries while saying little about far deadlier Russian attacks on Ukraine. He called for Zelenskiy to be replaced and said Russia's actions in Ukraine have been "fine".
Zelenskiy, who long avoided any criticism of the Trump administration, has increasingly pushed back against what he describes as a shift towards sympathy with Moscow.
On Thursday Zelenskiy snapped back at Witkoff for saluting Putin as a "humanitarian" during his visit to Russia, when the US envoy thanked Putin for releasing a 74-year-old American captured by Russian forces in Ukraine.
"Three waves of ballistic missiles have been launched at Kyiv by Russian 'humanitarians' since yesterday evening," Zelenskiy posted on X. "They used 21 missiles. Unfortunately, numerous sites across the city have been hit and damaged."
He said 2 people were killed and 34 injured, including five children, in attacks on a dozen Ukrainian regions.
Russia said it carried out a "massive strike" overnight on port infrastructure in Ukraine's Odesa region, as well as on vessels used by the Ukrainian military.
In Russia, two people were wounded near Moscow by drones launched towards the capital during the night, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram. Most of the drones were downed at long range, he added.
In the Russian border region of Belgorod, one man was killed and another wounded by Ukrainian drones, local officials said.
With the frontlines of the war largely static, both sides have escalated long-range air strikes this year. Russia has particularly targeted the Ukrainian power grid, while Ukraine has aimed at Russian oil refineries. Both have struck data centres, commercial warehouses and Black Sea shipping.
The war has ground on for more than 4-1/2 years, defying Trump's pledge during his 2024 election campaign that he could end it in a day. No breakthrough emerged from three short meetings in Istanbul last year and three rounds of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi and Geneva at the start of this year. REUTERS
