While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Oct 22, 2026
Global diesel prices seen staying high despite Russia deal
US President Donald Trump’s deal with Russia to supply diesel to US and global markets is unlikely to meaningfully lower diesel prices, market watchers and analysts said, noting that the promised volumes are too small to ease a global supply squeeze.
Diesel prices have shot to record highs during the US-Israeli war on Iran, creating a political liability for Trump and his Republican party as they campaign to maintain thin majorities in the US Congress in the Nov 3 midterm elections.
Critics of Trump’s move said lifting sanctions on Russian diesel could help Moscow fund further attacks on Ukraine, undermining years of efforts to curb Russian energy revenues and raising the risk the Kremlin could profit while consumers get little relief from high fuel prices.
Trump said Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tons, or 2.25 million barrels, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter”.
Russia frees retired US schoolteacher in goodwill gesture
Russia freed Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired US schoolteacher in custody since 2022, from prison on Oct 21 and took him to St Petersburg to fly back to the United States, after talks that Washington said were a step towards ending the war in Ukraine.
Russian President Vladimir Putin made the announcement at a meeting in St Petersburg with US envoy Steve Witkoff, who later said the talks will continue towards planned technical-level discussions involving the US, Russia and Ukraine.
Witkoff thanked Putin for Hubbard’s release and called the Russian leader a “humanitarian”, in footage of the exchange, a remark that drew sharp rebuke from Republican and Democratic lawmakers given Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Pope Leo will not need further cancer treatment
Pope Leo will not need any further therapy after undergoing lung cancer surgery last week, his doctors said on Oct 21, indicating that his tumour had not spread.
The announcement came as it was still unclear whether the US-born pope would proceed with a planned trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, scheduled for Nov 6-17.
The 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung removed in surgery on Oct 13 and was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.
PHP developers issue updates fixing vulnerabilities
Developers of the PHP programming language said a set of new updates fixing two previously identified critical vulnerabilities was now live, and acknowledged a delay in addressing a previously identified flaw.
Government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline on Oct 21 after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in PHP sent website operators around the world scrambling to protect their systems.
PHP underpins large parts of the internet and the vulnerabilities had raised concerns that a significant number of websites could be vulnerable to attack. The developers issued four patches to address two “critical” vulnerabilities that could allow hackers to execute code on vulnerable systems.
‘Mood of defeat’: Como hammer Manchester United
Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes said his side failed to apply enough pressure and adopted a “mood of defeat” after conceding early in their 4-1 Champions League loss at Como on Oct 21, a result that increased scrutiny on manager Michael Carrick.
Como opened the scoring in the second minute and United collapsed, with only a stoppage‑time consolation goal from Joshua Zirkzee making the scoreline slightly less severe.
“We started on the wrong foot, and they scored very early,” Fernandes told TNT Sports. “There was not enough pressure on the ball and not many good movements off the ball. There were many things not going our way.”

Meta ordered to pay US$25b to New Mexico after jury finds company misled consumers about data privacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
22:18:00 UTC
07:18:00 KST

Meta ordered to pay historic US$25b penalty to New Mexico for misleading consumers on data privacy
- A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay US$25 billion after a jury said it misled users about data privacy and Facebook data access linked to Cambridge Analytica.
- The state said Meta lied about who could access user data and how it handled hate speech and misinformation. It called the ruling a major win for consumer protection.
- Meta said it will appeal and called the case a “tax on speech”. Experts expect a long legal fight, and the money will go to New Mexico schools.
AI generated
NEW MEXICO – A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms on Oct 21 to pay the state US$25 billion (S$32 billion) after a jury found the company had misled consumers about the privacy of their data, hitting the company with one of the largest financial penalties in US history.
The ruling came in a case stemming from allegations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign, obtained data from millions of Facebook users without their consent. New Mexico had sued Meta, accusing it of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data.
“Facebook’s wrongdoing – over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public – goes to the heart of Facebook’s core business practices,” Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order, which came more than three weeks after the verdict.
He found that a penalty of more than US$219 billion was warranted based on state law, but reduced the figure to US$25 billion.
In a statement, C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal. “This ruling, and the Attorney-General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” he said.
“At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.”
New Mexico Attorney-General Raul Torrez said in a statement after the ruling the penalty was one of the largest financial penalties against a corporation in US history.
Meta previously faced a US$5 billion penalty from the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 over the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
Six other states settled their lawsuits against Meta related to Cambridge Analytica for US$459.2 million as part of a US$17.1 billion multistate settlement the company reached in August to resolve states’ claims that the company’s platforms had harmed teen mental health.
Lawsuit filed five years ago
New Mexico’s attorney-general had sued Meta in 2021 following revelations that Cambridge Analytica had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app.
The state accused Meta of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data, how the company handles hate speech and misinformation posted on the platform and other internal policies.
The company knew that third parties had broad access to users’ personal data, and it tolerated hate speech or other harmful content when it benefited the company’s bottom line, the state said.
Cambridge Analytica, now defunct, worked for Trump’s successful presidential campaign in 2016, and gained access to the personal information from millions of Facebook accounts for the purposes of voter profiling and targeting.
It obtained that information without users’ consent from a researcher who had been allowed by Facebook to deploy an app on its social media network.
“It has been a long time coming holding Big Tech accountable,” Torrez told a press conference in Albuquerque after Wednesday’s ruling.
“I think today’s judgment is a clear break with that past and a very clear warning to those in this space and beyond that we intend to protect our people and protect our consumers.”
Analyst Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson & Co, called the ruling costly but unlikely to impact the company’s value.
“Meta is worth nearly two trillion dollars, and will likely continue to appeal these cases and drag them out,” Luria said.
Experts expect long appeal fight
Legal experts and financial analysts said the penalty was likely to face a lengthy battle on appeal.
Jurors on Sept 25 found that 26 of 29 statements made by the company and its leadership on those issues were misleading. They said the company had committed more than 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws, based on the number of Facebook users or New Mexico residents who were the audience for each misleading statement.
State law allows a penalty of up to US$5,000 per violation, and directs that all of the money go to New Mexico’s school system, Torrez told reporters after the verdict.
At a hearing on Oct 1, Randi McGinn, a lawyer for New Mexico, had asked Mathew to award the state between US$35 billion and US$40 billion, saying that would be supported by the US Constitution’s protections on due process and the jury’s verdict.
“This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is money, and the value of its stock price,” McGinn said.
In court filings, Meta urged Mathew to cap the penalties at US$3.45 billion, saying a higher penalty ran the risk of scaring businesses out of the state. The evidence showed that Meta does not sell user data and New Mexico did not prove that any consumer had actually been misled, the company said in court filings.
Daryl Lim, an associate dean at Penn State Dickinson Law, said that while the US Constitution generally protects against excessive fines, because of the way New Mexico law is written, the large size of the penalty does not automatically mean it could be overturned.
Two juries sided with state
The verdict was the second in six months by a Santa Fe jury in a lawsuit brought by the state of New Mexico against Meta Platforms.
In the first trial, which ended in March, a Santa Fe jury found Meta misled users about young users’ safety on its Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp platforms and ordered the company to pay US$375 million in civil penalties.
After a second phase of that trial, a judge directed the company to pay US$567 million into a New Mexico fund for teen mental health and ordered Meta to implement measures to protect teen Facebook and Instagram users in New Mexico. REUTERS

Türkiye plans $2B investment in aviation, space industries over three years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
22:12:28 UTC
07:12:28 KST

Ankara has planned to allocate nearly $2 billion to its aviation and space industries over the next three years, according to the 2027 central government budget draft and budget justification.
The budget dedicated to the national space and aviation programme stood at $176 million this year and is set to surge by 181.7 percent to $495.7 million in 2027 to strengthen Türkiye's global competitiveness in the sector.
Financial commitments are projected to rise further to $616.9 million in 2028 and $745 million in 2029.
Under the spending framework, approximately $377.3 million will be directed towards the construction, operation, and servicing of air transport facilities, with total aviation infrastructure investments projected to reach $581.1 million in 2028 and $596.2 million in 2029 to meet rising domestic travel demand.
Ankara aims to accommodate 272 million airport passengers next year, including direct transit travellers, rising to 282 million in 2028 and 291 million by 2029.
Orbital infrastructure
The expanded space budget will support Türkiye's National Space Programme, dedicated research, testing infrastructure, and the commercialisation of high-value-added domestic technologies.
The push follows notable sector milestones in recent years, including the deployment of the country's first indigenous communications satellite, Turksat 6A, and the sub-metre Earth observation satellite, Imece.
Türkiye also completed its first crewed scientific space missions in 2024, when astronauts Alper Gezeravci and Tuva Cihangir Atasever conducted experiments in orbit.
The southwestern city of Antalya hosted the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) on October 5–9, ahead of preparations for Türkiye's maiden deep-space lunar mission scheduled for next year.
The lunar venture relies on a homegrown spacecraft featuring more than 80 percent domestic content and a hybrid propulsion system; the craft has completed assembly and is undergoing final testing.
Concurrently, the Turkish Space Agency is advancing efforts to establish a spaceport in Somalia to secure sovereign, independent access to orbit.

Websites pulled offline worldwide as AI finds critical security flaws
Vulnerabilities in code powering 70 per cent of the internet allow passwordless server takeovers, sparking a global race to patch
Government agencies and companies around the world shut down websites as they raced Thursday to protect themselves from hacks after artificial intelligence uncovered critical flaws in a widely used programming language called PHP.
Wiz, one of the cybersecurity firms that found the two flaws, estimated that PHP code helps run about 70 per cent of the world’s websites – from online stores and news outlets to government services.
It called the flaws “among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history”.
PHP programmers released a fix on Wednesday, and the US National Security Agency told organisations to patch their sites immediately or pull vulnerable systems offline.

Poland fumes as Ukrainian city celebrates ‘architect of genocide’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
22:07:03 UTC

Poland fumes as Ukrainian city celebrates ‘architect of genocide’
Poland has accused Kiev of making unacceptable “suicidal” moves after the Ukrainian city of Lviv dedicated 2027 to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and its leader, Nazi collaborator Roman Shukhevich.
To celebrate the 120th anniversary of Shukhevich’s birth and mark 85 years since the creation of the militant group that perpetrated mass killings of ethnic Poles, Jews, and Russians, the Lviv Regional Council decided on Tuesday to organize “cultural, memorial, scientific, and mass media events,” as well as exhibitions and national-patriotic rallies.
The announcement was met with widespread condemnation in Poland, which regards the UPA as perpetrators of genocide against Poles in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia and its leader, Shukhevich, as a key ‘architect’ of the massacres. From 1943 to 1945, Ukrainian nationalist militants murdered an estimated 100,000 ethnic Poles in the regions, which are now largely part of modern Ukraine.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the move a “suicidal tactic,” and Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz called it “unacceptable.” Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski condemned the announcement, calling for the resolution’s key sponsor, Lviv regional lawmaker Svyatoslav Sheremet, to be placed on Poland’s travel ban list.
The Ukrainian Foreign Ministry attempted to downplay the incident, blaming the Lviv regional authorities for making the “harmful decision.” The ministry also said the regional council did not consult any central authorities regarding “the consequences of their actions for bilateral relations with Poland.”
The resolution ultimately vanished from the Lviv council’s website without any explanation. Speaking to Polish media on Wednesday, Deputy Foreign Minister Marcin Bosacki said Warsaw received assurances from Kiev that the resolution would not be implemented.
“We take on faith the words of the administration of Vladimir Zelensky that this catastrophic decision will not be implemented,” Bosacki stated, calling the disappearance of the resolution from the council’s website a “good sign,” but cautioning against interpreting it as an official cancellation of the celebrations.
Ukraine’s increasingly open honoring of WWII-era nationalists and Nazi collaborators has drawn criticism from Warsaw, which remains one of Ukraine’s key backers in the conflict with Russia.
Poland regards the UPA and the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN), which collaborated with Nazi Germany during the early stages of its 1941 invasion of the Soviet Union, as perpetrators of genocide, while modern Ukraine cherishes them as freedom fighters and national heroes.
Earlier this year, Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky named a military unit after the ‘Heroes of the UPA’ and established a ‘pantheon of outstanding Ukrainians’ at Kiev’s main military cemetery, where OUN leader and Nazi collaborator Andrey Melnik was reinterred with state honors in May.

Hegseth Directs Air Force to Establish New Guard Special Tactics Squadron
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
22:06:39 UTC
07:06:39 KST

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has directed the Air Force to establish a new Special Tactics Squadron under the Florida Air National Guard, growing a small but elite group of special operators.
The Pentagon announced Hegseth’s order Oct. 21, releasing a brief Sept. 23 memo from Hegseth to Air Force Secretary Troy Meink, directing him to create the new squadron at Hurlburt Field “with an associated new organization at MacDill Air Force Base,” both in Florida.
Pentagon and Air Force spokespersons offered no further details. The Air National Guard did not immediately respond to a query.
Hurlburt is the headquarters of Air Force Special Operations Command, and MacDill is home to U.S. Special Operations Command. Connecting the new unit to both “creates an unparalleled ecosystem of combat-ready training and mission execution,” the Pentagon’s announcement states. “This move maximizes joint-force synergy, ensures seamless operational readiness, and provides the President with highly responsive, lethal options to counter pacing threats.”
Special tactics squadrons are some of the Air Force’s premier ground forces, consisting of combat controllers, pararescuemen, special reconnaissance, and Tactical Air Control Party specialists. They conduct a wide range of missions in covert, remote, or hostile areas, including combat search and rescue, airfield seizure, emergency air traffic controller, and coordination of close air support.
There are just a handful of special tactics squadrons across the Air Force, and only two in the Guard—the 123rd Special Tactics Squadron in Kentucky and the 125th Special Tactics Squadron in Oregon. The Florida Air National Guard has one special ops unit, the 249th Special Operations Squadron, which flies the CV-22 Osprey.
It is unclear how quickly the new unit will be established and be fully manned. Hegseth’s memo states that “any further resourcing for this direction, to include military construction, equipment, and manpower authorizations will be developed in the President’s Budget 2028 budget cycle.”
The memo also directs the National Guard Bureau and the Air Force to follow Air Force policy for establishing the new unit, “consistent with applicable DAF Strategic Basing process and environmental legal requirements.”
It is highly unusual—if not unprecedented—for the Secretary of Defense to direct the establishment of a squadron-level unit in any component.
Hegseth, a former Army officer, has praised special operations forces, seeing them as a model for innovation and acquisition reform, and they have played key roles in operations during his tenure, including Operation Absolute Resolve to seize Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January, Operation Rough Rider in Yemen in 2025, and the ongoing strikes against alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific.

Trump asks US Supreme Court to allow Big Bend border wall construction

Trump asks US Supreme Court to allow Big Bend border wall construction
Oct 21 - President Donald Trump's administration asked the US Supreme Court on Wednesday to let it proceed with a plan to build a US-Mexico border barrier in a remote region in West Texas that includes Big Bend National Park.
The Justice Department filed an emergency request for the court to lift a federal judge's order halting wall construction in the region while a lawsuit against the project brought by an environmental group and other challengers plays out.
The Republican president has long touted building or reinforcing barriers along the US-Mexico border as a signature part of his anti-immigration policies. But his administration's push to extend border infrastructure into the national park, around 250 miles (400 km) southeast of El Paso, has faced opposition from local officials, conservationists and some Texas Republicans.
The lawsuit was brought by the Center for Biological Diversity, a Big Bend-area river guide and a group seeking to preserve a historic church in Ruidosa, Texas, that says its fragile adobe structure is threatened by the border construction.
The plaintiffs challenged a series of waivers issued by the US Department of Homeland Security to expedite construction of roads and barriers in the Big Bend region, avoiding the application of a variety of environmental and conservation laws.
Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and the current Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who issued the waivers between February and July, found the region to be an "area of high illegal entry," requiring additional barriers to control the border.
US District Judge Kathleen Cardone in El Paso issued an injunction on October 2 halting the construction. In an opinion issued later, the judge found that the waivers exceeded the authority of Noem and Mullin.
The Justice Department in its request urged the Supreme Court to pause or overturn Cardone's injunction.
"Even assuming that the secretary's waiver authority implicates a question of 'vast economic and political significance,' Congress did clearly authorize the secretary both to build border barriers and to waive legal requirements in order to facilitate their expeditious construction," the Justice Department wrote.
In August, the administration paused construction in Big Bend after the project drew bipartisan criticism over its potential impact on the park's landscape and wildlife. Crews had begun clearing land in the park for roads and border security infrastructure, prompting protests and lawsuits seeking to halt the work. REUTERS

- Earnings: $2.95 adjusted vs. $2.86 expected
- Revenue: $17.10 billion vs. $16.82 billion expected
IBM's revenue grew about 5% from a year ago, according to a statement. Net income, at $2.19 billion, or $2.30 per share, increased from $1.74 billion, or $1.84 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude acquisition-related adjustments.
"Our clients are now deploying 'Super Intelligence' in ways that transform entire operating models, instead of simply addressing narrow or novel problems," IBM CEO Arvind Krishna was quoted as saying in a statement.

Consulting revenue, at $5.34 billion, was flat and just below StreetAccount's $5.37 billion consensus.
"AI is increasingly embedded in broader transformations our clients are undertaking, representing about 30% of our consulting revenue in the quarter and 35% of our backlog," Jim Kavanaugh, IBM's finance chief, said on a conference call with analysts.
The consulting unit's 27.4% gross margin narrowed from 28.9% in the second quarter.
"We reinvested productivity gains into digital assets, accelerating our transition towards a services as software model to capture the growing AI opportunity," Kavanaugh said.

As of Wednesday's close, IBM stock has come down 15%, while the S&P 500 index has gained 13%.
"I think the current street estimates for the year are about $32 billion of revenue," Kavanaugh said. "We feel comfortable with that $32 billion of revenue."

Roundup: UK inflation hits highest level since November 2025, adding pressure ahead of Budget

LONDON, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Britain's Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose by 3.5 percent year-on-year in September, marking its fastest increase since November 2025, according to data released by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) on Wednesday.
The latest reading also marks the third successive increase in inflation and is well above the Bank of England's 2 percent target.
Core CPI, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, rose by 2.8 percent year-on-year in September, up from 2.6 percent in August.
Transport costs, particularly motor fuels, made the largest upward contribution to the change in the annual CPI inflation rate. ONS data showed that average petrol prices in September reached their highest level since August 2022, while average diesel prices climbed to their highest level since July 2022.
Ahead of next week's Budget, today's data is a stark reminder of the growing price pressures in the UK economy, said Caterina Batog, research and economics analyst at the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC).
Inflation is casting a dark shadow over the businesses who are already struggling with a succession of high costs, she said, noting that BCC's latest survey of over 4,000 firms shows inflation remains the top concern of 60 percent of the respondents.
"With Christmas around the corner, consumers will be understandably concerned by the third increase in inflation in three months," said Harvir Dhillon, lead economist at the British Retail Consortium.
Attributing much of the situation to the sharp rise in petrol and diesel prices, he warned "the lifting of the Ofgem price cap this month will push up October's figure when published in November, having already driven up household energy bills and likely to do so again in January. Rises in the cost of household appliances and pharmaceuticals will further squeeze household budgets."
Citing persistently high inflation, Anna Leach, chief economist at the Institute of Directors, said "next week's Budget will need to tread a careful line."
Targeted support for those most exposed to rising energy costs could help cushion the immediate shock, but how that support is funded matters, she said, adding that further increases in the costs of doing business would undermine the very investment, hiring and economic resilience that the government needs to protect.
On the front of daily consumption, the upcoming Budget provides a crucial opportunity to tackle the high cost of living, Dhillon said. If the government can cut the cost of doing business, retailers will be in a better position to hold back price rises and increase investment in stores and jobs.
"A targeted tax reduction package to ease energy and business rates costs would help unlock the sustained growth we all want to see," Batog echoed. ■

UN, African officials call for investment on data systems
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:03:19 CST

Ethiopian President Taye Atske Selassie delivers a speech during the joint session of the Statistical Commission for Africa and the Regional Committee of United Nations Global Geospatial Information Management for Africa held in Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia, Oct. 21, 2026. (Xinhua)
ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- United Nations (UN) and African officials on Wednesday called for robust investment in data and statistical systems in Africa to help governments on the continent make informed decisions, anticipate emerging needs and spur development.
The call came during the joint session of the Statistical Commission for Africa and the Regional Committee of United Nations Global Geospatial Information Management for Africa held in Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia, under the theme "Unleashing the value of data in Africa: making official statistics a true mirror of the continent."
Speaking at the event, Claver Gatete, UN under-secretary-general and executive secretary of the UN Economic Commission for Africa, emphasized the need for African governments to modernize and adequately finance foundational data and statistical systems to produce data and statistics that reflect Africa's development realities.
"Africa needs reliable, forward-looking data and statistics on productive capacity, investment opportunities, trade flows and regional value chains to guide industrial policy and implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area," he said.
He warned that outdated and incomplete data and statistics can risk governments investing in wrong priorities, overlooking underserved communities and failing to identify opportunities for economic growth.
Noting that the production of high-quality data is a guarantee for Africa's development strategies and programs, Ethiopian President Taye Atske Selassie cautioned that using poor-quality data hinders evidence-based decision-making and evades sustainable development.
"Governments across Africa should remain committed to upholding and advocating for professional independence of official statistics, strengthen the legal and institutional frameworks, invest in their national statistical systems and use scientific evidence in their decision-making processes," Atske Selassie said.
Yusuf Murangwa, minister of finance and economic planning of Rwanda, said Africa's "data problem," involving a structural weakness not only in the availability of information but also in the ability to collect, analyze and use reliable evidence, remains a challenge to guide policy and make informed investment decisions.
"If we don't invest in statistics, we lose a lot of value. Decisions without good evidence are very expensive," Murangwa warned, urging African governments to support and allocate adequate resources for statistics development across the continent. ■

TASHKENT, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Uzbekistan will introduce a revised version of its Latin-based Uzbek alphabet on April 22, 2027, following a new law signed by Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev on Wednesday.
Under the legislation, all existing documents, national currency, and official securities issued prior to the effective date will remain fully valid. Official state symbols, signage and organizational insignia will also remain in use until replaced through natural wear or per an implementation program to be approved within two months.
The revised writing system updates the alphabet structure to 28 letters and an apostrophe. Several multi-letter combinations and specific character representations are replaced with individual letters, while the overall alphabet count is streamlined.
Uzbekistan first adopted a Latin-based script in 1993, which underwent subsequent modifications in 1995. While a full phase-out of Cyrillic was originally planned for 2000, both writing systems have continued in dual usage. The current reform stems from a 2020 presidential decree aimed at modernizing language policy and finalizing the transition. ■

Interview: China-Malta fishery cooperation delivers win-win results: Maltese minister
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:02:56 CST
07:02:56 KST

Maltese Minister for Agriculture, Fisheries and Food Supply Anton Refalo speaks during an interview with Xinhua in Qormi, Malta, Oct. 20, 2026. Fishery cooperation between China and Malta has delivered win-win results, Maltese Minister for Agriculture, Fisheries and Food Supply Anton Refalo has said. (Photo by Jonathan Borg/Xinhua)
by Diao Ze
VALLETTA, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Fishery cooperation between China and Malta has delivered win-win results, Maltese Minister for Agriculture, Fisheries and Food Supply Anton Refalo has said.
"Before we made the first agreement in 2023, bluefin tuna was only an exhibit at the China International Import Expo. Now it's a Chinese commodity," Refalo said Tuesday in an interview with Xinhua. Malta is one of the leading producers of farmed Atlantic bluefin tuna in the Mediterranean.
Describing the opening of the Chinese market as "a very important milestone" for Malta's fisheries sector, Refalo said it has allowed Maltese exporters to diversify their markets and reach a wider customer base. Calling the cooperation "a win-win situation," he said Malta looks forward to more trade and economic agreements with China.
Refalo also highlighted the significance of such cooperation for Europe. "Malta, being a member of the European Union, can show other European Union (EU) members how strategic and important the trade and economic relations are," he said.
"I have always considered China and its people as persons of goodwill," the minister said, adding that every country, "not only in the European Union but internationally, can have a lot to take and also to give."
Fishery cooperation between the two countries has continued to expand since 2023. In November 2025, Refalo led a delegation to China for the 8th China International Import Expo in Shanghai. During the trip, a protocol was signed in Beijing allowing Malta's wild-caught fishery products to enter the Chinese market for the first time.
Malta and China's general administration of customs are working toward the third agreement covering exports of fish oil and fishmeal made from bluefin tuna by-products, the minister added.
The cooperation has helped create jobs. Malta's official data showed that aquaculture industry has employed 532 people as of the end of April.
Science is another area of cooperation. The two countries are working together on bluefin tuna breeding research, and in July this year, a batch of fertilized bluefin tuna eggs from Malta cleared quarantine in China's Fujian Province for research purposes.
Expressing hope for extensive cooperation in fishery science and technology, Refalo said China has a lot of innovation to offer, and Malta can learn much from Chinese technique and knowledge-sharing.
Moreover, Refalo said China and Malta, which established diplomatic relations in 1972, have treated each other "as friends, as partners." Malta is committed to promoting friendship and advancing bilateral cooperation in such areas as the blue economy and tourism to achieve sustained growth, he added.
Refalo also said that as a small island state facing challenges such as insularity and climate change, Malta looks forward to further strengthening its relationship with China, which will help its people thrive.
"The Chinese people are our friends. They have always supported us in times of need," he noted. ■

News Analysis: Gulf recalibrates security amid Saudi-Houthi conflict
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:02:46 CST
07:02:46 KST

ADEN, Yemen, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- The renewed Saudi-Houthi conflict, more than another chapter in Yemen's long-running war, is emerging as a stress test for Gulf security, forcing regional states to balance old alliances against new threats, military deterrence against diplomacy, and external protection against self-reliance.
Different Gulf reactions -- from allegations about renewed Emirati involvement in Yemen to Oman's efforts to preserve mediation and Qatar's push for domestic defense production -- point to a broader recalibration: building stronger defenses while recognizing that military superiority alone cannot end the region's conflicts.
SHARED THREAT, UNEASY PARTNERSHIP
Citing unnamed sources in Yemen, The Guardian said the United Arab Emirates (UAE), once a key partner in the Saudi-led coalition, had agreed to resume payments to some government forces fighting the Houthi group.
Ahmed Naji, a senior Yemen analyst at the International Crisis Group, told Xinhua that it remains "too early" to speak of an Emirati return, given "unresolved differences with Saudi Arabia over Yemen."
The main driver for a possible UAE involvement would be the shared threat posed by Houthi expansion to both countries' interests, he said.
The UAE, analysts note, has strategic interests in safeguarding navigation through the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait and preventing shifts in Yemen's balance of power.
Yazeed Al-Jeddawy, research manager at the Sana'a Center for Strategic Studies, said he expected "limited and selective rapprochement (between the UAE and Saudi Arabia) driven by the common threat, rather than a full return to the partnership that existed at the beginning of the Yemen war."
Thabet Hussein, a military and strategic analyst, said any renewed UAE involvement would likely rest on "clearer agreements" with Riyadh defining the scope of cooperation to avoid a repeat of the disagreements that previously fractured their partnership.
Mohammed Al-Zghoul, director of the Iranian Studies Unit at the Emirates Policy Center in Abu Dhabi, told Xinhua that three distinct scenarios for the UAE should not be conflated: supporting allied Yemeni forces, helping defend Saudi territory and redeploying Emirati troops inside Yemen.
Financial or logistical support for local allies in Yemen would largely continue Abu Dhabi's existing approach of retaining influence without returning to direct warfare, he said.
"There are no serious indications that the UAE is moving toward returning its troop to Yemen," Al-Zghoul said.
OPEN CHANNELS, HARDENING POSITIONS
Oman has maintained channels of communication with the Houthis and sought to facilitate negotiations.
The challenge, Naji said, now lies less with the mediator than with the trajectory of the war, as both sides have hardened their positions and increasingly approach the conflict in "zero-sum" terms, leaving little room for negotiations in the near term.
"The problem is what each side can bring to the negotiating table under the current circumstances," Al-Jeddawy echoed.
The Houthis believe "military gains have strengthened their bargaining position" and are unlikely to return to earlier understandings without demanding greater concessions, he said.
Riyadh, by contrast, faces a different calculation. Returning to negotiations without first restoring some degree of deterrence could carry significant political and strategic costs, particularly after "Houthi attacks demonstrated the group's ability to threaten Saudi infrastructure and economic interests," he added.
Qatar, Kuwait and Bahrain, meanwhile, have adopted less direct approaches, combining solidarity with Saudi Arabia with support for diplomacy efforts.
RETHINKING REGIONAL SECURITY ORDER
Analysts say recent conflicts have prompted a broader reassessment of Gulf security, challenging long-held assumptions about how the region's security should be maintained.
Yemen is only one factor. "Tensions involving Iran, instability around strategic waterways and threats to economic security are pushing Gulf states to reconsider defense policies, expand military industries and reassess strategic partnerships," Naji said.
Qatar offered a fresh example this week with plans for a domestic defense-production hub focused on areas including ballistic-missile and drone defense and cybersecurity.
Al-Jeddawy described such moves as "a long-term transformation accelerated by successive wars and uncertainty surrounding the durability of U.S. security commitments."
"Gulf states cannot dispense with the United States in the foreseeable future," but they increasingly want to reduce excessive dependence, diversify partnerships and ensure they can protect critical infrastructure if outside assistance or supply chains are disrupted, he added.
The emerging Gulf strategy, analysts say, is therefore less about replacing one security umbrella than building more layers beneath it -- stronger national defenses, diversified partnerships and regional diplomacy.
The Saudi-Houthi confrontation is putting that model to an immediate test: whether Gulf states can build enough defensive autonomy to withstand the next missile or drone attack while creating a political framework capable of making the next attack less likely. ■

Why are uninsured vehicles not part of crash relief scheme? Supreme Court

Unknown Publisher

22:02:24 UTC

Union road transport ministry officials said the scheme will be notified as provided for under Central Motor Vehicle Act.
NEW DELHI: With Centre formulating a scheme to provide interim financial relief of Rs 2 lakh to families of road crash victims for deaths and Rs 1 lakh for grievous injuries, limited to accidents involving insured vehicles, SC has sought an explanation from govt on why it is not being extended to uninsured vehicles.Taking note that “Compensation to Victims (Interim Relief) Scheme, 2026” has not been notified or publicised, a bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and KV Viswanathan directed the govt to publicise it to ensure awareness. People must be made aware of their right to seek interim compensation, it said.
Union road transport ministry officials said the scheme will be notified as provided for under Central Motor Vehicle Act. Govt informed SC that the ministry shared the scheme with states and UTs on Feb 23. SC had directed the ministry in April 2025 to formulate the scheme.On why it covers only insured vehicles, officials said it was framed under provisions of MV Act dealing with insured vehicles. If the offender’s vehicle is uninsured, the matter will go to a Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal (MACT).
The apex court bench examined clause 6 of the scheme, which specifies that victims or legal heirs of the deceased can apply through a designated online portal, providing details of claims filed or pending before a MACT.
Officials said that Section 164 of the Act, which deals with compensation in cases of death or grievous injury, requires the vehicle owner or insurer to pay Rs 5 lakh and Rs 2.5 lakh for death and serious injury, respectively, under the “no-fault liability” provision. A claimant need not establish that death or injury resulted from wrongful act, neglect or default on the vehicle owner’s part.“Hence, interim relief was set at Rs 2 lakh for death and Rs 1 lakh for serious injury for immediate relief. Final compensation would be higher, depending on the order of MACT,” an official said.

Rosatom completes supply of engineered safety features actuation systems for Kudankulam N-plant units 3 and 4
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:57:28 UTC
06:57:28 KST

NEW DELHI: Russia state atomic energy corporation Rosatom’s division Rosatom Automated Control Systems has completed the supply of equipment for engineered safety features actuation system computerised subsystems (ESFAS CS) for units 3 and 4 of the Kudankulam nuclear power plant in Tamil Nadu. The role of the general designer and supplier of equipment in the project belongs to Atomstroyexport.In total, about 300 items of equipment were manufactured and delivered to the plant – four sets of ESFAS CS in accordance with the number of safety instrumentation and control trains, per each power unit featuring VVER-1000 reactors.
ESFAS is the system that monitors the process parameters of a power unit when there is a deviation from normal operation conditions. In case of an accident, the system automatically initiates the start of safety instrumentation and control systems and sends commands to actuators (boron injection pumps and other active protection means) in order to prevent a beyond-design-basis accident and bring the reactor plant to a safe state. The system also ensures reactor cooldown, which is a controlled decrease of coolant temperature and pressure down to safe values after the shutdown.
To avoid simultaneous failure, they are physically separated — located in different rooms — and have autonomous power supply from separate diesel generators.Specialists developing the ESFAS CS for units 3 and 4 relied on the operating experience of the same system at Kudankulam NPP units 1 and 2, which allowed them to implement a number of optimised solutions. One of such solutions is the application of non-programmable modules that process signals from sensors without the use of microprocessors. This helps to reduce the dependence of safety functions on application software and increases the resistance of equipment to potential common cause failures.The final delivery of ESFAS CS equipment was yet another step of equipping the power units with Russian automation, control and safety systems, implemented through industrial cooperation. Installation on the site will be followed by the pre-commissioning stage, which includes the off-line and integrated tests of the systems.
Following the tests, the systems will be prepared for commissioning and further operation at units 3 and 4 of the Kudankulam plant.Kudankulam plant features six power units with VVER-1000 reactors, with the total installed capacity of 6,000 MW. The first phase (units 1 and 2) was commissioned in 2013 and 2017, respectively. The second phase (Units 3 and 4) is under construction.

Airbnb hosts are melting down over a new policy banning them from making guests complete tasks that “would typically be performed by a cleaner,” like “stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes.”

Many guests, meanwhile, are celebrating. For years, travelers have complained about having to pay hefty cleaning fees as part of their Airbnb bookings, only to be required to complete a list of chores before checking out.
“The guest experience has become total ass,” one person said in a subreddit for Airbnb hosts. “Clean dishes and run in the dishwasher. Strip the beds, put all linen in the laundry room. Take out all garbage, put in garbage can, take to the curb. Honestly, knock it off.”
Airbnb noted in its Wednesday announcement that hosts can’t get around the new policy by putting cleaning tasks in the “Requests” section of their listings instead. Airbnb spokesperson Simon Letouze tells WIRED that hosts can still make “reasonable” requests, such as asking guests to put dirty dishes in the sink. Other examples Airbnb cites include asking guests to take short showers in areas with drought-related water restrictions, or telling them to place trash in bear-proof containers.
In a Facebook group for Airbnb hosts, one person posted what they claimed was a screenshot of their failed attempt to edit their property’s “Requests” section. They tried to ask guests to wash and air-dry dishes, put dirty towels in the laundry room, and take trash to a dumpster at an RV park they could find using a map on the refrigerator. But they realized they couldn’t hit Save. Airbnb's interface had underlined and highlighted the requests in red and displayed a pop-up that read “Guests shouldn't be asked to do this task.”
Hosts also can’t circumvent the new policy by giving guests a printed list of rules and asking them to sign it when they check in. On November 20, Airbnb is also banning hosts from requiring guests to sign separate contracts, with limited exceptions for local legal requirements, longer stays, or accessing “an optional amenity” like a “golf cart rental.”
If one of these situations applies, hosts have to mention it in the dedicated section of their listing. Airbnb adds that it “doesn’t help enforce the terms of these contracts.” Hosts who violate either policy, Airbnb warns, may receive warnings, or in severe situations, have their listings removed or be banned from the platform entirely.
In a Facebook group for Airbnb hosts, one person posted a letter they claimed to have sent to company executives, demanding the ability to set their own “common-sense expectations” for guests. They encouraged others to send their own versions. Another asked if they should raise their prices, while a third called for hosts to organize a platform-wide strike.
“Even if we all unlist our properties for just a day or two, we can send a powerful message,” they wrote. “Airbnb built its empire on OUR properties. It’s time we reminded them who actually holds the power.”
Some hosts haven’t given up on finding a way to ignore or get around the changes. On Reddit, one person said they would simply move their rules to other sections of their listing, like “Guest Access.” (Airbnb did not immediately respond to WIRED’s inquiry about whether this would work.) Another person said they would give the guests a “house manual,” require the guest to read it, and provide a “codeword” as proof. (Several pointed out that this is not only unenforceable but against current Airbnb policy.)
“First sentence of my requests section will now state ‘Here are my house rules!’” another person said, though it’s unclear whether Airbnb’s interface will allow this. They named “not smoking” as an example of one of their house rules, but Airbnb has said it enforces host-imposed smoking bans.
Unwanted smoking and other serious scenarios—like letting dirty dishes become “health hazards,” leaving “permanent stains on sheets,” and creating “mountains of rotting garbage”—were invoked by several hosts. But these policy adjustments, seemingly, will not change how any of these things are treated.
Airbnb already has its own ground rules that all guests must agree to. The general credo is to "treat your host’s home like your own," which translates to things like putting trash in the trash can and not leaving moldy dishes.
If a host finds that anything was damaged or went missing during a stay, guests are expected to pay a “reasonable” amount to repair or replace it. Hosts are also protected through the platform’s protection program, AirCover, which will reimburse up to $3 million for certain property damage caused by guests, including furniture, cars, and other belongings.
Additional cleaning costs, such as performing "smoke odor removal" or handling "pet accidents” are also covered by AirCover. Airbnb notes that the cleaning fees hosts are allowed to set are only meant to cover standard guest turnover tasks like laundry and vacuuming. Hosts can’t “charge guest fees for failing to perform specific cleaning or checkout tasks,” though they can still leave guest reviews “based on cleanliness.”
In the Airbnb Hosts subreddit, a few lurking guests were quick to bring up the cleaning fees, which are famously the subject of their ire. One self-described “mostly guest” said they’re not opposed to running the dishwasher or stripping the bed. “Just don’t charge me a cleaning fee over $100 then,” they said.
“Truth nuke,” another person replied. “Why would I have to pre-game the cleaners?”

Meta hit with $25-billion penalty for misleading Facebook users about data privacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:43:21 UTC
06:43:21 KST

Meta hit with $25-billion penalty for misleading Facebook users about data privacy
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Meta, the parent company of Facebook, was ordered by a New Mexico judge on Wednesday to pay $25 billion for misleading users about how it collects and safeguards user data.
The penalty, one of the largest ever levied against Meta or any other company, is the latest legal hit to the social media giant, which has grappled with lawsuits over allegations of social media addiction and child safety.
New Mexico sued the company in 2021 after revelations surfaced that a U.K. political consulting firm had harvested millions of Facebook users’ personal data without their consent. The major data privacy scandal sparked more scrutiny of Facebook and led to lawsuits, congressional hearings and multibillion-dollar fines.
A New Mexico jury dealt a blow to Meta, previously named Facebook, in September, finding that the social media company committed 43 million violations of the state’s consumer protection laws by making false and misleading statements about data privacy protections and efforts to combat misinformation and hate speech.
“Today’s result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable,” New Mexico state Atty. Gen. Raúl Torrez said in a statement.
As part of the jury’s ruling, Meta faced up to $5,000 for each willful violation, according to a news release about the verdict.
Meta said in a statement it plans to appeal the ruling.
“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico. At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal,” C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said in a statement.
Facebook was found to have deceived its users through statements and remarks made on its own platforms, interviews, earnings calls and other channels. The social media platform has privacy settings, but “they do not provide any meaningful control over their data in many ways,” and the company intentionally tried to mislead the public, according to the court’s judgment in the New Mexico case.
The judgment also found that Facebook committed to notifying users when an app misused their data and deliberately didn’t.
Meta made misleading statements about whether it sells people’s data and profits from misinformation or hate speech, along with other practices, the New Mexico jury found.
Meta has long grappled with data privacy lawsuits and complaints. The company has expanded beyond social networking and sells consumer gadgets, including smart glasses, that have also raised privacy concerns after allegations that people are being recorded without their knowledge.
The company has suffered from several high-profile legal blows this year that have resulted in multibillion-dollar penalties. In August, Meta agreed to pay $17 billion to resolve a child safety lawsuit filed by California and other states.
The company lost a child safety case in Los Angeles. New Mexico has also imposed other penalties on Meta this year. A New Mexico court ordered Meta to pay $942 million and take steps to make the platform safer after the state sued the company over allegations that it violated state consumer protection laws and enabled mental health harms to and sexual exploitation of young people.
In 2025, Meta reported roughly $200 billion in annual revenue and $60 billion in net income.
Meta reported third-quarter revenue of $64 billion on Wednesday, beating Wall Street’s expectations. But legal expenses totaling roughly $10 billion tied to the August agreement to resolve the case over the mental health of young people did affect Meta’s bottom line.
The company’s operating income that quarter was $13 billion, down 37% from the same period last year because of the legal costs.
Meta’s stock was up around 4% in after-hours trading.

New norms for DL: Driving tutorial pass mark may rise to 75%, select licence services to be free
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:43:14 UTC
06:43:14 KST

Under the proposal, the safe-driving tutorial would have to last at least 30 minutes. (Representative image)
NEW DELHI: Road transport ministry has proposed raising the pass mark for safe-driving tutorial assessment from 60% to 75% and waiving fees for specified driving-licence services availed through online Aadhaar authentication, along with charges for changes to licence particulars such as name and address.The proposed changes to driving licence rules are aimed at tightening assessment requirements and to ensure availing licence-related services without any hassle. The changes proposed in the draft notification to amend sections of the Central Motor Vehicles Rules published late Wednesday night also seek to streamline online driving licence services, specify acceptable identity and residence documents, and introduce time limits for processing applications to change licence particulars.Under the proposal, the safe-driving tutorial would have to last at least 30 minutes. The higher qualifying score of 70% is aimed at making the assessment more stringent. The draft also proposes a defined procedure for online applications to change driving licence particulars, including name and address. Licencing authorities would have to approve or reject applications for changes within 15 days, giving reasons for rejection.
An application for an address change that remains undecided for 30 days would be deemed approved.The proposed rules also specify documents that can be submitted as proof of identity, age and residence. These include Aadhaar, passport, voter identity card, recognised educational certificates and birth certificates, among other documents. Electricity and household gas bills not older than three months are among the proposed address-proof documents.
LIC policy would no more be accepted as a proof.The draft also provides for a consolidated application form covering services such as licence renewal, issuance of duplicate licences, addition of a vehicle class and changes to personal particulars. Specified applicant details would be retrieved electronically from the SARATHI portal wherever available.In another proposed change, a vehicle class would be deleted from a driving licence within seven days of an application to surrender it. However, applicants permanently surrendering a class would not be eligible to obtain a learner’s or driving licence for that class for one year.The draft notification invites objections and suggestions from stakeholders within 30 days of publication. The proposals will come into force after final notification.

NEW DELHI: Certain safety features of Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) will be made mandatory for cars, particularly taxis, as govt steps up efforts to reduce road crashes. From Oct 2030, all new car models would be required to be equipped with the advanced emergency braking system (AEBS), the most important ADAS feature, TOI has learnt.As for pre-2030 still-in production models, AEBS would mandatory from Oct 2032.The draft notification, with timelines for different ADAS safety features for cars, would be out soon, people aware of the development said, adding that focus would be more on taxis. They said the proposed timelines take into account the lead time that industry and users would need.ADAS is a set of more than 100 electronic technologies that increases safety by detecting potential hazards, warning the driver, and in some cases, automatically controlling brakes or steering to prevent a collision. At present, some cars have ADAS.
Starting Jan 2027, new truck and bus models will have AEBS — it detects an imminent collision with a vehicle or obstacle and automatically applies brakes, if the driver fails to respond adequately, preventing a crash or reducing its severity.
Blind spot information, moving off information and driver drowsiness detection and alert, and lane departure warning systems have been also made mandatory for these commercial vehicles.
It’s learnt that features, including automatic command steering functionalities, emergency lane keeping system, drowsiness and attention warning systems, would be made mandatory for taxis.The introduction of these norms could initially focus on ensuring compliance with Automotive Industry Standards for vehicles already equipped with AEBS or more advanced systems that can intervene in steering and lane-keeping, said Automobile and mobility expert Rama Pandey. “These technologies could prove a boon for commercial drivers who spend hours behind the wheel. By shifting more safety-critical & fatigue-inducing driving decisions to automated systems, ADAS could make driving safer and less strenuous,” he added.

The social effect of MAGA: The American nation breathes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21

The social effect of MAGA: The American nation breathes
Published 21 Oct, 2026 21:19
Despite the disappointment among voters regarding the state of the economy in the US in recent years, there are observable effects and trends of social improvement.
First and foremost, it’s important to note a significant decrease in the level of violent crime. Of course, after President Donald Trump’s controversial firing of the head of the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Erica McEntarfer, for publishing weak labor market figures, trust in American statistics has been considerably shaken. Thus, reports of achieving the lowest murder rate in history – 4.3 cases per 100,000 population – may be politically motivated and deliberately boastful. Nevertheless, a noticeable decline in the rate of murders and other violent crimes has indeed occurred in recent years. This can be attributed to increased federal funding and strengthening of the police force, as well as intensified efforts against illegal immigration during the Trump administration.
A particularly striking aspect of this is the comparison with Canada, which has been and remains a bastion of liberalism in immigration and domestic policy. Unlike the US, where the level of violent crime is traditionally high, Canada has always been perceived as a safe society. But now, everything is changing before our eyes.
Since 2015, the rate of violent crime per capita in the U.S. has decreased by 15.1%, while in Canada, on the contrary, it has increased by 36.9%. As a result, for the first time in history, the land of the maple leaf has surpassed the U.S. in terms of violent crime per capita.
Another significant trend: Gallup polls show that the perception of homosexual relationships as morally acceptable has stopped increasing and even declined in the US The share of those supporting same-sex marriage fell from 71% in 2023 to 64% in 2026. Support for gender transition practices among Americans decreased from 46% to 38%.
The most radical shift has occurred among Republicans. While Democrats’ acceptance of the morality of homosexual relationships remains at 80%, and independent voters have dropped from 74% in 2021 to 64% in 2026, among Republicans, the acknowledgment of homosexual relations plummeted from 56% in 2022 to 35% today (see chart). Only 5% of Republican voters consider gender transition morally acceptable – compared to 42% of independents and 60% of Democrats.
As we can see, the MAGA effect is concentrated within the Republican electorate and primarily manifests in the consolidation of Republicans based on traditional values. At the same time, there is an intensifying value conflict between conservative Republicans and the Democratic Party electorate.
Perhaps the most vivid manifestation of the MAGA effect is that in the summer of 2024, the trend of decreasing births among white Americans was replaced by steady growth, and by spring 2026, the proportion of newborns from white families reached 51.5%, the first increase in five years.
Let’s see if this trend can be maintained, but the mere fact of the growth in births among white Americans is quite remarkable – it demonstrates a surge of optimism in the WASP (White Anglo-Saxon Protestant) community and proves that they still have fight left in them. In an era of victorious globalization, WASPs in the US were already being metaphorically buried with a derogatory epitaph, yet they suddenly breathed life and showed they are ready to fight for their country, which their ancestors built.
It is noteworthy that conservative and religious Americans have twice as many children as their liberal and non-religious counterparts. Thus, the conservative American community reproduces itself (total fertility rate 2.22), while the liberal American environment naturally shrinks by half in each subsequent generation (total fertility rate 1.02), mainly replenishing itself through immigration.
The descendants of pilgrims and pioneers remember that the primary traditional value is the will to live. Everything one needs to know about MAGA can be boiled down to two points. First, it is the rise of the American spirit. Second, it serves as a visual reiteration of a biblical lesson: the salvation of those who are drowning is in the hands of the drowners themselves.

Putin agrees to resume talks on Ukraine war with Kyiv and Washington, Kremlin says
In short:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine as soon as next month.
The Russian leader has met with US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg.
What's next?
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he supports the proposal, and is hopeful the three-way talks will take place in early November.
The Kremlin says Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume three-way negotiations next month with Washington and Kyiv aimed at ending the war in Ukraine.
The Russian leader met US envoy Steve Witkoff for talks in a grand imperial palace in St Petersburg.
Mr Putin's foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said the focus would be on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends".
The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February before the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran.
Mr Witkoff's talks with Mr Putin about Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine took place as US President Donald Trump pushed Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has insisted that only a leaders' summit can break the impasse.
Latest proposals have little of value, Kremlin says
The Kremlin said the discussion in St Petersburg lasted about three hours and came a day after Mr Witkoff met Mr Zelenskyy and some European leaders in Norway's capital, Oslo.
Mr Ushakov said the proposals from the Oslo meeting "contained little of real value in the context of resolving the Ukrainian crisis".
However, he later told Russian state TV that while Moscow was not "fully satisfied" with the Oslo proposals, they were a step in the right direction.
Mr Zelenskyy said he supported the proposal for three-way talks.
"We have received feedback that … Russia supports a trilateral meeting at the level of our [negotiating] teams," he said.
"The American side has proposed holding it as soon as possible and we support that …The Ukrainian side has been in contact with its American partners. They will do everything to ensure that the meeting takes place as early as possible, in November. I think no later than early November."
Mr Zelenskyy said that Kyiv supported "any proposals for a ceasefire, an end to the war, an energy ceasefire as well as humanitarian initiatives".
Witkoff sees 'some degree of momentum' in peace efforts
Mr Witkoff and Mr Putin met at St Petersburg's Constantine Palace, with Mr Ushakov and Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev also at the table.
Mr Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined the discussion via a video link.
Before the meeting, Mr Witkoff said that there was "some degree of momentum" in talks.
In televised opening remarks, Mr Witkoff thanked Mr Putin for agreeing to send diesel to the US after Mr Trump lifted a ban despite anger from some US lawmakers, adding that the fuel would help reduce prices for American farmers and truckers.
Mr Putin said he was ready to consider restoring US-Russia economic ties and was prepared to discuss the US-led conflict with Iran.
He said Moscow stands ready to use its relationship with Tehran to help bring peace.
Mr Ushakov said that "large-scale joint economic projects that offer significant prospects for cooperation" between Russia and the US were discussed in detail with Mr Witkoff.
"Some of these are, in fact, nearing the implementation stage," he said.
Russia resumes attacks on Ukraine
Just as Russia indicated its readiness to join the trilateral peace talks, officials in Ukraine reported the capital Kyiv had been attacked with ballistic missiles on Wednesday evening, local time.
Homes, a petrol station and transport equipment were damaged and six people were injured.
Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram there were strikes in two districts on the east side of the Dnipro River bisecting the city, and posted on social media:
"Explosions in the capital. Kyiv is under ballistic attack.
"Stay in shelters!"
The city remained under a drone warning for more than two hours after the initial alert was declared.
Russian authorities also said they downed most of the 630 drones heading towards Moscow overnight.
Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram that two people were injured in the attack outside of the city.

KINSHASA, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Ebola infections in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have rebounded after a brief decline, while the virus's spread to other African countries is complicating efforts to contain an outbreak that has already claimed more than 4,600 lives, the World Health Organization (WHO) warned in its latest situation report Wednesday.
"The most recent seven-day moving average indicates a modest upward trend, suggesting renewed intensification of transmission," the WHO Regional Office for Africa said in the report, highlighting the outbreak's "widening international dimension and the growing complexity."
The DRC recorded 1,466 confirmed cases between Sept. 29 and Oct. 19, up 10.4 percent from the preceding 21-day period, while confirmed deaths rose 7.5 percent to 692, according to the report.
As of Oct. 19, the DRC had recorded 9,637 confirmed cases and 4,646 deaths across eight of its 26 provinces.
Meanwhile, the outbreak's international spread has added a new layer of complexity to containment efforts.
Kenya has reported nine confirmed cases, including one death, with all eight secondary infections linked to an imported case and detected among people already under quarantine, according to the WHO report.
Nigeria confirmed its first case on Tuesday, involving a woman who had travelled from Uganda earlier this month. The WHO warned that the prolonged interval between symptom onset and laboratory confirmation raised concerns about "potentially undetected exposures and secondary transmission".
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warned Tuesday that the outbreak had become the most geographically widespread Ebola epidemic on record, with infections reported across Central, Eastern and Western Africa.
In its latest assessment, the WHO said the outbreak remained "at a critical juncture," warning that escalating insecurity, population displacement and restricted humanitarian access in the DRC were "further challenging response operations and increasing the risk of undetected transmission." ■

Interview: Regular central bank dialogue underpins win-win China-EU economic and financial ties: ECB official
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:16:08 CST
06:16:08 KST

SHANGHAI/FRANKFURT, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- The European Central Bank (ECB) and the People's Bank of China (PBOC) maintain regular multi-channel exchanges, and deeper mutual understanding yields shared benefits amid extensive trade, technology and financial ties linking China and the euro area, according to a member of the ECB's executive board.
China and Europe are advancing financial connectivity through institutionalized central bank dialogue. The first annual governors' meeting between the PBOC and the ECB, held in Beijing in June 2025, established a high-level communication channel.
"We interact with the People's Bank of China in different venues," Philip R. Lane, member of the ECB's Executive Board, told Xinhua in an interview in Shanghai. "The more we understand one another, the more it benefits everyone."
Together with renewed bilateral currency swap facilities and joint work on green finance standards, this institutional mechanism underpins deeper China-Europe financial ties, while both sides demonstrate leadership in developing sustainable finance frameworks for global markets.
On green finance, Lane said both the ECB and the PBOC recognize the importance of the green transition and have led the Network for Greening the Financial System. "The PBOC and the ECB are leaders in that global effort," he said, describing their joint role as critical in adapting the financial system to the green transition and the risks posed by extreme weather events.
For cross-border payments, Lane said the G20 roadmap is the best way to advance global coordination. As issuers of two of the world's major currencies, China and the euro area stand to gain greatly from steady exchanges under the G20. Regarding China's Cross-Border Interbank Payment System, he said it is natural for China to develop local-currency settlement facilities given its rising weight in global trade.
Lane, who attended the 2026 Bund Summit in Shanghai, said there is substantial interest in Europe in using China's open-weight AI models. He also expressed appreciation for how China is exploring ways to leverage AI within a regulated framework to manage downside risks.
China's gross domestic product grew 4.5 percent year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics. Lane said China's economy is an important driver of the world economy. Its strong export performance creates positive spillovers: European consumers enjoy greater product variety with lower prices, and European manufacturers gain access to more intermediate goods. "More domestic consumption would benefit China and the euro area," he added.
Through pragmatic and productive discussions, China and the European Union have shown a willingness to deepen cooperation and work toward a stable, more balanced economic and trade relationship. The two sides agreed to continue discussing the possibility of lowering tariffs on certain goods under WTO rules and reached an understanding on the trade of hybrid vehicles consistent with WTO rules.
Recent agreements aim to adjust the pace of trade flows, enabling the European automotive sector to adjust "in a more gradual manner," Lane remarked. He voiced optimism over the outlook for China-EU trade and investment ties. "China's growing wealth also allows its savings to finance European investment, representing a financial spillover," he said.
Underpinned by renewable energy expansion that lessens fossil fuel dependence, government fiscal backing, and AI-fuelled investment and manufacturing improvements, the euro area economy has proved more resilient than expected, prompting the ECB to raise its 2026 and 2027 growth forecasts in September.
With energy prices and inflation rising sharply due to the conflict in the Middle East, Lane said policymakers aim to guide inflation back toward the 2-percent target while avoiding derailing economic expansion. He added the ECB has implemented two rate hikes and will not lock in future moves in advance. ■
