Children who later develop psychosis tend to have slightly smaller heads, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:00:49 UTC
05:00:49 KST

A longitudinal study tracking thousands of children from birth to mid-adolescence suggests that young people who develop psychotic disorders tend to have smaller heads throughout their early lives. Published in Psychological Medicine, the research indicates that these head size differences are largely tied to overall body height, pointing toward a broader pattern of altered physical growth rather than an isolated issue with brain expansion. The findings also point to distinct trajectories between males and females who experience milder psychotic symptoms.
Psychosis is a psychiatric condition in which a person loses some contact with reality. It often involves hallucinations, which are sensory experiences of things that are not present, and delusions, which are firmly held false beliefs. Psychosis exists on a spectrum, with clinical psychotic disorders like schizophrenia at the severe end, which disrupt daily life and typically emerge in late adolescence or early adulthood. A much larger segment of the population reports isolated psychotic experiences, such as occasionally hearing a voice or feeling unusually suspicious, without meeting the threshold for a clinical illness.
Even though psychotic disorders usually appear in young adulthood, the neurodevelopmental model of schizophrenia proposes that the underlying biological roots of these conditions begin during fetal development and early childhood. Adults diagnosed with schizophrenia tend to have slightly smaller total brain volumes than peers without the condition, even before they ever take psychiatric medications. Because performing brain scans on thousands of infants and children is costly and impractical, scientists often rely on head circumference, a simple tape-measure reading around the widest part of the skull that is routinely recorded by pediatricians, as an indirect indicator of early brain size.
“The study was motivated by the need to identify inexpensive and accessible biomarkers of psychosis risk,” study co-author Kate Merritt, a lecturer in human neuroscience in the Division of Psychiatry at University College London, told PsyPost. “If we can identify people who are more likely to develop psychosis, this could eventually help us target preventative interventions toward those at greatest risk.”
“Much of our work focuses on using MRI to identify biological markers that predict outcomes in psychosis, but MRI is expensive and not widely accessible,” Merritt explained. “We therefore wondered whether a much simpler measure, head circumference, might provide useful information. Head circumference is correlated with brain volume, so we looked at whether differences in head growth might be associated with psychosis risk.”
Prior research examining infant head size and later mental health has produced mixed results. Some studies, including a 2005 study of Swedish twins, found that babies born with smaller head circumferences and lower birth weights were more likely to develop schizophrenia as adults. Other studies found larger head sizes, no link at all, or differences that only appeared in females or vanished by early childhood. Most of this earlier work only looked at measurements taken at birth or during the first few months of life, leaving it unknown how head growth unfolds through later childhood and adolescence.
Scientists have also questioned whether a smaller head reflects a biological process restricted to the brain or a whole-body growth pattern. For example, a 2007 study of over 1.3 million Swedish men indicated that shorter adult height and lower body mass index were associated with a higher risk of schizophrenia. Similarly, a 2007 birth cohort study found that women who developed schizophrenia-spectrum disorders grew in height about one centimeter per year slower during early childhood than women without these conditions.
To determine whether head growth trajectories differ across the psychosis spectrum and whether those differences are independent of overall body size, Merritt, lead author Sarah A. Ashley of University College London, and their colleagues examined data from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children. This population-based project tracked children born to pregnant women in the Southwest of England between April 1991 and December 1992.
The researchers analyzed an overall sample of 3,866 participants, including 2,177 females and 1,689 males, who had complete background records and at least one head circumference measurement between birth and age 15. Head measurements were collected across up to 22 time points, with major assessments occurring during the first year of life, at age 7, and at age 15. On average, participants had about eight head circumference measurements recorded over their childhood.
When the participants reached age 17 or 18, trained psychologists interviewed them using a semi-structured assessment to evaluate whether they had experienced hallucinations, delusions, or thought interference since age 12. Thought interference refers to the belief that one’s private thoughts are being broadcast out loud, inserted into one’s mind, or taken away by an outside force. Based on these interviews, 339 participants (8.8 percent of the sample, comprising 218 females and 121 males) were classified as having definite psychotic experiences.
Within that group, 62 individuals (1.6 percent of the sample, comprising 49 females and 13 males) met the operational criteria for a psychotic disorder. This meant their experiences occurred at least once a month over the preceding six months and caused severe distress, impaired their social or work functioning, or prompted them to seek professional help. The remaining 3,527 participants served as the comparison control group.
To confirm that external head measurements accurately reflected internal brain size in their sample, the researchers also analyzed structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain scans from a subset of 347 participants at age 20. From these scans, they calculated total intracranial volume, which is the total space inside the skull cavity occupied by the brain and surrounding fluids.
In their statistical models, the authors controlled for several maternal and birth factors that can influence physical growth. These included the mother’s highest level of education, her pre-pregnancy body mass index, the length of the pregnancy, and the baby’s weight at birth. In a secondary step, the researchers added the child’s height across development to see if head size differences persisted when accounting for overall physical stature.
The neuroimaging analysis confirmed that childhood head circumference was a reliable proxy for young adult brain size. Head size at birth showed a moderate positive correlation with total intracranial volume at age 20, while head measurements taken at ages 7 and 15 showed strong correlations with adult intracranial volume across both males and females.
When looking at growth trajectories over time, the researchers found that young people who met criteria for a psychotic disorder at age 18 had consistently smaller head circumferences than the control group from birth right through to age 15. Across the developmental span, the psychotic disorder group had an average head circumference about 0.26 centimeters smaller than controls in the statistical model, a small fraction of overall head size. The gap did not widen or narrow as the children aged, indicating that the modeled gap was similar in size from birth through adolescence.
The difference remained after accounting for maternal education and maternal body mass index, and shrank only slightly, to about 0.20 centimeters, when length of pregnancy and birth weight were added, though at that point it fell just short of statistical significance. Sensitivity checks looking strictly at birth, age 7, and age 15 also found smaller head sizes in the psychotic disorder group at each milestone, with the differences reaching statistical significance at ages 7 and 15.
When the team examined the larger group of 339 young people who reported broader psychotic experiences, they discovered contrasting patterns between males and females. Females with psychotic experiences had consistently smaller head circumferences across childhood and adolescence compared to female controls, averaging about 0.27 centimeters smaller in the unadjusted trajectory model.
In contrast, males with psychotic experiences had larger head circumferences than male controls across the overall trajectory model, averaging about 0.35 centimeters larger. In the age-by-age checks, however, males with psychotic experiences had smaller heads at birth and larger heads at ages 7 and 15. Both of the overall sex-specific patterns remained intact after adjusting for maternal and birth characteristics.
The smaller head sizes seen in the psychotic disorder group and among females with psychotic experiences stand in contrast to findings in autism spectrum disorder, a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by differences in social communication and restricted or repetitive behaviors. “For me, one of the most interesting aspects of this finding is what it tells us when considered alongside our work in autism spectrum disorder,” Merritt noted. “In a separate paper, we found the opposite pattern, with larger head circumference associated with autism. This suggests that patterns of brain growth may differ across different forms of neurodevelopmental risk, rather than there being a single pattern of atypical brain development.”
The picture shifted when the researchers factored in the children’s height over time. After controlling for height across development, the head circumference differences between the psychotic disorder group and the control group shrank and were no longer statistically significant. The same thing happened among females with psychotic experiences: once height was taken into account, their smaller head size was no longer statistically significant. The raw height differences between groups at age 15.5 were small and not statistically tested: females in the psychotic disorder group averaged about 1.6 centimeters shorter than female controls, while the 13 males in that group averaged slightly taller than male controls.
In males with psychotic experiences, however, controlling for height did not change the outcome, and their head circumferences remained larger than those of male controls. Together, these results suggest that for individuals with psychotic disorders and females with psychotic experiences, a smaller head circumference may reflect a broader, whole-body growth restriction rather than an issue confined to brain growth.
The authors noted that hormones regulating early physical development might help explain why general growth restriction and sex differences appear across the psychosis spectrum. One candidate they pointed to is insulin-like growth factor-I, a hormone that manages both fetal and childhood physical growth and naturally circulates at different levels in males and females. Early environmental stressors, such as maternal infections during pregnancy or nutritional deficiencies, could also influence both overall physical stature and future mental health risk.
“The key takeaway is that head circumference is a potentially useful, inexpensive measure for understanding developmental differences associated with psychosis risk,” Merritt said. “However, these findings reflect differences between groups and cannot currently be used to predict psychosis in an individual. We would not want people to interpret a smaller head circumference as meaning that someone will develop psychosis. There are many factors that contribute to psychosis risk, and head circumference would need to be considered alongside other measures.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these findings. Because the study followed participants over nearly two decades, not every child had their head measured at every possible age, and the researchers had to rely on statistical modeling to chart continuous trajectories across gaps in time. In addition, the classification of psychotic disorder at age 18 was based on structured research interviews rather than formal clinical diagnoses from a medical doctor.
The total number of participants who met the criteria for a psychotic disorder was relatively small at 62 people, and only 13 of them were male. Because of this small male sample size in the disorder group, the researchers may not have had enough statistical power to detect sex differences among those with full psychotic disorders, and findings involving males in that group should be viewed cautiously. Future studies using larger, independent birth cohorts will be needed to verify these sex-specific growth patterns and examine the biological mechanisms that link early physical growth to adult mental health.
“In the longer term, we are interested in whether head circumference could be combined with other developmental, genetic and environmental risk measures to improve our ability to identify individuals who might benefit from early intervention,” Merritt added.
The study, “Course of head growth from birth to adolescence across the psychosis spectrum,” was authored by Sarah A. Ashley, Kate Merritt, Francesca Solmi, Pedro Luque Laguna, Yanakan Logeswaran, Derek K. Jones, David Linden, Anthony S. David, and Abraham Reichenberg.

How do we actually turn down the temperature in political debate?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:47:44 UTC
04:47:44 KST

analysis
After alleged attack on Helen Haines, how do we actually turn down the temperature?
Only two months ago, a group called Compassion in Politics Australia gained the first signatory to its "Civility Pledge".
Helen Haines.
The organisation, based on a similar foundation in the United Kingdom, aims to turn the tide of toxic debate and build a better politics.
As a start, it's asking elected officials to sign a simple pledge. "In my political life, I pledge to act with honesty, respect, and compassion," is all it states.
This week the independent MP was the victim of an attack widely described as shocking but unsurprising. Sadly predictable was the common reaction amongst MPs who have been at the receiving end of increasing threats and harassment.
Yesterday, security agencies briefed MPs on the risks to their safety. Security will no doubt be improved as much as practicable, without sacrificing MPs' ability to interact in their communities.
The more difficult question is what, if anything, can be done about the increasingly hostile political environment. What can be done to restore the "civility" that Haines, at least, pledged to pursue?
Civility was the word emphasised by the Governor-General late yesterday, who stood alongside the husband of Helen Haines in an effort to calm a worried nation.
"We don't have to all agree, but we can wrestle with the issue not the person," Sam Mostyn said from Melbourne's Alfred Hospital. Her message echoed the call to turn the temperature down.
"Words matter, whether spoken or in written form or increasingly in the virtual world."
This call for civility is something ASIO boss Mike Burgess has been going on about now for years.
"I genuinely believe the temperature of our security environment would be several degrees lower if we recommitted to conversing with civility, debating with respect and disagreeing with restraint," he said after the attack on Haines.
Burgess draws a line between words and actions: "ASIO has seen direct correlations between inflamed language, inflamed tensions and acts of violence."
The intelligence chief must feel at times he's talking to a brick wall. He warned against "inflamed language" and called for a return to civility after the October 7 Hamas attack on Israel in 2023, again after lifting the terrorism threat level to "probable" in 2024, and again after the Bondi terrorist attack in 2025.
Will anyone listen this time? Will an attack on one of their own force politicians to re-think their part in setting the tone of political discourse?
For some, the answer is clearly yes. There is a degree of self-reflection this week.
"We should all, every single one of us, me included, find ways to minimise the temperature of these debates," said shadow minister Jono Duniam, who will soon depart the Senate.
"We could all do better. I don't exclude myself or any political party," acknowledged the prime minister who, like Burgess, has repeatedly called for a more civil debate.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, by contrast, is worried about limiting robust argument. While condemning anything that intimidates or incites violence, he defended the role of vigorous debate.
"We have, like so few other countries in the world, avoided political violence. This is part of the great Australian achievement, and we've done that by having vigorous and rigorous debate and choice at the ballot box," he said.
"This is what's worked for us. We need to make sure it stays there."
It's certainly true — Australia has long enjoyed robust political debate while largely avoiding political violence.
But this misses the point being made by the ASIO boss. Times have changed.
We're now in an environment, according to Burgess, where "politically motivated violence is more likely than previous years".
Angus Taylor's own colleagues can recognise the deterioration, too.
"It's clear that the political environment has become more heated in recent years," said shadow minister James Paterson.
"In the last few years things have gotten much worse," said independent MP Monique Ryan, adding that "the 2025 election was completely different to 2022", with more aggression and anger. It's a common view, particularly among female politicians.
MPs are worried. For themselves, for their families, and for the fate of Australia's democracy.
So, what does it take to turn the temperature down?
"Gosh, if only I could say what the answer to that is," One Nation's Barnaby Joyce admitted on Radio National yesterday. "I don't know," he said.
It's rare to hear Barnaby Joyce stumped for an answer on anything. He's certainly not accepting any blame on the part of One Nation for raising the temperature.
Many might agree with Joyce that there are no easy solutions to counter the powerful domestic and global forces driving voter frustration, political polarisation, toxic online discourse and hate.
Politicians are certainly limited in what they can control. But they're not entirely powerless.
As Burgess says, language matters: "By all means, disagree. But consider how you disagree."
Signing a "Civility Pledge" might seem like a mere symbolic gesture, but it's something. If it's good enough for Helen Haines, why not others?
Compassion in Politics Australia issued a statement after the horrific attack on Monday, calling it "a stark reminder that compassion and civility in public life are not abstract ideals. They matter profoundly".
The attack on Helen Haines may prove to be just another brief interruption before regular political mud-slinging resumes. Or it could see all sides of politics try to course correct.
David Speers is national political lead and host of Insiders, which airs on ABC TV at 9am on Sunday or can be streamed anytime on ABC iview.

The announcement came as it was still unclear whether the US-born pope would proceed with a planned trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, scheduled for Nov 6-17.

Five Facts You Need To Know From The U.N.'s Major Emissions Gap Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:44:08 UTC
04:44:08 KST

The goal of limiting global warming to below 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels is largely out of reach. That’s according to the United Nations Environmental Program’s (UNEP) 2026 Emissions Gap report released on Wednesday, considered the definitive assessment of global climate action.
“We’ve spent decades postponing cuts to emissions and now we’re facing the consequences,” Anne Olhoff, director of the UNEP-Copenhagen Climate Centre, and one of the report’s authors, said after the report’s publication. “The world can still attain the goals of the Paris Agreement but we must work hard to not only meet but surpass our most ambitious climate targets. The longer we wait, the larger the risk that we jeopardize the temperature goal.”
While the report’s warning is stark, that doesn’t mean that all hope is lost. Coordinated efforts to reduce emissions can still have a meaningful impact on climate change, it says—but action must be taken quickly.
Here are the biggest takeaways from the Emissions Gap report.
The 1.5°C target is mostly out of reach
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, the world agreed to halt planetary warming at 2°C above pre-industrial temperatures and to pursue efforts to limit warming by 1.5°C. Doing so would provide a greater chance at avoiding the worst impacts of climate change. The window to avoid overshooting the 1.5°C goal, however, is now closed, the report finds.
But that doesn’t mean that there’s no hope for climate action. It is still possible to limit the overshoot and bring temperatures back below 1.5 degrees by the end of the century. Every fraction of a degree of warming above 1.5°C increases climate impacts, making the goal to limit as much warming beyond 1.5°C all the more important.
The world is on track to reach 2.8°C of warming by 2100
Under the terms of the Paris Agreement, countries must submit updated climate pledges, known as Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), which outline specific goals to reduce national emissions. Based on the policies currently in place under the NDCs submitted by over 150 nations, the planet is on track to reach 2.8°C of warming by the end of the century.
Based on this, today’s report concludes that global climate pledges are falling short. If countries meet their new NDCs, which set upgraded targets for 2035 and were due last year, global warming is still projected to reach 2.6°C by the end of the century.
Both scenarios would have devastating consequences—dramatically transforming sea levels and ecosystems, and triggering compounding climate extremes such as higher temperatures and drought, increasing the likelihood of wildfires.
We need to cut carbon emissions by 18% in the next four years
The report notes that it is still possible to peak warming at 1.7°C or 1.8°C. Doing so would require major changes. We would need to cut emissions by 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035, and 69% by 2040, relative to 2025 levels. This would require sustained emissions cuts along with carbon dioxide removal.
“Every additional fraction of a degree and additional year of warming above 1.5°C increases climate impacts and risks, such as the deadly floods, heat waves, and wildfires that have plagued many nations this year,” said UNEP executive director Inger Andersen. “So, we must pull out all the stops to minimize peak warming and return to 1.5°C by the end of the century.”
The U.S. is a major outlier for emissions
While emissions growth has slowed down in most G20 countries, emissions in the United States “far exceeded that of all other countries," the report says. That’s due to the increased electricity demand, in part due to data centers, and new policies that encouraged the use of fossil fuels like coal over clean energy sources.
The report includes a statement from the State Department, noting that the U.S. "does not endorse or agree with its analysis or conclusions, and has not provided comments to this report."
The Trump Administration’s decision to withdraw from the Paris Agreement also worsened the climate projections, as estimates no longer include climate action that would have been taken under the United States’s NDC targets.
The U.S. is the second largest emitter of climate-warming greenhouse gases, behind China, which has quickly become a world leader in renewable energy (while also ramping up coal production.)
Climate policies are reducing emissions
Since the adoption of the Paris Agreement just over a decade ago, global renewable electricity capacity has grown three times faster than anticipated, while solar PV build-out has increased seven times faster. If these trends were to continue, and coupled with more policies to support clean energy, the world would be on track to reach its renewable energy goals.
The report examined more than 200 climate policies and found that they target emission reductions across a wide range of sectors and countries. That’s an encouraging sign the report notes. All that’s left is for these solutions to be scaled faster.
“We have a wealth of success stories showing that emissions can be cut quickly,” said Andersen. “It is now up to nations to urgently put in place policies that spark fast, deep and sustained emissions reductions, and put the world on track for a more stable climate and more stable economies and societies.”

Quick hits: Sore Smith doesn't return as Marnus throws it away on horror day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:43:42 UTC
04:43:42 KST

Steve Smith doesn't return after reaching a major milestone and Marnus Labuschagne makes a mockery of an enormous reprieve as Australia is sent barrelling towards a chastening defeat in Gqeberha.
Here are the quick hits from day four of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.
1. Fiery Marco tears through the Aussies
Fresh from his swashbuckling 85 on day three, the towering Marco Jansen continued to terrorise the Australians on day four.
The left-arm seamer was at his fiery, probing best, with his aggression and accuracy proving all too much for the tourists in their first innings.
Jansen dismissed both Scott Boland and Travis Head early in the day, before a few tense exchanges with Marnus Labuschagne appeared to light a fuse somewhere deep in the big man.
He proceeded to treat Matt Renshaw to a send-off — seemingly in Afrikaans — upon having the Yorkshire-born Queenslander caught at gully, before sending Alex Carey packing in a double breakthrough in the shadows of lunch.
Unfortunately for the Aussies, Jansen wasn't done there, with the South African having Beau Webster caught in the cordon to claim his fifth wicket and continue Australia's horror day.
2. Sore Smith reaches 11,000 and doesn't return
Amid the carnage up the other end, Steve Smith was just about hanging in there.
Struggling with a neck issue, the Australian received running repairs at multiple points during his innings and never quite looked his usual self.
Even so, Smith was at the crease long enough to become just the 12th batter to score 11,000 Test match runs, joining Ricky Ponting and Allan Border as the only Australians in that rare air.
But the Australia vice-captain was in serious discomfort throughout his innings, and departed promptly after joining that exclusive club.
The stiff-necked Smith was bowled through the gate by Wiaan Mulder for 28 as Australia was asked to follow on after being skittled for just 99, their fourth-lowest Test total against the Proteas.
And in a massive blow for his team, the Australia vice-captain did not recover in time to return to the crease as wickets started falling in the tourists' second dig, remaining in training gear in the dugout as Australia limped towards stumps.
3. Two remarkable grabs, two very different reactions
We have been treated to some seriously sensational slip catching in Gqeberha.
With Australia 3-45 in its first innings and already beginning to teeter, the desperately out-of-touch Labuschagne drove unconvincingly, sending his thick edge flying low and hard towards the cordon.
Harmer dived dramatically to his left, using his sizeable left hand to pluck the quickly dropping ball from the air in front of second slip.
And the off-spinner was absolutely pumped with his effort, throwing his head back and roaring as he got to his feet.
It provided quite some contrast to Renshaw's bewilderment after pouching his similarly excellent catch earlier in the Test.
4. Marnus throws it away after enormous reprieve
With Australia beginning its second innings needing 326 runs to just make South Africa bat again, Labuschagne had a golden opportunity to revive his sputtering Test career and make up for his rash dismissal earlier in the day.
Coming in after the early departure of Nic Maddinson, the signs were good for the Queenslander, who knuckled down with Head to push Australia towards 100.
And it was beginning to feel like Labuschagne might have finally been on for a score when he was the beneficiary of a huge reprieve in the 28th over.
Given out LBW to a Harmer off break, Labuschagne reviewed the decision in a blink and it was high drama as both camps waited for ball tracking to take an unusually long time to build.
Eventually, the technology projected the ball to be missing leg stump by what surely wasn't much more than a coat of paint.
Helmet off and head back, Labuschagne was making no secret of his relief.
But only moments later, he threw it all away, mistiming his slog and holing out to long-on for 39.
It was an ugly, ugly dismissal and one that left Australia once again on the rack with shadows lengthening in St George's.
5. Consecutive night shifts for Boland
With Australia proceeding to lose both Renshaw and Webster late on, Boland once again found himself batting in the dying embers of a day.
It was the second consecutive evening the Victorian had been called on as nightwatchman, and for the second consecutive evening, he made his way through to stumps.
Again, he betrayed no hint of annoyance with his sacrificial role, instead digging in and bravely finding his way through a couple of overs of twilight finger spin.
It was another committed shift from Boland — but boy, it's some reward for taking a five-wicket haul on his return to the team.
He'll begin day five alongside Head (87*) with Australia 4-156 and still 170 runs away from making South Africa bat again.

- Israelis living abroad are paying thousands of dollars to fly home and vote
Israelis living abroad are paying thousands of dollars to fly home and vote
Many Israelis view this election as a sliding doors moment, and are willing to fork out on flight fees and hotel costs to make a difference.
Around 1 million Israelis eligible to vote in the October 27 parliamentary election live outside the country. Yet Israel is one of the few democracies that requires citizens to be physically present to cast a ballot, with no general postal or proxy voting and no voting at embassies except for diplomats and official emissaries.
That has not stopped tens of thousands from making the trip. The AID Coalition’s Fly & Vote initiative estimates that more than 50,000 Israelis living abroad, many of them in the United States, plan to return to Israel to vote, often at a cost of thousands of dollars. For a large proportion of them, this is their first time doing so.
“It’s my duty”
Revital Ganon Baruch moved to California in 2011 with her husband and two children. She had never felt the need to return to vote, but this year she is taking a 14-hour flight because she believes Israel needs change.
“I think the elections are very crucial,” she said. “I felt that if I won’t do it, I would feel bad with myself,”
“It’s an effort of time and money, but if I feel as Israeli as I feel, it’s my duty to do it now.”
She added that she once questioned whether she had the right to vote from abroad. “But the way this government is running Israel is affecting people outside of Israel too.”
Why this election feels different
For many expatriates, the election has become a pivotal moment for Israel’s future, shaped by demographic change, the October 7 massacre, the war in Gaza, the hostage crisis and years of political division.
Ido Kadman, an Israeli living in New York who left the country in 1994, pointed to the growing political influence of ultra-Orthodox communities. “We have generations and decades of Hasidic Jews coming in droves to vote,” he said, arguing that many had “never served in the military, paid taxes, or done anything to actually contribute to this country.”
Others say October 7 was the catalyst. Many are angry at Benjamin Netanyahu’s government over its handling of the attack, the hostages and the war, as well as its judicial overhaul plans and dependence on far-right coalition partners.
Every vote counts
If around 50,000 expatriates vote, their ballots could be worth roughly two Knesset seats. With polls suggesting a close race, organizers believe the number, and the influence that could reach, could be higher.
Nadav Nir, an Israeli living in Berlin, said the tightness of the race made the journey worthwhile. “With the two blocs and everything being so close, I would say every vote counts,” he said.
Nadav, an active climate campaigner, acknowledged the environmental cost of flying, but said he saw it as a necessary trade-off. “Letting go a little of my climate-related worldview, to be a tiny help in this huge crisis that Israel is facing, was obvious for me.”
Who can vote?
Israeli citizens can vote as long as they are in Israel on election day, regardless of how long they have lived outside of the country.
Maya Gur Arieh was born in Israel, moved to Canada as a child and later returned to Israel as a young adult. She moved to London a month ago for her studies, but she and family members in Canada who have not lived in Israel for years are flying back to vote.
“We’re all angry Israelis living abroad,” she said. “It’s still very much our home, and we just want the future of the country to be much brighter.”
Israel’s Law of Return allows any Jew to obtain citizenship, preserving voting rights even for people who have spent most of their lives abroad.
Marco Greenberg, an American-Israeli living in New York, was born in Hollywood and lived in Israel for only three years, between 1993 and 1996. He sees no contradiction in returning to vote.
“I think it’s the right of being a citizen,” he said. “I was granted citizenship. I have every right to take full advantage of that.”
Many believe that it is unfair to that people can vote in elections in countries they were not born in, and have not lived in for a long time.
Marco said reactions within his own family had been mixed. “Some say, all the honor to you, it’s so patriotic. Others don’t say that. They say, WTF.”
He argued, however, that the connection between Israel and its diaspora citizens strengthens the country. “Having a strong relationship between the Jewish people in Israel and Israeli citizens around the globe is only an advantage to the state of Israel.”
Will the laws ever change?
Every expatriate interviewed for this report, both on and off the record, said they planned to vote for parties in the opposition bloc seeking to unseat Netanyahu.
That may explain why the prime minister has shown little interest in changing Israel’s voting rules. Many Israelis left the country in recent years amid dissatisfaction with his government, and making it easier for them to vote from abroad would likely benefit the opposition.
The issue is also legally and politically sensitive. Likud challenged Fly & Vote, an initiative that made it easier for Israelis living in the U.S. to fly to Israel for the October election, arguing that it amounted to improper election interference, before withdrawing its petition under a compromise that bars the group from subsidizing tickets or adding group flights.
And while the opposition may be tempted to loosen the rules if it takes power, the combination of Israel’s Law of Return and overseas voting could open the door to foreign interference. The concern among politicians is that a foreign group or organisation could encourage Jews abroad to obtain Israeli citizenship, remain outside the country, and vote according to that group’s agenda.
For now, Israelis abroad must pay their own way home. But for the tens of thousands making that journey, the cost is an investment in what they see as the future of their homeland.

Who are the terrorists? J&amp;K and Ladakh high court questions ‘vague’ detention order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:16:29 UTC
04:16:29 KST

SRINAGAR: J&K and Ladakh HC has summoned the Srinagar deputy commissioner for a personal appearance over a “vague” preventive detention order under Public Safety Act that accused a 28-year-old man of supporting “aforementioned terrorists” without identifying a single one, prompting the court to question whether the officer had independently assessed the case or merely reproduced a police dossier.A single bench of Justice Wasim Nargal said preventive detention, which allows authorities to deprive a person of liberty without a regular criminal trial, demands the “highest degree of constitutional responsibility and procedural diligence”.“The safeguards embodied in Articles 21 and 22 of the Constitution of India are not empty formalities,” the court said, adding that the detaining authority must independently assess the material and satisfy itself that legal conditions for detention are met.The court directed the DC to appear with the detention order, police dossier, material placed before him and records showing his consideration of the case and subjective satisfaction before ordering detention under PSA.HC was hearing a habeas corpus petition filed by Zubair Amin Bangroo of Srinagar, challenging his detention under an order dated Jan 13, 2026. His counsel Nida Nazir said the allegations were vague, no FIR had been registered against him and the detention order appeared to have been passed hurriedly.
The order accused Bangroo of developing close links with terrorists, supporting them logistically and morally, and allowing his home and other safe locations to be used as hideouts. However, Nazir said it neither identified the terrorists nor named the network or associates with whom Bangroo was allegedly in contact.
HC found that the detention grounds referred to “aforementioned terrorists” without any preceding reference identifying a terrorist. The phrase raised a compelling question about whether the DC had independently formulated the grounds or simply reproduced the police dossier, the court said.“Personal liberty occupies a position of paramount importance in the constitutional scheme. Its deprivation, even for a single day, constitutes an injury which cannot subsequently be undone by the mere restoration of liberty,” the court said.

US busts ring accused of arranging hundreds of sham marriages in Massachusetts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:10:20 UTC
04:10:20 KST

US busts ring accused of arranging hundreds of sham marriages in Massachusetts
- Federal prosecutors charged six people over a 12-year scheme in Massachusetts that allegedly arranged hundreds of sham marriages to help immigrants get green cards and possible US citizenship.
- US Attorney Leah Foley said Jennifer Gonzalez was the alleged mastermind, charging US$38,000 to US$40,000 per marriage and making over US$6 million in profit.
- The Justice Department said the case fits President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, and the investigation may lead to more charges against people who gained legal status through the scheme.
AI generated
BOSTON - Federal prosecutors on Oct 21 charged six people with participating in a long-running scheme to allegedly arrange hundreds of sham marriages in Massachusetts, in order to help immigrants unlawfully obtain green cards and potential US citizenship.
US Attorney Leah Foley during a press conference in Boston said the scheme’s alleged mastermind, Jennifer Gonzalez, helped organise sham marriages for over a decade in Massachusetts, a Democratic-led state the defendant described as a “sanctuary” jurisdiction where “you get a lot of help as an immigrant.”
It marked the latest such case by the US Department of Justice as part of Republican President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown. In August, it brought one of the largest such cases when in New York it charged 11 people over a scheme prosecutors said facilitated about 1,000 sham marriages.
Gonzalez, 43, told a cooperating witness posing as a client that her group helped obtain hundreds of permanent resident cards, or green cards, for non-citizens living illegally in Massachusetts, charging US$38,000 to US$40,000 (S$48,000 to S$51,000) for marriages to US citizens, according to a criminal complaint.
Authorities said the operation ran about 12 years and averaged about 18 to 20 fraudulent marriages annually, generating over US$6 million in profits.
Gonzalez, a US-born citizen, told the witness her goal was “for you to get the American Dream,” but that her business had become more difficult after Trump in 2025 returned to office, the complaint said.
Foley, whom the Trump administration appointed as the state’s top federal prosecutor, called it a sophisticated scheme that Gonzalez was “operating with impunity under the last administration.”
“My hope is that today the charged defendants and others like them realize that the American dream is not for sale,” Foley said.
“It is earned. And when you try to pilfer it for profit, we will hold you accountable.”
Gonzalez is charged with harbouring immigrants living illegally in the United States and marriage fraud. Her lawyer did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Other defendants include people accused of aiding Gonzalez’s scheme or entering into sham marriages with immigrants.
Foley said Gonzalez entered such a marriage herself and obtained food stamp benefits from Massachusetts without listing any income from her scheme, which she used to buy property in the Dominican Republic.
Foley said the investigation was ongoing and could result in future charges against anyone found to have obtained legal status through the scheme. REUTERS

Meta to pay New Mexico a historic US$25 billion in Cambridge Analytica Facebook case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Meta to pay New Mexico a historic US$25 billion in Cambridge Analytica Facebook case
The company was accused of lying to Facebook users about its privacy policies and how it handled their data in the wake of the scandal
Meta Platforms was ordered to pay a groundbreaking US$25 billion civil penalty to the state of New Mexico in a consumer deception case spurred by the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
The fine issued by state court Judge Francis Mathew is among the largest verdicts issued in US legal history.
The award comes after a jury in Santa Fe determined that Meta had violated the state’s consumer protection over 43 million times based on widely viewed deceptive statements made by the company and its top executives about how it handled hate speech and user data.
Under New Mexico’s Unfair Practices Act, Mathew could issue penalties of up to US$5,000 per violation.

Iran cautions Egypt against Yemen meddling as Sisi insists on limited Saudi defence role
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:08:18 UTC
04:08:18 KST

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said that any interference in the Yemen war by Egypt or any other country would make the situation "more difficult", even as Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el Sisi stressed that Cairo’s role is limited to defending Saudi territory and not launching attacks into Yemen.
"Egypt has sufficient experience to avoid entangling itself in such a highly complex conflict," said Iran's top diplomat in an interview with Iraqi state broadcaster Al-Iraqiya on Wednesday.
"We believe that any foreign presence or interference will only make resolving this issue more difficult," Araghchi noted.
Araghchi added that Egypt has said it "will not enter Yemen or engage in a war against Yemen".
Sisi also said on Wednesday that Egypt’s military support for Saudi Arabia does not include launching attacks on Yemen, stressing that Cairo’s role is limited to defending the Kingdom’s territory and borders.
“The Egyptian military effort is intended to defend the Kingdom’s territory and does not include an attack on Yemen,” el Sisi said.
Vote on October 26
Egypt’s parliament postponed a vote on authorising potential military support to help defend Saudi Arabia, rescheduling the decision for October 26 as regional security tensions rise.
Sisi asked lawmakers to approve military support for Saudi Arabia if requested by the kingdom, which has come under near-daily attacks from the Houthi militia.
The Egyptian president said Cairo was not seeking to "confront or attack anyone", adding: "We are speaking only about defence."
He explained that Egypt’s military role involves defending Saudi Arabia’s territory and borders, as well as those of any other Arab country that requests Cairo’s assistance.
Sisi stressed that Egyptian military efforts would not extend beyond Egypt’s borders or those of a fellow Arab country whose security and stability Cairo seeks to protect.
He also emphasised that Arab national security is "indivisible", saying the stability of Gulf countries is closely linked to Egypt’s national security.
Houthi attacks
The Egyptian president said Cairo’s support for Gulf countries reflects its commitment to collective Arab security.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthi militia seized the capital, Sanaa, and several provinces in 2014.
A Saudi-led coalition intervened the following year in support of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
A United Nations-brokered truce that took effect in April 2022 brought a period of relative calm after years of fighting.
Recent Houthi militia attacks on Saudi Arabia have renewed concerns about the durability of that calm and the risk of further regional instability.

US preparing to issue ordered departure of some personnel from Gulf embassies, say US officials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:06:27 UTC
04:06:27 KST

US orders diplomats to depart Saudi Arabia amid Houthi strikes
JERUSALEM/ISTANBUL/DUBAI – The US State Department has ordered some diplomats and family members to depart from its missions in Saudi Arabia and plans to withdraw family members from a number of other US missions in the region, US officials told Reuters.
The order came as attacks in Saudi Arabia killed at least one person and injured eight others at a civilian airport in Dammam and two people were killed in a drone attack on an oil field.
State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said in a post on X that the department ordered the departure of “non-emergency US government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only” amid attacks by the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen on civilian targets in the country.
Washington had returned some diplomatic personnel to the region in recent months after many were pulled out when Tehran launched attacks on US facilities after the US-Israeli war on Iran began in late February.
“Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions,” Pigott said.
Four US officials told Reuters that US missions in other Gulf states would also be ordering family members to leave. Pigott did not address changes to other missions outside Saudi Arabia.
The latest withdrawals follow an escalation of the fighting in Yemen, opening another front in the regional conflict triggered by the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The wider conflict has snarled global energy trade and hurt Gulf economies.
After the departure order, Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority on Oct 21 reported an attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam that killed one person and injured eight others.
Earlier in the day, two people were killed after Saudi air defences intercepted a drone that was attempting to hit a facility at Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oilfield, the energy ministry said.
The US embassy in Riyadh issued a security alert on Oct 21 about possible further attacks by the Houthis on Saudi Arabia, after recent deadly strikes including on Riyadh’s airport.
The embassy and a CIA station hosted there came under attack by drones in early March, as Iran began launching attacks across the region. REUTERS

France unveils AI literary prize amid debate over authorship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:03:43 UTC
04:03:43 KST

Three tech entrepreneurs in France on Wednesday said they had launched what they claimed was the first literary prize for books written with artificial intelligence.
Named the "Prix Pascal", it does not have a jury yet or declared prize money, but the initiative is intended to challenge other prizes which are struggling with how to regulate AI and its use by authors.
"The prize is open to anyone who writes in French, anywhere in the French-speaking world, with no requirement of nationality or residence, and without a publisher," said the three entrepreneurs, Philippe Rodriguez, Albin Serviant and Gilles Mentre, in a statement sent to AFP.
"Only the work itself matters: an unpublished work of fiction, in French, co-written with an artificial intelligence, that dares to do what has never been read before," they added.
France's literary world has been roiled since September by allegations that top-selling debut novelist Thelyson Orelien used AI to write his book "It was Either That or Die".
It won the prestigious FNAC prize in early September before Orelien was accused of cheating, which led to him being ejected from the shortlist for the Goncourt, France's top prize.
After weeks of denials, Orelien's original publisher in Canada, Boreal, said on Wednesday that it had "confirmed" that he had used artificial intelligence in the writing process.
Initiatives to label books as written by humans are gaining ground in the industry, while the organisers of established literary prizes are rewriting their rules to exclude AI-generated submissions.
But the issue poses thorny questions: will authors be allowed to use services such as ChatGPT or Claude for research or writing advice? When does AI-assisted research become AI writing?
Submissions for the debut Prix Pascal will be accepted until November 30 with the prize set to be handed out in mid-December, the organisers said.

Albares and his Thai counterpart strengthen bilateral relations at the 4th Spain–Thailand Forum

- During their meeting, the two Ministers held consultations and signed two agreements
The Minister for Foreign Affairs, European Union and Cooperation, José Manuel Albares, met on Wednesday with his Thai counterpart, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Sihasak Phuangketkeow, with whom he discussed bilateral relations, the EU’s agenda with Thailand and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), and the regional and global situation. The meeting between the two Ministers took place within the framework of the annual Political Consultations mechanism, which the two countries have maintained since 2017 and which is being held at ministerial level for the first time.
Albares welcomed his counterpart, highlighting the growing exchanges between Spain and Thailand and their shared commitment to further strengthening bilateral relations in areas such as political dialogue, multilateralism, connectivity and the energy transition. In the Minister’s words, the meeting “seeks to lay the foundations for a closer and more strategic partnership”, in line with Spain’s Asia-Pacific Strategy 2026–2029. In this spirit, the two Ministers signed two agreements during their meeting.
The two Ministers also inaugurated the 4th Spain–Thailand Forum, held at the headquarters of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, European Union and Cooperation and co-organised by Casa Asia.
Signing of agreements
Before holding the consultations, the Ministers signed an agreement waiving visa requirements for holders of official and service passports, aimed at facilitating exchanges of visits, and a memorandum of cooperation between their diplomatic schools, which provides, among other areas, for Spanish-language training for members of the Thai foreign service and the exchange of experts.
4th Spain–Thailand Forum and bilateral relations
The meeting between the Ministers took place ahead of the 4th Spain–Thailand Forum, hosted this year by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, European Union and Cooperation in its capacity as the holder of Casa Asia’s rotating presidency (2026). The Forum, launched in 2023 and organised by Casa Asia and the International Studies Centre of the Devawongse Varopakarn Institute of Foreign Affairs (DVIFA), is a valuable public diplomacy instrument aimed at facilitating dialogue on shared challenges. This year’s edition is being held under the theme “Innovation, Technology and Cooperation for a Shared Digital Future”.
During his opening remarks, Albares highlighted the Forum as a crucial public diplomacy instrument for bringing Spanish and Thai societies closer together, as both seek to strengthen their economic resilience by diversifying their partners. This priority is reflected in Spain’s new Strategy, which identifies Thailand as a key partner within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). Bilateral relations are currently excellent, driven by record levels of trade, a growing presence of Thai investment in Spain and extensive opportunities for cooperation in key sectors such as energy, infrastructure and technology.

Russia has said it is ready to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine in November, with discussions potentially taking place in Abu Dhabi.
President Vladimir Putin conveyed Moscow’s position to US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff during three hours of talks in St Petersburg on Wednesday, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov told reporters on Wednesday.
“Our president informed Steve Witkoff that we are, in principle, prepared to resume the aforementioned trilateral negotiations around the 10th of November,” Ushakov said.
The meeting was Putin and Witkoff’s ninth in-person encounter.
Ushakov said the situation in Ukraine was a central topic, with Moscow’s readiness to resume negotiations particularly concerning the creation of a post-war “security system” for Moscow and Kiev.
Putin praised Washington’s mediation efforts, Ushakov said. The Vesti news outlet also quoted the Kremlin aide as saying the talks could take place in the Emirati capital, Abu Dhabi.
Moscow and Kiev held three rounds of US-mediated negotiations earlier this year, on January 23–24, February 4–5 and February 17–18. Abu Dhabi hosted the first two rounds, while the third took place in Geneva.
Diplomacy on Iran
Ushakov said Putin also confirmed Russia’s willingness to help find political and diplomatic solutions concerning Iran.
“Vladimir Putin emphasised that diplomatic opportunities are far from exhausted. And that it is possible and necessary to reach an agreement with Tehran, our strategic partner,” he said.
He also said Witkoff briefed Putin on the substance of talks he took part in on Tuesday in Oslo, which included Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and leaders of Finland and Norway, and that the US sensed "some new nuances in the behaviour of the European leaders."
“They mentioned this to us, but, truth be told, these nuances do not entirely satisfy us,” he said.
The discussions also covered the implementation of agreements on Russian diesel supplies to the US and global markets following a phone call between Putin and US President Donald Trump earlier this month.
“The parties also held a detailed discussion on other large-scale joint economic projects, which offer significant prospects for cooperation between the two nations. Some of these initiatives are now nearing the implementation stage,” Ushakov said.
American prisoner released
During the meeting at Constantine Palace, Witkoff announced that Russia had released 73-year-old American Stephen Hubbard.
Hubbard was sentenced by the Moscow City Court on October 7, 2024, to six years and 10 months in a penal colony after being convicted of fighting alongside Ukrainian forces.
Ushakov said Russian officials handed Hubbard over to Witkoff at St Petersburg’s Pulkovo Airport for his return to the US.
The envoy thanked Putin on Trump’s behalf for the “gesture of goodwill”, saying the release would be appreciated by the US president and the American public, Ushakov added.

Could software cloning change the way we use the internet?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

An AI-cloned free tool is being dubbed 'the end of software'
It is being called "the end of software" and the dawn of a new era of AI-powered piracy.
New AI tools are disrupting the tech industry, making it relatively easy and fast to clone an existing piece of software and replicate its features.
Earlier this month, a small team of developers used AI tools to create near-identical, free versions of two commonly used products: Microsoft Office, with programs such as Word and Excel, and Adobe Creative, which includes Photoshop.
Around the same time, a different tool called Reverse Engineer Anything that helps developers use AI to deconstruct and replicate features in other pieces of software shot to the top of trending projects on software repository GitHub.
For some, this new generation of tools will disrupt software in the same way MP3 file-sharing networks in the late 1990s changed how we listened to music and watched movies, replacing CDs and DVDs with streaming.
But whether this will give more power to users or further concentrate power in the hands of AI companies remains to be seen.
'Set the clock back' to the 1990s internet
Brandon Thomas is one of the developers who recently announced they had used AI tools to copy the Microsoft Office and Adobe Creative suites.
A 15-year veteran of the US tech industry, he sees himself fighting a "war" for the future of the internet.
In the 1990s, "Everything [online] was nerdy, hackable and weird," he told the ABC.
"Everything in this era could be inspected, copied, shared with friends, remixed. It was amazing."
But over time, the internet became more standardised and bland. Spaces for innovation and personalisation, like Geocities or Myspace, were replaced by closed ecosystems that tightly controlled user access.
"Everything became a walled garden fiefdom, extractive and rent seeking,"
he said.
This is "enshittification", a term coined by writer Cory Doctorow in 2022 to describe the perceived decline of online spaces.
Social media platforms like Facebook initially attracted users with clean, chronological feeds and personal connections, then pivoted to intrusive ads and sponsored content.
Search engines became crowded with sponsored ads and affiliate-marketing spam, pushing out organic search results.
Software makers shifted to subscription-only models with automated billing and predatory cancellation fees, in some cases worth 50 per cent of the annual contract.
For some, AI is part of the problem, as "slop" content floods online spaces.
But for Mr Thomas, AI is the solution.
"AI flips the tide of this war in a way legislation never did," he said.
"We can build anything, even triple-A video games and operating systems.
"This is the most excited I've felt for the future in a long time.
"I think we have a great opportunity to take back the internet from the monopolistic platforms that became rent-seekers and behaved badly to us as users and customers."
How AI is making software easier to copy
Think of a piece of software like a cake from a bakery.
To copy the recipe, you could break into the bakery and steal the list of ingredients (the source code), for which you would be quickly prosecuted.
Or you could reverse engineer the cake by tearing it apart, tasting it, and studying it under a microscope. This is known as "decompiling".
You can then bake the cake based on what you learnt. Each time you bake the cake, you tweak the recipe so the result more closely matches your description.
Queensland University of Technology (QUT) digital economy expert Marek Kowalkiewicz said AI dramatically sped up this process.
"[AI-powered reverse engineering] is not very different from having a bunch of human software developers doing the same thing, but it's way faster and cheaper," Professor Kowalkiewicz told the ABC.
"In the past, I could have hired 100 developers to create a copy. Now it's not expensive anymore."
Reverse Engineer Anything, the viral tool on GitHub, dramatically streamlines the reverse-engineering process by allowing a user without coding skills to replicate features from other software at no cost.
The mood is giddy and chaotic in reverse-engineering forums where users share their projects.
These include hacking into the control systems of cars to replace factory dashboards, playing old games that have lost vendor support, or just figuring out ways to remove ads popping up on their smart TVs.
One user wants to make a free version of their therapy practice's management software. Someone else wants their printer to accept less expensive third-party ink cartridges.
One user writes:
"I'm so excited for all the good and bad stuff that will happen onward."
Software could be recreated legally
AI-generated software cloning means some tech companies face similar issues to musicians, authors and artists who have seen big tech steal their work to train AI.
These tech companies have trained the AI models being used to reverse engineer their own software.
"All those big players will be probably now be lobbying for legislative change and more protection of software," Professor Kowalkiewicz said.
"It's an arms race."
But copyright law was not equipped to deal with the emerging scale of the software cloning issue, according to Malcolm Burrows, a lawyer at Dundas Lawyers.
Software in Australia is protected under copyright as a class of literary work.
Reverse-engineered software is illegal where it is a "substantial reproduction" of an original.
But this will be hard to prove where AI tools have been used to copy software without access to the source code.
"It's going to get very grey in terms of source code and reproduction of software," Mr Burrows said.
Tool 'devalues work of developers'
While Mr Thomas and others dream of a retro internet, some fear a dystopian future.
The new AI tools may further entrench the power of AI companies and generate a rash of low-quality "slop" software.
QUT computer scientist Aaron Snoswell said the tools devalued the work of developers and would lead to more cost cutting and worse software.
"I think for the software industry it creates more of the same headaches and exacerbates the existing AI pain points," Dr Snoswell said.
"Companies are probably going to try to automate even more software development labour with AI."
This trend was already apparent among independent game developers.
"I'm seeing all these indie game developers who have spent 14 years developing their dream game … and then someone in one weekend can create a functional copy," Dr Snoswell said.
"What point is there in building with human effort, with human soul, if if can be stolen like that?"

New Mexico sues to stop payouts to Jeffrey Epstein's lawyer, accountant
Oct 21 - New Mexico has filed a civil lawsuit to block payments from Jeffrey Epstein's estate to the late sex offender's lawyer and accountant, and to recover damages for survivors of his alleged sexual abuse, the state's top law enforcement official said on Wednesday.
The suit is the first law enforcement action against Epstein's longtime personal attorney Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Kahn, according to New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez.
The lawsuit alleges Indyke and Kahn facilitated, financed, and concealed Epstein's sex trafficking operation, including at his ranch 30 miles south of New Mexico's capital Santa Fe. They are co-executors of Epstein's estate, valued at $107 million, and respectively eligible for bequests of $50 million and $25 million from it, according to the complaint.
Daniel Weiner, a lawyer representing Indyke and Kahn, rejected allegations the two "knowingly" facilitated Epstein's abuse of women, saying the crimes took place "behind closed doors, in secluded locations" when neither was present.
The suit will test whether authorities are able to pin down allegations that a network of people and financial arrangements helped sustain and conceal Epstein's operations.
“Jeffrey Epstein did not operate alone, and his death does not end the pursuit of accountability for the people who helped make his crimes possible,” Torrez said at a press conference in Albuquerque. He was joined by two survivors of Epstein's alleged abuse, Julia Molchanova and Anouska De Georgiou.
Indyke and Kahn have already been named in civil lawsuits against the Epstein estate, including a complaint last month seeking damages for people pictured in the late financier's collection of child sexual abuse material.
"Not a single woman has ever accused Mr. Indyke or Mr. Kahn of committing sexual abuse or witnessing sexual abuse," Weiner said in a statement, adding that the New Mexico attorney general's office had made no effort to interview the men before filing the lawsuit.
New Mexico's civil action comes after the Democratic-run state in February reopened an investigation into activities at Epstein's Zorro Ranch in New Mexico, where he is accused of abusing women and girls for nearly three decades.
Eight months into the probe, New Mexico has yet to file any criminal charges.
The state has sued the US Department of Justice for access to unredacted files on Epstein, accusing the Trump administration of stonewalling its investigation.
The DOJ said it provided some files but was prevented from handing over most material due to privacy protections.
Molchanova and De Georgiou, both prominent survivors of Epstein's sex trafficking network, applauded the New Mexico lawsuit to stop Indyke and Kahn profiting any further from the late sex-offender's estate.
"Accountability cannot end with Epstein and Maxwell, it must extend to those who knowingly made their abuse possible, especially those who stand to profit from it," said De Georgiou, a key witness at the trial of Epstein's partner Ghislaine Maxwell, convicted and sentenced to 20 years in prison in 2022 for sex trafficking of a minor and related conspiracy. British forces board German warship by air and sea
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:38:53 BST
03:38:53 KST

Royal Marines boarded the German support ship FGS Berlin by air and by sea during Exercise Strike Warrior, fast-roping from a Merlin helicopter while a second team climbed from a rigid inflatable boat, according to Defence Operations.
The post said the commandos were “making an entrance the commando way” and had boarded the vessel “sharpening their skills alongside NATO allies”, adding: “Training together to defend together.”
⚓ Making an entrance the commando way@RoyalMarines boarded German warship FGS Berlin by air and sea during Exercise Strike Warrior, sharpening their skills alongside @NATO allies.
🛡️Training together to defend together.#ExStrikeWarrior #SW26 pic.twitter.com/F2D1ya5Mhf
— Defence Operations 🇬🇧 (@DefenceOps) October 21, 2026
FGS Berlin is the lead ship of the German Navy’s Berlin class replenishment vessels and was serving as flagship of Standing NATO Maritime Group One, the alliance’s permanent naval force in northern European waters, which is currently under French command.
The boarding was carried out by personnel from K Company, 42 Commando, the Royal Marines unit that specialises in maritime interdiction. One team went up the ship’s side from a rigid inflatable boat using caving ladders, a physically demanding method in strong winds but one that preserves surprise, while another fast-roped onto the deck from a Merlin of 824 Naval Air Squadron, which is quicker but noisier.
Once aboard, the teams cleared the ship compartment by compartment carrying short-barrelled L119A1 rifles, prioritising the bridge and control rooms. A simulated casualty allowed commando and Royal Navy personnel to rehearse evacuating a wounded man from inside a ship.
Exercise Strike Warrior ran from 28 September to 9 October and involved more than two thousand personnel, eight warships and nineteen aircraft across Cape Wrath, the Western Isles, the North-West Approaches, Galloway, the Borders and the North Sea. The Royal Navy describes it as the largest test of the United Kingdom Commando Force in fifteen years, and the first time since the war in Afghanistan that all of its specialist elements have trained together.
The exercise rehearses allied crisis-response operations in the High North and the North Atlantic. Alongside Britain it drew in forces from the Netherlands, Canada, Germany, Norway and the United States, with the Portuguese frigate NRP Dom Francisco de Almeida, the Dutch frigate HNLMS Van Amstel and the Royal Canadian Navy frigate HMCS St John’s taking part.
Elsewhere in the exercise, soldiers of 148 (Meiktila) Commando Forward Observation Battery were carried to the Scottish coast aboard the German submarine U36, a Type 212A boat, before going ashore near Cape Wrath to direct naval gunfire from Portuguese, Dutch and Canadian warships onto simulated targets.
This publication reported when NATO warships arrived in Glasgow ahead of Strike Warrior and when Merlin helicopters headed to Scotland to protect the submarine force.

More young people are choosing to be child-free. Dita's decision was based on fear of the future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:36:40 UTC
03:36:40 KST

The Feed's latest debate brings together a panel of online voices to discuss the question: Why Are More People Choosing a Child-Free Life, and Should Having Kids Still Be a Priority? It can be streamed now on YouTube.
Dita has a husband she loves, financial security and — on paper — the foundations for family life.
But the 37-year-old and her partner have decided not to have children, citing fears about the world their children would inherit as one of the main reasons.
"I'm very pessimistic. I'm surrounded by fear," Dita said during The Feed's debate.
Although Dita believes her husband would make a wonderful father, her concerns about artificial intelligence, climate change and global conflict have reinforced her reluctance to bring a child into a world she cannot control.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The "nail in the coffin" was hearing about a doctor who had been charged with generating AI child sexual abuse material.
"Imagine a world where a man can just walk out, take a picture of your child and then upload it to AI … and be like, 'can you create child pornography of this?'" Dita said.
I'd rather protect my child from that and not give birth at all.
The decision is part of a broader trend — more young people are choosing to go child-free — resulting in Australia’s fertility rate falling to 1.481 births per woman in 2024, according to the ABS. A fertility rate of about 2.1 is generally considered necessary to maintain a population without migration.
A generation rethinking parenthood
The sense of uncertainty was reflected in Monash University's 2024 Australian Youth Barometer where affordable housing, employment and climate change were the three key issues identified as needing immediate action. The barometer, based on 620 young Australians aged 18-24, found that only about half of respondents thought they would have children in the future.
And according to the Growing up in Australia research report from the Australian Institute of Family Studies, 65 per cent of the 4,407 young people surveyed were at least "somewhat concerned" about climate change, with higher environmental concern linked with lower hopes of having children.
Fewer Australians want to become parents, with the number of people reporting that they do not want children rising from 8 per cent in 2005 to 14 per cent in 2023, according to data from the annual Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia survey.
"The cost of raising children and being able to buy a house are all factors becoming increasingly important in people's decision to have a child," Dr Pelin Akyol, a research manager at economic think tank the e61 Institute told The Feed.
A 2026 analysis commissioned for The Parenthood, a non-profit parental advocacy organisation, found that the cost of raising a family with children has increased 134 per cent since 2003 — and the yearly cost of raising two or more kids is about $36,500.
Akyol also said women are increasingly needing to prioritise their careers which is resulting in delaying — or entirely reconsidering — having children.
"Women put more emphasis on having time and energy for their career and they're reporting how important this factor is in their decision to have a child."
"We know that in Australia, the desired number of children is higher than the realised number of children," Akyol said.
Doubts about suitability
But concerns about the world are only part of the decision. Dr Imogene Smith, a clinical psychologist and researcher at Melbourne's Cairnmillar Institute, said some young people were also questioning whether parenthood suited them personally, including whether they felt capable of being a good parent.
"People list something central to their identity … for example, 'I'm not maternal or paternal' as a primary reason [not to have kids]," Smith said.
"Things like fear of overpopulation or the environment often seem to be secondary to that — although it doesn't mean it's any less important."
Smith said changing social expectations had also given young people more freedom to question whether parenthood was right for them. Previous generations often viewed having children as the expected path, whereas today the decision is more openly discussed.
"We have much more social discourse around decision making and this decision in particular ... which means that it's front of people's minds and people know that they have a choice and they're exercising that choice," Smith said.
The pressure to be a good parent
For those who do want to become parents, Smith said social media had made information more accessible, but had also left some prospective parents confused about how to raise children.
"Over the course of the last 50 years, we now have so many different 'expert opinions' about how to raise your child that people are reporting feeling confused now," Smith said.
Akyol said these expectations could affect how people perceive the cost of raising a child.
"Depending on a person's preferences about parenthood, they may also see the cost of having a child differently," she said.
"With the increasing role of social media in our life, people's view about being a better parent might have changed as well. We see parents providing a lot to their kids."
Stephanie Bastiaan, head of advocacy at Women's Forum Australia, a conservative think tank, said modern society was exaggerating the difficulties of parenthood.
"I do think we overthink it, particularly in this day and age where we're so top-heavy with influencers and content online," she said.
I just wonder if we're getting a bit soft as a culture.
Bastiaan, a mother of five with another one on the way, said negative media narratives and concerns about children's wellbeing were overshadowing the positive aspects of raising a family and increasing fear in young people.
"We've got a generation of kids coming out with poor mental health because we are instilling all this fear," she said.
Bastiaan acknowledged the strain on working parents, particularly women, who she said often shoulder much of the emotional and practical burden of raising children.
"If you have both parents in an economy where they have to work, then you've got them coming home after a day of work. They then have two hours where they've got to emotionally give to their kids," Bastiaan said.
We don't ever hear the joy of giving to a child.
"And you can see why there's such a high rate of burnout, particularly for women where that usually falls to them."
But Bastiaan argued that society also needed to talk more about the positive aspects of motherhood and family life.
"I feel sad that you're giving up something that's so beautiful because of that fear," she told Dita during the debate.
'If we don’t have children, we will go extinct'
George Mamalis, from conservative political advocacy group Turning Point Australia, believes negative attitudes towards having kids are having impacts on Australia’s future.
"The youth, they’re obsessed with climate change," Mamalis said on The Feed’s debate.
"I've actually heard in interviews kids saying they're not going to have kids because they're worried about climate change."
Mamalis believes people who opt out of parenthood are "selfish" and "entitled".
"It means that you're relying on those who are willing to have children," he said.
The fact is, if we don't have children, we will go extinct.
Lower fertility will be the main driver of slower population growth and faster ageing over the next four decades, according to the latest Intergenerational Report, however Australia’s population, which hit 28 million in June, is projected to grow to 39.3 million by 2065-66.
Being a 'good enough' parent
Smith said one way to ease the pressure was to reconsider what it means to be a good parent. She pointed to British paediatrician Donald Winnicott's concept of the "good enough parent", which emphasises providing children with the care, safety and love they need without striving for perfection.
"It has a very specific definition, and it means that you do enough to keep that child safe and happy and loved," Smith said.
The concept does not mean neglecting children's needs, Smith said, but recognising that parents cannot do everything perfectly.
She said the constant stream of parenting advice could make people feel they needed to meet unrealistic standards before they were ready to have children.
"The more they hear about how hard parenthood is, the more they're disinclined to participate," she said.
For Dita, the decision is also shaped by her own childhood. Growing up in a single-parent household, she watched her Indian-born mother work multiple jobs to support the family.
"I saw my mum struggle a lot," she said.
Dita said that although they could afford to provide for a child, she worried she and her husband’s demanding working hours would leave them without the time and energy to meet a child's emotional needs.
"We know that we would probably make terrible parents," she said.
Yet Dita has not ruled out motherhood entirely. If the obstacles were removed, she said she might reconsider. For now, she believes the decision should remain a personal one.
"At the end of the day, it's my body, my mind, my feelings, my choice. That's it."
