====================================================================================================

‘This Is Not a Drill’: Critical PHP Vulnerabilities Are Setting the Internet on Fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:26:19 UTC
23:26:19 KST

Internet security and web administration teams around the world are scrambling to prevent widespread disaster. On Wednesday, the developers behind the much-used PHP programming language released emergency security updates designed to fix critical flaws that could be exploited to allow attackers to gain dangerous remote control of victim systems.
The PHP Foundation detailed the two critical vulnerabilities—CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619—which impact “all PHP installations serving web requests” going back to PHP version 5, released in July 2004. However, only PHP 8.2 and newer are still supported and will receive patches, according to the alert. The PHP Foundation noted, though, that some PHP distributions and third-party vendors still produce legacy fixes. The caveat is significant because ubiquitous and foundational web layers like PHP can persist forgotten and un-updated in historic internet infrastructure.
“There are no complete mitigations, updating is the only safe choice,” the PHP Foundation wrote in its advisories. Security experts warn of the potential dire consequences of overlooking unpatched systems.
“This is not a drill,” says Lukasz Olejnik, an independent security consultant and visiting senior research fellow at King’s College London. Since its development in the 1990s, PHP has evolved into an essential scripting language for web development and is used across vast swaths of the internet in websites and software. Everything from publishing systems like WordPress and Drupal to e-commerce platforms like Adobe’s Magento are built on PHP.
Olejnik likens the widespread use of the programming language to critical infrastructure.
“The impact is enormous,” he says of PHP’s security flaws, adding that millions of systems could be impacted. “Especially if attackers would turn to exploiting these vulnerabilities fast. Worst case is wormable malware affecting big chunks of the internet.”
The overriding fear for security teams and developers is that malicious hackers could quickly jump upon the vulnerabilities and begin exploiting deployments before they are fixed. Internet infrastructure company Cloudflare reported it was “seeing early attacks emerging” before the PHP Foundation had detailed the vulnerabilities and released fixes. “We expect mass attacks to start within 15 minutes of the release,” security firm Sansec wrote ahead of the fixes, which were released just before 10 am ET on Wednesday.
“Most of the web runs on PHP and this bug is in a file upload interface that’s like a front door with no lock,” says longtime security and compliance consultant Davi Ottenheimer. “An attacker does not need to know which site they are hitting or even the actual software it runs. They send one crafted upload to any server they can find, and that is the entire attack.”
Ahead of the updated versions of PHP becoming available, some organizations took their websites offline as a precautionary measure. Multiple sites belonging to the Finnish government, including the National Land Survey, were inaccessible, according to reports. French government websites and the Port of Rotterdam’s website were also offline, according to Reuters.
“Everybody should patch immediately, exploitation may happen very fast and at a scale,” says Olejnik. “AI makes exploiting such vulnerabilities of immediate importance. Like, indeed, a minute or so.”
Security company Wiz, which is owned by Google, claimed its researchers discovered the vulnerabilities in PHP partially using AI tools, while OpenAI and security firm Calif also say they independently discovered the issues and worked together. Dubbing an exploitation demonstration php2shell , the Wiz researchers write that in some cases the vulnerabilities can be exploited “fairly easily.”
“The vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers or read sensitive process memory,” Wiz writes in its research. “That memory may contain passwords, authentication tokens, API keys and certificates belonging to other requests or the server itself.”
Details of the upcoming vulnerabilities first appeared from the maintainers behind PHP on October 20. In a short post on the PHP website, the PHP Foundation wrote it was giving “advance notice” of the security flaws and upcoming release of the fixes. While omitting specific details about the vulnerabilities or the versions impacted, it said both flaws are considered to have a “critical” 9.2 score out of 10 on the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS).
“We reserve the right to release earlier should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild,” the security warning on the PHP site said ahead of Wednesday’s release. According to reports from Bleeping Computer and Ars Technica, some details about the vulnerabilities may have leaked before they were due to officially be published.
The early warning from the PHP Foundation may have given some developers, security teams, and companies enough of a heads up to start preparing to update systems using PHP. Ahead of the details being published, warnings from the EU’s Computer Emergency Response Team (EU-CERT) and Australia's cybersecurity agency said IT teams should be prepared to update their systems as soon as possible, with the potential for websites to be taken offline while fixes are applied.
Similarly, the UK’s National Cyber Security Center (NCSC) published an alert saying organizations should “prepare for immediate updating of systems” using PHP. “Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organizations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated,” the agency wrote online.
The NCSC advises that organizations and businesses should identify systems running PHP across their tech infrastructure. There should be a particular focus on systems using PHP that are connected to the internet, including monitoring them for any potential exploitation. The next step is applying PHP updates as they are available and monitoring for updates from software companies as they may use PHP within their apps or services.
“If you find signs of compromise, isolate the system, preserve your web server and PHP logs, and report it to your local FBI field office,” Brett Leatherman, the FBI’s cyber assistant director posted online. “Those reports help us identify the actors involved and warn other organizations before they become victims.”

SpaceX stock jumps 8% after earnings beat and Musk hints at Tesla tie-up
Unknown

2026-10-21
14:21:39 UTC
23:21:39 KST

SpaceX stock jumped 10% Wednesday after the company reported surging revenue growth in its third quarter, and owner Elon Musk floated a potential SpaceX-Tesla merger.
The space company, which made its debut on the Nasdaq in the biggest initial public offering ever in June, reported third-quarter revenue on Tuesday of $14.6 billion, up 161% from the previous year, and beating LSEG consensus estimates of $12.72 billion.
Meanwhile, its operating income came in at $2.8 billion, with net income of $4.4 billion, after reporting a net loss of $1.05 billion in the same period a year earlier.
On an earnings call, Musk said he's considering a combination with Tesla — which would mark the largest merger in history — and that the boards of both companies have created specific committees to discuss a consolidation.
"I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained from cooperating," Musk said on the call. Tesla is set to report third-quarter earnings after the closing bell on Wednesday.
Shares of other space stocks, including Rocket Lab, Intuitive Machines and AST SpaceMobile climbed on Wednesday.
SpaceX forecasts first-quarter 2027 revenue between $33 billion and $37 billion, beating the average analyst estimate of $22.2 billion, according to LSEG.
"We delivered another strong quarter in Q3. Revenue grew an impressive 161% year-over-year, fueled by continued momentum in Connectivity and a clear inflection in our Super Intelligence business," SpaceX's chief financial officer, Bret Johnsen, said in the earnings release.
Johnsen pinned the strong results on recurring revenue from its satellite internet business, Starlink, and significant expansion of its Super Intelligence [SI] infrastructure.
The company has dived into artificial intelligence this year, which it's now calling SI. The segment is its largest business unit, with revenue soaring ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million in the same quarter last year.
Bull case for AI cloud providers
Commentary on computing during the earnings call supported "continued pricing power and shorter payback periods" for AI cloud providers, Truist Securities analysts said in a Tuesday note.
"Despite market concerns relating to financing for AI cloud providers this past week, we believe SpaceX's third-quarter 2026 represents the first data point during the earnings season to support the bull case for AI cloud providers," they added.
They explained that demand appears "insatiable," with SpaceX noting that it could rent out its capacity several times over. The analysts said Coreweave and Nebius are set to benefit and capture demand as "pricing power will more than offset higher rates."
The shares of neoclouds Nebius and Coreweave traded marginally lower, while Iren and Applied Digital climbed in early trading on Wednesday.
— CNBC's Lora Kolodny contributed to this report.

MSM ‘sources’ contradict Musk on Starlink for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:16:55 UTC
23:16:55 KST

MSM ‘sources’ contradict Musk on Starlink for Ukraine
The Wall Street Journal has challenged Elon Musk’s denials over alleged restrictions on satellite services used for Ukrainian drone strikes deep inside Russia. The outlet has cited anonymous White House sources who have claimed that the SpaceX founder and Starlink owner had personally ordered restricting the service.
Ukrainian officials last week claimed that SpaceX’s Starlink satellite communications service and its military-grade version, Starshield, which Kiev uses for frontline drone operations, stopped working on drones traveling faster than 160 kph (100 mph). Neither Starlink nor SpaceX has publicly acknowledged a technical “signal or service failure,” leaving the questions of whether an actual service restriction took place, and if so what could have caused it, unconfirmed.
What has Ukraine claimed about Starshield?
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky initially claimed, without evidence, that Kiev had been told “technical malfunctions” had caused a service slowdown. He later shifted the blame to Washington. On NBC’s ‘Meet the Press’ on Sunday Zelensky claimed, again without citing evidence nor being asked to provide it, that an order had come from the US government. According to Zelensky, Kiev had even secretly despatched cars to the EU, where they could drive "legally" at 180kph (110mph) where tests allegedly surfaced discrepancies in Starlink performance between the EU and Ukraine.
What has Musk said about Starshield?
Musk has categorically denied that he instructed SpaceX to restrict either service, nor has he confirmed that any restriction or slowdown took place.
The WSJ cited anonymous sources who contradicted him, alleging on Tuesday that he personally ordered speed limits on Ukrainian hardware connected to the satellite network.
Even the WSJ's sources accounts differed. Some claimed that Musk acted unilaterally; others said he consulted senior administration officials, including President Donald Trump, before making the decision. The outlet also claimed that SpaceX representatives contacted the White House to coordinate their accounts of whether the restrictions had been agreed on with the administration.
What has the US government said about Starshield?
Musk earlier insisted that Starshield is owned and controlled by the US government, meaning any speed or usage restrictions are determined by the US military and ultimately Trump – who denied that he ordered the restrictions, though he said on Monday he “would like to find out” who did. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent both said the administration was not behind the restrictions, with Bessent rebuking Zelensky for making “reckless” allegations.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio also rejected the claims. Questioned about the allegation during a visit to India on Wednesday, he warned Kiev against escalating the dispute, saying Ukraine “would not exist” as a sovereign state without US support.
Relations between Zelensky and Washington have effectively collapsed in recent weeks over sanctions on Russia and Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. Both Musk and Trump have sharply criticized Ukraine’s attacks on Russian diesel refineries, blaming them for global fuel shortages and soaring prices at the pump.
Speaking at the Oval Office on Tuesday, Trump warned Zelensky that he is “going to have to want to make a deal.” He also criticized the cost of supporting Kiev, saying the US has received “absolutely nothing back” except “grief, death and tremendous monetary loss.”
What did Kiev say about Starshield?
Despite Zelensky’s evidence-free assertions and there being no record in the public sphere to support it, the Western press and Ukrainian diplomats are echoing the claims regardless. Ukraine’s ambassador in Washington, Denis Senik, said on Tuesday that Kiev is still “waiting for the official response from contacts with the Pentagon and SpaceX” to understand what happened.
What did the Kremlin say about Starshield?
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said last week that Moscow is unaware of the reported Starlink restrictions, but stressed that “overall, of course, it would be better if such amazing technology… was not used for military purposes at all.” Moscow has condemned Western military assistance for Kiev, arguing that it only prolongs the conflict and obstructs peace efforts.
Is there any proof Starshield was slowed down?
There is no proof on the public record or in the public domain that the Starshield was affected. The only suggestions supporting the idea such an incident took place are Vladimir Zelensky's uncontested claim that Ukrainians sent cars to the EU with Starlink terminals to compare data and the claims of an anonymous Ukrainian officer who told German media giant Axel Springer's Global Reporter's Network, seemingly during the alleged service restriction, that all operations were on hold.

Global diesel prices seen staying high despite Trump’s deal with Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:15:00 UTC
23:15:00 KST

Global diesel prices seen staying high despite Trump’s deal with Russia
- Trump’s deal with Russia is unlikely to cut diesel prices much. Analysts said the promised volumes are too small to ease the global supply squeeze.
- US diesel prices have stayed above US$6 a gallon since September. The issue has become a political risk for Trump and Republicans before the Nov 3 midterm elections.
- Russia may struggle to deliver the extra fuel because of weak refining, high freight costs and sanctions. The International Energy Agency warned shortages could last until 2027.
AI generated
NEW YORK – US President Donald Trump’s deal with Russia to supply diesel to US and global markets is unlikely to meaningfully lower diesel prices, market watchers and analysts said, noting that the promised volumes are too small to ease a global supply squeeze.
Diesel prices have shot to record highs during the US-Israeli war on Iran, creating a political liability for Trump and his Republican party as they campaign to maintain thin majorities in the US Congress in the Nov 3 midterm elections.
Critics of Trump’s move said lifting sanctions on Russian diesel could help Moscow fund further attacks on Ukraine, undermining years of efforts to curb Russian energy revenues and raising the risk the Kremlin could profit while consumers get little relief from high fuel prices.
Trump said Russia would immediately export 300,000 tonnes, or 2.25 million barrels, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter”.
Analysts have said it may not be possible for Russia to produce enough excess diesel in the near-term to meet those ambitious goals, while a strained global tanker market may also make timely shipments difficult.
Analysts also said the announced volumes are unlikely to meaningfully lower diesel prices.
US retail diesel prices topped US$6 a gallon in September for the first time ever and have remained above that level since.
Big promises, limited impact
Michelle Brouhard, head of policy and geopolitical risk at Kpler, said it would take an additional 400,000 barrels per day of diesel supply to materially ease prices in the current market.
But the initial shipment of roughly 2.2 million barrels would amount to only about 73,000 bpd if distributed over a month.
She said that volume on its own would probably not significantly affect global diesel prices.
Caspian Conran, lead economist at consulting firm Baringa, estimated that the market would require an additional 850,000 bpd of supply to produce an immediate softening in prices.
Trump initially said Russia would immediately supply diesel to the US and global markets to help bring down fuel prices, but later said the Russian cargoes would be released to global markets rather than shipped to the US.
This raised questions about whether the deal will deliver the domestic supply relief the president promised.
“The diesel that Putin was going to sell, they were going to make it available to the global market one way or the other,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said over the weekend. “The only difference is how much of it the US was going to get.”
White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said Trump announced that “massive amounts” of Russian diesel will supply the global markets and will lower prices at home and abroad.
“President Trump continues to secure good deals, not just for the United States, but for the world,” Rogers said.
Strained refining system, high freight rates
It was unclear whether Russia can substantially increase diesel exports in the near term due to limited Russian export availability and elevated freight costs.
Shipping data on Oct 20 showed some Russian diesel cargoes were returning to their traditional destinations after the US suspended sanctions and secured the lifting of an export ban.
At least two tankers were signalling trips to Turkey and Brazil.
Data also showed Russia has resumed diesel export loadings from the Baltic port of Primorsk following an agreement between Washington and Moscow to supply fuel to global markets.
Disruptions to diesel exports from Russia, the world’s second-largest diesel exporter after the US, and the Middle East reached 1.3 million barrels per day in September, about 4.5% of global diesel and gasoil demand.
The International Energy Agency has warned shortages could persist into 2027.
“We question whether Russia’s refineries could even support an increase in exports with, by some estimates, up to 45% of Russia’s refining capacity currently offline,” said Mary Melton, an analyst with tanker company Braemar.
Delivering the announced volumes in addition to existing exports would require Russia to produce roughly 384,000 to 509,000 barrels per day of diesel, the Energy Policy Research Foundation said in a note.
Russia currently produces about 1.4 million barrels per day and consumes roughly 1.2 million barrels per day domestically, leaving little surplus available for export.
Traders noted the country is currently importing distillates and lacks sufficient production and surplus volumes.
While an end to attacks could allow damaged facilities to begin repairs and eventually return to international markets, sources said that is unlikely to happen before the end of the year, a view widely shared across the market.
Ukraine resumed its attacks on Russian refineries last week with a strike on a plant in the Ryazan region.
Moreover, freight rates for Russian oil and fuel exports have also risen sharply amid heightened security risks in the Black Sea.

What to Say When Someone Cuts in Line in Front of You
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:05:54 UTC
23:05:54 KST

Wait a second. You’ve been standing in line for 20 minutes, famished and desperate to order one of the viral bagels that keep selling out—or for six hours outside a concert venue, determined to claim a spot at the barricade to see your favorite band.
And then someone strolls up and slips in line ahead of you. Apparently, the rest of you have been standing around for the ambiance.
How much of a sin are line-cutters committing? “You are ripping the fabric of society apart,” says Nick Leighton, an etiquette expert and co-host of the podcast Were You Raised by Wolves? Queue-jumpers have to live with that, he adds. “But worse, we have to live with you.”
Here’s exactly how to handle this maddening situation—including when and how best to speak up.
When to speak up about someone cutting in line
If a stranger jumping ahead of you feels strangely personal, Richard C. Larson, a professor emeritus of data, systems, and society at MIT who has studied queuing, understands why. “We only have a finite number of minutes of life on Earth,” he says. The cutter’s implied message: “A minute of my life is worth more than a minute of yours.”
Before you decide whether to confront the offender, think about what speaking up would accomplish. Are you trying to reclaim your turn or get revenge? Sometimes, the impulse is “to sort of let them know you think they’re a jerk,” says Ryan Martin, a professor of psychology and dean of the College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences at the University of Wisconsin–Green Bay, known online as the Anger Professor because he studies strong emotions.
Martin would speak up to help someone recognize “that what they did wasn’t OK and that I wanted them to go to the back of the line,” he says. But he’d also consider: “What is going to allow me to have the kind of night I want to have?” If you spend the concert replaying a confrontation instead of singing your happy heart out, you’ve lost more than your place in line.
Leighton's gut check for situations like these is to ask yourself: Is this the hill you want to die on? “That’s always a good etiquette question,” he says.
Consider your safety, too. If the person seems hostile or you feel uneasy approaching them, you can ask staff for help or let the cut go. “Health and safety always trumps etiquette,” Leighton says.
What to say—if you do decide to say something
Marie Helweg-Larsen, a professor of psychology at Dickinson College who studies social norms, has explored what makes line-cutting so rage-inducing. For a 2008 study, she and a colleague surveyed U2 fans waiting for prime concert-floor spots, asking how they would react to hypothetical line-cutting scenarios.
Interestingly, fans reacted just as negatively to someone cutting behind them as ahead of them—even though their own place wasn’t affected. “You have to have people follow the rules,” she says, “or your investment into the line falls apart.” Helweg-Larsen’s co-author also heard fans invoke a higher authority when someone misbehaved: “Bono wouldn’t like that!”
You don’t need a rock star’s moral authority—or a grand speech—to point out where the line starts. Helweg-Larsen’s suggested opener: “Excuse me, but the line starts down there.” Aim for an “‘I’m just trying to be helpful’ kind of vibe,” she says.
That approach gives the person a chance to correct their mistake without having to defend their character. And you don’t have to believe it was an innocent oversight to deliver the message graciously. “Even if they’re doing it on purpose, you still need to use that tone,” Leighton says.
He’s been on the receiving end of a polite correction himself: At a deli, he once joined what he thought was the back of the line, only to discover he’d guessed wrong. He was happy for someone to point him in the right direction.
If you decide to speak up, do it promptly. “Your window of opportunity is short,” Leighton says. “As soon as it happens, that’s when you need to say something.” Waiting until you’ve spent five minutes glaring at the back of someone’s head won’t make the conversation any easier.
For a line that represents a serious investment of time, Martin suggests spelling that out: “Hey, I’m not sure you noticed, but there’s actually a really long line here, and people have been waiting all day.” You’ve identified the problem and given them an opening to say “Oops.”
Of course, some situations are murkier than a stranger breezing past the entire queue. Someone returning from a bathroom break is different from four friends arriving hours later to join the person who saved their places. Leighton is sympathetic to a water or restroom run. Holding spots all day for a last-minute entourage? “I don’t love that,” he says.
What to do if a line-cutter won’t move
Sometimes, your kind reminder won’t be met with the same level of helpfulness: They saw the line. They’re staying put. Now what?
If you feel comfortable continuing, Martin suggests a firmer follow-up: “I really think you should go back to the back of the line.” You’re making a direct request without adding an insult.
Larson advises skipping any confrontational nicknames or demands—like “What do you think you’re doing, bud?” You’re pointing someone toward the back of the line, not challenging them to a duel.
If the person still refuses to move, resist the urge to keep arguing. “We can’t control everybody,” Martin says. Continuing to push someone who’s already refused could lead to “a more significant confrontation.”
At a concert venue, amusement park, or other staffed location, you can ask an employee or security person to step in. “You can always appeal to a higher authority,” Leighton says. Whether they’ll enforce the rules is another question, but it’s an option worth trying when the cutting is particularly egregious.
If you decide to drop it, drop the parting shot, too. A sarcastic “Must be nice!” might feel irresistible, but Leighton advises against adding more rudeness to the encounter. “It will not achieve anything,” he says.
As Larson puts it, “A fight can ruin your whole day—or life.”

====================================================================================================

Extraversion is linked to faster relief from depressive symptoms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:00:45 UTC
23:00:45 KST

As patients receive inpatient treatment for depression, their personality traits often shift in tandem with their recovering mood, pointing to a deeply intertwined relationship between character and mental health. Individuals with higher average levels of neuroticism experience a slower recovery across a wide range of depressive symptoms, while those who lean toward extraversion or agreeableness tend to bounce back faster. These findings were recently published in the Journal of Affective Disorders.
Mental health professionals classify human personality into five broad domains, often called the Big Five. Neuroticism involves a tendency to experience negative emotions like sadness and worry. Extraversion reflects how outgoing, enthusiastic, and socially engaged a person is. Openness describes a willingness to try new things and embrace novel ideas.
Agreeableness involves being cooperative, empathetic, and trusting. Finally, conscientiousness is characterized by being organized, reliable, and goal-oriented. Together, these traits shape how individuals perceive the world and interact with others.
Depression is a highly varied condition. Two people diagnosed with major depressive disorder might experience entirely different challenges. One might sleep too much and feel constantly guilty, while another might suffer from insomnia and a total loss of appetite. Standard therapies help many people, but about one third of patients do not see their symptoms improve.
Researchers want to know why some people respond well to therapy while others do not. Personality is a prime suspect in this investigation. Prior studies have established a strong link between personality dimensions and psychiatric conditions. Neuroticism is generally viewed as a risk factor for mental health struggles, whereas extraversion and conscientiousness are often seen as protective traits.
Mara Carlotta Berg and Maike Richter, along with senior authors Mitja Back and Nils Opel, led the new investigation. The team includes researchers from the University of Münster and Charité Universitätsmedizin Berlin in Germany. They wanted to understand how personality and depression evolve together over time. They also wanted to look beyond total depression scores to see how specific symptoms respond to treatment in people with different personality profiles.
The research team recruited 334 psychiatric patients receiving care at a German university hospital. The participants had been diagnosed with affective or psychotic disorders, such as major depressive disorder or bipolar disorder. To be included in the analysis, patients needed to stay in the hospital for at least four weeks. This minimum duration allowed the research team to track their progress over a meaningful timeframe.
Patients completed digital questionnaires upon admission and then again roughly every two weeks. The final assessment took place shortly before they were discharged from the hospital. One questionnaire measured the severity of 21 different depressive symptoms experienced over the previous two weeks. This assessment included questions about mood, suicidal thoughts, and physical complaints.
A second questionnaire assessed the Big Five personality traits. The researchers opted for a very brief, 15-item version of a standard personality test. This shortened format reduced the burden on patients who were already dealing with severe mental health challenges. The research team then used statistical models to track how these scores shifted and interacted from admission to discharge.
The overall severity of depression dropped substantially across the study population as patients received inpatient care. Alongside this clinical improvement, the researchers observed coordinated shifts in how patients described their own personalities. Neuroticism scores went down over the course of the hospital stay. At the same time, scores for conscientiousness and extraversion went up.
The statistical models revealed a synchronized relationship between personality and mood. Patients who reported the steepest drops in neuroticism also experienced the largest reductions in their overall depression scores. The reverse was true for agreeableness, conscientiousness, and extraversion. For those three traits, greater increases over the course of treatment were tied to larger mood improvements.
The researchers then broke the depression data down to the level of individual symptoms. They wanted to see if a patient’s average personality profile during their stay influenced the speed of their recovery for specific issues. They found that higher average neuroticism was associated with slower improvement across 14 distinct symptoms.
These lingering issues spanned emotional problems like sadness, irritability, and suicidal thoughts, to physical complaints like insomnia, appetite loss, and somatic worries. The broad impact of neuroticism aligns with its reputation as a general vulnerability factor in mental health. Patients with high neuroticism often experience heightened emotional reactivity and persistent rumination, which might make these symptoms harder to shake.
Other personality traits were linked to faster recovery in specific areas. Patients with higher average extraversion saw quicker relief from seven symptoms, including work difficulty, indecisiveness, and pessimism. Higher average agreeableness mapped onto faster improvements in self-blame, guilt, and body image concerns. Openness was associated with a quicker return of sexual interest and a faster reduction in feelings of guilt.
Conscientiousness was the only trait that did not show these item-by-item associations with recovery speed. While conscientiousness increased overall as patients felt better, it did not seem to dictate the pace at which individual depressive symptoms faded. The researchers suspect that the benefits of conscientiousness might operate through broader behavioral habits that are not captured by specific symptom questions.
The study relies on observational data gathered during naturalistic treatment. Because patients received different types of therapy for varying lengths of time, the results cannot establish that personality directly caused the symptoms to change. The researchers note that the brief personality questionnaire used in the study has limited precision. The short test may have reduced the reliability of the measurements, particularly for the extraversion trait.
It is also difficult to separate true personality changes from a recovering mood. When people are deeply depressed, they often view themselves through a negative lens. The observed changes in personality traits might reflect enduring psychological growth. Alternatively, they might simply represent a return to the patient’s normal baseline as their depression lifts.
Future studies could track patients for months or years after discharge to see if the personality changes stick. Researchers could also use more comprehensive personality tests to confirm the symptom-specific findings. Understanding these patterns could eventually help mental health professionals design more personalized treatments.
Psychiatry is gradually moving toward precision medicine, where care is tailored to the individual rather than the diagnosis alone. If a clinician knows a patient has high neuroticism, they might anticipate a slower recovery and deploy targeted interventions earlier. These targeted interventions could focus specifically on emotion regulation or persistent rumination. Conversely, highly extraverted patients might benefit most from socially engaging group therapies.
The study, “Big Five personality dimensions and their association with depressive symptom severity over the treatment course,” was authored by Mara Carlotta Berg, Maike Richter, Marius Gruber, Janik Goltermann, Luise Victoria Claaß, Julian Herpertz, Ramona Leenings, Lara Gutfleisch, Jonathan Mathias Fasshauer, Michael Storck, Rogério Blitz, Udo Dannlowski, Mitja Back, and Nils Opel.

Military satellites could be refuelled in orbit
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:00:44 BST
23:00:44 KST

Life extension of the in-service SKYNET 5 military communications satellites would use in-orbit servicing, assembly and manufacturing technologies, and any requirement for future defence satellites to be capable of refuelling will be considered on a capability-by-capability basis, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Olly Glover, the Liberal Democrat member for Didcot and Wantage, asked whether the Secretary of State will set out whether future defence satellites will be required to be refuelled.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence, said: “In-Orbit Servicing, Assembly and Manufacturing was one of four prioritised sub-sectors in the UK’s National Space Strategy. As part of our Defence Investment Plan the life extension of the in-service SKYNET 5 military communications satellites, would utilise ISAM technologies. The Ministry of Defence continues to consider the potential benefits of emerging in-orbit servicing technologies, including satellite refuelling, which could enhance the resilience, flexibility and operational life of Defence space capabilities. Any requirement for future Defence satellites to be capable of refuelling would be considered on a capability-by-capability basis, taking account of operational requirements, technological maturity and value for money.”
A geostationary communications satellite spends most of its propellant on station keeping, nudging itself back into position against the pull of the sun and moon, and it dies when the tanks run dry even though the radios still work.
SKYNET 5 was launched between 2007 and 2012 and built by Airbus, carrying British secure military communications across most of the globe, and the fleet has already run well past its original design life. SKYNET 6A is under construction with Airbus for launch later this decade, and this publication reported when the contract was awarded, with the wider SKYNET Enduring Capability programme covering the ground segment and future spacecraft.

The Iranian foreign minister reiterated that Tehran had already handed over to the United States, via Qatar, a seven-day plan that envisages the restoration of the navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, and it particularly stipulates that "the Strait would reopen on Day 6, with the resumption of talks for a final deal commencing on Day 7."
"If the plan is implemented, life in the region will begin to return to normal. As a career diplomat, I am obliged to do my utmost to give diplomacy a chance, even when hope of success is scant," Araghchi said.
"If the US again chooses military action over diplomacy, I can say with complete and utter confidence that it will result in an even greater strategic failure," he added.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, in the early morning hours of July 8, the US resumed large-scale strikes against Iran, accusing it of violating the terms of the agreements reached on the Strait of Hormuz.
Nearly 25% of global oil trade and about 20% of the liquefied natural gas trade are transported through the strait. The US administration then effectively indicated that it would stop using large-scale military force against Iran and instead seek to economically strangle the country through sanctions.

Peek into hidden worlds revealed by the 2026 Nikon Small World contest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:00:31 UTC
23:00:31 KST

Peek into hidden worlds revealed by the 2026 Nikon Small World contest
Winners include ink droplets frozen in flight and what a molting tardigrade leaves behind
Nestled within a rebuilt inkjet printer, droplets of ink hang suspended above a page. Seen through a microscope, the droplets reveal how an inkjet printer produces crisp, uniform letters.
Ole Bielfeldt, a design student in Cologne, Germany, has been photographing the microscopic world since about 2021. His interest began as a quarantine hobby, when an old school microscope from his attic gave him a way to explore while stuck at home during the pandemic.
His printer image won first place in the 2026 Nikon Small World photomicrography competition. To capture the winning photo, he built a custom rig that moved the paper instead of the printer’s ink nozzles, keeping the nozzles stationary and in focus.
The mini side of ‘macro’
Ole Bielfeldt created this custom rig to catch impossibly fast ink droplets midflight. The contraption is only a bit larger than his head. Swipe through to see what word the printer was spitting out ink to spell.
Bielfeldt estimates that the droplets traveled at nearly 20 meters per second — too fast for even his best slow-motion camera to resolve. To freeze their motion, Bielfeldt worked in darkness, illuminating the scene with a single brief flash. He instructed the printer to repeatedly spell out “macro,” a nod to his social media handle, macrofying.
Before this project, a printer was “like magic,” Bielfeldt says. Photographing its inner workings helped him understand how it operates.
Bielfeldt no longer takes the magic printers spit out for granted. “It’s so, so advanced technically, but at the same time it’s so, so common,” he says.
His photograph is one of 86 images recognized in this year’s competition, whose winners were announced October 21. Here are some of our other favorites.
Did you capture my jumping side?
This pollen-dusted jumping spider offers a close look at the bristling hairs and some of its eight eyes that are easy to miss with the naked eye.
John-Oliver Dum’s fascination with spiders began as a childhood fear. Dum says he suffered a particularly painful arachnid-inflicted bite when he was young. Several years ago, when he was inspired to study the movements of a curly hair tarantula (Tliltocatl albopilosus), Dum became passionate about capturing their beauty.
Preparations for his photographs can begin years before he submits them to a competition. His wife grows plants selected for their pollen, which Dum uses in his images.
“The biggest challenge was finding a spider like this on the right plants, with the right pollen attached to it, at exactly the right time of year and at exactly the right moment,” he says. “You need to understand not only the spider’s behavior, but also the surrounding insect and plant life and their seasonal rhythms.”
Dum hopes the photograph, which won second place, encourages viewers to look more closely, too. “We first have to see the beauty of this largely unknown world before we can truly understand what we may be destroying,” he says.
Seeing a mouse eye in a new way
It’s not a leaf and it’s not a flower. This cross section of a mouse eye is crisscrossed in fractals of blood vessels and tethered by the optic nerve.
Cell biologists Sinem Karaman and Satu Paavonsalo at the University of Helsinki visualize vascular networks, like blood vessels, to study how they work within tissues. The arrangement, Paavonsalo says, could even point to mechanisms underlying how these systems stop working in obesity and diabetes.
Paavonsalo says the duo set out to capture a mouse eye in 3-D, different from the flattened retinas typically used in her research. After meticulous mounting which required several attempts for an arrangement she was satisfied with, Paavonsalo still didn’t know for certain the image would turn out right.
“I had to hope that the sample was correctly positioned and that the staining was detected throughout the sample,” Paavonsalo says, which made her excitement upon seeing the image even more pronounced. The image won 19th place in the competition.
A tardigrade Easter egg
A water bear emerges from its shed cuticle, and oh! What’s that left behind? This egg will be protected by its mother’s discarded skin.
The tardigrade (Hypsibius exemplaris) is one of nature’s toughest creatures, able to survive space by going into a state of suspended animation. This species, emerging from its former skin, is only about two-and-a-half times as wide as a strand of hair. Evolutionary developmental biologist Gonzalo Quiroga-Artigas captured the image during his studies of these tiny wonders at the University of Montpellier in France.
In the tardigrade life cycle, “egg laying is closely synchronized with molting,” says Quiroga-Artigas. Tardigrades can lay up to about a dozen eggs at once, and the moment one sheds its old cuticle happens quickly enough that it’s easy to miss.
Snapping this image demanded painstaking mounting and imaging of many specimens. Quiroga-Artigas chose this particular one, which won 12th, because “the egg looks almost like a precious gem being left behind by its mother.”
The stretch of a slime mold
This slime mold (Hemitrichia sp.) was found in the heart of Brooklyn, N.Y., sprouting from a decaying log in Prospect Park. The image features the mold’s gelatinous fruiting bodies, which release spores as part of reproduction. To bring the delicate structures into sharp detail, Eric Epstein stacked 240 images.
First, Epstein searched local parks for slime molds to photograph, carefully cutting pieces of waterlogged wood free without disturbing his subjects. “In this liquidy state, any touch would demolish” the fruiting bodies, he says.
One species of slime mold closely mirrors the cosmic web of gas and dark matter connecting galaxies, which helps scientists to more accurately map the cosmos. Another species has fascinated researchers for its ability to pack a store of bacteria to feed the next generation, when it’s near death.
Epstein hopes the photograph hints “at [a] vast array of activity beyond our unaided perception.” The image won sixth place in the competition.
A brain full of stars
This cell could have become anything in the body. Through some scientific nudging, it burst into a brilliant neuron.
Clusters of nuclei, looking like flashpoints in an intricate web, were captured by undergraduate student Faith Fernandes and structural cell biologist James Glover at the University of California, Berkeley.
The image commemorates the team’s first attempt at crafting neurons from a particular kind of stem cell. “I was so instantly enamored with this piece that I made it my computer wallpaper as soon as it was taken,” Fernandes says.
The eruption of color depicts human induced pluripotent stem cells, which can become any type of cell in the body, that have developed into neurons. The neurotubules, which contribute to the structure of and transportation of intracellular molecules, appear blue. Orange indicates where the DNA is located.
The stem cells are created by reprogramming adult cells to a stage before the cell was locked into a path to become a specific type of cell. They are studied for their many potential applications in regenerative medicine.
Fernandes says she hopes that studying these cells will illuminate ways to address neurodegeneration in diseases such as Parkinson’s disease. Already, researchers have used these cells to regrow eye tissue, address premature aging in mouse studies and grow organs. The shot won an Image of Distinction title in the competition.

AI Guardrails Aren’t Stopping Criminal Hackers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

As AI adoption spreads among both malicious hackers and defenders, even relatively unsophisticated cybercriminals are incorporating agentic AI into their campaigns and getting around model safeguards, according to new details published on Wednesday about recent successful attacks by four different threat groups.
Researchers from the threat intelligence firm CrowdStrike looked at the AI infrastructure powering attacks perpetrated between May and August by four previously unreported groups—one that operates in Chinese, one in Spanish and English, one in Indonesian, and one in Russian. The former two exhibited sophisticated AI “harnesses,” the software that supports and guides a model to carry out tasks. The latter two showed less technical prowess, researchers found, but were still able to compromise multiple targets. All had left their AI infrastructure openly accessible on web servers, allowing the researchers to analyze their activity and which models they used—largely versions of Anthropic’s Claude as well as versions of the open-weight Deepseek models. All the actors devised ways to allow their campaigns to run autonomously over relatively long periods of time.
“You can leverage different models for different aspects in the operation. Model routing and selection is very important because it’s expensive and a lot of times would be overkill to use newer models,” says Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike's senior vice president of counter adversary work. The researchers observed the attackers using both open- and closed-weight models; in almost all cases, they were using older versions rather than working with frontier models. Meyers notes that doing as much as possible with older models is common in legitimate AI usage, too, as costs mount.
The attackers also used multiple models to take advantage of differences in the guardrails meant to prevent people from using AI to carry out digital attacks.
“The models don't all have equivalent guardrails and protections, even from one company,” Meyers says. He adds about the sophistication of the hacking campaigns overall that “these attacks are not using new exploits or novel vulnerabilities. They’re really just taking advantage of the speed and the volume that you can use AI for in conducting these operations targeting the bulk of security hygiene issues in a lot of these environments—things that were preventable but weren’t prevented.”
The researchers found that all four threat actors circumvented AI safeguards, often by convincing a model that the activity was all legitimate and authorized, often for penetration testing or other security evaluation. One method used by many of the groups involves adding files to an agent’s working directory to try to show that tasks are approved and authorized. The attackers also used traditional jailbreaking methods, crafting prompts and narratives framing their hacking as authorized and benign, and proactively addressing potential questions or concerns the models might raise. The more sophisticated actors were typically more strategic in their world-building, while the less sophisticated actors sometimes resorted to more crude and aggressive prompts that tried to bully the models into accepting that the activity was legitimate.
The Chinese-speaking actor also used what's known as a “run time patch,” in this case a tool known as ClawGod, to add functionality on top of Claude Code and attempt to remove the “CYBER_RISK_INSTRUCTION” from the Claude Code system prompt, an instruction directing Claude Code to only participate in authorized security testing, not abusive or destructive hacking.
The actor that worked in Spanish and English targeted Argentine health care entities and successfully compromised at least 15 organizations. CrowdStrike researchers see evidence that the actor stole credentials and medical records from at least one of these victims. The actor special built a penetration testing harness, the kind an organization would use to test its own infrastructure, to find and fix vulnerabilities. Using models including Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Haiku 4.5, and Deepseek V4 Pro, the group set up a full infrastructure for autonomous attacks involving a “Supervisor” Claude Code agent to direct the steps of an attack and an “Executor” agent to carry them out.
The attacker working in Chinese also built penetration testing harnesses to guide Claude Code in reconnaissance and then autonomously attack once a human had selected a course of action. The researchers found that the actor successfully compromised government targets in both Brazil and Colombia and also targeted private organizations in Brazil and the United States in a range of sectors that include biotech, healthcare, food and beverage, retail, technology, and travel.
According to the researchers, the Chinese-speaking actor primarily relied on Claude Opus 4.8, but also used other models including Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Deepseek Chat. The actor accessed Claude through an AI proxy service based in China but set up multiple fallbacks to other AI tools if Claude was not available through the proxy.
Anthropic did not provide comment ahead of publication, and Deepseek did not immediately respond to WIRED's requests for comment.
The researchers say that both the Russian-speaking actor, which seems to have been focused on financially motivated “e-crime,” and the Indonesian-speaking actor (the least sophisticated of the four) used more basic, publicly available skills and harnesses to carry out their attacks. But both were still successful at compromising targets. This included multiple Indonesian government domains, a Bangladeshi government domain, and some private-sector targets, in the case of the Indonesian-speaking actor.
“What we are seeing is humans are doing some of the initial probing in these situations and then they’re engaging the AI for the hacking at scale,” CrowdStrike’s Meyers says. “I find it interesting that even with agentic attacks with all of these capabilities, we could still see that there’s a human behind it and what they’re up to.”

Russia willing to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine – Moscow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:59:26 UTC
22:59:26 KST

Russia willing to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine – Moscow
Russia is ready to resume three-way negotiations with the US and Ukraine to discuss security arrangements for when the conflict has ended, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov has said.
The announcement followed nearly three hours of talks between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff at Constantine Palace in St. Petersburg on Wednesday. Jared Kushner joined by video link after illness prevented him from traveling.
Ushakov said Putin told Witkoff that Moscow was “in principle, ready to resume” trilateral negotiations in mid-November, with the main topic being a post-conflict security system for Russia and Ukraine. Witkoff indicated that Trump would welcome the proposal, the aide added.
The presidential aide noted that earlier attempts to restart trilateral talks were derailed by Kiev having carried out massive attacks on Moscow and other cities during Russia’s recent parliamentary elections. Polling stations were targeted on the main voting day, with election commission personnel killed.
However, the situation has since been “re-evaluated, taking into account the signals received from the Americans,” Ushakov said, adding that Putin had praised the mediation efforts of Trump, his administration, and special representatives in seeking mutually acceptable solutions.
The Russian president also presented an “objective picture of the situation along the line of contact, where Russian troops hold complete strategic initiative,” and noted that Moscow’s forces are conducting a “relentless offensive in all key areas” and effectively destroying military-industrial, energy, and logistics facilities in Ukraine.
Beyond Ukraine, the participants discussed the October diesel agreement, under which Washington eased sanctions on Russian fuel exports. Both sides said the deal served their interests and would help stabilize global fuel markets. Other joint economic projects are also approaching implementation, Ushakov added.
Russia, Ukraine and the US last held talks in Geneva in February, following two rounds in Abu Dhabi. Further negotiations, however, were put on hold after the US and Israel launched their war against Iran, disrupting access to the UAE.
Ushakov told Russian media that Abu Dhabi was again being examined as a possible venue for renewed talks, noting that Putin has yet to choose the members of a future Russian delegation.
Asked by reporters whether the Ukraine conflict was approaching its end, Ushakov suggested it is “moving in that direction.”

American regime change ops cause chaos every time – US ambassador
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:50:06 UTC
22:50:06 KST

US ambassador makes regime change ‘disaster’ confession
Washington has been involved in nearly two dozen regime change operations across the Middle East, each ending in disaster, US Ambassador to Türkiye Tom Barrack has said.
Barrack criticized American efforts to manipulate the region and impose change through military force during an interview at the Global Security Forum in Qatar on Tuesday. He warned that his remarks would be “real” rather than “diplomatic.”
“If you take the greater Middle East, including the Levant, the Gulf, the Caucases, Central Asia, North Africa, we’ve had 23 regime changes. None of them have worked,” he said, stressing that the US had been involved in all of them in one way or another and bore responsibility for the outcomes.
The diplomat added that “kinetic reactions have never worked” either, referring to US military interventions and their “unintended consequences.” The latest US-Israeli war on Iran, which began in late February, has also plunged the region into chaos.
Barrack acknowledged that fomenting “conflict and controversy” had previously benefited Washington because “the more off base the region was, the more [Washington] could manipulate fossil fuels for its own benefit.” That is no longer the case, he said.
According to Barrack, the US “no longer wants to own [what it] doesn’t need to own” and envisions a different role for itself in the Middle East. “The bargain is not to own, not to control, but to tend, not to leave,” he said.
The envoy contrasted the proposed approach with the arrangement Washington reached with Saudi Arabia in 1974 following the oil shock triggered by the Yom Kippur War between Israel and several Arab nations.
Under the old arrangement, Saudi Arabia continued pricing its oil exclusively in US dollars and invested much of its revenues in American assets, while also purchasing US weapons and expecting American troops stationed in the region to rescue it in case of a major conflict.
The US confrontation with Iran, culminating in two open wars since 2025, has crumbled the foundations of that relationship.
Barrack urged friendly Middle Eastern nations to temper their expectations of American assistance, saying the US is not offering “a commitment to open seas and open trade at any cost.” Washington should “do a better job of defining: here’s what we’re willing to do, here’s what we’re not willing to do,” he added.
The diplomat repeatedly deflected questions critical of Israel, its regional policies, and its role in pushing Washington toward war with Iran.
“We leave Israel out of this because it’s so delicate to talk about,” Barrack said.
He also acknowledged that the Israeli government was reluctant to make any concessions on national security and described a “failure” of the Abraham Accords, a series of normalization agreements Israel signed with several Arab nations in 2020.

Swiss barn owls are changing colour, study shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:48:00 UTC
22:48:00 KST

Swiss barn owls are changing colour, study shows
Over the course of thirty years, the plumage of Swiss barn owls has become more reddish-brown and spotted. A long-term study by the University of Lausanne interprets this as a sign of rapidly advancing evolution, as it announced on Wednesday.
According to the study report, published in the journal Nature Communications, alongside owls with immaculate white plumage, the scientists had observed an increasing number of specimens with plumage ranging from golden-brown to deep red. This was neither a chance finding nor purely cosmetic in nature.
According to the long-term study, the colour change is the result of a rapidly advancing evolutionary process. It is linked to fertility and hunting strategies, and thus also to food intake.
More
Almost extinct owl is making a comeback in Switzerland
The scientists have identified a gene that could be linked to traits such as stress management or aggression, whilst also playing a role in pigmentation. Ultimately, however, it remains difficult to determine exactly which ecological factors account for the varying colouration.
White barn owls use moonlight to hunt their prey – mostly field mice. The red owls, on the other hand, feed predominantly on voles. The mottled plumage, in turn, is linked to immunity and the ability to cope better with stressful situations such as food shortages or parasite infestations.
Not least, the study demonstrates that evolution does not only take place over millions of years, but also within timeframes of just a few decades. Against the backdrop of climate change, this is seen as an encouraging sign. The ability to adapt quickly could help living organisms cope swiftly with environmental changes.

Government websites go dark as vulnerabilities in programming language send shudder across internet
Oct 21 - Government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline on Wednesday after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language sent website operators scrambling to protect their systems.
Developers of the PHP programming language said Tuesday they had identified two critical vulnerabilities and urged users to update their sites as soon as a fix was released. With reports that hackers were already exploiting the flaws to break into websites, government agencies in the Netherlands and Finland were among those that took sites offline as a precaution.
PHP underpins large parts of the internet, raising concerns that a significant number of websites could be vulnerable to attack.
"PHP is everywhere. It quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," cybersecurity company Huntress said in a blog post.
Dane Knecht, the chief technology officer of Web and cloud security firm Cloudflare, said that attacks were emerging and Cloudflare was updating its firewall rules as a stopgap measure.
"We are seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up. This is a STOPGAP only. Patch as soon as PHP releases the update," he said on X.
Wordfence, a security plugin that protects WordPress websites, said all WordPress sites run on a PHP-installed server. It warned that automatic updates would not apply the fix and advised site owners to find out who is responsible for updating PHP on their sites.
Cybersecurity agencies in Europe, Australia, Japan and Britain have urged PHP users to update immediately or take websites offline until patches can be applied. The Dutch cybersecurity agency itself went offline, saying it had done so as a precaution because of the vulnerabilities.
Officials have said that all PHP versions from PHP 5 onward could be affected, although PHP has not yet disclosed which versions are vulnerable. REUTERS

Investors are questioning neoclouds' business model but Nebius says AI computing prices are rising
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:44:12 UTC
22:44:12 KST

BERLIN — Nebius is seeing AI computing prices rise more than expected, a top executive told CNBC on Wednesday, offering a bullish view as neocloud firms' business model comes under increasing scrutiny.
Investors have grown wary after CoreWeave, one of the biggest neocloud players, saw the spread on its five-year credit default swaps hit levels generally viewed as signs of distress. The yields on CoreWeave's bonds also climbed.
The CoreWeave developments and questions around the amount of debt being used to fund the data center buildout have weighed heavily on other neoclouds like Iren and Nebius, whose stocks have dropped sharply over the last month.
Marc Boroditsky, chief revenue officer at Nebius, said his company wasn't in CoreWeave's position because "we're not carrying the kind of debt that they are."
He also said that if the AI infrastructure company brought its 2027 capacity online, it would sell out. There could be "the same type of dynamic" in 2028, supporting a positive longer-term demand outlook, he said, as companies race to secure access to computing power.
When asked whether he sees the price per megawatt continuing to rise ahead of expectations, Boroditsky replied: "Yeah."
Nebius is among a new wave of Neocloud companies that are investing billions to buy up Nvidia's graphics processing units, build data centers and rent that capacity.
Nebius ran an auction for computing capacity on Tuesday, which showed continued price rises, the revenue chief said. "We're seeing continued upward mobility in terms of the kind of price per megawatt," he told CNBC.
Price per megawatt, a key measure among new cloud companies, shows how much a company can charge customers for a certain amount of computing capacity.
Chase Lochmiller, CEO of Crusoe, an Nvidia-backed AI company that is building data centers, was also bullish on pricing, saying the company was seeing rising prices for GPUs, including older Nvidia chips.
"We're seeing higher pricing today for A100s than we saw in 2020 or 2021. We're seeing higher pricing for H100s than what we saw when they were first deployed in 2023," Lochmiller said.
"There's tremendous demand and a lot of it is because the underlying model capabilities have gotten so much more advanced that people are just creating so much more value out of the compute infrastructure."
The comments come amid an investor debate over how quickly Nvidia's GPUs lose their economic value as more powerful chips enter the market.
The ability to continue renting out older chips at attractive prices is crucial to AI infrastructure companies that need to recover their investments and generate profits, while spending billions on GPUs.
Lochmiller's comments suggest that, at least for Crusoe, older generations of Nvidia chips are commanding higher rental prices than when they were first deployed, potentially strengthening the economics of its AI cloud business.
SpaceX boost
Nebius stock rose on Wednesday after SpaceX reported revenue at its AI business jumped ninefold to $7.56 billion. SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen said pricing is "currently tracking slightly above the high end of the $30 to $50 per watt range," underscoring the pricing power for those renting out compute capacity.
Cloud providers CoreWeave, Iren, and Applied Digital also rose in premarket trading on Wednesday following Johnsen's comments.
"I'm thrilled by SpaceX's results. It's confirming what we already know, which is that it's a very dynamic market and that supply continues to fall far behind demand," Boroditsky said.

====================================================================================================

China Focus: Panda homeland takes a new path amid changing times
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:38:07 CST
22:38:07 KST

CHENGDU, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Deep in the mountains of southwest China's Sichuan Province stands a Catholic church that looks like a traditional wooden Chinese courtyard house, yet its interior follows Gothic design.
Visitors flock to the Dengchigou church in Baoxing County year-round, but most are not there to pray. They come for the giant panda, an animal that continues to shape the memories, identity and economic profile of the region.
In 1869, French missionary and naturalist Armand David arrived in Muping, as Baoxing was then called, and spent more than eight months at the Dengchigou church. There, he encountered an animal known locally as the "black-and-white bear," which was found to belong to a species totally new to science -- the giant panda.
For Li Yunjun, 48, who grew up in these mountains, giant pandas have always been part of life. He recalls how his parents' generation rescued starving pandas during widespread bamboo flowering in the 1980s, carrying weakened animals on makeshift stretchers for treatment.
Back then, wild pandas occasionally wandered near villagers' homes in search of food. "If one came to our home looking for food, we'd just let it eat whatever it wanted," Li said.
Li and other villagers were relocated from the mountains to a new village in 2016, but pandas still occasionally paid a visit. In July 2021, villagers spotted one near a riverbank and watched from a distance without disturbing it. The animal eventually returned to the forest.
If a panda is found injured or ill, villagers report it to local authorities, who arrange for experts to examine the animal before it is taken by "panda ambulance" to a veterinary hospital, Li said.
The peaceful encounters contrast with a darker chapter of the panda's history, documented at the Dengchigou church, part of which now serves as the giant panda origins museum.
Among its exhibits are photographs of Western expeditions in the 1920s and 1930s, when pandas were hunted for foreign museum collections.
The images recall an era of foreign aggression and domestic turmoil in China, when another chapter of history was unfolding in the same mountains.
In June 1935, the Communist Party of China (CPC)-led Red Army reached Baoxing after crossing the Dadu River and capturing the Luding Bridge. The soldiers then climbed Jiajin Mountain, the first major snow-capped mountain on their Long March.
The Long March, an epic military trek from 1934 to 1936, saw Red Army troops cross mountains and marshlands while battling better-armed Kuomintang forces, some marching as far as 12,500 kilometers.
The journey preserved the Red Army and gave the CPC a new foothold in northwest China, from which it built up its strength, fought back against invading Japanese troops and eventually toppled the corrupt Kuomintang regime, leading to the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949.
There are no known records of Red Army soldiers encountering giant pandas, but the animals, too, would see their fortunes change dramatically in the decades ahead.
For years, Baoxing relied heavily on white marble mining, logging and small hydropower projects, which provided jobs but put pressure on the environment.
That development model began to shift in 1998 when China banned commercial logging in natural forests along the upper Yangtze River. Dan Zhaohui, who had built roads for timber transport in Baoxing, joined reforestation efforts.
Three years later, he became a forest ranger, patrolling 1,250 hectares of mountainous terrain. "Over the years, I have encountered giant pandas, golden snub-nosed monkeys and other wildlife," he said. "The animals have come back."
Decades of conservation efforts have helped bring giant pandas back from the brink. Sichuan's wild panda population rose from 909 in the 1980s to 1,387 in the fourth national survey released in 2015, while their habitat expanded to more than 2 million hectares. The International Union for Conservation of Nature has reclassified the giant panda from "endangered" to "vulnerable."
At the 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics, panda mascot Bing Dwen Dwen became a sensation, with souvenirs quickly selling out. Once hunted for foreign museum collections, giant pandas have become a global symbol of friendship and conservation.
Protecting the animals and their habitat, however, has required difficult economic trade-offs.
Nearly 40 percent of Ya'an, the city that administers Baoxing, now lies inside the Giant Panda National Park. In Baoxing itself, more than 80 percent of the territory is included in the park.
The closure of mines and small hydropower facilities in protected areas has forced Baoxing to seek new sources of growth.
"The transition has been painful, but moving away from the old economic model is necessary. We must find new paths toward greener, higher-quality development," said Li Lun, director of Baoxing County's bureau of economy, commerce and technology.
Tourism has emerged as a source of growth. In 2025, Baoxing received 4.63 million tourist visits, up 10.28 percent year on year, while tourism revenue rose 10.41 percent to 4.09 billion yuan (about 608.7 million U.S. dollars), according to local authorities.
For Li Yunjun, the shift has meant leaving behind the marble trucks he once drove through the mountains.
He used to earn about 60,000 to 70,000 yuan a year hauling marble. He remembers the dust from blasting and the muddy Baoxing River during the mining boom.
In 2016, he sold his truck and opened a guesthouse in Dengchigou. Its seven rooms are often booked ahead of holidays, and his family's annual income now exceeds 100,000 yuan.
"Instead of hauling stone out of the mountains, I now welcome visitors drawn by giant pandas and the surrounding forests," he said.
But pandas are not the only draw for travelers to Baoxing. Many also come to trace the Long March. The Memorial Hall of the Red Army Crossing Jiajin Mountain receives over 300,000 visits annually, according to guide He Mengyu.
She said more student groups are coming from outside Sichuan, while foreign visitors who come for the pandas often extend their trips to Long March sites too. Some even ask where they can try making the straw sandals once worn by Red Army soldiers, an experience available in Dengchigou.
Jiajin Mountain, at the border of Baoxing and Xiaojin counties, has become a hiking destination for outdoor enthusiasts. As of August 2026, the Jiajin Mountain scenic area had recorded 13,327 tourist visits so far this year, up 1.45 percent year on year.
For Li Yunjun, the transformation is visible much closer to home.
"The Baoxing River has become clear again," he said. "The mountains are still the same, but the way we live with them has changed." ■

Australian researchers suggest gut's nervous system evolved before brain
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:37:26 CST
22:37:26 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Australian researchers have proposed that the nervous system in the gut may have evolved before the brain, challenging traditional theories about the evolution of the nervous system.
Researchers from Flinders University in South Australia argue that the gut's nervous system may have served as the body's original "brain," with the brain evolving later to support its functions, according to a university statement released on Wednesday.
The theory, published in The Journal of Physiology, draws on evidence from physiology and evolutionary biology to suggest that the nervous system may have originated in the gut to help early organisms obtain the energy needed for survival.
The enteric nervous system, often referred to as the body's "second brain," can sense its environment, process information and coordinate complex responses independently, according to the researchers.
The researchers said the theory could open up new avenues for studying conditions linked to the gut and nervous system, including obesity, diabetes, Parkinson's disease and digestive disorders. ■

====================================================================================================

China Focus: China makes significant progress in climate action, charts green path
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:37:25 CST
22:37:25 KST

The State Council Information Office (SCIO) holds a press conference on China's proactive efforts in addressing climate change and leading global climate governance, in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 21, 2026. (Xinhua/Pan Xu)
BEIJING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- China has achieved significant results in tackling climate change in recent years, gradually forging a green and low-carbon development path, a senior environment official said on Wednesday.
Li Gao, vice minister of ecology and environment, made the remarks at a news conference, where an annual report on China's policies and actions on climate change was released by the Ministry of Ecology and Environment.
The report showed that in 2025, China's carbon dioxide emissions per unit of GDP fell by 17.7 percent compared with 2020 levels. Non-fossil energy accounted for 21.7 percent of total energy consumption last year, while combined installed capacity of wind and solar power reached 1.84 billion kilowatts. Forest stock volume stood at 20.99 billion cubic meters in 2025.
This progress is backed by the country's sustained efforts to accelerate its green and low-carbon transformation.
China has built the world's largest and most complete clean energy industrial chain, with green and low-carbon industries becoming an important engine of economic growth, Li said.
By mid-2026, the country's total installed renewable energy capacity had reached 2.46 billion kilowatts, accounting for 60.7 percent of total national power generation capacity. At the end of July, installed solar power capacity had surpassed coal power for the first time in China's history, making it the country's largest single power source.
Moreover, China's combined installed capacity of operational and approved nuclear power units has risen to first place globally. New energy vehicle production and sales, meanwhile, have ranked first in the world for 11 consecutive years.
Li noted that the country has established the world's largest carbon emission trading market, covering about 8.3 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide, or more than 65 percent of the country's total emissions. Cumulative allowance trading volume recently surpassed 1 billion tonnes.
China has long placed high importance on addressing climate change. It has set the dual carbon goals of peaking carbon dioxide emissions before 2030 and achieving carbon neutrality before 2060.
China last year announced its 2035 nationally determined contributions, including a target of reducing economy-wide net greenhouse gas emissions by 7 percent to 10 percent from peak levels, while striving to do better.
It represented the first time China had put forward an absolute emission reduction target covering all greenhouse gases across the entire economy, Li said.
The country is also actively participating in and leading global climate governance while helping other developing countries build their capacity to address climate change.
China has signed South-South cooperation memoranda of understanding on climate change with 46 developing countries, helped build low-carbon demonstration zones, implemented a series of flagship climate projects, and trained more than 10,000 officials and technical personnel from over 120 developing countries.
China in 2023 launched the "Africa Solar Belt" photovoltaic project, which has helped nearly 20,000 households in five African countries gain access to electricity and lighting. By 2027, this flagship project is expected to benefit 50,000 African households.
Looking ahead, China's commitment to addressing climate change will not waver.
In July, the government released a national climate change plan for the 2026-2030 period, targeting a 17-percent reduction in carbon dioxide emissions per unit of GDP by 2030 compared with 2025 levels. The plan also vowed to deliver the country's carbon peaking target on schedule and fulfill the 2030 nationally determined contributions.
Li said China will promote green and low-carbon development in key sectors including energy, industry, transport, and urban and rural construction, accelerate the development of the national carbon market, and advance the building of a climate adaptive society.
Also on Wednesday, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology released an action plan on controlling both the total amount and intensity of carbon emissions across the industrial and information technology sectors for the 2026-2030 period to speed up China's green and low-carbon transition.
The plan called for improving carbon emission management in key industries, accelerating the development of zero-carbon factories, zero-carbon computing facilities and low-carbon supply chains, establishing a carbon footprint management system for industrial products, and setting up carbon accounting mechanisms.
By 2030, the plan targeted the formulation and implementation of around 400 carbon footprint accounting standards for key industrial products, the establishment of roughly 500 national-level zero-carbon factories and zero-carbon computing facilities, and an over 10-percent reduction in energy consumption per unit of value-added output of major industrial enterprises. ■
