Across China: Extended-stay travel gains ground among China's older people
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:37:24 CST
22:37:24 KST

This undated file photo shows elderly people practicing musical instruments at the Huangshan mutual aid community in Huangshan District of Huangshan City, east China's Anhui Province. (Xinhua)
HEFEI, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- On a recent autumn morning in Xiongcun Village in east China's Anhui Province, Bi Sheng sipped coffee in his small studio while answering emails.
A short walk away, craftsmen were renovating an old house, waiting for the 55-year-old to review designs and select timber.
A native of Beijing, Bi first visited villages in Shexian County of Huangshan City, southern Anhui, more than a decade ago for a design project. Drawn to the area's rich cultural heritage, he eventually bought a house there and embraced what he described as a semi-retired life.
"Every village has its own stories, and history is everywhere. That was beyond my expectations," he said.
His new life has given Bi something he missed in the city: close-knit neighborhood ties. His new neighbors sometimes bring him freshly caught fish or vegetables they have grown themselves.
"In cities, many people don't even know their neighbors," he said.
Bi is part of a growing trend in China, where many older people are traveling to spend extended periods in places with beautiful scenery, rich culture and opportunities to build social connections, particularly after retirement.
From July 2024 to June 2025, China recorded more than 84.3 million extended-stay visits by older travelers, averaging more than 7 million a month, according to a report released by the China Association of Ageing.
To cash in on this fast-growing market, many regions offer services tailored to older travelers, ranging from age-friendly accommodations and traditional wellness treatments to activities that help newcomers build social connections.
In Shexian County, at the foot of Mount Huangshan and within easy reach of major eastern cities such as Shanghai and Hangzhou, local authorities have developed eight wellness-themed guesthouses, said Xu Yuhong, deputy director of the county's health commission. These guesthouses received 13,300 guests from January to July this year, he said.
Wu Zenghe is one of the guesthouse managers. He converted three traditional Huizhou-style buildings into a guesthouse catering to older travelers.
"People who travel after retirement are more interested in in-depth experiences than in simply rushing from one tourist attraction to another," Wu said.
His guesthouse features specially designed doors and windows to block noise and light, as well as herbal sachets intended to aid sleep. It also offers an artificial intelligence-powered health consultation device, acupuncture, moxibustion and medicinal baths.
So far this year, it has welcomed several thousand older visitors from across China, including hundreds who stayed for more than a week.
In Yunnan Province in southwest China, some markets have been renovated to better accommodate older people, while eligible visitors can receive discounts at tourist attractions and use public services such as universities for older adults. In Heilongjiang Province in northeast China, localities are exploring cross-border extended-stay and wellness initiatives for older visitors.
At the same time, as older travelers spend weeks or months away from home, many want a stable social network and a sense of belonging.
About 2,600 older people from across China live in the Huangshan mutual aid community in Huangshan District, Huangshan City.
Li Jiankang, a 66-year-old from Nanjing, capital of neighboring Jiangsu Province, was among the community's first residents. His daily routine includes running, tending a vegetable garden, playing the saxophone, and joining other residents for table tennis or swimming.
He said he has made many friends and found a fulfilling rhythm to life in Huangshan.
The community has established more than 20 interest groups covering sports, agriculture and music, giving residents opportunities to connect through shared interests. It has also set up mutual aid groups so residents can care for one another.
"Many older people who live alone can feel isolated, and some may even struggle with their mental health. That is why we hope to help them find comfort and companionship through mutual support," said Li Junping, manager of the community. "A sense of being needed is often the main reason residents choose to stay."
For Li Jiankang, this sense of connection is central to the experience.
"To me, the Chinese character for 'mutual' looks like two hands clasped together," he said. "Everyone here extends a hand to help others, and people can feel the bonds between us." ■

====================================================================================================

U.S. Midterms Loom Over a Deadlock Between Trump and Tehran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:35:00 UTC
22:35:00 KST

Iran may have found a weapon in the American electoral calendar. With the midterm elections two weeks away, Tehran is intensifying attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, calculating that higher energy prices will deepen President Donald Trump’s political troubles and make another U.S. military campaign too costly to contemplate.
The wager is seductive: an American president anxious about diesel prices and his party’s prospects in the midterms, Iran seems to believe, will have little appetite for another major war.
Trump’s declaration that he will refrain from striking Iran before the Nov. 3 vote appears to vindicate this view, even as he periodically threatens to use force again. Having survived two rounds of war and absorbed punishing economic losses, Iran’s leaders believe they can endure a little longer. By disrupting Gulf commerce, they gain leverage their conventional forces cannot provide. They also hope to make that leverage permanent and compel Washington to accept Tehran’s authority over passage through the world’s most important energy chokepoint.
Yet the past nine months of war against Iran have made it clear that renewed military conflict before the midterms or after the elections is unlikely to resolve the disputes between the U.S. and Iran. The two countries will eventually have to sit across the negotiating table to resolve their long-running disputes.
Miscalculations in Tehran and Washington
Tehran may be misreading how political peril shapes an adversary’s decisions. Trump could decide that appearing powerless as Iranian attacks push up prices is more damaging than another round of military strikes. Reports that his administration has considered fresh strikes suggest the military option remains in play. A serious attack on American forces could turn Trump’s promise of restraint into a political liability overnight.
The political situation in Israel adds a combustible variable. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces an Oct. 27 election with his bloc struggling to secure a majority. He has staked his political reputation on the claim that only he can neutralize the Iranian threat.
With Tehran rebuilding its missile and drone capabilities and uncertainty surrounding its nuclear program, Netanyahu may see renewed strikes as both a strategic opportunity and a means of restoring his standing at home. Such a gamble could deepen Israel’s insecurity, but electoral desperation seldom improves anyone’s judgment.
The convergence of these calculations makes the coming weeks particularly perilous. Iran thinks Trump’s electoral weakness will constrain him. Trump and Netanyahu might each conclude that a show of force could rescue their political fortunes. Each side imagines it can calibrate the violence and manage the aftermath. The experience of this year’s conflict, in which successive rounds of fighting outran diplomatic efforts to contain them, offers little reason for that confidence.
Even if October passes without another conflagration, November brings its own hazards. After the midterm elections, the political constraints Trump has publicly imposed on himself will disappear. With substantial American forces already positioned in the region, Washington may be tempted to break the deadlock through another round of attacks. Tehran, fearing another surprise attack, might choose to strike Israel or U.S. military assets in the region first. What might seem like prudent preparation in Washington or Tehran could help bring about the war it is meant to deter.
The underlying impasse is as stubborn as ever. Washington wants a nuclear agreement and believes its blockade will ultimately compel Iran to negotiate. Tehran insists on upfront economic relief and an end to the war before substantive talks on the nuclear issue can begin.
America can point to tankers still transiting Hormuz, but shipping that depends on costly military protection and remains under threat is a poor substitute for normal trade. Iran can inflict considerable damage on the oil exports of its Gulf neighbors, but it has so far failed to turn that leverage into meaningful American concessions.
Dangers of a wider war
Another surge in hostilities would widen this gulf rather than bridge it. American and Israeli aircraft can destroy missile launchers, production facilities, and infrastructure, but Iran has repeatedly demonstrated that it can retaliate and survive. Iran’s response could extend further to target Gulf energy infrastructure, maritime commerce, data centers, and other critical networks.
The Houthi confrontation with Saudi Arabia already offers a grim illustration of how quickly the costs can spread. The war in Yemen has been reignited with devastating consequences, including deadly attacks on civilian airports and a spiraling cycle of retaliation. The fighting now threatens to draw in Turkey and Pakistan to support Saudi Arabia, as the three countries recently signed a mutual security pact known as the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement.
A new campaign could leave Iran poorer, Israel more exposed, and the U.S. burdened with an even more expensive regional commitment, while markets around the world absorb another shock.
The outlines of a diplomatic bargain have been visible for months: reciprocal steps to reopen Hormuz, calibrated sanctions relief, and a resumption of nuclear negotiations. The difficulty lies in sequencing and trust. Tehran fears that surrendering its maritime leverage first would invite fresh demands; Washington worries that easing pressure would reward coercion without securing lasting constraints on Iran’s nuclear program. Addressing those fears will require reciprocal steps and credible verification. More bombing won’t help.
Leaders contemplating an October surprise or an offensive after the midterms must remember that uncomfortable truth. Military force may alter the balance of pain without resolving the disputes each side will eventually have to confront across the negotiating table.
After another round of death and destruction, they could find themselves negotiating over the same issues, with less trust, greater bitterness, and far fewer resources to rebuild what they have broken. Their choices will be no easier then; the cost of reaching an agreement will be far greater.

The Indian Government’s Job Statistics Are Misleading
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:35:00 UTC
22:35:00 KST

The Indian government claims that the formal job market in the country is booming. It cites as proof payroll data from the Employees’ Provident Fund Organization (EPFO).
The Employees’ Provident Fund is a mandatory government-backed retirement savings scheme in India for salaried workers. The question, however, is: does a rising EPFO count really amount to more good jobs?
The official story goes as follows. The Economic Survey 2023-24 reported that net EPFO payroll additions more than doubled, from 6.11 million in FY2018-19 to 13.15 million. The survey called it “healthy growth in formal employment.” The Union Labor Ministry hailed it as a “growing formal employment landscape.”
The Indian government has now gone further and linked formalization of employment directly to “quality jobs.” In August 2026, it promoted the Pradhan Mantri Viksit Bharat Rozgar Yojana as a scheme to expand formal employment, designed to encourage first-time employment and to reward employers for creating new formal jobs through EPFO.
Formalization is valuable. A worker brought under EPF coverage gains access to an institutional mechanism for retirement savings and social security. An enterprise complying with labor regulations represents progress over one that does not.
However, these claims ignore reality. An EPFO “net subscriber addition” is not a net new job. It can include a person moving from one EPFO-covered employer to another; an existing worker newly brought into EPFO coverage; a worker previously outside formal coverage becoming covered; workers rejoining after an employment break; changes resulting from EPFO administrative coverage; and, importantly, formalization of an already existing informal job.
September 2026 EPFO data showed contributors in 12 traditionally labor-intensive sectors (garments, textiles, leather, jute, beedi, tea, brick-making, cashew, coir, cotton ginning, diamond cutting, and others) fell 1.3 percent, from 5,536,000 in 2023-24 to 5,464,000 in 2025-26. These are precisely the sectors India must expand to absorb workers leaving agriculture.
There is a further fundamental statistical problem.
EPFO payroll statistics measure movements into and out of the EPF system. The monthly payroll series records first-time subscribers, members exiting coverage, and earlier members who rejoin. The government itself cautions that the numbers are provisional because employee records are continuously updated.
The Economic Survey 2025-26 carried the government’s claims further: organized manufacturing added 5.7 million jobs. This is potentially more interesting because it is not based on EPFO figures.
The National Sample Survey or NSS Survey uses Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) data and says organized manufacturing employment increased by more than 5.7 million between FY2015 and FY2024; grew at about 4 percent compounded annual growth rate (CAGR); and increased by more than 1 million in FY2024 alone, a 6 percent year-on-year increase.
This is probably the strongest official evidence currently being cited for actual employment expansion in the organized sector, rather than simply formalization. But there is a major definitional qualification: The ASI’s “persons engaged” category includes working proprietors, family members, and unpaid workers, as well as employees. So it is not synonymous with regular wage/salaried formal jobs.
The government is also pointing to the rise in regular salaried employment. Regular wage/salaried employment increased from 22.4 percent of workers in 2024 to 23.6 percent in 2025. That is a meaningful movement toward wage employment, although it is still very far from the claim that most new employment is formal.
In fact, what takes the wind out of the government’s claims is that the increase in organized manufacturing has been accompanied by growing contractualization. According to ASI, contract workers accounted for only about 13 percent of the formal manufacturing workforce in 1993-94. However, this share rose sharply to 20 percent by 1999-2000 and further to 37.8 percent in 2018-19. As per the latest ASI data (2022-23), it has reached 40.7 percent. So much for the claim of formalization – the ILO defines it as work with social security, and contract work does not offer that.
The percentage share of contract labor in capital-intensive industries has increased from 19.5 percent in 1999-2000 to 46 percent in 2018-2019, whereas it has increased from 22 percent in 1999-2000 to 33 percent in 2018-2019 in labor-intensive enterprises.
As though that is not enough, if EPFO was really creating so many new jobs, how is it that India’s Periodic Labor Force Survey (PLFS) continues to show that India’s share of informal workers without social insurance (i.e. pensions, death/disability insurance, maternity benefits, etc.) was 90 percent in 2004-5, 90 percent in 2017-18, and still 90 percent in 2024.
Job quality also matters: duration, earnings, working conditions, social protection, security of tenure, and prospects for advancement. India’s employment challenge has historically been not only unemployment but also underemployment, low productivity, and poor-quality work.
The latest PLFS data illustrate this complexity. Even after the increase in regular wage employment, 56.2 percent of workers in 2025 remained self-employed (mostly own-account and unpaid family labor) and another 20.20 percent were casual wage laborers. Agriculture still accounted for 43 percent of employment in 2025 (42 percent in 2019). The largest addition to the workforce since 2020 has been in agriculture (rising from 200 million to 280 million in 2024).
This matters most for the young. A graduate in a low-paid, insecure job is technically employed but not upwardly mobile. As we estimate in our new book, “India Out of Work,” real wages for casual and regular workers, and for the 53 percent of workers who are self-employed, have stagnated for 12 years. If non-farm jobs have grown at half the required rate (12 million a year) for a dozen years the Modi government has been in power, leaving youth unemployment double its 2012 level, from 6 percent to 12 percent in 2024, how can real wages rise, however loudly the government touts its low inflation?
The real test of India’s labor market is not how many names enter an EPFO database but whether the economy creates enough stable, productive, and decently paid jobs. If it did, the youth (those aged 15-29 years) not in education, employment, and training, would not have jumped from 50 million in 2012 to 100 million in 2024. Clearly, many became “discouraged workers” who stopped looking for work.

Telehealth Giant Hims Wants to Test Every Dude for Low Testosterone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:34:37 UTC
22:34:37 KST

Talk of testosterone deficiency is hard to escape these days, with podcasters and politicians obsessing over how to avoid a “low T” lifestyle.
As the hormone’s cultural salience deepens, demand is growing. In a timely move, telehealth giant Hims just launched a testosterone replacement therapy service for cisgender men.
The direct-to-consumer juggernaut will offer two types of injectable treatments, as well as an oral pill option that can be sent to patients after they take an at-home capillary blood test. Peter Stahl, a urologist and a senior vice president of men’s health at Hims, wants to “cast as wide a net, and get as many people tested, as possible.”
Hims, which started out selling erectile dysfunction medications, has expanded into women’s health and grown from a startup to a publicly traded company serving 2.9 million customers since it launched in 2017. Offering testosterone replacement therapy, or TRT, is both a new phase for the health platform and a doubling down on men’s health care. “When we first started, we didn't have the capabilities to take care of a complex condition like testosterone deficiency,” Stahl says. “We've finally grown up.”
The company will compete with a wide array of online clinics offering testosterone therapy, many of which have cropped up in the past few years using turnkey telehealth services to launch quickly. Many of these services market the medication as a lifestyle enhancer or anti-aging solution.
Stahl sees testosterone deficiency as a medical condition that’s “really underdiagnosed” and “really misunderstood.” Testosterone became a controlled substance following the 1990 Anabolic Steroids Control Act, and for decades, taking it has carried an association with muscle-obsessed gym rats. “That created a lot of stigma,” he says. Older research also showed that testosterone therapy came with cardiovascular risks, though more recent findings suggest those concerns were overestimated.
Testosterone levels have become a MAGA fixation. This fall, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth announced a mandatory testosterone deficiency screening for most male troops in the US armed services. Texas Republicans have been hurling the phrase “low T” as a masculinity-questioning insult in a hotly contested Senate midterm race between Ken Paxton and James Talarico.
A survey of 2,000 American men this summer commissioned by Hims indicates that they are increasingly willing to talk to one another about testosterone treatment, but the stigma persists around taking medication to address low levels.
Because testosterone is a controlled substance, it can’t be dispensed like many other treatments popular with digital clinics. Unlike GLP-1s and estrogen-based hormone replacement therapy, which are now often prescribed by clinicians after patients simply fill out a quick questionnaire, TRT requires "synchronous" care. That means any would-be users have to have a video chat with a clinician before getting a prescription, and for ongoing monitoring.
“It's important to remember that testosterone therapy can cause infertility, and you don't give it to someone trying to conceive,” says urologist Mohit Khera, the director of Baylor College of Medicine’s Laboratory for Andrology Research at McNair Medical Institute. Khera sees telehealth TRT services as promising ways to expand access to the medication, “as long as it’s monitored appropriately.”
While laboratory testing can show whether testosterone levels are below thresholds set by groups like the American Urological Association to indicate potential issues, diagnoses aren’t made based on bloodwork alone. Instead, clinicians assess labs along with patients’ symptoms and medical history. Common symptoms of hypogonadism (the technical term for the diagnosis) include sexual dysfunction and muscle loss. Stahl calls it a “powerful biomarker” for understanding someone’s health.
“Quite frankly, it’s underutilized,” he says, noting that men with low testosterone have a 35 percent increased risk in overall mortality.
The test doesn’t require a standard blood draw. Instead, Hims will send patients a Tasso blood collection device, a round single-use wearable that sticks to the upper arm and punctures the skin with microneedles to collect a small sample. (It may sound suspiciously like Theranos, but Tasso devices have a solid track record.) From there, the patient sends the collection off to a lab that will conduct an analysis of a broad selection of 21 different biomarkers to assess health, including triglycerides and thyroid hormones as well as testosterone.
Based on the results, a patient might be prescribed a compounded injectable testosterone, a commercially available injectable testosterone, an oral pill—or something else entirely, if their testosterone levels are not low. Stahl sees hormone testing as a way to persuade otherwise-reticent men to go see a doctor. “Getting screened for testosterone deficiency is much more exciting to a young man who's feeling good than getting tested for high cholesterol,” he says. “So we're trying to leverage that opportunity as much as we possibly can.”
Hims’ expansion comes at a Wild West moment for online testosterone sales. In 2022, urology researchers went undercover to test how digital clinics prescribed the medication, and found that six of seven platforms in the analysis offered testosterone replacement therapy despite reported normal levels of the hormone.
Although he wants to test people widely, Stahl has a more conservative philosophy about who should actually get a prescription for testosterone, especially in comparison to digital clinics that explicitly offer it as an anti-aging treatment or lifestyle enhancement: “If you're asymptomatic, it doesn't matter what your testosterone level is, you're not going to get treated on our platform.”

Doctors, engineers and computer scientists leave Israel. Researchers sound alarm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:27:37 UTC
22:27:37 KST

Seven years ago, when Benjamin Netanyahu celebrated his 70th birthday, one of the people who came to wish him well him was May Golan – then a Knesset member and now the social equality minister. At the time Netanyahu was the leader of the opposition, having failed to form a coalition after the 2021 election.
Golan ceremoniously proclaimed to Netanyahu that masses of Israelis would leave the country if he weren't the prime minister. "Young people in Israel don't see their future and their children's future in the country if you don't continue to lead it," she told him.
Netanyahu was elected for a sixth term as prime minister at the end of 2022 and since 2023, there has been a dramatic increase in the number of Israelis who left the country. This number reached almost 70,000 in 2025, compared to less than 40,000 in 2009-2023, a jump of dozens of percent. The emigrants were primarily young families with children. Concurrently, the number of returning Israelis has fallen to a low not seen in many years.
Researchers at Tel Aviv University warn of a loss of equilibrium and damage that will lead to the collapse of the Israeli economy if the emigration trend continues. They note that while the current situation is not dangerous, it could quickly spiral into an extreme scenario.
According to a forthcoming report on the subject by Prof. Itai Ater of the School of Management, Prof. Netai Bergman, head of the School of Economics, and Doron Zamir of the School of Economics, emigration from Israel is particularly pronounced in several groups: those with a bachelor's degree or higher, those with degrees in science, engineering or computer science, and doctors.
"The continuation of the emigration trend could lead to a dangerous decline in the stock of skilled human capital available to the Israeli economy, which is the State of Israel's primary resource," the report states.
The researchers warn that additional negative shocks could lead to a surge in the number of emigrants. "Every additional emigrant increases the incentive for others to leave, due to the growth of networks of Israeli immigrants abroad and due to the consequences for the Israeli economy, social cohesion and public service. This will have severe macroeconomic consequences," they write.
'A stream that will become a flood'
The researchers have been tracking trends in emigration from Israel in recent years. According to the report, the number of Israelis who returned home in 2023-2024 is the lowest since 2009. Israel's negative migration balance (the number of those leaving minus the number of those returning) is also the highest since 2009.
According to Central Bureau of Statistics definitions, emigrants are defined as Israeli residents who spent 12 full months abroad, with three of those months being consecutive. The researchers excluded from the data new immigrants to Israel who emigrated within three years of making aliyah, thereby nullifying the excuse for the high figures that Netanyahu gave in the Knesset in January when he said that that a large portion of those leaving Israel are immigrants from Ukraine who returned to their country.
According to Central Bureau of Statistics data analyzed in the report, an average of 32,000 Israelis left Israel each year between 2009 and 2019, but in 2023-2024 the number jumped to about 50,000 per year (an increase of more than 50 percent); in 2025 that number reached 69,000. Concurrently, in 2024, the number of returning Israelis fell below 20,000 per year for the first time since 2009. Israel's negative migration balance rose from an average of 10,500 people in the previous decade examined (2010-2019) to about 30,000 people in 2024 – almost threefold.
An extended analysis by the researchers shows that the emigration rate (emigrants per 1,000 people in the population) of those who have a higher education (bachelor's degree or higher), doctors, engineers and those with science degrees almost doubled between 2019 and 2024, and increased at a faster rate than the increase in the emigration rate in the general population.
While the emigration rate in the general population increased 1.74-fold during these years, it increased 1.75-fold among doctors, 1.87-fold among those with a bachelor's degree, 1.9-fold among engineers, and almost doubled among those with technological qualifications. According to another publication by the researchers from September, close to 1,400 doctors left Israel in 2023-2025 – almost double the number from the corresponding period a decade earlier (2013-2015).
"The great concern stems from the fact that the people leaving are Israel's best human capital, who contribute to society and to the economy," Ater says. "If the trend is not stopped, this stream will become a flood that will endanger Israel's ability to exist as an independent and advanced state."
"We know of countries like Turkey, Iran, Russia, Venezuela and South Africa that have undergone similar processes and have not managed to recover," Ater adds. "In Israel, there is also a large, unskilled ultra-Orthodox group that doesn't study the core curriculum and puts Israel's ability to survive a large wave of emigration of skilled Israelis at risk. As a country that relies on high-tech, our greatest resource is human capital. A large emigration rate will also harm security, not just the economy."
"This is not just about the brain drain and the weakening of research and development, but also a real blow to the country's security and resilience," says Prof. David Harel, president of the National Academy of Sciences. "Israel's scientific and technological capabilities in engineering, cybersecurity and computer science are a vital component of national security, from the development of advanced defense systems to Israel's cyber capabilities."
The Tel Aviv University researchers say the increase in the number of Israelis who left was already noticeable in the third quarter of 2023 – before the October 7 massacre. According to Ater, it's still too early to determine whether the end of the Gaza war led to a decrease in the number of emigrants or an increase in the number of returnees. "The election is a pivotal event," he says. "For many people, the results will influence the decision of whether to leave or to stay."
Young people, families with children
The researchers say a particularly significant change occurred among young families. The main increase in emigration rates was among adults aged 35 to 45 and children aged 0-14 – families with children. The emigration rate in these groups almost doubled.
High-income earners are more prominent among emigrants from Israel. The share of highest earners (in the upper third) among emigrants increased from 24.5 percent in 2009 to 33.5 percent in 2024; close to half of those leaving earned above the median wage. The researchers noted, however, that education and skillset predict emigration more than income.
"The loss of high-value human capital has a real economic cost," the report states. According to an Israel Tax Authority report published this year, the loss of tax revenue from emigration increased from half a billion shekels ($161 million in today's dollars) in 2019 to 1.2 billion shekels in 2024. If the emigration trend continues, the tax loss is expected to reach 3.5 billion shekels per year within five years.

Germany's military warns of 'significant' Russian sabotage threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

13:26:21 UTC
22:26:21 KST

Germany's military warns of 'significant' Russian sabotage threat
BERLIN, Oct 21 - Germany's armed forces classified the threat of Russian sabotage against their own troops and facilities as "significant" for the first time, the second-highest level on their internal threat scale, according to a Bundeswehr assessment reported by German broadcasters WDR and the Sueddeutsche Zeitung on Wednesday.
A defence ministry spokesperson confirmed the assessment, telling reporters: "We are noting that we face a significant sabotage threat overall for the Bundeswehr."
The reassessment was triggered by the discovery in mid-September of a crashed drone carrying a tin of high explosives near the Wunstorf air base in Lower Saxony, WDR and Sueddeutsche Zeitung reported.
CROSSED 'RED LINE'
The internal document, seen by WDR and the Sueddeutsche Zeitung, said Russia had crossed "a previously anticipated red line of harmful intent involving kinetic and/or lethal effects" against Germany and the Bundeswehr through the use of weaponised drones.
The Wunstorf drone resembles one laden with explosives that was used in a failed attack at Leipzig/Halle airport in August. But unlike the Leipzig incident, which authorities said targeted civilian cargo aircraft, investigators believe the Wunstorf drone was aimed at Bundeswehr aircraft, the document is cited as saying.
Germany has blamed Russia for the Leipzig attack.
Moscow denied involvement and has consistently rejected accusations of carrying out sabotage or hybrid attacks in Europe.
The report also cited a pattern of suspected Russian reconnaissance across Germany, including drone overflights of the Arrow 3 missile defence site in Saxony-Anhalt, and a camouflaged camera found filming a strategically important railway station in Minden, Westphalia.
Intelligence services expect the situation to worsen in the short term, with further actions likely in the near future, the document says, according to WDR and Sueddeutsche Zeitung.
The defence ministry spokesperson said preventive measures were being tailored to individual sites and could range from increased guard patrols to additional technical security such as infrared cameras and fence surveillance systems.
The assessment comes just over a week after German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Germany faced a "shadow war" and called for expanded intelligence powers.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Wednesday that Russian disinformation and hybrid attacks posed the biggest threat to Germany. "My view is that our people are still underestimating this big threat to our society... This is a fundamental attack against the entire political order we achieved after 1990." REUTERS

Cartel-linked mom wanted for child's 1997 murder caught in Mexico
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:25:11 UTC
22:25:11 KST

Cartel-linked woman wanted in brutal 1997 murder of her child in Arizona is captured in Mexico
A woman linked to drug cartels and accused of torturing and murdering her daughter in Arizona in 1997 has been captured in Mexico nearly 30 years after the crime, officials said Wednesday.
Anna Marlene Somoza was connected to a "major transnational drug trafficking network" along the Arizona border through the 1980s and 1990s, the U.S. Marshals Service said in a news release. She was arrested for selling and transporting marijuana in 1993, and agreed to act as a confidential informant for Arizona law enforcement.
In November 1993, Somoza had a daughter, Crystal Reyes. The child was born in Nogales, Mexico. Her father was Darren Stockwell, a law enforcement officer and U.S. citizen, the U.S. Marshals said.
Somoza and Crystal then moved to Ahwatukee, Arizona, to live with her boyfriend, narcotics detective Avelino Tamala. The U.S. Marshals Service said that Somoza and Tamala began an "improper romantic relationship" while she was a law enforcement source.
While living with Somoza and Tamala, Crystal was allegedly subject to "severe physical abuse," including being bound and gagged in a small dog kennel for weeks at a time, the U.S. Marshals said. The abuse "escalated fatally" on January 30, 1997, when Crystal suffocated inside a sealed cardboard box, the agency said.
Nearly a year later, in November 1998, human bone fragments were found in Mobile, Arizona. The bones could not be identified. In 1999, Somoza and Tamala were arrested on drug and weapon offenses. DNA was collected. When compared to the bones, the analysis "could not eliminate Somoza as the maternal source," the U.S. Marshals said. But without a paternal DNA source, an identification could not be made. In 2008, Somoza was released from prison.
The case went cold until 2014, when Stockwell was located and interviewed by cold case detectives. A sample of his DNA was collected and analyzed, allowing investigators to identify the bone fragments as Crystal's.
Somoza and Tamala were indicted on charges of first-degree murder on December 12, 2014. Arrest warrants were issued. Tamala was arrested that day by the U.S. Marshals and Arizona's WANTED Violent Offender Task Force. The task force quickly determined that Somoza had fled to Mexico. They began collaborating with the U.S. Marshal Service Mexico Foreign Field Office, but Somoza could not be found. In 2016, Tamala was sentenced to life in prison.
Federal, state and local officials continued to investigate the case for the next 12 years, the U.S. Marshals said. "Extensive investigative efforts" were taken to locate Somoza, but law enforcement found that she "had taken deliberate and extensive measures to evade detection by law enforcement." The long search was also "affected by her close connections with cartels," officials said.
In September 2026, members of a U.S. Marshals task force became aware that Somoza was in Cernavaca, Mexico. On Sunday, Mexican police and Interpol officers were able to arrest Somoza in Xochitepec, Mexico.
Efforts to extradite Somoza are underway. She will face charges in Arizona, the U.S. Marshals said.
Attorney Juan Rocha, who teaches at Arizona State University, told CBS affiliate KPHO-TV that Mexico often seeks assurance the death penalty will not be pursued. Prosecutors have not publicly said whether they will seek the death penalty against Somoza.
"No one can hide from American justice forever," said Timothy Courchaine, U.S. Attorney for the District of Arizona, in the news release. "The United States Attorney's office stands in partnership with both our federal and critically our state partners to ensure defendants have their day in court. We look forward to now working alongside our Mexican partners to bring this fugitive back to Arizona."

Roku Pro Series OLED TV Review (2026)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:21:18 UTC
22:21:18 KST

While I had the Apple TV app running, I tuned into some live MLB soccer. The action: sharp and smooth (and dull, obviously, because soccer), and the same was true when I switched over to an NFL game on DirecTV. That’s as expected with a 120-Hz refresh rate.
Speaking of which, that rate, coupled with low-latency game mode (which kicked on automatically) served my Xbox experiences well. From the 1930s palette of the cartoonish Cuphead to the candy-colored arcade racing of Burnout: Paradise, everything looked crisp and vivid, with fast response times and zero blur.
For my color investigations, I clicked into Planet Earth II on HBO Max, Pixar’s Coco on Disney+, various “8K” nature videos on YouTube, and an Inglorious Basterds 4K Blu-ray played on the Xbox. Across the board, the Roku Pro Series produced vibrant, richly detailed color—but with less of the “pop” I’ve witnessed on high-end LG and Sony OLEDs. That’s partially due to the panel’s limited brightness.
Whether that’s a bad thing is open for debate; some would argue that higher-end OLEDs oversaturate, the shiny colors more of a distraction than an enhancement. Discuss.
A notable Roku innovation is Smart Picture Max, which automatically detects the type of content you’re watching and adjusts various display settings accordingly. Though it’s hard to gauge the impact of this on things like color and brightness, there’s one clearly quantifiable benefit: motion-smoothing. Smart Picture Max disables it for most TV shows and movies, meaning you don’t get the dreaded soap-opera effect. That alone gives the Pro Series a leg up over most OLEDs, which require manual tinkering to disable this heinous feature (and again to re-enable it for sports and gaming, the only situations in which it’s not heinous).
The one catch here is that any Dolby Vision content overrides Smart Picture Max, leaving motion-smoothing switched on. Fortunately, Roku makes it refreshingly easy to modify that and other picture settings; just press the star button on the remote. I found (and toggled off) smoothing with just a few clicks. Another nice perk: Any change you make applies instantly to whatever you’re viewing, so you can immediately gauge whether it’s what you want; you don’t have to exit the menu to see the results.
On the audio front, the presence of Dolby Atmos does nothing to improve the TV’s speakers, which produce plenty of volume but get harsh and shrill the higher you go. Indeed, the opening measures of Nick Perito’s “The Green Leaves of Summer” in Inglorious Basterds were deeply unpleasant, even at a modest volume. This came as something of a surprise, as Roku’s previous Pro Series TV sounded much better overall. The speakers here are tolerable at low volumes in a small room; for everything else, you’re going to want a soundbar.
In the end, Roku’s first OLED won’t win over any die-hard fans of premium panels; it’s a budget model through and through, probably on par with LG’s similarly affordable B6. But it’s still an OLED, with all the vivid color, pitch-black black, and strong contrast that technology affords. And the Roku remote, interface, and automated image adjustments contribute to a splendid user experience. Watch for the next sale (Black Friday, anyone?) and you’ll feel like you’re getting a steal.

AI generated
HOUSTON, Texas - Texas Democrats’ best chance at a statewide win in more than three decades is facing a wall of Republican money, with Elon Musk and other donors pouring hundreds of millions into a late effort to rescue Senate candidate Ken Paxton.
With two weeks until the Nov 3 election and early voting under way, however, it is unclear how much impact the spending can still have.
Polls show few undecided voters remain, and Republicans say their biggest challenge is turning out their own voters, many of whom are frustrated by the cost of living and the war with Iran launched by US President Donald Trump, who has endorsed Paxton.
“The money being spent now isn’t for persuasion. It’s for mobilisation,” said pollster James Henson, director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas. “In most of the statewide polling we’ve seen, Republicans are suffering from an enthusiasm gap.”
Republican strategists say internal polling shows that gap has narrowed considerably.
“We’ve seen it collapse, thank God. It was one of our concerns,” said Dave Carney, a longtime Republican strategist and chief adviser to Texas Governor Greg Abbott.
That turnout challenge helps explain the tone of Republican advertising.
Rather than focusing on inflation and the economy, which polls consistently show are among voters’ top concerns, Republicans in Texas and other battleground states have leaned heavily on culture-war themes to energise their base.
Republican groups have spent more than US$100 million (S$127.73 million) nationally since Aug 1 on more than 200 ads accusing Democrats of backing “sex change” procedures for children, according to an analysis of AdImpact data by FactCheck.org.
Texas-sized spending
Combined advertising spending in the race between Paxton, the state’s Republican attorney-general, and Democrat James Talarico has topped US$500 million, according to ad-tracking data, putting it on pace to become the most expensive US Senate contest ever.
Talarico has held a small but consistent lead over Paxton, though generally within the margin of error, making it Texas’ most competitive statewide race since 1994, Henson said.
Outside groups backing Paxton have spent about US$239 million, more than five times the roughly US$45 million spent by the largest Democratic-aligned groups. Texas PAC, a Republican super PAC, alone has accounted for nearly US$149 million.
The group was launched by the Senate Leadership Fund, the main Republican Senate super PAC.
Musk, who lives in Texas and has relocated SpaceX, Tesla, X and other businesses there, has contributed US$158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, which subsequently transferred matching sums to Texas PAC, according to federal filings.
Talarico has offset the outside-spending disadvantage with grassroots fundraising.
His campaign says it raised US$64 million from July through September, more than triple Paxton’s total, with 97% of donations under US$100.
He spent US$61 million on ads through September, according to AdImpact, while the biggest Democratic outside group, Lone Star Rising PAC, has spent US$19.3 million.
The influx of Republican money arrived relatively late in the campaign, with Trump’s MAGA Inc super PAC not beginning major spending until early September.
“I think the cavalry arrived just in the nick of time for Paxton,” said Republican donor and oil businessman Dan Eberhart.
Going negative
Much of that spending has funded attacks portraying Talarico as out of step with Texas voters on culture-war issues.
Independent fact checkers say the ads distort Talarico’s record, and Henson said their goal is “arousing negative sentiment among Republican voters” to boost turnout.
Texas PAC ads tell voters that Talarico is “for they/them, not you” and accuse him of supporting taxpayer-funded sex-change surgeries for minors.
PolitiFact rated that claim false, noting that while Talarico opposed a 2023 ban on gender-transition care for minors, he has said he opposes gender-reassignment surgery for children.
A Paxton campaign ad featured an AI-generated Talarico reading from a fictional “King James (Talarico) Bible” that combined excerpts of his past remarks, including one describing God as “non-binary.”
FactCheck.org said the ad lacked key context.
Talarico has responded by casting Paxton as “the most corrupt politician in Texas.”
Paxton was impeached by the Republican-controlled Texas House in 2023 on abuse-of-office allegations but was acquitted by the state Senate.
Separate state securities-fraud charges dating to 2015 were dropped in 2024 under an agreement requiring community service, ethics training and restitution.
Paxton denied wrongdoing.
The Paxton campaign did not respond to requests for comment. It has previously said Talarico raises the allegations to distract from his own record.
Some voters say the Republican attacks are unconvincing.
Sal Anthony Rodriguez, a 32-year-old Houston operations manager who voted for Trump in 2020 and 2024, said he now supports Talarico, partly because of what he views as misleading attacks.
“I’ve seen a lot of ads saying that he is in 100% support for transgender surgeries on kids, and a quick Google search showed that that was not accurate,” Rodriguez said.
Democrats argue the focus on cultural issues reflects Republican difficulty addressing voters’ economic concerns.
“Voters are really pissed off about the state of their lives right now, and you can only run so many trans ads at people who are sick of paying US$6 for diesel,” said Chuck Rocha, a senior adviser to the Talarico campaign. REUTERS

Is China Getting Involved in the Japan-Russia Territorial Dispute?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:20:00 UTC
22:20:00 KST

According to information released by the government of Russia’s Sakhalin Oblast on October 13, a delegation from China’s Heilongjiang Province, including government officials and entrepreneurs, recently visited Iturup Island (Etorofu in Japanese). The island is part of the Southern Kuril Islands, known as the Northern Territories in Japan, which are currently under Russian de facto control, though Japan claims sovereignty over them.
The Chinese group’s visit led to an immediate expression of dissatisfaction from Tokyo, with Japanese Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu declaring it “absolutely unacceptable.” In response, Beijing stated that it “consistently advocates for respecting and upholding the outcomes of the victory [of World War II].” A Japanese media outlet suggested that this reflects “a coordinated stance between China and Russia regarding the Northern Territories issue and a joint approach in dealing with Japan.”
The islands in question were under Japanese control until they were occupied by the Soviet Union at the end of World War II. The Japanese government has maintained its claim ever since. Tokyo has made repeated attempts to advance negotiations on the territorial issue with Russia by leveraging economic cooperation and investment. Ultimately, however, these efforts have not yielded satisfactory results.
Despite possessing abundant fishery and mineral resources, the economic potential of these islands remains largely untapped due to the lagging economic development of the Russian Far East, inadequate infrastructure, and high transportation costs. In 2022, Russia announced the establishment of a special economic zone on the islands to foster economic growth. If Chinese enterprises become more involved in the economic development of the Southern Kuril Islands in the future, it would not only exert political pressure on Japan but could also strengthen Russia’s de facto control over these islands.
Although maps currently published in China label these islands as Japanese territory under Russian occupation, Beijing generally avoids taking an explicit stance on their sovereignty. In August 2026, following Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to Iturup Island, the Chinese and Russian ambassadors to Japan co-authored an article stating: “The preservation of historical memory of World War II and its outcomes is particularly important for our countries.” This appeared to imply China’s acknowledgment of the status quo without an overt declaration. Some Japanese media outlets perceive Beijing as shifting away from the position it held during the later Mao era and moving toward the Russian side.
It remains unclear whether this delegation’s visit was intentionally orchestrated by Beijing. However, given that the delegation included officials from the Heilongjiang provincial government, the visit clearly had at least the tacit approval of the authorities.
Over the past few months, Japanese lawmakers from various political parties have visited Taiwan, and most notably, a group of 27 Japanese parliamentarians arrived in Taiwan around the same time as this delegation’s visit. Beijing typically views such actions as an infringement upon China’s territorial sovereignty. Consequently, this visit by the Chinese delegation may well be a countermeasure by Beijing against Japan.
One disadvantage for Japan is that it is involved in territorial or maritime disputes with nearly all of its neighbors. These disputes currently remain largely a matter of bilateral relations between Japan and the respective countries involved. However, the Chinese delegation’s visit to the Southern Kuril Islands against the backdrop of deteriorating China-Japan relations may signal that Beijing has deployed a diplomatic card against Japan that had previously received little attention.
The deepening of China-Russia relations has further complicated this issue. In recent years, the frequent joint patrols conducted by Chinese and Russian military aircraft and naval vessels in the vicinity of Japan have drawn concern from Tokyo.
Concurrently, China and Russia have aligned their historical narratives. In May 2025, the two nations issued a joint statement commemorating their respective victories in the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the Great Patriotic War, while also pledging to strengthen bilateral cooperation and uphold the authority of international law. The statement characterized both China and Russia as “pivotal forces in the fight against militarism and fascism” and asserts their commitment to “defending the outcomes of the Second World War” and resisting any “resurgence of militarism.” This aligns with Beijing’s accusations that Japan is pursuing a “new-type militarism.”
Given these shared historical perceptions, China and Russia can be expected to coordinate more closely on historical and security-related issues in their diplomatic approaches toward Japan.
However, it remains highly likely that Beijing will continue to avoid formally recognizing Russian sovereignty over the islands. This is not only because China needs to maintain diplomatic maneuvering room vis-à-vis Japan, but also because it seeks to avoid becoming entirely tethered to Russia’s interests.
Japan’s response, meanwhile, is constrained by both its own policy toward Russia and the state of its relations with China. Japan’s continued imposition of sanctions against Russia makes any substantive improvement in its relations with Moscow in the near term highly unlikely. At the same time, there are no signs of any meaningful improvement in Tokyo’s relations with China. Against this backdrop, it is difficult for Japan to effectively counter the activities of China and Russia in the region.
More significantly, should China begin to actively engage in economic activities or even pursue military cooperation with Russia on the islands, the issue could gradually evolve from a bilateral dispute between Japan and Russia into a new variable affecting China-Japan relations and, by extension, the security landscape of Northeast Asia.

Mortgage rates drop for the first time in 2 months, but demand still falls further
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:13:48 UTC
22:13:48 KST

Mortgage demand took another leg lower, despite a brief respite from rising interest rates.
Total mortgage application volume fell 5.3% last week compared with the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index.
The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, dropped last week to 7.41% from 7.50%, with points falling to 0.75 from 0.83 including the origination fee for loans with a 20% down payment.
"Mortgage rates decreased for the first time in over two months," said Joel Kan, an MBA economist, in a release. "However, lower rates were not enough to boost application activity, as both purchase and refinance applications continued to decline."
Applications to refinance a home loan, which are most sensitive to weekly moves, fell just 2% week to week, a smaller drop than some previous weeks when rates were moving higher. Refinance demand was still 59% lower than the same week one year ago. With rates now over a full percentage point higher than they were a year ago, there is a very small pool of borrowers who can benefit from a refinance.
Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home declined a steeper 7% for the week and were 18% lower from the year before. Buyers are reacting less to the weekly move in rates but more to the overall higher level. A report from the National Association of Realtors on Tuesday showed a sharp drop in September pending home sales. These are measured by signed contracts, so it showed the real-time impact of rising rates during the month. Rates remained at that higher level in October.
For those buyers in the market, a continued high share are opting for adjustable-rate mortgages, or ARMs, which offer lower rates but are considered riskier because they will eventually reset to whatever the market rate is at the end of their term.
"The ARM share held steady at 10.5 percent, as ARM rates remained almost a full percentage point lower than the 30-year fixed rate, giving qualified borrowers a lower rate option to purchase a home," Kan added.
Mortgage rates haven't done much to start this week, according to a separate survey from Mortgage News Daily. Last week was a particularly volatile week for rates, due to multiple monthly inflation reports. This week the moves have seemed to follow oil prices.
"But we'd caution against placing too much emphasis on the oil price correlation," wrote Matthew Graham, chief operating officer at Mortgage News Daily. "It's been highly unreliable for more than a month."
Correction: The National Association of Realtors on Tuesday reported September pending home sales. An earlier version misstated the day.

UN warns climate pledges leave world far off track for 1.5°C goal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:10:37 UTC
22:10:37 KST

Current climate pledges would cut global greenhouse gas emissions by only 11 percent to 15 percent by 2035, far short of the 45 percent reduction needed to help bring warming back below 1.5°C by the end of the century, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) warned Wednesday.
In its Emissions Gap Report 2026, UNEP said emissions must fall 18 percent by 2030, 45 percent by 2035 and 69 percent by 2040 from 2025 levels to limit peak warming to around 1.7°C-1.8°C before potentially returning to 1.5°C or below by 2100.
However, fully implementing countries' existing climate pledges would cut emissions by only 5 percent to 8 percent by 2030 and 11 percent to 15 percent by 2035.
The report found that current climate policies could lead to 2.8°C of global warming this century, while fulfilling all national climate commitments would limit warming to 2.6°C.
Even meeting additional net-zero targets alongside national climate commitments would limit warming to only 2.1°C, according to UNEP.
"Every additional fraction of a degree and additional year of warming above 1.5°C increases climate impacts and risks, such as the deadly floods, heatwaves and wildfires that have plagued many nations this year," UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen said in the report.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres stressed that exceeding the 1.5°C threshold does not mean abandoning efforts to reverse warming.
"Overshoot is not surrender. We can still keep it as small and as short as possible — and bring temperatures back below 1.°C degrees by the end of the century," he said.
The report also found that returning to 1.5°C would require removing and permanently storing approximately 320 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere this century, a task facing significant technological and economic challenges.
Despite the warnings, UNEP noted that renewable energy expansion and climate policies have already reduced emissions in several countries.
"It is now up to nations to urgently put in place policies that spark fast, deep and sustained emissions reductions, and put the world on track for a more stable climate and more stable economies and societies," Andersen said.
The report warned that without urgent action, keeping peak warming below 1.7-1.8°C "will quickly become impossible."

World falling ‘dangerously short’ on climate action, UN chief warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:09:58 UTC
22:09:58 KST

World falling ‘dangerously short’ on climate action, UN chief warns
- UN report says current climate pledges are far too weak, putting the world on track for 2.6 deg C warming by 2100 and missing the Paris goals.
- UN chief Antonio Guterres warned that 1.5 deg C is already out of reach, with record emissions causing floods, heatwaves, wildfires and rising inequality.
- The report says 2025 emissions stayed near record highs, with the US the biggest driver of increases, and calls for urgent cuts and 5,000 gigawatts more renewables.
AI generated
PARIS – Global commitments to cut planet-heating emissions are falling far short of the Paris climate goals and put the world on course for 2.6 deg C warming this century, the UN warned on Oct 21.
The report by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) lays bare the chasm between rhetoric and action when it comes to tackling global warming, and the challenge before political leaders at November’s COP31 climate summit.
Even if countries deliver their latest climate pledges in full, global temperatures could still rise 2.6 deg C above pre-industrial levels by 2100, said the annual Emissions Gap Report.
That would blow past the historic goal agreed in 2015 in Paris: keeping warming well below 2 deg C while striving for a safer 1.5 deg C. Any chance of keeping to 1.5 deg C has been “lost” due to decades of insufficient action, the report said.
“The world can no longer avoid overshooting the 1.5 degree limit, and the consequences are already devastating,” said UN chief Antonio Guterres in a statement to launch the closely watched report.
“Deadly floods, brutal heatwaves, raging wildfires, lost lives, crippled economies, deepening inequalities, and those least responsible are suffering first and worst,” he said.
Overall, global greenhouse gas emissions in 2025 were broadly on a par with record levels in 2024, with the difference between the two years too small to call, the report said.
Carbon emissions just from burning coal, oil and gas – the main driver of climate change – rose slightly in 2025 compared to the previous year.
Guterres said deep and immediate cuts were needed to protect humanity from worsening impacts, but instead “emissions remain at record levels, and national climate plans and current policies fall dangerously short”.
Sticking just with current policies would see warming hit 2.8 deg C by the end of the century, the report said.
No country immune
Scientists warn that every additional fraction of a degree above 1.5 deg C increases extreme weather events and the likelihood of irreversible changes to the planet, from dying coral reefs to melting permafrost.
The world has already warmed roughly 1.4 deg C relative to pre-industrial times, and crossing 1.5 deg C is expected in a matter of years.
This latest UNEP warming outlook is worse than in 2025 because of the formal withdrawal of the United States from the Paris accord and upward revisions of historical emissions, said report co-author Anne Olhoff.
Emissions growth slowed among the G-20, but the US was a “major exception”, it added.
The Group of 20 major economies (G-20) accounts for three-quarters of global emissions.
Among the world’s top six emitters, preliminary data for 2025 showed emissions increases in the US, Indonesia and China, and decreases in India, Russia and the European Union.
But the US increase of 133 megatonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent “far exceeded” that of any other country, driven by higher electricity demand and a rebound of coal power generation.
The next-largest increase was recorded in Turkey, which is hosting the UN climate summit in Antalya from Nov 9 to 20.
The US is the world’s second-largest polluter, behind China.
US President Donald Trump has called climate change a hoax and rolled back clean energy policies while boosting fossil fuel production.
UNEP executive secretary Inger Andersen said she would not put the blame “squarely on one nation”, saying every country, especially those in the G-20, has “a specific duty to find a way to phase down their carbon emissions”.
To limit the overshoot beyond 1.5 deg C, Andersen said the world has an “urgent to-do item”: adding another 5,000 gigawatts of renewable energy over the next five years.
‘Historic failure’
The report details a scenario with a 50% chance of bringing global warming back down to 1.5 deg C by 2100.
To get there, warming must peak around 1.8 deg C by 2050, and vast amounts of carbon dioxide would have to be removed from the atmosphere to bring temperatures down further.
But this scenario assumes immediate emissions cuts of 6% per year, every year, until 2035, nowhere near current projections.
Some climate-vulnerable developing nations have accused bigger emitters of abandoning the Paris goals, and a showdown over the 1.5 deg C target is expected at COP31.
“This is a historic failure of political leadership,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Kenya-based think tank Power Shift Africa.
“The science has been clear for decades, but governments have chosen delay over action,” Adow said. “The consequences will be measured in lives lost, not just degrees of warming.” AFP

====================================================================================================

Too much RNA can starve cells of energy, scientists discover
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:02:34 UTC
22:02:34 KST

Too much RNA can starve cells of energy, scientists discover
- Date:
- October 21, 2026
- Source:
- Texas A&M University
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered an unexpected danger lurking inside cells: too much RNA can damage the structures responsible for producing energy. A new study found that excess RNA, including the normally essential messenger RNA (mRNA), can directly disrupt mitochondria without relying on the immune system. The discovery could help explain how viral infections and certain aging-related diseases damage cells.
- Share:
Scientists have uncovered a surprising way that viruses can interfere with the body's cells. When too much RNA accumulates inside a cell, it can damage the structures that produce energy, potentially leaving the cell struggling to function normally.
A new study led by researchers at the Texas A&M College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences (VMBS) found that excess RNA produced during poxvirus infections can impair mitochondria, the tiny structures responsible for generating most of the energy cells need to survive.
Published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the research reveals an unexpected connection between RNA buildup and cellular energy production. The findings could have implications far beyond viral infections, potentially helping scientists better understand aging-related diseases and improve RNA-based medical treatments, including mRNA vaccines.
"Scientists have long known that RNA degradation helps control protein production and remove defective RNA," said Dr. Zhilong Yang, a professor in VMBS' Department of Veterinary Pathobiology. "Our study reveals another important role: it helps cells maintain the energy they need to function properly."
Cells constantly produce and break down RNA as part of their normal activities. This cleanup process, known as RNA degradation, helps regulate protein production, eliminate faulty RNA, and control immune responses. The new findings suggest it also performs another essential function by protecting the cell's energy supply.
Why Too Much RNA Can Damage Cells
RNA plays several important roles in keeping cells functioning. Messenger RNA (mRNA), for example, carries genetic instructions that tell cells which proteins to produce. These proteins are needed for nearly everything cells do, from maintaining their structure to carrying out essential chemical reactions.
Another type, double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), frequently appears during viral infections. Its presence can serve as a warning signal, alerting the immune system that a virus may have entered the cell.
Viruses often generate large quantities of RNA as they reproduce inside infected cells. Ordinarily, cellular cleanup systems help prevent RNA from accumulating to harmful levels. However, when RNA production exceeds the cell's ability to break it down, the excess material can interfere with mitochondria and reduce energy production.
Scientists already understood that excessive double-stranded RNA could provoke potentially harmful immune responses. What surprised the researchers was discovering that too much ordinary messenger RNA could also damage mitochondria.
"MRNA is a normal component of our cells, but it seems like with many good things, if we get too much, that can become a problem for the cell," Yang said. "When too much RNA builds up, including mRNA, it can damage the mitochondria and interfere with the cell's ability to produce energy."
This creates an unusual challenge for viruses. Although viruses depend entirely on the cells they infect to supply energy and manufacture proteins, producing excessive amounts of viral RNA can damage the very machinery they need to reproduce.
According to Yang, poxviruses, a group that includes the viruses responsible for smallpox and mpox, appear to have ways of managing this problem. They use RNA cleanup mechanisms to remove excess RNA, helping infected cells remain functional long enough for viral replication to continue.
"If the cell is not healthy, the virus would not replicate well," Yang said. "The virus needs to keep RNA levels balanced inside the cell."
Scientists Discover RNA Can Directly Damage Mitochondria
One of the study's most unexpected findings emerged when researchers investigated exactly how excess RNA affects mitochondria.
Initially, the team suspected that RNA buildup was damaging these cellular powerhouses indirectly by activating the immune system. Certain types of RNA are known to trigger defensive responses, which can place additional stress on infected cells.
However, experiments revealed that the damage did not require an immune response.
"When we isolated only the mitochondria and added RNA, we still saw mitochondrial damage," said Dr. Djamal Brahim Belhaouari, the study's first author. "That was the moment we realized this could be a previously unknown cellular response to RNA."
The researchers also observed that mitochondrial problems developed before substantial immune activation occurred. Furthermore, the damage did not depend on the immune pathways normally activated during infection.
Together, these results indicate that excess RNA itself can interfere with mitochondrial function, rather than simply causing damage through the body's response to a virus.
The precise mechanism remains unclear, but the researchers have proposed a possible explanation involving electrical charges.
Mitochondria produce energy by maintaining an electrical and chemical difference across their inner membranes. This difference helps drive the production of ATP, the molecule cells use as their primary energy source.
RNA carries a negative electrical charge. The researchers suspect that when unusually large amounts accumulate near mitochondria, they may disturb the electrical conditions required for efficient energy production.
"We think the negatively charged RNA may accumulate around mitochondria and disrupt the electrical balance needed for energy production, although how it happens is unknown," Yang said. "This is a new concept that we are continuing to explore."
What the Discovery Could Mean for Aging and Disease
Although the experiments focused on viral infections, the findings raise questions about whether RNA buildup might contribute to other health problems.
Abnormal RNA accumulation has been observed in several conditions, including certain cancers, neurodegenerative diseases, and disorders associated with aging. Neurodegenerative diseases involve the progressive deterioration of nerve cells, as occurs in conditions such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease.
Because mitochondria are essential for maintaining healthy cells, disruptions to their energy production could potentially contribute to cellular dysfunction in some of these conditions.
The researchers suggest that excess RNA may represent one previously unrecognized source of mitochondrial stress. However, further studies are needed to determine how broadly this mechanism operates and whether it directly contributes to these diseases.
"We think this has quite broad translational implications," Brahim Belhaouari said. "Too much double-stranded RNA or mRNA that cannot be degraded effectively may contribute to disease processes in some contexts."
Potential Implications for mRNA Vaccines and Future Treatments
The discovery could also provide useful information for scientists developing medicines that rely on RNA.
RNA-based therapies, including mRNA vaccines, work by introducing RNA instructions into cells to produce specific proteins. Understanding how cells respond to RNA, process it, and eventually break it down is important for designing these treatments.
By identifying another way excessive RNA can affect cellular health, the findings may help researchers optimize future RNA-based therapies and vaccines. The study does not establish that existing mRNA vaccines cause mitochondrial damage in people.
"Understanding this mechanism could help researchers design and optimize future RNA-based therapeutics and vaccines by better understanding how cells respond to large amounts of RNA," Yang said.
More broadly, the research suggests that controlling RNA levels is important for more than maintaining accurate protein production or managing immune activity. It may also be essential for keeping mitochondria functioning and ensuring cells have enough energy.
For the scientists, the most striking result was that even a molecule cells depend on every day can become harmful when it accumulates beyond normal levels.
"Scientists already knew that too much double-stranded RNA can be harmful," Yang said. "What surprised us was finding out that too much mRNA -- something cells normally need every day -- can also damage mitochondria and interfere with the cell's ability to produce energy."
Research reported in this study was supported, in part, by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (R01AI143709 to Z.Y.) and Texas A&M University. The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official views of the NIH.

Journal Reference:
- Djamal Brahim Belhaouari, Anil Pant, Santiago Navarro-Forero, Fernando Cantu, Zhilong Yang. Perturbation of RNA homeostasis impairs mitochondrial respiration during poxvirus infection through excess RNA accumulation. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2026; 123 (22) DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2605194123

Libya’s maritime deal with Türkiye angers EU states
Libya’s eastern-based parliament has approved a disputed maritime agreement with Türkiye, drawing condemnation from Greece and Cyprus over competing boundaries and energy rights in the Mediterranean.
The House of Representatives voted unanimously on Tuesday to endorse the agreement, which was first signed in November 2019 between Ankara and Libya’s internationally recognized government in Tripoli. Lawmakers also overturned a 2020 decision to sever political ties with Türkiye.
The agreement demarcates maritime jurisdiction between the two countries in an area contested by Greece, Egypt, and Cyprus.
The Greek Foreign Ministry called the parliamentary decision “unilateral [and] legally unfounded,” saying the deal disregards Greek islands’ rights to maritime zones between the Turkish and Libyan coasts.
“The memorandum remains illegal, null and void, contravenes international law of the sea, and infringes upon the sovereign rights of states in the region,” the ministry said in a statement.
It argued that Türkiye and Libya lack opposite or adjacent coastlines providing a lawful basis for the boundary, warning that Greece would take action to defend its sovereign rights. Cyprus also condemned the decision, calling the memorandum “illegal, null and void.”
Ankara welcomed the vote, saying the agreement safeguards “the mutual rights and interests” of both countries under international law and the principle of equity, while deepening cooperation between Türkiye and Libya. “Türkiye will continue to work with all partners to foster trust, stability and peace in the Mediterranean basin, in line with its commitment to international law,” the Foreign Ministry stated.
The eastern Mediterranean has seen a wave of offshore gas discoveries since 2009, opening new export opportunities while intensifying disputes over maritime boundaries and drilling rights. Major finds off Israel, Cyprus, and Egypt have attracted international energy companies, including Chevron and Eni, to the region, according to a US Energy Information Administration report.
Greece and Egypt signed an overlapping maritime agreement in 2020, which Türkiye rejects. Athens also approved offshore exploration south of Crete by a consortium led by Chevron last year, prompting Turkish objections.
The move on Tuesday comes amid improving ties between Türkiye and Libya’s eastern authorities, who are aligned with military commander Khalifa Haftar. Ankara helped Tripoli repel his forces’ 2019-2020 campaign to capture the capital, but has since expanded diplomatic contacts and investment in the east. The country remains divided between Abdul Hamid Dbeibah’s government in the capital, Tripoli, in western Libya, and an eastern administration led by Osama Hammad and backed by Haftar.
Officials from both rival administrations welcomed the parliamentary approval. The Tripoli-based Foreign Ministry called it a “positive development toward strengthening bilateral relations” with Türkiye. Haftar’s son Saddam, the deputy commander of the Libyan National Army, called it a move toward overcoming past differences, putting Libya’s national interests first.
