House values drop in all capital cities for first time in 15 years, Domain says
In short:
House prices have fallen across every capital city for the first time in 15 years, Domain reports.
Data shows Australia's most expensive homes have recorded the biggest drops this year, while lower-value homes have remained largely stable.
Experts say rising interest rates and lower market confidence are driving the downturn.
House prices have fallen 4.7 per cent, the steepest quarterly drop on record, according to new data from Domain.
Prices dropped in every capital city in the September quarter, the first time in 15 years and only the second time on record.
The real estate platform's data showed the sharpest decline was in Perth, where prices dropped 7.4 per cent.
Combined capital city house prices fell to $1,226,566. Domain said markets that started the year in very different positions "are now moving in the same direction".
Australia's biggest property markets, Sydney and Melbourne, recorded their largest quarterly house price drop in four years, falling 4.7 per cent and 3.3 per cent, respectively.
Unit prices also fell 3.5 per cent, marking the second consecutive quarter both property types declined.
It marked a clear shift in the housing cycle, according to Nicola Powell, Domain's chief residential economist.
"What began as weakness concentrated in some cities has broadened considerably," Dr Powell said.
"The balance of power has shifted towards buyers.
"Homes are taking longer to sell, there is greater scope to negotiate, and sellers are having to be more realistic about price expectations."
The cumulative impact of rising rates, lower affordability, and cost-of-living pressures has reduced demand, according to Gerard Burg of data firm Cotality.
"It's been a demand-led downturn," Mr Burg said.
Australia's most valuable homes falling the most
While all major markets across the country have joined the downturn, prices have not been dropping equally within cities.
Australia's most valuable homes are dropping the most, while lower value homes were relatively stable in three months to September, according to property data firm Cotality.
In Sydney, the most valuable quartile of homes dropped more than twice as much as the least valuable quartile.
Nationwide, lower-value homes have seen a much slower price drop, Cotality said.
Prices grew in Darwin's lowest value quartile.
The sharper downturn in more expensive properties reflects fewer buyers and higher borrowing costs, according to property economist Cameron Kusher.
"They've typically seen larger increases in values over recent years and when you see that market slowdown, there's overall fewer buyers for those properties," he said.
However, he said the ultra-top end of the market had remained largely stable.
Mr Burg agreed, saying lower-priced homes remained affordable to more buyers.
"The median house really appears kind of out of reach of the median income household across much of the country," he said.
Prices were falling before federal budget
The federal budget was a factor, but not the only factor, in house price falls, according to Mr Kusher.
House prices peaked last year and had already begun to drop before the changes to investment taxes in May's federal budget, Mr Kusher and Mr Burg both noted.
Mr Burg said prices were already falling in many capital cities, and three consecutive interest rate hikes had dampened market confidence.
Auction activity, a common gauge of market confidence, has roughly halved from last year, with 1,423 auctions across capital cities last week, according to Cotality.
"Confidence has really evaporated. Affordability is very stretched and borrowing capacity is reduced dramatically," Mr Kusher said.
"People just aren't in a position or able to pay the prices that a lot of these properties are worth at the moment."
He said home ownership rates had not moved much since the May budget changes, due to lower buyer confidence and stretched affordability.
"The first time is pretty scary as it is, and I think a lot of them are looking at it and saying, 'Well, prices are falling, why would I jump in now when there's quite a lot for sale, if I wait another six or 12 months properties will probably be cheaper,'" he said.
"I just don't think first home buyers have that urgency anymore."
He said prices would be unlikely to return to their previous heights, at least not in the short term.
"I think this downturn is probably going to drag on a bit longer than people expect, and it probably will until it looks like interest rates are going to actually be reduced again," he said.

E-scooter and e-bike hospitalisations on the rise in Australia, report finds
In short:
A report from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) has found e-scooter hospitalisations have more than tripled since 2019.
There were 4,089 hospitalisations involving e-scooter in the 2024-25 compared to 1,291 in 2019-20.
Two-thirds of those hospitalised in 2024-25 were male with largest increase in young boys aged between 12 and 15.
Teenage boys riding e-scooters drove a sharp rise in hospitalisations over the last five years, according to a report from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW).
The number of boys aged 12 to 15 hospitalised following e-scooter falls saw a 15-fold increase between 2019/20 and 2024/25.
Boys in that cohort were four times more likely than girls to end up in hospital because of an e-scooter fall.
It also found hospitalisation rates increased for e-bike riders, but these data were harder to capture because of how these injuries were classified.
The report found e-scooter-related deaths increased over the past decade from seven in 2014/15 to 20 in 2024/25; however, the proportion of deaths was stable.
New codes introduced in July this year will help better differentiate between e-mobility devices such as e-scooters and e-bikes, the report said.
AIHW spokesperson Jacqueline Rek said the improved data will help better understand the risks surrounding e-mobility devices.
"Meaning these findings should not be interpreted as precise counts of injuries involving e-scooters or e-bikes alone," Ms Rek said.
"This report provides the first national view on this topic, while also highlighting where more data is needed."
What can improve safety?
E-bikes and e-scooters are now mainstream, with almost 1 million privately owned by Queenslanders, according to University of Queensland research.
Richard J Buning, who worked on the research, said improving safety was crucial given the growth.
"Every single year over the last five years, the growth in e-mobility device purchases has risen by 30 per cent," he said.
Dr Buning said unsafe devices such as over-powered e-bikes were among his chief concerns.
Last year, the federal government introduced stronger e-bike import standards similar to those in the European Union (EU), limiting access to unsafe devices.
"It's these unsafe, uncompliant, illegal devices that are creating much of the problems of people riding really fast on high-powered devices," Dr Buning said.
"But the safe, compliant devices, they don't provide more power than just a normal typical average fit person can provide."
Dr Buning highlighted Queensland as one jurisdiction in the country leading e-mobility device regulation.
People riding e-bikes in the state must be 16 or older and hold a valid driver's licence, including a learner licence.
Children aged between 12 and 17 (where 16- and 17-year-olds do not hold a driver's licence) will only be able to ride an e-bike or e-scooter with parental supervision.
Dr Buning disagreed with licensing e-bikes but praised the state's e-bike assurance scheme, which followed EU regulations.
It will mean from March 2027, all e-bikes in the state must have a compliance label to ride in public.
"So stopping those things from being sold and making sure that the public knows if they buy one of these devices that are uncompliant, they cannot legally ride it on the road," he said.
Dr Buning also suggested more targeted initiatives to better educate those who are riding unsafely, which was mostly younger people.
"Ideally we can get into schools and teach them how to ride a device safely. That's probably going to take out the majority of the problematic behaviour,"
he said.
"Because the vast majority of people that use e-bikes are actually much older, 70 per cent of e-mobility device users are over the age of 40.
"That highly visible behaviour may be obscuring public perception of an overall quite inclusive and sustainable transport mode."

====================================================================================================

Older adults tell the story of their lives differently, and it may not be a sign of decline, new psychology study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:00:44 UTC
22:00:44 KST

A new study published in Psychology and Aging indicates that having to switch between recalling different types of personal memories makes it harder for both young and older adults to follow instructions accurately. Beyond the mental effort of juggling changing rules, the findings suggest that older adults tend to include more general personal facts and fewer specific details than younger adults, whether they are recalling a one-time event or a recurring routine.
Autobiographical memory is the mental system that allows people to recollect their own life history. It encompasses two main kinds of information: episodic memory and personal semantic memory. Episodic memories are rich recollections of unique events tied to a specific time and place, such as a particular birthday dinner last month. Personal semantic memories are broader facts about one’s life that are not tied to a single episode, such as general self-knowledge. Falling between the two are memories of repeated events, like a weekly habit of cooking with a friend, which summarize many similar occasions while still carrying some sensory and contextual detail.
As people age, the balance between these forms of recall tends to change. A benchmark 2002 study of younger and older adults found that when asked to describe past life events, younger adults mostly shared specific details about what happened, where they were, and how they felt, whereas older adults shared fewer time-and-place details and favored general, factual knowledge.
“A typical example would be that if a young adult is telling you about their last birthday party, they are more likely to include specific contextual and perceptual details (such as the specific time and place, what clothes people wore at that party, or specific details about what they said),” senior author Louis Renoult, a professor of cognitive neuroscience and the postgraduate research director in the School of Psychology at the University of East Anglia, told PsyPost. “In contrast, when remembering the same event, older adults would typically provide more factual background knowledge about similar birthday parties or other celebrations they would have attended, or more general knowledge they have about the people involved, for example.”
This pattern raised questions about whether the shift toward general memories comes from changes in how memories are stored or from age-related declines in executive control, which is the set of mental skills used to manage goals, stay focused, and filter out irrelevant thoughts. A 2013 study explored this by changing how instructions were given while participants listened to musical clips, finding that younger adults adjusted how specific their memories were to match the rules, while older adults did not adjust their recall as much when task demands grew more complex.
To test how mental flexibility affects memory recall, another 2013 study of university students introduced a test requiring participants to rapidly alternate between recalling unique, one-time events and repeated routines. The students were less accurate at providing specific memories when they had to switch back and forth compared to when they followed a single rule at a time.
“In the field, people generally assume that the greater reliance on factual knowledge (and semantic memory) in aging would constitute a compensation, due to a less efficient episodic memory,” explained Renoult, who also recently discussed memory and aging on a podcast episode. “However, tests commonly used to assess semantic and episodic memory are rarely well matched in difficulty, and most tests of autobiographical memory focus on episodic memory only. Due to these issues, my research group has developed new memory tests to study semantic and episodic memory in parallel, in conditions where they are well matched experimentally to better understand memory changes as we get older.”
To examine whether mental switching places an extra burden on older adults during memory recall and how it interacts with the broader shift toward factual details, Renoult and his colleagues carried out the new study. The work was led by Greta Melega while she was completing her doctorate at the University of East Anglia; she is now a postdoctoral researcher at Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin (“and also an elite European Ultimate Frisbee player (!),” Renoult noted).
The researchers recruited 45 younger adults and 45 older adults, all of whom were native English speakers without psychiatric or neurological conditions. After excluding participants who did not finish the study, had poor audio recordings, fell below a cognitive screening threshold, or did not pass an initial training check, the final sample included 37 older adults aged 60 to 85 and 37 younger adults aged 18 to 33.
The two age groups had similar levels of education and did not differ in self-reported symptoms of depression or anxiety, which the authors measured because mood can influence how specifically people recall the past. A subset of 30 younger and 30 older participants also completed standard tests of attention and working memory, showing no statistically significant differences between the age groups.
Participants completed an online memory task where they saw 21 neutral, easy-to-visualize cue words on a screen, one at a time. Depending on the prompt, they had up to one minute to think of either a specific memory (a unique event lasting less than a day, such as having “a good time at Jane’s party last month in London”) or a categoric memory (a repeated event that happened multiple times in a similar way, such as “When I go to Jane’s house, we usually cook together and watch a movie afterwards”).
Once a memory came to mind, they pressed a button and spoke aloud for up to two minutes to describe it in as much detail as possible. After each description, participants had five seconds per question to rate how vivid and emotional the memory was, whether they saw it through their own eyes or as an outside observer, and how long ago it took place.
The experiment was divided into two parts: a baseline block and a switching block. In the baseline block, participants followed one instruction at a time, recalling three specific memories in a row and three categoric memories in a row. In the 14-trial switching block, the instructions to recall specific or categoric memories changed unpredictably every two or three trials. This allowed the scientists to compare “switch trials,” where the rule had just changed from the previous prompt, with “remain trials,” where the rule stayed the same as the prompt right before it.
The research team evaluated the recorded narratives in two ways. First, they measured accuracy, defined as the percentage of memories that matched the prompt given on that trial. Second, for the memories that matched the instructions, the researchers broke the transcripts down to count the exact types of details produced: episodic details (specific sights, times, and feelings of a one-time event), repeated event details (context and sensory details of a recurring routine), semantic details (general facts and personal background knowledge), and other statements like repetitions. Because older adults spoke longer on average than younger adults (about 45 seconds versus 27 seconds) and produced more total details per memory (an average of 11.00 details compared to 7.41), the authors analyzed the proportion of each detail type rather than raw counts.
When looking at overall accuracy, both younger and older participants had a harder time following instructions when they had to juggle both rules in the switching block, dropping from 82 percent accuracy in the baseline block to 73 percent in the switching block. Within the switching block itself, accuracy did not differ between switch trials and remain trials, suggesting that the mental cost came from keeping two different rules in mind at once rather than the immediate act of switching from one trial to the next.
Older adults were not disproportionately harmed by the switching block compared to younger adults. Across the experiment, the two age groups were equally accurate when asked to recall specific, one-time events, with older adults succeeding on 81 percent of trials and younger adults on 80 percent. However, older adults were less accurate than younger adults when instructed to recall categoric, repeated events, matching the instructions 68 percent of the time compared to 81 percent for younger adults. When participants failed to provide a proper categoric memory, they most often defaulted to sharing general personal facts instead of an actual recurring event.
When the researchers examined how participants elaborated on their accurate memories, strong age differences appeared regardless of whether participants were in the baseline or switching block. Even when older adults successfully recalled a unique, one-time event, only 66 percent of the details they shared were specific episodic details, compared to 79 percent for younger adults. In turn, general semantic facts made up 18 percent of older adults’ descriptions of unique events, compared to 13 percent for younger adults.
A similar pattern emerged for categoric memories: older adults included a smaller proportion of on-target repeated event details than younger adults (48 percent versus 72 percent) and a much larger proportion of general semantic information across both blocks (40 to 42 percent for older adults, versus 15 to 24 percent for younger adults).
“As observed previously, older adults consistently produced more semantic (factual) details but less episodic (specific) elements than young adults,” Renoult said. “However, crucially, this was not only observed under specific (episodic) instructions, but also under categoric (semantic) instructions. This suggests that remembering the past using more factual knowledge is adaptive and meaningful to older adults, and not necessarily the result of a compensation, or of a general decline in their memory abilities.”
The study itself did not test what purpose, if any, this narrative style serves.
Increased task demands in the switching block also altered the makeup of memory details. Under categoric instructions, moving to the switching block reduced the proportion of target repeated event details from 67 percent to 54 percent across participants. The paper reports a similar shift under specific instructions, but its figures for that comparison duplicate those given elsewhere, so the size of that effect is uncertain.
The subjective ratings highlighted additional differences in how the two age groups experienced their memories. Even though older adults included proportionally fewer specific details in their stories, they rated their specific memories as more vivid than younger adults did (an average of 3.81 versus 3.53 on a 5-point scale) and rated their memories overall as more emotional (2.92 versus 2.46). Regarding the age of the memories, younger adults mostly drew from the past five years, especially the past year, whereas older adults recalled memories from more than 10 years ago on 39 percent of specific trials and 48 percent of categoric trials, compared to just 15 percent and 7 percent for younger adults.
“It is important to realize that, even though young and older adults remember their past differently (with different narrative style), in these studies participants of both age groups are able to follow the overall instructions and retrieve the relevant type of information in most trials (i.e., they produce the correct type of memory, even if with different amount of details),” Renoult noted. “Nonetheless, the results that we report in this study are consistent with previous findings from our group using different methods.”
Renoult also emphasized that differences in how older adults recount their past should not be mistaken for a broad loss of memory function. “Sometimes people have gloomy views of aging, but not all types of memory decline when we get older, as shown in studies such as ours: Semantic memory (general knowledge of the world) is well preserved in older adults (who sometimes outperform young adults in these tasks).”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. The study’s design and analysis plan were not preregistered. Because the baseline block was always completed before the switching block so participants could learn the rules, fatigue or the possibility that the easiest memories were used up first could have contributed to the drop in performance during the switching phase. The number of trials was also kept relatively small to prevent tiredness during online testing, which meant the authors could not separately test whether switching rules hurt one memory type more than the other.
In addition, the older adults in this sample performed just as well as the younger undergraduate students on standard cognitive tests of working memory and attention. Because executive control often declines with age, this high-performing group of older adults might not reflect the broader aging population, which could explain why they had no trouble finding specific memories when prompted. The participants were also predominantly female, and they were allowed to choose memories from any point in their lives; future studies could restrict recall to specific time periods and use standardized follow-up prompts to see if older adults can retrieve more specific sensory details when encouraged to do so.
Looking ahead, the research team plans to explore how the social context of a conversation shapes the way people recount their lives. “We are interested to investigate social elements that may influence memory retrieval in aging, such as with whom one is sharing their memories,” Renoult said. “One related bias in the literature is that older adults are typically interviewed by a young adult (e.g., a PhD student, or a research assistant). It is possible that, in such cases, older adults include more general knowledge to provide additional background information for someone of a different age group.”
The study, “Age-Related Differences in Autobiographical Memory Recall: Impact of Retrieval Mode Switching,” was authored by Greta Melega, Alice Bush, Tabitha James, Riccardo Sacripante, and Louis Renoult.

No decisions yet on new RAF jet trainer, says Pollard
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:00:16 BST
22:00:16 KST

The Jet Training System programme is ongoing and no final procurement decisions have been made, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what comparative assessment the Secretary of State has made of the effectiveness of the Collins Aerospace ACES 5 ejection seat fitted to the Boeing T-7A Red Hawk against the Martin-Baker seats used across the rest of the RAF fleet.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “The Jet Training System programme is ongoing and no final procurement decisions have been made.”
The Jet Training System will replace the Hawk T2 that trains fast jet pilots at RAF Valley, with the older Hawk T1 already retired and the T2 fleet running towards the end of the decade. A competition is expected, and Boeing, Saab and BAE Systems have offered the T-7A Red Hawk with local assembly in the United Kingdom, with Leonardo’s M-346 among the alternatives.
Ejection seats carry unusual weight in a British competition because Martin-Baker is a British company that has equipped almost every RAF type since the 1940s and holds a worldwide position built on that record. Choosing an airframe fitted with the American ACES 5 would move that work, and swapping a seat into an airframe designed around a different one is a design and certification exercise in its own right.
The T-7A’s escape system drew sustained criticism during American testing, with problems identified around the performance of the seat and canopy for pilots at the light end of the weight range and around the sequencing of the escape itself, and Boeing has worked through a series of modifications. Programme delays in the United States have pushed initial operating capability for the American air force to the end of the decade.
Martin-Baker’s Mk16 variants are fitted to Typhoon, the F-35 and the Hawk, which means an RAF trainer on a different seat would put student pilots through a different escape system from the one they meet on the front line.

Poland has no Patriot missiles to spare for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:57:54 UTC
21:57:54 KST

Poland has no Patriot missiles to spare for Ukraine
Poland does not have enough Patriot air defense missiles to hand over to Ukraine, Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski has said, urging other NATO members to supply Kiev with the scarce interceptors.
In an interview with the Polish Press Agency published on Monday, Sikorski warned of growing pressure on Western air defenses, citing the US-Israeli bombing campaign against Iran.
“Following the attacks on Iran, the shortage of interceptor missiles has indeed increased, and Russia is producing more missiles than we have interceptors to neutralize them. This is a real problem,” he said.
“There are NATO countries that still have such resources to contribute, but Poland is not one of them,” Sikorski said, adding that Warsaw “can only join the calls for countries possessing Patriot missiles to share them with Ukraine.”
The issue sparked a political scandal in Poland in July, when the government came under fire over the transfer of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine as part of a wider NATO-backed aid package. Opposition politicians accused Warsaw of sacrificing its own security to arm Kiev, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk insisted the deliveries would not compromise the country’s defenses.
Poland has emerged as one of the EU’s most rapidly militarizing nations, with defense spending reaching 4.7% of GDP. Warsaw has also been one of Kiev’s staunchest backers, pouring billions into military and other aid while serving as a crucial hub for Western arms shipments.
Yet Poland now faces delays in replenishing its own arsenal, with deliveries of US-made PAC-3 MSE Patriot interceptors pushed back as the war with Iran drains American weapons stocks, Polish General Ireneusz Nowak warned earlier this month.
Relations with Kiev have also soured over Ukraine’s honoring of Nazi collaborators linked to the World War II-era Volhynia massacres, in which Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) militants associated with the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN) killed an estimated 100,000 ethnic Poles. Warsaw recognizes the killings as genocide, while Kiev continues to honor figures including OUN leader Stepan Bandera.
Tensions flared again this year after Zelensky awarded a Ukrainian military unit the honorary title “Heroes of the UPA.” Polish President Karol Nawrocki subsequently stripped him of the country’s highest honor, politicians on both sides renounced state decorations, and Warsaw threatened to obstruct Ukraine’s EU accession.
The ammunition crunch is spreading across NATO. In July, the Netherlands said it had exhausted its capacity to supply Ukraine with Patriot missiles from its own stocks, having already provided interceptors and helped assemble a complete Patriot system for Kiev.
Meanwhile, Kiev is facing a critical shortage of air defense ammunition as Russia intensifies strikes on Ukrainian military and energy infrastructure. Moscow has said the attacks are in retaliation for Kiev’s continued strikes on Russian territory, including civilian targets and energy facilities.
Vladimir Zelensky has requested 300 Patriot interceptors from European backers and complained that Washington has approved only some of the missiles purchased through a NATO-backed initiative. The White House has also delayed approving additional transfers as US President Donald Trump presses Ukraine to reach a negotiated settlement with Russia.
Moscow has repeatedly maintained that Western weapons deliveries prolong the conflict, obstruct peace efforts, and risk drawing NATO countries into a direct confrontation with Russia.

Egypt rejects Libyan approval of maritime deal with Turkey
Oct 21 - Egypt's Foreign Ministry on Wednesday rejected the maritime boundaries deal that Libya's eastern parliament ratified with Turkey, saying in a statement that the ratification will have no legal impact on Cairo.
The deal approved on Tuesday is part of a years-old dispute over competing claims to sea borders and energy exploration rights in the eastern Mediterranean.
• "Egypt reaffirms that this memorandum is null and void ... possesses no legal effect," Egypt's Foreign Ministry said
• Israel said on Wednesday it "strongly" condemned the Libyan eastern parliament's approval, which also drew swift criticism from Greece
• "Regretfully, once again we see Turkey working to destabilise the east Mediterranean region," the Israeli Foreign Ministry said in a statement
• Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan rejected the criticism, saying the agreement was legitimate and that the Libyan parliament's ratification was simply a formality as the deal was already in effect for Ankara.
• "There are countries reacting to this. We know why they are reacting. Some are doing so because they need to, some really do have strategic problems with this issue. However, this is an entirely legitimate deal, both from a legal and a statutory perspective. There is no need to argue this," Fidan told state media in Brussels
• A statement by the EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas issued later said: "The EU has a strategic interest in a stable and secure environment in the Eastern Mediterranean and urges all countries to respect the sovereign rights of all Member States, in accordance with EU and international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea"
• The Libya-Turkey maritime deal was originally agreed in 2019 by Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli in the west, but the rival eastern administration had withheld its approval for years
• Greece, Egypt and Cyprus have long been opposed to a maritime-boundaries deal between Libya and Turkey, as they see it as an infringement on their own maritime claims.
• The Greek Ambassador to the United Nations, Aglaia Balta, briefed the UN Security Council about the issue on Wednesday, arguing it would impact security and stability in the eastern Mediterranean, said Greek diplomatic sources. REUTERS

Married couples can use double surnames from 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:54:00 UTC
21:54:00 KST

Married couples can use double surnames from 2027
From January 1, 2027, married couples will once again be able to use a double surname in Switzerland. The government will bring this amendment to the Civil Code, which was passed by parliament, into force on that date.
From next year spouses will once again be able to use a double surname with or without a hyphen. However children will not be allowed this privilege.
Double surnames were allowed in Switzerland until an amendment to the Civil Code in 2013. From that year onwards, couples intending to marry had to choose a shared surname or retain their respective surnames. Only an unofficial “alliance name” was permitted. This refers to the unofficial double surname with a hyphen.
More
Why double surnames are stirring controversy in Switzerland
Under the amendments adopted by the government, people who are already married will be able to apply to the registry office for an official double surname from 2027 onwards. In future, the alliance name – which differs from the official surname – will no longer be included in passports or on identity cards.
However, a transitional period will continue to allow the alliance name to be recorded in identity documents to enable the authorities to make the necessary technical adjustments.
The governing Federal Council has not yet determined the duration of this transitional period. It will bring the relevant amendment to the Identification Documents Act into force in due course and announce the end of the period well in advance.

NEW DELHI: A special executive magistrate (SEM) court in Delhi on Wednesday accepted the surety bonds of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka and ordered their release, officials said.The court said they may be released from jail if they are not in custody in any other case. The order came after Delhi Police sought a three-day extension of their judicial custody.The two leaders have been in police custody for 7 days.
On their way back, Saurav Das in the brief interaction with media responded to the court's order saying, "Truth has triumphed."
Ashutosh Ranka also had a message to share before stepping inside his car to leave. Surrounded by media, Ranka before heading inside held his fist up and said, "Inquilab Zindabaad!"
The CJP founder and leader Abhijeet Dipke shared his reaction to the court's release order. Taking to his X account, Dipke shared a clip from the climax scene of Shah Rukh Khan's movie Chak De India.
'Pursue alternative remedy'
Earlier in the day, Das and Ranka challenged the extension of their custody before the Delhi high court. The court asked them to await the SEM's decision and approach the appropriate appellate or revisional forum if their grievance persisted. The activists subsequently withdrew their plea.Delhi HC also questioned why they had invoked its writ jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution when an alternative legal remedy was available.
“Your second incident. You are a person who has actually broken a bond. Your remedy actually lies in revision,” the court observed while hearing the challenge to the SEM's October 19 order.The bench also questioned whether authorities could impose stricter surety conditions following an alleged second breach of a peace bond.“Once you have broken peace for the second time, are the authorities not entitled to insist upon everything?” the court asked.The court further expressed concern that breaching barricades at Jantar Mantar could encourage others to violate prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS).“The two petitioners here are at the forefront. When you go and break a barricade, the chances of 10 or 20 more people in violation of 163 are very high,” the court observed.
Advocate Abhik Chimni, appearing for the petitioners, argued that the SEM lacked jurisdiction to extend their custody and that their sureties had been wrongly rejected. The High Court clarified that it had not expressed any opinion on the merits of the case before permitting the withdrawal of the plea.
CJP leaders detained after Jantar Mantar protest

Their custody was extended by two days on October 19.The activists challenged the extension under Sections 126 and 170 of the BNSS, arguing that their continued detention was illegal and that the allegations did not establish an imminent threat to peace and tranquillity.

New report points to widespread and systematic Israeli sexual violence against Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:52:26 UTC
21:52:26 KST

Content warning: This article contains descriptions of sexual violence and abuse that readers may find distressing.
Sexual violence against Palestinians has become part of a widespread and systematic pattern of abuse under Israeli occupation, with a new report laying out incidents of rape, genital torture, forced nudity and sexual humiliation across detention facilities, military operations and displacement sites.
The report in the British Medical Journal collates evidence from medical, humanitarian, and human rights organisations and examines the scale of the abuses to highlight the failure to secure accountability.
The report comes a few weeks after the third anniversary of the start of Israel’s genocidal war against Palestine that has killed more than 75,000 people and displaced millions in the devastated enclave of Gaza.
Sexual violence is part of a wider campaign of abuse that terrorises Palestinian communities and helps drive their forced displacement, according to Dr Nick Maynard, an Oxford-based consultant surgeon who has travelled to Gaza multiple times to provide medical care and co-author of the new report.
“It is important to understand that the evidence we have provided of sexual violence against Palestinians must not be considered as isolated incidents but a part of a widespread systematic pattern of severe physical and sexual abuse of Palestinians throughout the (occupied) West Bank and in Gaza,” Maynard tells TRT World.
“This behaviour is designed to break the will of the Palestinian people and clearly represents a fundamental and core part of their policy of forced displacement of Palestinian people and ethnic cleansing,” he adds.
In March 2025, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry concluded that sexual and gender-based violence against Palestinians was increasingly being used as a method of war.
It found that forced public stripping, sexual harassment and assault formed part of Israeli security forces’ standard operating procedures, with sexualised torture committed with explicit orders or implicit encouragement from senior civilian and military leadership.
The Commission documented a pattern of sexual violence, torture and other inhumane acts amounting to war crimes and crimes against humanity.
The evidence includes rape and sexual assault against Palestinian detainees, attacks targeting their genitals, threats of rape against detainees and their family members, and repeated strip searches conducted in degrading circumstances.
Life-altering injuries
The documented abuse against Palestinian detainees includes sexual violence and beatings that have left them with devastating and sometimes permanent injuries.
In one documented case, a Palestinian detainee suffered a rectal rupture requiring surgery and the formation of a stoma.
Other accounts describe detainees losing one or both testicles after beatings targeting their genitals.
The abuse has also extended beyond detention.
Palestinian men, women and children in Gaza were subjected to prolonged forced nudity during Israeli military operations, including being forced to walk naked in public.
Israeli soldiers also photographed and filmed Palestinian women’s underwear in homes they had raided, posting images online to humiliate them.
The UN’s 2026 report on conflict-related sexual violence verified sexual violence against 31 Palestinian men, women and children in Gaza and the occupied West Bank across 2023 to 2025.
Nine victims were subjected to rape or gang rape, in some cases repeatedly. The documented abuses included genital violence, forced nudity, threats of rape and invasive searches without apparent security justification.
Maynard, who has travelled to Gaza repeatedly since 2010, including on three occasions since October 7, 2023, says he witnessed appalling atrocities including mass casualties caused by bombings in densely populated civilian areas, with children among those killed.
During his work, Maynard collected detailed testimonies from two healthcare workers and one civilian who had been abducted and detained in Israeli prisons. Their accounts included descriptions of torture and sexual violence.
“I have worked in the hospitals with many patients who died because of the lack of resources, and clearly many of them would have survived if we had had adequate resources.”
“The lack of adequate medical resources, as a direct result of the direct targeting of healthcare facilities and the Israeli blockade stopping adequate aid and resources coming into Gaza, meant that patients suffering from trauma often were not able to get adequate medical care and support and this applied to those with trauma from sexual violence,” Maynard says.
“Those who were tortured and underwent sexual violence in Israeli detention centres and prisons were also denied medical care while in custody,” he adds.
Sexual violence drives fear and displacement
For Palestinians, sexual violence and threats have also shaped everyday life under occupation, including during military raids, at checkpoints and in displacement sites.
Reports document women being forced to undress in front of soldiers, subjected to sexual assault and threatened with rape, sometimes in front of their children.
Other accounts describe Israeli soldiers exposing their genitals to women and girls, while Palestinian women in the occupied West Bank have faced sexual harassment and threats from Israeli settlers.
In one study involving 39 displaced households in Area C of the occupied West Bank, more than 70 percent identified threats to women and children, particularly sexualised violence, as a decisive reason for leaving their homes.
The findings illustrate how sexual violence can contribute to an environment of coercion and displacement, alongside other forms of violence and intimidation faced by Palestinian communities.
Children are also among those affected.
In 2025, more than half of 165 Palestinian children aged 12 to 17 who had been detained by Israeli authorities reported witnessing or experiencing sexual violence in detention, including rape threats, forced stripping and genital assault, according to research cited in the BMJ article.
Underreporting and impunity
The scale of documented abuse is compounded by the barriers survivors face in reporting violence and obtaining care.
Fear of reprisals, shame, stigma, and distrust of complaint mechanisms can keep survivors from coming forward. Limited access for independent investigators also limits evidence collection and verification.
“We believe these abuses are greatly underreported for many reasons. Victims frequently refuse to report their injuries out of fear of further abuse and attacks on themselves and their families,” Maynard says.
“It is challenging to document the full extent of sexual violence as Israel has repeatedly refused to allow independent investigators to review what is going on,” he adds.
The accountability record is also troubling.
The UN Commission found that the Israeli civilian and military justice systems had failed to ensure accountability for sexual crimes against Palestinians.
Of 1,260 cases of offences by Israeli soldiers against Palestinians known to the military law enforcement system between 2017 and 2021, only 11 resulted in indictments.
Neve Gordon, professor of human rights and humanitarian law at Queen Mary University of London, said credible allegations required independent investigation, including into those who ordered or enabled the abuse.
Sexual violence can constitute a war crime and, where the legal requirements are met, a crime against humanity.
Establishing criminal responsibility requires investigators to examine individual incidents, preserve evidence and determine the roles of direct perpetrators and those in positions of command.
“The UN needs to be allowed to send in independent teams to investigate such reports of sexual violence and ensure not only that victims of this violence have access to all appropriate specialist medical care but also that perpetrators must be held accountable,” Maynard says.
“Western governments such as the UK government have an obligation under international law to prevent these violations and to make sure international humanitarian law is upheld.”
“These governments must do more to protect Palestinians and must insist on independent monitoring and investigation,” he adds.

Israel’s election may change its leader, but not Iran war policy

- The Iran conflict may deepen. Netanyahu talks of toppling Tehran’s rulers, while analysts warn of a long, risky struggle that could drive Iran towards nuclear deterrence.
AI generated
DUBAI - Israel’s election next week may change its leader, but not its strategy: Iran will remain its chief adversary, military force will continue to be its preferred tool and Palestinian statehood a distant prospect, regional policymakers and analysts say.
That is because the strategic assumptions underpinning Israeli policy were hardened by the Oct 7, 2023, attacks on southern Israeli communities by Palestinian militant group Hamas and by the wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
If anything, Israel could toughen its security policy, the analysts said, as victory for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu with the backing of far-right coalition partners could embolden him to step up the war with Iran, tighten Israel’s grip on the occupied West Bank and push diplomacy further to the margins.
Israel’s security doctrine now rests on three pillars: breaking Iran, holding buffer zones beyond its borders and using force to deter enemies.
The real divide is one of degree rather than direction – how aggressively Israel fights its wars, how far it expands Jewish settlements in the West Bank and whether any leader opts for diplomacy, the analysts said.
From Tehran to Riyadh, the Oct 27 election is not seen as a potential turning point but as a test of whether the Middle East is settling into a long confrontation, where wars ebb and flow while the underlying conflicts are unresolved.
“If Netanyahu is elected, he’ll do whatever he thinks he wants to do,” said Aviv Bushinsky, a former adviser to Netanyahu. “Expansion of the settlements will continue. The wars against Iran, Hamas and Hezbollah will continue.”
“What you see now is what you’ll see after the election, maybe even more aggressively,” he said. “As long as Iran is in such a situation, it’s a waste of time talking about Palestine.”
Netanyahu said on Oct 18 that Israel must prioritise “prevention and offence over containment and defence”, including pre-emptive strikes to thwart emerging threats, while establishing Israel as a regional power and maximising its independence in armaments.
Why the course is unlikely to change
The election pits Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud and its ultra nationalist allies against an opposition led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party.
Palestinian analyst Ghassan al-Khatib sees no prospect of a fundamental shift in policy towards the Palestinians, with Israeli political parties competing to project harder-line positions as public opinion moves further to the right.
“The substance of the policy remains the same: No to a Palestinian state and yes to further settlement expansion. On this, they are all in agreement,” he said.
A government led by Netanyahu’s opponents might seek to repair Israel’s international standing by curbing some settler violence or pursuing settlement expansion with less fanfare.
But such changes would be a shift in style rather than substance, al-Khatib said.
Michael Young of the Carnegie Middle East Center said Israel’s security establishment and much of its political class share a common strategic outlook, centred on confronting Iran, maintaining “forward defence” and preserving military deterrence, reducing the scope for big policy shifts.
Joost Hiltermann of the International Crisis Group, who has conducted research in the West Bank, said growing settler violence, mounting Palestinian frustration and the absence of a “political horizon” had created combustible conditions, where even a minor trigger could spark a wider uprising.
‘Venomous octopus’
Some regional policymakers ask whether Israel’s confrontation with Iran has become the organising principle of Middle East security, regardless of who wins the election.
US President Donald Trump’s praise of Netanyahu as a “great warrior prime minister” has reinforced expectations that the Israeli leader will try to finish the campaign against Tehran if he retains power.
Netanyahu has made clear his ambitions extend beyond containing Iran to toppling its clerical rulers.
“Completing the task means toppling the terrorist regime in Iran, the head of the venomous octopus,” he said in a speech this week.
But military and political analysts question whether anything short of a US-Israeli ground invasion would force Tehran to abandon what it views as its core security interests in what it sees as an existential fight.
After surviving months of war, Iran may be betting it can outlast its opponents while continuing to exert pressure through regional allies.
“This is a quagmire,” Young said. “The Iranians can outlast Trump.”
Hezbollah in Lebanon and Hamas in Gaza have been weakened, but the broader network of Iran-aligned groups has survived and the conflict could strengthen Tehran’s determination to pursue a nuclear deterrent, the analysts said.
For all the alarm Netanyahu causes in the Arab world, some Gulf leaders still see him as the Israeli politician most likely to keep Iran under pressure.
This creates a dilemma for them. They oppose what they view as his expansionist policies but want Iranian influence curbed.
“Netanyahu’s policies in Gaza, the West Bank, Syria and Lebanon are damaging,” said Abdulaziz Sager, chairman of the Gulf Research Centre.
“As for Iran, a settlement is needed before the conflict escalates further. If Iran’s role is not curbed, the region could be heading toward 50 years of Iranian hegemony.” REUTERS

China Focus: China-initiated Luban Workshops empower global youth with practical skills
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:48:57 CST
21:48:57 KST

TIANJIN, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- At an automotive industrial park in north China's Tianjin Municipality, Egyptian students Abdelrahman Ayman Zaky and Adham Ayman are gaining hands-on experience in new energy vehicle (NEV) chassis systems alongside their Chinese peers.
Having acquired vocational skills at an Egyptian Luban Workshop, the two came to China to deepen their expertise. Adham, 20, hopes to improve his Chinese and vehicle maintenance skills before returning to Egypt to pursue a career as an automotive engineer.
Their experience highlights the mission of the China-initiated Luban Workshops, which over the past decade have equipped young people worldwide with useful skills, fostered local talent, and supported industrial development.
Named after Luban, an ancient Chinese craftsman and inventor who lived more than 2,500 years ago, the initiative draws on a longstanding Chinese tradition of craftsmanship and innovation.
Jointly established by Chinese and foreign educational institutions, Luban Workshops now offer vocational education and skills-training programs in 32 countries.
In Egypt, Luban Workshops are helping students like Adham translate classroom learning into engineering capabilities.
Mohamed Mostafa, a student at an Egyptian Luban Workshop now studying at Tianjin Light Industry Vocational Technical College, said hands-on practice has strengthened his ability to tackle real-world engineering challenges.
"In the EPIP (Engineering Practice and Innovation Project) classroom, we don't just work on simulated problems. We work on real-world engineering problems in teams, discussing solutions, refining our techniques and testing them again and again. We break down complex challenges to achieve the best results and meet engineering standards," Mostafa said.
He added that he has shared the approach with students in Egypt, where they have applied the same methods to develop their own projects.
The two Egyptian Luban Workshops have provided formal education to more than 3,100 people and skills training on over 4,000 occasions, creating new opportunities for industrial cooperation.
Wang Baolong, dean of the School of Mechanical Engineering at Tianjin Light Industry Vocational Technical College, said graduates trained in advanced technologies can meet the needs of local businesses, strengthening Chinese companies' confidence in investing in and establishing factories in Egypt while supporting local economic development.
An employment training base jointly established by the Egyptian Luban Workshops and the China-Egypt TEDA Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone has provided young Egyptians with a direct pathway to employment.
"After receiving professional technical training, these young people can operate production equipment proficiently. They are exactly the kind of skilled workers that companies need," Wang added.
Beyond teaching technical skills, the workshops also help build local capacity for sustained vocational training. While setting up training centers and supplying advanced equipment, Chinese partners send teachers and technicians to train local instructors and arrange exchanges and learning opportunities in China.
In 2016, the Tianjin Bohai Vocational Technical College and the Ayutthaya Technical College in Thailand jointly established the world's first Luban Workshop. Over the past decade, all six of the workshop's internationalized majors have been incorporated into Thailand's national education system.
"We are not just cultivating talent for the local area, but leaving the whole system behind. Chinese standards and models are truly integrating into and promoting local development," said Mei Wentao, a staff member at the Tianjin Bohai Vocational Technical College.
More than 100 Chinese companies in Thailand operate businesses ranging from NEV components to vehicle distribution. In August 2025, the China-Thailand automotive intelligent manufacturing industry-education integration community was established in Thailand. With a steady supply of skilled graduates, companies can recruit directly from schools, helping young Thai people find jobs more easily and quickly.
In Central Asia, the Tajik Luban Workshop is helping local young people explore new career opportunities. In nearly four years of operation, it has provided learning and training opportunities to more than 3,600 undergraduate and postgraduate students.
When Bakhtiyor Bozorzoda enrolled at the Tajik Technical University, he was uncertain about his chosen major in geodesy and cartography. Advanced surveying equipment, digital mapping technologies, and virtual simulation courses at the Tajik Luban Workshop helped him recognize the field's potential and develop a stronger interest in surveying.
During his studies, Bozorzoda gained hands-on experience with high-precision instruments and digital mapping technologies.
"I hope to continue my studies in China in the future, learn more advanced surveying technologies and contribute to infrastructure development in Tajikistan," he said.
Today, Luban Workshops have become a hallmark of China's international vocational education cooperation. Data from China's Ministry of Education show that the country has established 38 Luban Workshops in 32 countries, providing formal education to more than 30,000 students and non-degree training to over 160,000 people.
The Luban Workshops reflect a commitment to harmony, coexistence and the common good in Chinese cultural tradition. By responding to local needs, they help young people in different countries acquire skills that can benefit them throughout their careers, said Tian Xuejun, president of the China Education Association for International Exchange, at the 2026 World Vocational and Technical Education Development Conference, held in Tianjin from Oct. 15 to 17.
China has the world's largest vocational education system, with 9,151 secondary vocational schools, 1,554 higher vocational colleges and 124 vocational undergraduate institutions.
As of the end of 2025, China's vocational education catalog covered 19 major categories, 97 subcategories and 1,491 majors, spanning virtually all sectors of the national economy and all 41 major industrial categories.
China is continuing to strengthen its vocational education system to support the development of emerging industries and expand opportunities for people both at home and abroad. At the 2026 World Vocational and Technical Education Development Conference, representatives from 45 countries jointly released the Framework of World Vocational and Technical Education Standards developed under China's leadership.
The framework calls for improving vocational school systems, establishing lifelong education and training opportunities for all, developing teaching materials through industry-education collaboration, building teaching teams through school-enterprise partnerships, and using artificial intelligence to drive reform in education and teaching. ■

====================================================================================================

Ruined by NATO, divided without Gaddafi: Can Libya’s new deal hold?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:48:31 UTC
21:48:31 KST

Ruined by NATO, divided without Gaddafi: Can Libya’s new deal hold?
The long-awaited agreement between Libya’s rival factions was finally signed on August 30 under the auspices of the United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL). On that day, the mission gathered the two negotiating delegations at its Tripoli headquarters to formalize the text ironed out during earlier rounds of talks in Rome and Tunis. UNSMIL invited foreign diplomats, media representatives, and Libyan delegations to the event, where UN Special Representative Hanna Tetteh hailed the accord in her opening remarks as “another important milestone in Libya’s journey toward stability and national unity.”
This, however, bore a resemblance to previous diplomatic milestones – most notably the 2015 Libyan Political Agreement (LPA) signed in Skhirat, Morocco. The LPA established the rules of the political game in the fractured country; rules to which none of the domestic political actors seem fully committed, yet from which none completely depart. In a sense, Skhirat remains the ultimate reference point for every subsequent UN roadmap in Libya.
In the vacuum left by the 2011 NATO intervention and the brutal murder of Muammar Gaddafi, Libya has seen a continuous parade of diplomatic accords. Yet the fundamental problem has never been a shortage of roadmaps, but rather their consolidation into nationally accepted political facts that elites cannot simply manipulate at will.
The August 30 agreement has two main parts. The first is restructuring the High National Elections Commission (HNEC), the agency in charge of organizing elections. In practice, this means replacing its leadership to settle disputes over appointments and regional representation. Although these changes were long delayed by regional quotas and political patronage stemming from the 2015 Skhirat agreement, rivals can still negotiate them with relative ease.
The 24-month timeline to hold elections was also established. However, the countdown is designed to govern the transition only once a single, unified executive authority and unified national institutions are established to oversee the voting process.
The second component concerns the central objective of UNSMIL’s latest roadmap: agreeing on viable election laws, an issue on which the UN has failed to make meaningful progress since the collapse of the planned 2021 elections.
Libya remains divided between rival power centers: the Government of National Unity (GNU), led by Abdul Hamid Dbeibah in Tripoli, the western part of the country, and the Libyan National Army (LNA) command in the east led by General Khalifa Haftar. These exist alongside two political institutions: the Tripoli-based High Council of state (HCS) and the eastern-based House of Representatives (HoR). To break the deadlock, UNSMIL established a smaller negotiating group known as the ‘Smaller Convening’, or the ‘4+4’. It brings together eight representatives from the GNU, Haftar’s military command, the HCS, and the HoR.
This mechanism directly mirrors the ill-fated 2021 Geneva process, Libyan Political Dialogue Framework, which ultimately hardened Libya’s institutional divide and brought the country closer to a permanent de facto partition than at any point since its formal unification in 1951. The UN Security Council issued a delayed presidential statement endorsing the deal, and thus repeating a familiar ritual that seems to elevates elite compromise over structural reform. Seeking to seize the political initiative, Speaker Aguila Saleh brought the 4+4 framework to the HoR floor for an immediate vote where it was approved by the majority of members.
The ‘4+4’ format developed alongside (and ultimately eclipsed) UNSMIL’s broader Structured Dialogue. Even before those conclusions were finalized, UNSMIL was already facilitating a parallel ‘Smaller Convening’ behind closed doors – the 4+4 was born. As Hanna Tetteh told the Security Council on June 18, the explicit goal of this smaller format was to bypass the paralysis between the legislative bodies and force an accord on the roadmap’s first two steps: reconstituting the elections commission’s board and resolving the contested electoral framework. Thus, the ‘4+4’ was a deliberate strategy to concentrate decision-making among the political and military figures deemed capable of enforcing an outcome.
After the HoR approved the agreement on September 14, the HCS formally rejected it on October 5, along with the related laws and decisions issued by the House, arguing that they bypassed the constitutional, legal and consensual frameworks governing the political process. In her October 14 briefing to the UN Security Council, Tetteh acknowledged this rejection but maintained that the agreement offers an actionable path to presidential and legislative elections under a single, unified executive authority within 24 months.
She also announced that UNSMIL would meet members of the 4+4 committee later this month to examine the possibility of establishing a broadly representative national mechanism under Article 5 of the agreement in consultation with the Security Council. This proposal implicitly acknowledges that the 4+4 mini-dialogue alone may not be sufficient to advance the roadmap.
Another significant development is the removal of Aguila Saleh as speaker of the HoR after 12 years in office. On October 7, the eastern-based parliament elected Al-Salhin Abdulnabi as his successor, ending Saleh’s long tenure amid growing discontent over his leadership. The change is particularly significant because Saleh had been accused of being a prominent obstacle to previous attempts to move Libya’s political process forward. Tetteh acknowledged the transition, expressing her appreciation to Saleh for “his leadership and engagement over his 12-year tenure of service.” Her emphasis on the change in parliamentary leadership is noteworthy: The departure of a figure long associated with resistance to political roadmaps could create new room for maneuver, although it does not by itself guarantee that the House will cooperate with the UN initiative or that the entrenched political divisions will be overcome.
Ultimately, the structural core of the August 30 agreement rests on a fundamental contradiction: 4+4 does not equal 1. Combining four delegates from Tripoli’s political-institutional structures, including representatives of the HCS, with four delegates representing the eastern power structure in Benghazi does not produce a unified state. Instead, it seems to function as a shared enterprise in which rival political elites, rather than competing to build a single nation, recognize that their mutual survival depends on dividing power and maintaining exclusive control over the state apparatus.
Setting a 24-month timetable neither offers a guarantee that elections will actually occur; instead, it grants entrenched factions another two years of status quo protection without imposing any penalty for non-compliance.
Still, the UN Security Council appeared to endorse the latest UNSMIL plan. Following Tetteh’s briefing on October 14, the Council reaffirmed its support for the agreement, despite concerns over its implementation and the High Council of State’s rejection.
By prioritizing elite consensus over an enforceable constitutional baseline, the international community risks continuing to repeat a flawed equation. Until UNSMIL and foreign powers break this cycle and align their strategy with the Libyan public’s demand for genuine democratic renewal, every new agreement risks becoming another monument to the status quo. In the end, the ‘4+4’ framework offers no viable fallback or alternative path forward if it fails.
Last week, the UNSC did not vote to extend UNSMIL’s mandate, which expires on October 31. However, this is largely a technicality, since the Council has already approved UNSMIL’s roadmap.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

Across China: East China's Liangzhu offers Chinese wisdom for sustainable tourism
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:48:22 CST
21:48:22 KST

HANGZHOU, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- A silver self-driving shuttle glided past golden rice fields on the outskirts of Hangzhou in east China's Zhejiang Province, linking several cultural landmarks, including the Liangzhu ruins, where an early regional state flourished over five millennia ago.
This route, launched earlier this month, points to a question facing many World Heritage sites: how to protect fragile ruins without turning them into isolated monuments, and how to let surrounding communities share in their value without putting the heritage at risk.
This year marks 90 years since the Liangzhu ruins were first discovered. From Oct. 18 to 20, the fourth Liangzhu Forum brought together officials, archaeologists and scholars from about 60 countries and regions in Hangzhou to discuss issues including advances in technologies for protecting and utilizing cultural relics and sustainable tourism.
"UNESCO believes that sustainable tourism can help safeguard cultural heritage by raising awareness of the importance of heritage for future generations, improving cultural understanding and strengthening local livelihoods," said Nayef Al-Fayez, UNESCO assistant director-general for culture, in his video speech.
"Liangzhu was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2019. Much of Liangzhu's ancient city layout and its water conservancy system lie beneath the surface, so non-specialist visitors may easily miss what makes the site remarkable," said Wang Shu, director of the Hangzhou Liangzhu Archaeological Site Administrative District Management Committee.
"If the public cannot see or understand it, the social value of the heritage cannot be fully realized. Our focus is on how to translate archaeological evidence into cultural experiences that the public can understand, participate in and share," Wang added.
Technology is helping make such translation possible. At the Liangzhu Museum, visitors can put on augmented reality glasses and watch a virtual exhibit appear to float out of its display case, revealing intricate carvings from every angle without touching the original.
In the virtual reality experience at the ruins, tourists can drift through ancient waterways on a bamboo raft, stand atop the palace to take in the city's grand layout, or walk into a virtual altar to witness a sacred ceremony firsthand.
"Just as tourism needs heritage, heritage also needs tourism," said Michael David Robinson, vice chair and non-executive director for culture, UK National Commission for UNESCO, adding that management plans and clear rules are needed to prevent excessive damage. "You have to ensure that the tourists understand how sensitive some of the archaeology is."
At many sites, conservation has focused on the ruins themselves and the museums built to tell their stories, while development in surrounding areas has followed a separate course. Residents may live alongside extraordinary cultural heritage yet have few opportunities to benefit from it.
Liangzhu's efforts have offered a window into China's practice regarding this global issue.
That effort now stretches across a 634-square-kilometer cultural corridor linking the Liangzhu ruins with the nearby Grand Canal, the world's oldest artificial waterway system and a UNESCO World Heritage Site inscribed in 2014, and with surrounding hills, waterways, woodlands and cultural institutions.
"Archaeology shows that over 5,000 years ago, Liangzhu was an early thriving regional state. Today, the same land is still buzzing with innovation and entrepreneurship," Wang said. "Liangzhu is using a corridor-style development approach to strike a balance between protection and growth."
"We have been trying to bring rural communities, urban centers and industry together to let culture benefit people," said Yao Huimin, deputy director of the Liangzhu Museum.
Driven by Liangzhu's cultural resources, the corridor has gathered more than 1,000 cultural enterprises above the designated size. In the first half of 2026, it added 50 such enterprises, with combined revenue exceeding 89.1 billion yuan (around 13.26 billion U.S. dollars), up 37 percent year on year.
Rather than simply restricting construction, Liangzhu has sought ways to turn protection into opportunity for its villages, which are home to residents who have lived on the heritage belt for generations.
In Xin'gang Village, idle land left by the closure of six furniture and brick factories in 2016 was transformed into a standard football pitch. This field quickly drew city dwellers to the countryside, hosting 12 corporate league matches in its first year.
This single move set off a chain reaction. Xin'gang has since built more sports venues, becoming a sports hub on Hangzhou's outskirts. The model is spreading across villages in Liangzhu, with softball, rugby, archery, tennis and pickleball centers now in use.
Raphael Callou Neves Barros, director general for culture, Organization of Ibero-American States, emphasized the need for continuous dialogue with local communities and to ensure tourism does not undermine the sustainability of culture and heritage.
The deeper value of sustainable tourism lies in what visitors take away and what they leave behind, Barros added. They take away not just a sightseeing experience, but an understanding of a civilization. And they leave behind not only short-term consumption, but a positive force supporting heritage protection, community development and the continuation of local culture.
"Heritage conservation does not end at the fence. Its true destination is people's hearts," said Liu Jiecheng, deputy director of Peking University's Institute for Cultural Innovation. ■

Nvidia announces plug and play Vera Rubin racks that can be shipped on a truck
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:43:49 UTC
21:43:49 KST

Nvidia announced Wednesday a new product that will put seven of its Vera Rubin AI racks into a shipping container, the company's latest effort to move up the stack and offer complete systems for artificial intelligence computing.
The DSX Pod AI Factory is roughly the size of a standard shipping container and weighs about 28,000 kilograms (nearly 62,000 pounds), Nvidia said. It's designed to be shipped on a truck on normal roads and all the cabling and liquid cooling for the Pod are assembled at the factory, the company said.
"The only thing that has to happen when it gets to the site is it's placed in its location, connected to the rest of the other containers, and validated through final burning and testing," Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale computing at Nvidia, said on a call with reporters this week.
The DSX Pod AI factory will reduce the time for a new AI data center to start serving tokens from six months to 14 days, according to the company. Nvidia said the pod is intended for customers worldwide and could help address deployment challenges faced by European customers.
Nvidia did not announce a price for the system, but analysts say a single Vera Rubin rack can cost more than $7 million.
The DSX Pod is a reference design that will ship from Nvidia's manufacturing partners. Nvidia said it was working with manufacturers including Foxconn, Gigabyte, Lenovo, HPE, Quanta and Pegatron. Nvidia expects deliveries to start in early 2027.
Nvidia, once a chip company, now offers networking, storage and other data center needs to its customers. Its AI systems have evolved from single graphics processing unit chips to servers with four or eight GPUs, then to entire racks and now to the DSX Pod, a containerized building block with several racks already integrated.
"What we offer into one gigawatt went from about $18 billion or so per gigawatt, to $20-something billion per gigawatt, to now $40-plus billion per gigawatt," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said recently on a podcast. Gigawatts refer to the size of data center infrastructure by how much power is used. "My sense is that's going to keep going up."

See one of the most iconic meteor showers at its peak this week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:43:17 UTC
21:43:17 KST

Bright flashes of shooting stars are set to streak across the night sky this week as the Orionids meteor shower hits its peak—and if you’re lucky (and patient), you could spot dozens of these meteors.
NASA estimates stargazers might see three to six meteors per hour in suburban areas, with even more shooting stars likely to be seen in rural areas with less light pollution. Night owls can rejoice: the “prime viewing window” will occur after the moon sets around 3 A.M. over the nights of October 21 and October 22, NASA says.
The Orionids’ shooting stars are particularly fast and bright. They travel at around 41 miles per second, and the fastest ones can leave fiery trails of debris in their wake or even ignite into fireballs.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Meteor showers are the beautiful remains of debris trailing from comets and asteroids. As that debris hits our atmosphere, it burns up, creating the light shows we know as meteor showers and love to view. The Orionids gets their name from the constellation Orion because the shower seems to flow from that direction, but that’s not their true origin. These meteors were once part of Halley’s Comet.
The comet sheds rock, dust and ice as it shoots through the solar system. This iconic space rock is visible from Earth once every 75 to 76 years or so—it is famous for its brightness, appearing in historical records stretching back for millennia. Although we won’t see Halley’s again until 2061, the Orionids offer a glimpse of its leftovers.
If you can’t catch the Orionids, look out for a spooky full moon that’s traditionally called the “hunter’s moon” next week, on October 26. Plus, the Taurid meteor showers, which have been shooting across the sky since September, are set to peak next month: you can catch the Southern Taurids’ peak on November 4–5 and the Northern Taurids’ peak on November 11–12.

France Protests: How Fuel Prices, Student Anger are Driving Riots and Unrest
