France Protests: How Fuel Prices, Student Anger are Driving Riots and Unrest

====================================================================================================

Why Europe's student protests signal a deeper education crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:40:03 UTC
21:40:03 KST

A wave of youth-led protests has swept across Europe, from France and Belgium to Spain, Portugal, Germany, Italy, Albania, and Greece, reflecting growing frustration among young people who feel the political establishment is increasingly ignoring their educational needs.
The protest in France began at the Saint-Exupéry high school in a Paris suburb before spreading to schools across the country.
French high school students and their peers across Europe have demanded better educational facilities, more teachers, smaller classes and adequate funding and learning resources.
While university students, trade unions, and other parts of French society have backed the protests and consider the demands legitimate, the demonstrations have also been marked by looting and violence, prompting President Emmanuel Macron to call on security forces to restore “calm and order”.
Emmanuel Dupuy, a French political scientist at the Catholic University of Lille, which has also witnessed these protests, says there is "a big difference" between earlier student protests and the violence that erupted over the weekend, when more than 3,000 stores were damaged or looted across France.
Videos also showed Limoges' historic town hall in flames.
While Dupuy describes the latest violent protests as riots, he sees student protests, from high schools to universities, as driven by legitimate demands over poor school conditions, from infrastructure to teacher shortages, and growing concerns about whether their education will help them secure jobs.
"The same sort of resentment" has become a powerful trend not only in France but also among young people in other European countries, the French professor tells TRT World
Beyond France, massive student protests erupted in Italy, with more than 400,000 people participating over the weekend, while similar protests against education budget cuts turned violent in Belgium.
“France reflects a wider European challenge affecting students, teachers and families,” Riyad Rogiest, a Ghent-based Belgian teacher, tells TRT World, referring to a growing education crisis across Europe.
This challenge is “particularly visible in schools serving socially disadvantaged communities”, where problems often accumulate, he adds.
“The anger we see in France is not simply about education budgets. It is also about young people who feel increasingly abandoned by the system.”
Education ‘falls victim’ to economics
Under Macron, a former Rothschild investment banker, the government has cut public spending, reduced corporate taxes and employer social contributions, and replaced the wealth tax with a narrower levy on property assets.
But France continues to face sluggish economic growth and mounting public debt, which reached 119.1 percent of GDP in the second quarter of 2026.
From the COVID-19 crisis to recent US-Europe tensions over NATO defence spending and ongoing escalations in the Strait of Hormuz, which have driven up energy prices, successive crises have put additional pressure on public finances, raising questions about governments' spending priorities, including investment in education.
These policies “have had some consequences and education is one of their victims,” Dupuy tells TRT World, referring to education spending cuts.
He says the current Macron government has not sufficiently considered the need to invest in education.
Dupuy also believes that the French education crisis extends beyond Macron’s governments.
“We haven't sufficiently invested in education over the last 20 years, and we're paying the price for that,” he says. “It has collapsed and is in very poor shape.”
While France and many developed European countries have long been admired by non-Western populations for their educational, economic and political standards, the current protests have shocked many international observers.
This international perception no longer reflects the realities on the ground in Europe, as "a sort of dream land" for non-European education "no longer exists in our countries," says Dupuy.
He also points to how the rise of AI has contributed to the decline of French education.
"New specialities like artificial intelligence are more linked to human resources, or management, which has never been a sort of French excellency," he says, noting that France has traditionally excelled in law and other social sciences.
Like France, other European countries also suffer from "the same reasons of shifting priorities" from education to sectors such as health, defence and AI, Dupuy adds.
"We didn't understand how low our investment was in education. But the situation is now so dire that there was an obligation to improve conditions for the sake of the new generation," he says.
‘Teachers are overwhelmed’
Among other measures, France's draft 2027 budget, which proposes eliminating 1,588 teaching posts in a country already facing overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages, has drawn criticism from teachers' unions amid growing student unrest.
In 2019, Macron's proposed pension reforms sparked widespread protests, adding to public anger after the Yellow Vest movement began in 2018 over fuel tax increases.
Despite continued opposition, Macron's government enacted a new pension reform in 2023, gradually raising the retirement age from 62 to 64, although the timetable was subsequently suspended until 2028.
But Macron’s position has been significantly weakened in recent years, as his decision to call snap elections in 2024 led to a divided parliament and further weakened his centrist allies. Since then, France has seen repeated changes of prime minister, with successive governments struggling to secure parliamentary support.
Amid growing protests, Education Minister Édouard Geffray announced plans to deploy 3,000 substitute teachers to schools facing shortages, a measure backed by Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu.
But experts say this may not resolve the structural problems facing education systems in France and other European countries.
“We are facing a serious teacher shortage, while the teaching profession is becoming less attractive. Teachers are increasingly expected to be educators, psychologists, social workers, mediators and administrators simultaneously. Many experience exhaustion or burnout,” Rogiest says.
On the other hand, many young people carry frustrations from home into the classroom, as financial difficulties, family conflicts, parental separation, social media and a lack of emotional support deeply affect their behaviour and motivation, he adds.
These behavioural problems require additional meetings, administrative reports, and constant follow-up, leaving less time for teaching and personal interaction with students.
In Belgium, for example, new rules introduced in September 2026 require secondary schools, in principle, to organise supervision or alternative activities when lessons are cancelled.
Although limited exceptions exist, Rogiest says this creates additional organisational pressure on teachers.
He also notes that the current digital age makes his job difficult in certain ways, as students are increasingly influenced by social media and constant digital stimulation, which creates unrealistic teaching expectations.
“We expect teachers to solve society's problems inside the classroom, while giving them fewer resources and less time to build relationships with their students,” he says.
“This is neither fair to teachers nor beneficial to children.”
Future of European education
Europe has been facing not only rising inflation, which has increased the cost of living, but also growing political divisions between left-wing and far-right groups, both of which accuse mainstream politics of social and economic problems.
While worsening economic conditions hit classrooms, leading to various cuts in the educational sector, political divisions do not help countries meet the new generation’s demands, exposing deep social insecurity in the new digital age.
“European education has many strengths, but I am deeply concerned about its increasing focus on economic productivity rather than human development,” Rogiest says.
“Historically, we spoke about the humaniora: an educational tradition that sought to develop the whole human being, intellectually, morally, culturally and socially.”
But today, education is increasingly reduced to obtaining qualifications, entering the labour market, becoming economically productive, and paying taxes, he adds.
While earning a decent salary is important for a decent life, education must be much more than professional training, according to Rogiest.
“We should not only ask what profession our students will have, but what kind of human beings they will become.”
From this perspective, Rogiest says the future of European education depends on restoring its human dimension.
“We need smaller classes, better support for teachers, more investment in mental health and stronger cooperation between schools and families.”
While digital education and artificial intelligence offer enormous opportunities, young people “need guidance in developing concentration, discipline, empathy, responsibility and critical thinking,” he says.
Without these fundamental skills, modern technologies will help students little, he adds. This also requires restoring the dignity and attractiveness of the teaching profession.
“Education should not simply produce skilled workers for the economy,” Rogiest tells TRT World.
“It should develop responsible, compassionate and thoughtful human beings who can contribute positively to society. That is the educational vision Europe needs to rediscover.”

Afghanistan’s Wakhan Transit Road Is a Long Shot to Connect with China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:40:00 UTC
21:40:00 KST

On October 4, Taliban officials inaugurated the 121-kilometer-long Wakhan Transit Road connecting Afghanistan to China via the Wakhan Corridor after approximately three years of construction work. The road stretches from Afghanistan’s Broghil border area, on the Afghanistan-Pakistan border, along Badakhshan province’s Wakhan district, finally reaching the border with China. According to Afghanistan’s de facto government under the Taliban, beyond China, the road will connect the country with third parties like Central Asian countries and global markets.
This corridor is expected to play a significant role for Afghanistan’s trade as well as its regional transit. Its opening marks an important milestone for the Taliban since the corridor was ignored for years due to security concerns.
A remote region in northeast Afghanistan, the Wakhan Corridor is 350 kilometers long and 13 to 65 km wide. The corridor, which shares borders with Pakistan (through the Durand Line, which the Taliban has started referring to as a “hypothetical” line), Tajikistan, and China, was created as a buffer zone between the Russian and British empires in 1895-96 when the Anglo-Russian Boundary Commission awarded the area to Afghanistan. Once a part of the famous Silk Road trade route, the Wakhan Corridor has been closed for regular transit for almost a century now.
Taliban Minister of Rural Rehabilitation and Development Abdul Latif Mansour, speaking at the inauguration ceremony, said that the road held “political, economic, and strategic significance” for Afghanistan. “The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan has prioritized such public projects, especially in provinces that are most in need,” Mansour said, according to Tolo News. He further emphasized the homegrown nature of the project, saying, “There are no foreign engineers or advisers; all the engineers are Afghans.”
Governor of Badakhshan Rahmatullah Najib highlighted the road’s opening as a milestone. “After 45 years of war in the country, the Afghan people are witnessing the completion of such a major project in one of Afghanistan’s most remote areas,” Tolo News paraphrased Najib as saying.
This project is said to have cost 365 million Afghanis ($5.6 million) and was funded by the Taliban’s Ministry of Rural Rehabilitation and Development.
According to Afghanistan’s Deputy Prime Minister for Economic Affairs’ website, this trade route will benefit Afghanistan by providing direct access to imports from and exports to China. The minister highlighted that China is Afghanistan’s largest trading partner, with annual trade exceeding $1 billion between the two countries. The website claimed that the Wakhan Corridor is now the “closest, safest, and most reliable” route for China to export its goods not only to Afghanistan, but to the Central Asian countries, and beyond: to the Arab world, Turkiye, Iran, and the European countries.
That assumption is questionable; China has direct borders with three Central Asian countries – Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan – and has invested millions in upgrading its trade and transit infrastructure to the region. China already has well-developed rail links with Kazakhstan. The Khorgos Gateway, which opened for operations in 2012 on the China-Kazakhstan border, is the world’s largest dry port. And construction on the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan (CKU) railway is underway. It’s unclear why China would choose to route exports to Central Asia via Afghanistan.
The benefits for Afghanistan are more obvious. Due to the ongoing conflict between Afghanistan and Pakistan, trade across their border has come to a halt. That cuts off landlocked Afghanistan’s primary trade and transit route for reaching third countries. If the Wakhan Corridor route becomes fully operational, it will provide an alternative route for Afghanistan to trade with the regional countries, particularly with China. Afghanistan could then connect directly with China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), rather than linking itself to the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) as previously discussed.
In 2016, Afghanistan – then under the Republic government – and China signed a memorandum of understanding to integrate Afghanistan into the BRI. The following year in December, foreign ministers from Afghanistan, China, and Pakistan agreed to discuss ways to extend the CPEC to Afghanistan. In 2023, Afghanistan – now ruled by the Taliban – again reiterated its intention to join CPEC. This was also discussed during last year’s trilateral foreign ministers’ dialogue in Kabul. However, there has been no further progress in this regard due to the ongoing conflict between Pakistan and Afghanistan.
The Taliban government views the new road via the Wakhan Corridor as an opportunity to lessen Pakistan’s leverage. Islamabad has a history of closing the border crossings between the countries, affecting trade and inflicting heavy losses on Afghanistan’s economy. Thus, the de facto regime is jubilant with the inauguration of the Wakhan transit road.
As per Afghanistan’s Deputy Minister for Economic Affairs’ website, “With the opening of the Wakhan Corridor, Afghanistan will be forever freed from the pressure of neighboring countries, which often exploit the Karachi route, Gwadar Port, and Chabahar for political purposes and cause heavy financial losses to our traders and compatriots every year.”
Even though the inauguration of the route is expected to alleviate the transportation challenges for the residents of Pamir and Wakhan, its role as a trans-regional route, or even just connecting Afghanistan to China, seems to be a distant dream.
Despite the Taliban regime’s completion of the road, China still has not opened its border with Afghanistan, arguably due to security concerns vis-à-vis the crossing. Moreover, China neither sent its representative to the inaugural ceremony on October 4, nor did it acknowledge the road’s completion diplomatically.
China built the road that the Taliban’s Wakhan transit road aimed to link up with over a decade ago. The goal wasn’t to increase trade, but to secure its militarized border with Afghanistan by advancing access for its armed patrols. The Taliban refer to the transit route as a trading link to gain access to Chinese markets; Chinese media refers to this approximately 76-kilometer-long border as a “major counterterrorism front line.” This media framing aligns with Chinese officials’ narrative that Uyghurs in the region have frequently visited the corridor in order to “return to Xinjiang for Jihad.”
China’s major security concern in Afghanistan is the potential threat from the members of the East Turkestan Islamic Movement (ETIM), a group that seeks self-determination for the Uyghurs and independence of Xinjiang province from the Chinese government.
According to some estimates, there are over 3,000 Uyghurs living in Afghanistan. China has asked the Taliban to ensure that Uyghur separatists would not be allowed to use Afghan soil as a base for their activities in Xinjiang. Besides this, China wants the Taliban to extradite Uyghurs affiliated with ETIM to China.
China’s lukewarm reaction to the Taliban’s completion of the Wakhan transit route emanates mainly from its security concerns. Until the Taliban completely secure the route and convince Beijing that it will not be used as a route by ETIM members to infiltrate Xinjiang, the use of the Wakhan Corridor as a trade route between the two countries will remain a distant dream.

Hong Kong to tighten media access to land records, triggering concerns
Some legislators also urge government to explain details and streamline applications to support investigative reporting
Hong Kong lawmakers and the media industry have raised concerns about the authorities’ plan to tighten arrangements for journalists searching land records, with some legislators urging the government to explain operational details and streamline the application to support investigative reporting.
The Hong Kong Journalists Association voiced objections on Wednesday, after the government tabled eight pieces of subsidiary legislation, including the Land Titles Regulation that covers land record search arrangements, at the Legislative Council for negative vetting.
Negative vetting involves enacting the law first and scrutinising it later. Most provisions, including the tightened search arrangements, will take effect in the first half of next year.
The association said authorities had not justified the changes and had not consulted the public beforehand, stressing that the arrangements would weaken the public’s power to monitor the property market.

As the Kremlin Seizes Control of European Companies, U.S. Rivals Remain Largely Spared
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:20:32 UTC
21:20:32 KST

Russia has deepened a crackdown on European companies in response to Europe's support for Ukraine, while largely sparing U.S. firms as Moscow courts business ties with Washington, Russian officials and U.S. businesspeople said.
Of the 20 foreign-owned firms President Vladimir Putin has placed under temporary administration since U.S. President Donald Trump's inauguration in January 2025, only three were linked to the United States, with the rest controlled by European companies, a Reuters analysis of official data shows.
A person close to Russian financial regulators said that it is not in Moscow's interest to take a tough line on American companies while business negotiations with Washington are underway.
U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff met with Putin in St. Petersburg on Wednesday for talks aimed at resolving the war in Ukraine. Russian news agencies reported that Putin told Witkoff he was interested in restoring economic ties with the United States.
Ukraine and its allies have voiced concerns that the U.S. is backing away from its support of Kyiv, and Trump has criticized Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries even as European leaders have lined up behind Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Russia, citing Europe's wartime support for Ukraine and involvement in "direct battlefield hostilities," has taken control of the local units of Swiss food group Nestle and retailers Auchan and Metro since last month.
Last week, the Kremlin seized control of the local assets of four smaller companies from France, Germany, Sweden and Belgium.
"Their country of origin was one of the factors taken into account in making the decision," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, adding that these countries were involved in "illegal expropriations of Russian property."
Nestle, which said in September it would take steps to protect its rights in Russia, declined to comment further. The other companies did not respond to requests for comment.
A spokesperson for Switzerland's State Secretariat for Economic Affairs said that the available information supported the perception that more European than U.S. firms were being targeted.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment. Commenting on the report after its publication, the Kremlin said that U.S. companies were better treated than their European rivals because of Trump's efforts to achieve peace in Ukraine.
"The American administration is doing a lot to help bring about a peaceful settlement. The European capitals are doing nothing to help while doing a lot to prolong the military action," Peskov told reporters.
Russia's relations with the Trump administration, meanwhile, have warmed. The U.S. announced a deal this month to buy Russian diesel, and other deals, including those on gas, have been discussed at meetings in recent months.
Trump also signed an executive order on Saturday waiving key sanctions and tariffs on Russian goods.
Russian negotiator Kirill Dmitriev, a U.S.-educated investment banker who heads the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) and has pushed in talks for the return and expansion of American firms, hailed the move as a "historic moment."
Trump's envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner have used the prospect of multibillion-dollar deals with Russia as an incentive to push Putin toward a peaceful settlement since the start of peace talks in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, in February 2025.
Dmitriev said last week that Russia and the U.S. would soon announce new joint initiatives that could move ahead before the war ends. The U.S. has previously signaled that deals are unlikely while the conflict continues.
One person familiar with the situation said that some Russian officials who do not support peace efforts could still push for the Kremlin to seize more American firms.
The RDIF's only current partnership with a U.S. company is a joint investment with New York-listed Titan International in a tire factory in Volgograd.
Another person familiar with the situation said Dmitriev has in private highlighted this as an example of a thriving U.S. business in Russia.
Titan did not respond to a request for comment.
Trump's commitment to economic cooperation with Russia and ongoing talks have helped protect the interests of American companies, two U.S. businesspeople in Moscow said.
American Chamber of Commerce Russia President Robert Agee said in December last year that European firms in Russia were less optimistic than American ones, citing European foreign policy. The chamber estimates there are around 300 U.S. firms remaining in Russia.
"We have Trump, and they don't, and our hopes are linked to him," Agee told Russian media last year. Agee and the chamber declined to comment further for this story.
Russia did target some mid-sized U.S. firms during its property redistribution drive after the start of the war. One report estimated that the Kremlin seized more than $50 billion worth of private property from both Russian and foreign owners.
The European Commission in Brussels declined to comment on the number of EU firms being targeted relative to U.S. ones, but said the recent asset seizures were without due process and amounted to "forced expropriation in all but name."
"This follows a clear pattern of economic retaliation," a Commission spokesperson told Reuters, adding that the moves showed "Russia is not a safe environment for business."
"The EU has measures in place to respond. We can sanction those profiting from forced expropriations," the spokesperson added.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Texas’ University of St. Thomas Professor Yeh Yao-yuan (葉耀元) warned Thursday that China is interfering in elections to deepen political divisions and undermine public trust in democracy, CNA reported.
Speaking at a National Taiwan University Hospital forum on election interference and democratic defense, Yeh said Beijing's main goal was not necessarily to help particular candidates win or lose elections. Instead, he said, China seeks to turn voters against one another and undermine confidence in democracy.
Yeh said China uses disinformation and online influence campaigns to reinforce existing political divisions. He warned that growing distrust could deepen disagreements over national defense and relations with China, leaving Taiwan more vulnerable to outside pressure.
China's interference should not be judged solely by election results, the professor said. The greater concern, Yeh said, is whether people with different political views become increasingly unwilling to accept one another.
The National Security Bureau has also warned of growing Chinese information campaigns ahead of the Nov. 28 local elections. The bureau said that it identified about 2.5 million items of contentious online content from January to September, up from 1.69 million during the same period last year, per Liberty Times.
China uses fake accounts, AI-generated videos, and coordinated online campaigns to spread misleading information, the bureau said. Social media and online forums were among the main platforms used for such activity.
Tsai Ming-yen (蔡明彥), the bureau's director-general, said that Chinese election interference was becoming more targeted. He identified six methods, namely illegal campaign funding, subsidized trips to China, discounted flights, disinformation, illegal betting, and cyberattacks, per SETN.
Yeh called for a foreign agents law to address activities carried out on behalf of foreign governments. He said stronger legal measures were needed to protect Taiwan's democracy from outside interference.
Hung Pu-chao (洪浦釗), director of the University of Taipei's Center for Global Strategy and Democratic Resilience, warned that China could step up election interference. He said Beijing would use the results to assess its efforts to influence Taiwan ahead of the Chinese Communist Party's 21st National Congress in 2027, per CTS News.
Hung said Greater Taipei could be major targets because of their political importance and competitive elections. The director warned that foreign funding and local networks could also be used to influence election campaigns.
He urged national security, law enforcement, and election agencies to share more intelligence and investigate suspicious foreign funding and coordinated online campaigns. Hung also called for tougher penalties to ensure elections are decided by voters.

Macron targets Trump over French riots
French President Emmanuel Macron has slammed as “stupid” and “unacceptable” remarks by foreign leaders about the unrest gripping France, in an apparent swipe at US President Donald Trump, who blamed the violence on Paris’ lax border policies.
France has been rocked by some of its worst riots in years, sparked last month by teacher shortages and crumbling schools before escalating into nationwide protests over inequality, soaring living costs and public service cuts.
Hundreds of thousands took to the streets over the weekend as demonstrations descended into clashes with police, arson and looting. Nearly 2,400 people were arrested, around 1,000 officers injured, hundreds of businesses looted and buildings torched, with damage estimated at “hundreds of millions of euros.”
Trump pours fuel on the fire
Trump claimed that “migrants, jihadists, and communists” had “conquered, looted, and burned” France, accusing Macron of failing to secure its borders. He urged European leaders to “close their borders,” before seizing on the unrest to rally Republicans ahead of the November 3 midterms, warning that scenes of “burning steeples and raging fires” were “what the Radical Dumocrats want to do to AMERICA” with their own migration agenda.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Macron accused outside actors of manipulating information about the events to their gain.
“There was foreign manipulation of information, which gave rise to unacceptable and stupid comments from many people, including foreign leaders,” he said. “We have had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false… These people annoy me.”

Russia, the usual suspect

However, yet again, she presented no evidence connecting either country to the crisis.
Moscow says look closer to home

Responding to Rama’s accusations, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told him to look closer to home.
“These are citizens of your own country who took to the streets to protest. Don’t shift your responsibility onto others. Deal with your own domestic problems,” she said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, meanwhile, described the unrest sweeping the EU as evidence of “a major crisis… bordering on chaos.”

Death Just Got Out of This Truck (guest post)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:36:06 UTC
21:36:06 KST

“There are, I find, things I want philosophy to do that it cannot. Or that I cannot do with it.”
That’s Amy Olberding, professor of philosophy at the University of Oklahoma, on the limits of philosophy that life sometimes makes vivid.
The guest post by her, below, is an excerpt from her truly remarkable book, Kill All The Chickens, which was published last month, and which you should all buy today (Amazon, Bookshop).
The book is a beautiful example of an academic philosopher breaking free of the standard publishing conventions of the profession (at which she was perfectly adept) to produce writing that is full of wisdom and personality, and that, even as it confronts us with an exploration of life’s difficulties, is nonetheless a pleasure to read.
Death Just Got Out of This Truck
by Amy Olberding
Maybe we should just skip the middle step and throw it all straight in the toilet? This is what I ask my mother as we together stand and consider the overburdened farm table. We are bereaved and so a steady stream of neighbors has come by to deliver casseroles and pies, lunch meats and cookies, chicken and potato salad. If death were an appetite, we’d have the means to satisfy and send him off by now. But he is not an appetite, nor have we any of our own.
Mine are a people of uneasy stomachs. I remember one night spent in the ER alongside some uncles and cousins, waiting to hear what the doctors would make of my grandfather’s alarming stroke-like swoon. That night we shared the TUMS bottle the way others might pass a flask. Bringing food to us bereaved is like giving a dog a pencil. There’s just not much that we can do with it, at least not much that anyone could count useful.
Grief is an affliction physical and material. It roils the gut and stops the sleep. It can put a tremble in the limbs, a quiver in the voice, a restless agitation run all through. It makes the knees want to let go, the body just to sink. It is tired but cannot ever really rest, a breath you cannot really catch. It can make the gaze go vacant, blank. Grief is eyes that see too much, make sense of little. How long have I now stared out the window into nothing, seeing nothing? Grief sets the body all awry. The body wants, but what? Something it can now no longer have, a voice in the ear gone mute, a touch tactile, now but memory. We stare at food; we do not eat it.
My book on death, the one I will not write, was originally going to have a chapter on the body. It seemed to me that one of the troubles with philosophy on grief is that it misses out on bodies. The philosopher’s talk is all of what loss means, what grief can make you think. It speaks to what the mind and heart may feel, but not the stalling, empty mind or trembling heart. It speaks to one who speaks and thinks, not the instinctive, aching animal, not the raw creature all sensation without sense. This is not a novelty where philosophy is concerned—philosophers have long neglected the cruder materiality from which thought transpires. But still, I wanted some way to make philosophy answer not to thought or feeling or meaning, but to the brute stuff upon which all the rest is set. I wanted some way to make loss less like an experience of the mind and thought, to make loss on the page more like itself in life, an experience altogether nauseating. Before the reasoning or meaning, first the gut.
There are, I find, things I want philosophy to do that it cannot. Or that I cannot do with it. There is nothing wrong with thought, with seeking out some sense. But what can be made sense is rarely all there is; it leaves in remainder much, too much. Worse still, even good sense can be misleading. You can get your thoughts in careful order, root out all mistake, prepare to read the vexations of experience with well-honed training pitched to make vexations yield. But all that practiced thought and careful habits of the mind can leave you unready for what comes. Don’t trust them more than they can bear. The body is not a prison, but neither can thought escape its meaty and substantial bonds. I cannot make philosophy bend to this, I think, not in a way that is not all false and false confidence.
Many years ago now, when the farm was still a working dairy and the place was hectic with cows and work, my grandfather hired a milker to come in and help. The milker had a love of the drink and would sometimes cry off work for a hangover, but he was, I suppose, reliable enough that they kept him on. One day, he’d taken the farm’s yellow truck into town to retrieve some feed. At a four-way stop sign, he was briefly bested by a fancy man in a fancy car, the kind of man who didn’t want to wait on a beater truck that got there first and instead just blew the stop sign so he’d get ahead. The milker would have none of this, so he drove that yellow truck right up to and behind the man’s bumper for blocks that soon turned into miles. Finally, the fancy man pulled over in a parking lot, the milker close behind. Both men got out of their vehicles. The fancy man planted his feet wide and bellowed out a caution meant to be severe: I have to warn you that I just got out of karate! The milker didn’t even pause before he answered quietly, Well, I just got out of this yellow truck. Before aught else could happen, the milker’s fist had found that fancy man and laid him flat.
Karate class is fine and so, too, is philosophy. But make no mistake, you can’t really get ahead of it. Loss comes at you like a fist.
“Death Just Got Out of This Truck,” from Kill All The Chickens by Amy Olberding.

MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. Production of components for the Dobrynya Nikitich cargo unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), used in Russia’s special military operation in Ukraine, is planned to be fully localized, a spokesman for the Svarog Research and Production Center told TASS.

On foreign companies’ assets

‘Former inmates want to come back to visit’: inside Florida’s prison zoo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:30:04 UTC
21:30:04 KST

At the Monroe County detention center on Stock Island in the Florida Keys, most of the prisoners do the type of work you’d typically imagine people doing in jail. Preparing meals in the kitchens, cleaning the common areas, working in the laundry, and so on.
But for about five prisoners at a time the work looks a little more exotic. They’re working in the jail’s on-site zoo, taking care of animals including a capybara, a kinkajou, a zebu and an ostrich.
The zoo was started in 1994, after a sheriff’s deputy noticed that ducks living near the jail were often getting hit by cars while crossing a highway. He gathered a group of prisoners and relocated the flock to a disused area beneath the jail, which sits on stilts as it is in a hurricane-prone area.
Word of the rescue spread, and people started showing up at the jail to drop off rescued or unwanted animals. “People started bringing in a goat, a pig, a cow, pets they’d gotten that they didn’t want or couldn’t keep,” said Jeanne Selander, the zoo’s supervisor. “We got a blind horse from the Miami area that had been abandoned, and then the sheriff thought, ‘Well, there’s a need for this.’”
The Monroe County detention center is the only correctional facility in the world with its own zoo. There was, briefly, another one. In Venezuela, a gang took over a prison and installed various resort-style amenities for the prisoners, including a pool, night club, and a zoo, with big cats, monkeys and flamingoes. But the Venezuelan government forcefully retook control of that prison a few years ago. Several of the zoo’s animals were reportedly killed in the battle for the prison and the ones that survived were relocated.
According to Selander, all of the animals in her zoo were either rescued, donated or confiscated. Rocky the fox was rescued from a fur farm in Minnesota. Jack the ostrich was donated as a tax write-off by a breeder that was unable to sell him because he’s blind in one eye. Harriet Houdini, a red-tailed boa constrictor, was donated by a school after the teacher that kept her as a class pet retired. “I had some alligators one time that came from a raid on a crack house,” said Selander.
But the zoo doesn’t accept all of the animals it is offered. Selander said she previously declined a camel and a bear as they presented too much of a risk to the residents.
You are unable to see the zoo from the inside as the building’s windows are frosted. Selander said that, when she is upstairs in the jail, the prisoners will ask her about the sounds they can hear coming from outside. She has been told that, from inside the jail, the peacock can sound like a woman screaming.
The prisoners that work on the zoo spend around six hours a day feeding and cleaning the animals, and performing maintenance tasks. Those selected are typically low-level offenders and are not allowed to have charges for violence or animal abuse. “It’s kind of hard to get down [to the zoo] because if you have a high bond or you’re in any way shape or form a risk to run away, they’re not going to let you come outside,” said Peter Faraco, a former inmate who worked on the zoo in 2021.
Inside the jail, prisoners sleep on concrete bunk beds with no pillows. “Stuck in them cells all day, or in the kitchen; it’s not that nice,” said Rodney Cox, who previously worked on the zoo. “There’s no air.”
Boredom is also an issue. “It’s a lot of time,” said Nicholas Sheldrake, a current inmate who is working in the zoo. “It’s just very boring. Watching the same TV shows and movies over and over, hoping a football or baseball game or something comes on.”
The zoo offers a respite for the prisoners that get to work there. “I love it down here,” said Sheldrake. “It makes my time go by fast. Nobody bothers me. I love working with the animals and talking to them.”
“And we can see stuff like birds and trees,” he added.
It is important to Selander that the zoo not look like it is part of a jail, as she hopes to make it appealing to visitors on the zoo’s regular open days. She has planted trees around the property, and had inmates paint murals of animals on the walls and support pillars. “People will come in, they’re like, ‘You don’t even realize you’re at a jail,’” she said.
In the 20 years she has worked there, she said, the number of visitors on open days has grown from about a dozen to more than 300.
Studies have shown that access to animals can have a positive effect on incarcerated people, leading to improvements in mental health, as well as a decrease in reoffending after release.
There are animal programmes of various kinds in prisons around the world. There are prisoners in Chile living alongside cats, and in New Zealand training service dogs, and in the UK receiving equine therapy, and in South Africa raising birds. Selander said that she believes working on the zoo has had a positive effect on the prisoners she has worked with, and has, over the years, received positive feedback from her workers.
She was recently out for brunch and her server was a man who’d worked at the zoo. “He was like, ‘I wanted to thank you, Miss Jeannie … Being able to be on the farm and have peace while I served my time just made it so much easier,’” she said.
Selander said that it’s not uncommon for former incarcerated zoo workers to come back and visit during open days to see the animals. Some will bring their family members. “One of the greatest compliments is that the inmates want to come back to visit,” she said. “What a compliment. Who wants to come back to jail?”

Ukraine will receive weapons through NATO’s new mechanism — the Ministry of Defence explained its features and advantages
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:25:57 EEST
21:25:57 KST

Ukraine will receive weapons through NATO’s new mechanism — the Ministry of Defence explained its features and advantages
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine has joined the NSPA partnership and will be able to procure weapons faster. Ukrainian manufacturers will gain access to the Agency’s tenders.
For the first time, Ukraine will have the opportunity to procure military equipment through the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA – NATO Support and Procurement Agency). The Ministry of Defence announced this and added that it will open opportunities for Ukraine’s defence industry both to receive and provide services through the Agency, reports UNN.
Details
According to the Ministry of Defence, this is provided for by the Cooperation Agreement between the Government of Ukraine and the NATO Support and Procurement Organization (NSPO) on the Security Cooperation Support Partnership (SCSP).
On 13 August 2026, the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine approved the draft Agreement, and on 14 October 2026, the Agreement was signed by Ukraine’s Minister of Defence, Yevhenii Khmara.
Ukraine becomes a partner in the NSPA procurement system
According to the ministry, the partnership was created to ensure stable and long-term support for Ukraine. It will make it possible to consolidate requests for assistance from Ukraine, capability coalitions and other NATO structures, as well as to use the Agency’s existing procurement and supply mechanisms. The Agreement was developed so that Ukraine could join the Partnership and communicate its needs, as well as conduct defence procurement.
Ukraine is developing cooperation with NATO in the area of procurement, and participation in this Partnership provides a unique opportunity to gain access to all the services and capabilities of the NATO Support and Procurement Agency for our needs. Ukraine is the first and only country (and, moreover, a non-NATO member) for which a separate Partnership has been created as a single point of entry to the Agency’s operations, while Ukrainian industry has also been granted broad access to the Agency’s tenders.Mstyslav BanikDeputy Minister of Defence of Ukraine
The Deputy Minister of Defence noted that this expands Ukraine’s access to NATO markets with vetted suppliers.
Details of the agreement on Ukraine’s participation in NATO procurement
Through participation in the SCSP, Ukraine will potentially be able to use the capabilities of 45 NSPA partnerships, which cover various weapons systems and provide for their procurement, maintenance and support throughout their entire life cycle.
The Agreement provides for:
-  Faster procurement for the needs of the Defence Forces. Ukraine’s requests will be able to be processed through existing NSPA contracts or by concluding new ones.This will make it possible to meet Ukraine’s needs more quickly through the emergency-response procurement mechanism. 
-  To conclude a new contract, NSPA may announce a tender in accordance with Ukraine’s needs – both foreign and Ukrainian companies will participate in it simultaneously. 
-  More advantageous procurement conditions. NSPA will be able to combine Ukraine’s needs with those of other countries. Consolidated orders strengthen negotiating positions and make it possible to obtain better pricing conditions. 
-  More flexible procedures. To accelerate procurement and supply within the partnership, the Agency will be able to adapt standard mechanisms to Ukraine’s needs. 
In addition, procurement will have several sources of financing. It may be financed from Ukraine’s state budget, by international partners or through joint financing.
New opportunities for Ukrainian defence-industry manufacturers
The Ministry of Defence added that another important area is the involvement of Ukrainian defence companies in NSPA procurement.
Ukraine’s defence industry is developing rapidly, increasing its production capabilities and creating new solutions. We want our partners to gain access to this experience and technology, and Ukrainian manufacturers to gain access to new cooperation opportunities. This is a partnership from which both sides will benefit.
Manufacturers will have the opportunity to register in the Agency’s supplier database, submit proposals, participate in tenders on an equal footing with foreign companies and conclude contracts with NSPA. The relevant mechanism is provided for a period of 5 years, starting in April 2025.
For Ukraine’s defence industry, this is an opportunity to attract new orders, expand production and gradually integrate into international defence supply chains.
Practical consultations for manufacturers
The signing of the Agreement was announced on October 14 during the NSPA Industry Outreach Event, which the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine organized jointly with the NATO Support and Procurement Agency.
The event brought together around 150 representatives of Ukrainian defense industry enterprises.
During the meeting, manufacturers received information about registration in the NSPA system, preparing and submitting proposals, undergoing tender procedures, and requirements for potential suppliers. NSPA brings together capabilities in the areas of procurement, logistics, medical and infrastructure support, and also provides operational and system support and services to NATO member states, the Alliance’s military command authorities, and partner countries.
This partnership will help deepen the integration of Ukrainian industry with opportunities for growth, while enabling allies and partners to adopt Ukrainian experience in combat-tested innovation and operational experience. Our goal is to continue strengthening Ukraine’s industrial base and incorporating this experience into the supply and sustainment of capabilities.
The Ministry of Defense continues to work on developing cooperation with NATO and expanding Ukraine’s access to the means needed by the Security and Defense Forces in the fight against the enemy. It is also working to involve Ukrainian manufacturers in international procurement mechanisms, secure new orders, and scale up production for the needs of the Defense Forces.
We would like to remind you
As the Financial Times wrote, NATO will allow Ukraine to purchase weapons, ammunition, and military equipment through its centralized procurement agency, potentially enabling Kyiv to receive defense supplies "faster and more cheaply."

Trump, Putin and Xi can decide Ukraine’s fate without it: will there be a "Yalta 2.0"
Kyiv • UNN
Steve Witkoff proposed a trilateral meeting of the leaders of the United States, Russia and China to discuss ending the war in Ukraine. An expert warned against negotiations without Kyiv.
U.S. President Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff proposed that Russia hold a trilateral meeting involving China next month to discuss a plan to end the war in Ukraine. This is reported by Financial News, according to UNN.
Details
The proposal is for U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Chinese President Xi Jinping to meet and reach a settlement on Ukraine.
The proposal is being compared to the Yalta Conference, when the top leaders of the United States, Great Britain, and the USSR gathered in Yalta on the Crimean Peninsula in February 1945 and agreed on the post-World War II world order. At that time, the division of Germany and Korea was also discussed
Additionally
The president of the International Institute for Security Studies, Oleksii Buriachenko, said in a comment to UNN that only the Kremlin is interested in possible trilateral talks between Russia, the United States, and China. In particular, it wants to raise the possibility of resolving Russia’s war against Ukraine without the participation of Kyiv and Europe. For the United States and China, other issues remain priorities.
According to him, the possibility of trilateral talks arose against the backdrop of preparations for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, which is to be held in China this year.
In the expert’s view, it is precisely the location of the summit that creates conditions for a potential meeting between Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin, and Xi Jinping, but this does not mean that Russia’s war against Ukraine will become the main topic of the talks, because, according to the expert, the initiative to discuss it in such a format is primarily beneficial to Moscow.
Despite this, the political scientist does not believe that the potential meeting itself will have direct political consequences for Ukraine. In his view, the main risk is that discussing the war without Kyiv could gradually come to be perceived as an altogether acceptable format of international politics. Therefore, it is important for Ukraine not only to state that such talks are unacceptable, but also to seek partners who will likewise support this position.

France has recorded its first case of infection with the Shamonda virus.

France has recorded its first case of infection with the Shamonda virus.
Kyiv • UNN
France has recorded the first human infection with the Shamonda virus; the patient died. Authorities said there is no threat to the population.
France has recorded its first case of a person infected with the Shamonda virus — the patient died, although medical officials assure that there is no threat to the population. BBC reports this, UNN writes.
The patient died, but the authorities stress that this was an exceptional case and that, in general, the virus does not pose a threat to people
The Shamonda virus is usually transmitted among animals through the bites of small blood-sucking insects. It has been circulating in Africa and Asia for several decades, and was first detected in Europe this summer.
A joint statement by France's ministries of health and agriculture said that the deceased patient had serious problems with their immune system, making this case exceptional.
Background information
The Shamonda virus is an orthobunyavirus spread through the bites of small blood-sucking insects, mainly biting midges. The virus's main hosts are livestock, in which it causes fever.
The virus circulated in Africa and Asia for decades, and was first detected in animals in Europe in the summer of 2026. It does not pose a mass threat to humans. The case in France was the first recorded instance of a human infection, and the fatal outcome was caused by the patient having severe immunodeficiency.

Will deposit rates rise - NBU has issued a forecast

Will deposit rates rise - NBU has issued a forecast
Kyiv • UNN
Customer funds in banks increased, primarily due to households. Financial institutions expect an increase in deposit rates and the cost of funding.
Banks are attracting more funds from clients, primarily households, and expect deposit rates for businesses and households to rise. This is evidenced by the results of the NBU survey on bank funding for the third quarter of 2026, UNN reports.
Details
The volume of client funds in banks increased, primarily those of households, while the cost of attracting them rose mainly due to the increased cost of business funds
The regulator briefly outlined the results of the survey for the third quarter of 2026:
-  the volume of banks’ liabilities increased overall, mainly due to growth in household funds; 
-  the volume of wholesale funding has been growing since mid-2025, primarily due to loans attracted from international financial organizations and development banks; 
-  going forward, banks expect an increase in the volume of household and corporate funds, as well as wholesale funding; 
-  the average cost of borrowing rose due to the increased cost of corporate funds and, to some extent, household funds, while the cost of wholesale funds remained almost unchanged; 
-  banks forecast an increase in the cost of funding and higher deposit rates for businesses and households, as well as an increase in the cost of wholesale funding; 
-  the share of liabilities in foreign currency increased slightly, but it is expected to remain unchanged going forward; 
-  the maturity of funding increased, and financial institutions expect it to continue increasing; 
-  the majority of banks reported an increase in total capital over the past 12 months and expect this trend to continue; 
-  banks once again identified profitability as the key factor behind the increase in capital; 
-  for the first time since the first quarter of 2025, respondents expect the cost of capital to rise. 
For reference
The survey on bank funding was conducted from September 16 to October 7, 2026, among bank managers responsible for liability management. Responses were provided by 25 financial institutions accounting for 95% of the banking system’s total assets. The survey results reflect the respondents’ views and are not NBU estimates or forecasts.

President's economic adviser: Politics has been emotionally draining
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:21:00 UTC
21:21:00 KST

President's economic adviser: Politics has been emotionally draining
In an interview with ERR, Maris Lauri reflects on the Reform Party's electoral prospects, the challenges of coalition government and the importance of avoiding costly election promises.
What led you to decide to leave politics? Was it perhaps because you didn't see much of a future for the Reform Party in the upcoming Riigikogu elections?
The president's offer was very appealing and I've been in politics for 12 years. The past few years have been somewhat emotionally exhausting. And I felt this was an opportunity to do something similar to what I'd done professionally earlier in my life, without moving too far away from politics and Estonian affairs.
It certainly wasn't because I thought I wouldn't have any prospects or opportunities if I ran in the Riigikogu elections. That was definitely not on my mind.
But what prospects do you see for the Reform Party to succeed in the upcoming Riigikogu elections?
There's always an opportunity to achieve a good result. There are still quite a few months until the elections. And as we've seen over the past decade, things can sometimes change very quickly.
We've had a very strong team and plenty of good ideas. I'm deeply convinced that Estonia needs a center-right liberal party in politics. There are plenty of voters who want that and it's simply necessary. The entire political spectrum needs to be represented — nature abhors a vacuum.
On the one hand, it's understandable that people have been disappointed and perhaps even angry about things that have happened. But things can always be changed and improved and lessons can certainly be learned.
Are you referring to the confusion over taxes or the "tax festival" as it was called at one point? Various taxes were proposed — tax increases, which were then scrapped, followed by announcements that taxes would be cut. Is that what you had in mind?
No, I'm talking about a broader range of issues. There have been various crises and these have been global crises, not just ones affecting Estonia. They've made people more sensitive and frustrated, not just in Estonia but across society in other parts of the world as well.
In situations like these, perhaps the best decisions haven't always been made or there hasn't been enough explanation of why certain decisions were taken.
It's also true that we've had governments made up of different coalitions, with partners holding opposing views. Coalition governments always involve finding compromises and quite often those compromises have reflected the positions of our partners much more than those of the Reform Party.
But the biggest party always ends up taking the blame, as unfortunately often happens in life.
So perhaps there hasn't been enough explanation of why certain decisions were made and the best choices haven't always been made or things haven't always turned out for the best in difficult circumstances.
Even now, in recent weeks, we've seen quite a lot of blame directed at the former coalition partner, the Social Democratic Party, when explaining the situation. The argument seems to be that the Social Democrats prevented the government from governing properly and making the right decisions that reflect the Reform Party's principles. You just said things should be explained better. Is that what you consider a better explanation?
I haven't heard any direct accusations against one party or another. It's perfectly natural for political parties to have different views of the world and that's why they debate these issues. They debate them in the Riigikogu, among themselves and certainly in public as well. That's simply inevitable.
We can't expect people with different political views to agree on everything.
There isn't even 100 percent agreement within any single party. People still debate, discuss and ultimately choose what they feel is the best option at that moment and what they can agree on. And if they can't reach an agreement, then that's how it is.
There are undoubtedly situations where coalition partners have such opposing positions that they simply can't reach an agreement on certain issues.
I think that's happened in every government. One partner doesn't like a particular issue or proposed solution, so no agreement can be reached and no solution emerges.
What would you consider the achievement closest to your heart from your time in politics?
There have been various achievements and it's difficult to immediately single out one or another.
One important change has certainly been marriage equality, which was already being debated more than 12 years ago when we were discussing the Registered Partnership Act. That issue also stirred a lot of strong emotions. Now that marriage equality has been adopted, the whole issue has settled down.
Another little project of mine at the Riigikogu is the Foresight Center, a think tank that provides an opportunity to discuss and analyze Estonia's development prospects.
I spearheaded the legislation and the ideas behind how such a center should operate and what requirements it should meet. So I hope the Foresight Center will continue doing valuable work for Estonian society for many years to come.
Now that you're leaving politics, what's your final piece of economic advice for the Reform Party?
I think it's important that when a party goes into an election, it focuses not on handing out lots of money or giving people gifts, but on taking steps and pursuing policies that genuinely make life better in Estonia.
People generally understand and appreciate that.
The idea that handing out money will win votes... It won't. At some point, it leads to disappointment.
It's worth relying on people who share your worldview rather than those who are simply looking for the biggest promises and the most money.
I recall that the Reform Party itself was involved in handing out money quite generously in the social welfare sector not long ago. There was the €20 increase in the single-parent benefit.
Having a right-wing worldview doesn't mean you don't spend money on social issues or that you approach them coldly.
A liberal worldview values individual freedom, but it also values responsibility — responsibility for the consequences of one's own actions, as well as responsibility toward people who are economically disadvantaged or in a worse position due to circumstances beyond their control.
So helping vulnerable people is a perfectly normal and logical part of a liberal worldview.
But what kind of economic advice do you think the president needs and how can you be useful to her?
The specific responsibilities will certainly become clearer over time and we'll sit down and discuss them in more detail.
But the president has various meetings to attend and when she's spoken about her role as being, so to speak, the mortar between the bricks, that also means she needs to be able to understand economic issues and explain them to people.
That's certainly where I can help — by helping her understand these issues, articulate her views and, more broadly, explain to the public why certain decisions are made, which policies are good and which may be less effective and what the strengths and weaknesses of different approaches are. That will certainly be part of my role.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Estonia receives €32 million from EU for drone surveillance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:52:00 UTC
20:52:00 KST

Estonia receives €32 million from EU for drone surveillance
Estonia will be able to significantly boost its drone surveillance, as the European Union has allocated over €30 million for the cause, Minister of Interior Igor Taro (Eesti 200) said on Thursday.
"Last week, we learned that Estonia will receive €32 million from the European Union to strengthen drone surveillance along the eastern border. [This has been] a very pressing issue for us," Taro said at the government's weekly press conference on Thursday.
"To put the figures into perspective, we have allocated €4 million for other infrastructure along the eastern border next year, while drone defense will receive €32 million," Taro added, explaining the significance of the amount.
No migration crisis
The interior minister also discussed migration pressure originating from Belarus, highlighting how much it has increased this year.
"While a total of 39 people were apprehended in Estonia last year for illegally transiting through the country after crossing the Latvia-Belarus border, that number had already reached 406 as of October 20 this year," he said.
Although this places considerable pressure on the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA), there is still no reason to speak of a migration crisis, Taro assured.
"Our emergency plans are designed for entirely different magnitudes. We are nowhere near that point, and even if the emergency plan were activated, there would still be a substantial reserve of capacity, meaning that resources are available and nobody would be overwhelmed as a result," he said.
According to figures provided by Taro, nearly 50 patrols are involved in managing migration-related matters in Estonia every day.
"Our police officers have worked more than 8,000 hours of overtime, and as of today, we have returned 134 people apprehended for illegal transit to Latvia, with more awaiting return shortly," he said.
The interior minister said the number of attempted illegal border crossings at the Latvia-Belarus border is now clearly declining, having fallen from 340 prevented attempts to 122 over three weeks.
"But the threat has not disappeared, and our preparedness must remain high. More of these people may still come toward Estonia. But the main conclusion is that Estonia is managing this situation," he stressed.
